title: Oriental rugs: types, structure, woven dates and signatures, knot counts, labels and dyes
applies_to: Hand-knotted pile rugs, flatweaves and bags from Iran, the Caucasus, Anatolia, Central Asia, Afghanistan, China, Tibet, India and Pakistan, and the machine-made and tufted rugs sold beside them. A type names where rugs with these features were made; the same names are woven elsewhere. A woven date is the year the weaver wove in, not proof of age.

types.title: Oriental rug types: where, by whom, how they are made, and how to tell them apart
caveats: A type names where rugs with these features were woven. The same names are used for rugs woven elsewhere in the same designs, and the trade uses many of them for a look or a grade rather than a place: each sheet says how.

The structure on each sheet (the knot, the knots to the inch, the warps, the wefts, the sides and the ends) comes first from Hawley (1913) and the other early handbooks, checked against later books, Turkish and Indian registrations and museum records. Rugs vary within a type, and so do the books: where they disagree, the sheet shows each.
Knot counts are knots per square inch: the number of knots in an inch across the rug times the number of rows in an inch along it.
A type is not a verdict on a rug. Only someone who can handle a rug can say what it is, and none of this says what it is worth.

groups.name: Persian city and workshop rugs
groups.blurb: Rugs woven in town workshops and home looms in and around Iran's weaving cities (Tabriz, Kashan, Isfahan, Nain, Qom, Kerman, Mashhad and others), usually on cotton foundations, finely knotted, with curving floral designs drawn on paper first. The city name on a tag is a trade name: it can mean the city, a grade, or only a look.

groups.name: Arak (Sultanabad) district rugs
groups.blurb: The villages and town looms around Arak, called Sultanabad until the 1930s, produced the Farahan, Sarouk, Mahal, Mushkabad and Lilihan rugs that filled American homes from the 1880s to the 1950s. Most of these names are grades or looks more than places.

groups.name: Khorasan (northeast Iran) rugs
groups.blurb: Rugs from Mashhad and the towns of Khorasan province (Birjand, Dorokhsh, Kashmar and others), often with a purplish cochineal red and, in many grades, knots tied over four warps instead of two (jufti).

groups.name: Northwest Persia: the Heriz district and Azerbaijan
groups.blurb: Village and tribal rugs of Iranian Azerbaijan and Zanjan, mostly Turkic-speaking weavers using the symmetric knot: the heavy, angular Heriz carpets and their grade names (Gorevan, Mehriban, Serapi, Ahar), Karaja runners, Sarab camel-ground runners, Caucasian-style Ardabil and Meshkin rugs, and Shahsavan bags and soumaks.

groups.name: Kurdish weaving of western Iran
groups.blurb: Rugs of Iranian Kurdistan and Kurdish groups elsewhere: the stiff, heavy Bijars, the very fine, thin Senneh rugs and kilims, and Kurdish village and tribal rugs (often wool foundations, shaded blue grounds, Mina Khani designs). 'Mosul' is an old trade name for coarse Kurdish rugs.

groups.name: Hamadan market and its villages
groups.blurb: Hundreds of villages around Hamadan weave rugs with symmetric knots and, as a rule, a single thick weft between rows on a cotton warp, which leaves a checkered back. 'Hamadan' is the market name; better rugs are sold under village names.

groups.name: Central and west-central Persia: Bakhtiari, Joshaghan, Varamin, Lurs
groups.blurb: Village and tribal rugs of the Zagros and the central plateau: Bakhtiari garden-panel rugs of Chaharmahal, the lozenge-lattice Joshaghan design, Yalameh, Varamin Mina Khani rugs and bags, and Lur tribal weaving.

groups.name: Fars: Shiraz market, Qashqai, Khamseh and gabbehs
groups.blurb: Tribal and village rugs of Fars sold through Shiraz: Qashqai and Khamseh rugs and bags, Neyriz, Abadeh and gabbehs. Wool foundations, red-dyed wefts, barber-pole side wrapping and striped end webs are typical of older tribal pieces.

groups.name: Southeast and east: Afshar and Baluch
groups.blurb: Afshar rugs of Kerman province (Sirjan, Shahr-e Babak) and the dark, small Baluch rugs of Khorasan and western Afghanistan.

groups.name: Caucasian rugs
groups.blurb: Village rugs of the Caucasus (today Azerbaijan, Armenia, Georgia and Russian Dagestan), mostly 1850-1930: symmetric knots, wool warps, bold geometric designs. Western trade names (Kazak, Karabagh, Shirvan, Kuba, Daghestan) often differ from the regional names used in Azerbaijan and Armenia, and many are attributions by design rather than by proven place.

groups.name: Anatolian (Turkish) rugs
groups.blurb: Rugs and carpets of Anatolia (Asian Turkey): village prayer rugs, nomadic Yörük and Kurdish rugs, the export carpets of Uşak and İzmir (Smyrna), and silk and art-silk workshop rugs of Hereke and Kayseri. Almost all use the symmetric (Turkish) knot; old village rugs are wool throughout with red wefts.

groups.name: Turkmen (Turkoman) rugs
groups.blurb: Pile weavings of the Turkmen tribes of Central Asia (today Turkmenistan, northern Afghanistan and northeastern Iran): floor carpets and many bags, door hangings and animal trappings, mostly red with rows of octagonal guls and wool throughout. The trade sold most of them as 'Bokhara'.

groups.name: Afghan, Uzbek and Kyrgyz rugs
groups.blurb: Rugs woven in Afghanistan since the late 1800s, mainly by Ersari and other Turkmen in the north, with Uzbek, Baluch and Pashtun weavers, plus the refugee-era rugs of the 1980s-2000s (war rugs, 'Kazak', chobi) often woven across the border in Pakistan. Uzbek and Kyrgyz pile rugs of Central Asia are included here.

groups.name: East Turkestan (Xinjiang) rugs
groups.blurb: Rugs from the oasis towns of Xinjiang in western China (Khotan, Kashgar, Yarkand), woven by Uyghur weavers: Chinese-looking motifs and colors on cotton (earlier wool) foundations, long sold in the West as 'Samarkand'.

groups.name: Chinese rugs
groups.blurb: Rugs of northern China: Ningxia and Inner Mongolia (Baotou), the export workshops of Beijing and Tianjin from the 1880s to the 1930s (including the 'art deco' rugs of Nichols and Fette), the line-graded export rugs since the 1960s, and silk rugs in Persian designs since the 1980s.

groups.name: Tibetan rugs
groups.blurb: Rugs of the Tibetan plateau, woven by looping the pile yarn around a rod and cutting the loops rather than tying each knot separately, in sleeping and sitting rugs, saddle rugs and monastery pieces; and the Tibetan-style rugs made by refugees in Nepal and India since about 1960.

groups.name: Japanese rugs
groups.blurb: Japanese dantsu (緞通), hand-woven floor rugs with a cotton pile from Saga (Nabeshima), Sakai and Akō, made since the Edo period and exported in the Meiji era; and the wool rugs in Chinese and French designs that Japan made for the American market in the 1950s-60s.

groups.name: India
groups.blurb: Hand-knotted, flat-woven, felt and embroidered rugs made in India, from British-era jail and factory carpets (Agra, Lahore, Amritsar) to the modern export trade of Uttar Pradesh, Jaipur and Kashmir. Most were made for Western importers in copied designs, often under trade names.

groups.name: Pakistan
groups.blurb: Export rugs woven in Pakistan since the 1950s: 'Bokhara' rugs in Turkmen gul designs, Pak-Persian rugs in Persian designs, and hand-spun, vegetable-dyed Chobi and 'Ziegler' qualities learned from Afghan refugees.

groups.name: Other hand-made rugs sold beside oriental rugs
groups.blurb: Hand-made rugs from Romania, Bulgaria, Albania, Greece, Egypt, Morocco, Nepal, China and Japan, many in Persian or Chinese designs, and viscose 'art silk' rugs. The label or trade name often names a design, not the country.

groups.name: Machine-made rugs in oriental designs
groups.blurb: Rugs woven on power looms (Wilton, Axminster and their modern successors) in patterns copied from hand-knotted oriental rugs, made in the United States from the late 1800s and in Belgium, Egypt, Turkey and elsewhere later. They have no knots; turning the rug over and parting the pile usually shows this.

groups.name: Classical court-carpet designs
groups.blurb: Designs of the great carpets of Safavid Persia and Mamluk Egypt (the Ardabil carpets, vase, Polonaise, hunting and garden carpets, Mamluk and Cairene carpets) that modern rugs copy. On a modern rug the name describes the design, not where or when it was woven.

rows.name: Tabriz
rows.region: Tabriz, capital of Iranian Azerbaijan (northwest Iran), city workshops and factories; Tabriz is also the market for Heriz-area village rugs, Karaja, Ardabil and Serab rugs, which are not Tabriz rugs.
rows.made_by: City workshops and factories run by Tabrizi merchants and master weavers, and before World War I also by foreign firms; weavers often worked from paper cartoons and could copy any design to order.
rows.date_note: Tabriz was the market for Persia's export trade from the mid-19th century and its own export weaving was organized by local investors from about the 1870s. Rugs readers own are mostly from the 1880s on; production continues.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric (Hawley and May 'Ghiordes'; Mumford 'the Turkish system'; Stone 'symmetric'). Lewis 1920 alone says 'nearly always the Senna'. Tabriz weavers tie knots with a hooked knife (qollab), which Jacobsen says makes the four-warp jufti knot impractical.
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: 12-20 knots per inch across x 10-22 down = 120-440. Lewis: 120-440. Stone (modern factory rugs): about 40-400. In Iran, Tabriz grades are stated in raj (knots per gereh of about 7 cm): computed here, assuming the same count both ways, 30 raj is about 120 kpsi, 40 raj about 210, 50 raj about 330, 60 raj about 470, 70 raj about 650 (Stone gives the anchor: 20 raj is about 53 kpsi).
structure.weft_color: white or pink (Hawley; May 'usually undyed or pink'); Lewis says older pieces had weft dyed the main color
structure.wefts_note: Two passes of fine weft after each row of knots (Hawley, May, Stone 'double-wefted').
structure.pile_note: Wool clipped short; Hawley and May call it harsh to the touch and less silky than Kerman or Kashan wool. A few rugs are silk (Stone).
structure.sides: A two-cord selvage (Hawley). Lewis: older pieces usually overcast, newer ones usually selvaged.
structure.ends: Narrow plain-woven band (web) and loose warp fringe at both ends (Hawley); a few strands of colored wool may run through the web (Lewis).
structure.handle: Firm and stiff; so closely woven that edges may curl (Lewis).
structure.back: Fine, even grain; warps hidden and the white or pink weft partly visible (Hawley).

design.field: Large central medallion on an ivory, blue or red field; concentric medallions; copies of classical carpets (vase, hunting, Ardabil, prayer and pictorial designs); cartouche borders with Persian verses.
design.border: Five to eight stripes with an outer edging; main stripe often palmettes or cartouches rather than a continuous vine.
design.colors: Red, blue and ivory; ivory fields common; modern rugs in many colorings.
design.sizes: All sizes, most large and nearly square (Hawley 9-18 ft long); Jacobsen: mostly 7 x 10 ft and up, plus 6.5 x 4.5 ft.

look_alikes.name: Kashan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kashan (and Sarouk) wefts are blue and the knot is asymmetric; Tabriz wefts are white or pink and the knot symmetric.

look_alikes.name: 'Kermanshah' (old American trade name)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Hawley compares Tabriz with 'Kermanshahs': Tabriz is finer, its wool harsher and its colors stronger; 'Kermanshah' borders carry a continuous vine and a pink edging.

look_alikes.name: Mashhad (Meshed)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The Turkbaff grade of Mashhad was introduced by Tabriz merchants and is made like a Tabriz (symmetric knot); a purplish cochineal-red field points to Mashhad.

look_alikes.name: Yazd
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Jacobsen says pre-war Yazd rugs in the Herati design were so like Tabriz that a photograph could be either; structure must be checked.

rows.trade_use: 'Tabriz' names rugs made in the city in any grade; grades are quoted in raj (e.g. '50 raj'). 'Hadji Jalili' (Haji Jalili) is used for fine late-19th-century Tabriz rugs in soft colors; 'Taba Tabriz' for a thick modern rust-and-ivory type.
rows.what_it_tells: A symmetric-knotted, double-wefted rug on a cotton (sometimes linen) foundation with depressed warps, pinkish or white wefts and short harsh wool, in a formal Persian city design, is typical of Tabriz.
rows.cautions: Quality ranges from coarse to among the finest made, so the name says little about grade. 'Hadji Jalili' is an attribution, not a documented signature. Romanian, Indian and other workshops copy Tabriz designs.

facts.text: Tabriz became the main market for Persia's carpet export trade in the second half of the 19th century.
Export weaving in Tabriz was first organized by Persian (Tabrizi) investors and merchants, not foreign firms.
Before World War I Tabriz weavers worked for exporting companies that prescribed the workmanship and designs.
facts.quote: the weavers are in the employ of foreign companies who prescribe the character of workmanship

facts.text: Tabriz rugs are tied with the symmetric (Turkish, Ghiordes) knot.
facts.quote: The fineness of the knots ... is incredible when it is remembered that the Turkish system is used.

facts.text: Tabriz foundations are usually cotton; Hawley says a very large number have finely spun linen warps.
facts.quote: A feature peculiar to a very large number of these rugs is the adoption of very finely spun linen for the warp

facts.text: Tabriz wefts are usually white or pink, unlike the blue wefts of Sarouk and Kashan.
Tabriz rugs are double-wefted with one warp of each pair deeply depressed.
Tabriz pile is clipped short and is harsh rather than silky.
Hawley's Tabriz knot count is 12-20 per inch horizontally and 10-22 vertically (120-440 per square inch); Lewis gives the same range; Stone gives about 40-400 for modern factory rugs.
In Iran, density is quoted in raj, the number of knots per gereh (a length of about 6.25-7 cm); Stone equates 20 raj with about 53 knots per square inch.
Tabriz weavers tie knots with a hooked knife (qollab).
Tabriz workshops copy classical designs, including the vase design, and add cartouche borders with Persian verses.
Stone says high-quality late-19th-century Tabriz rugs are attributed to a designer 'Haji Jalil', but there is no conclusive evidence he existed.
Stone names Sadakiani and Faradji as early 20th-century Tabriz weaver-designers.

'Tabriz hand-woven carpet' is a registered geographical indication, nationally (Industrial Property Office 6-GI (21 Feb 2010)) and internationally (WIPO Lisbon register AO 914, 27 Jan 2013); the registered area is the city of Tabriz and six rural districts.
facts.quote: (AO 914) فرش دستبافت تبریز / Tabriz Handmade Carpet

says.text: Knot, Ghiordes [symmetric].
Ghiordes knot with buried alternate warps; this combination 'absolutely' distinguishes Tabriz.
the Turkish system is used
symmetric knot
Knot.—Nearly always the Senna, occasionally Ghiordes.
A putative designer; no conclusive evidence Haji Jalil existed; high-quality Tabriz rugs may be so attributed.
A master weaver from Marand near Tabriz with a large workshop, active from about 1850 or the early 1880s to 1900, known for a lighter palette; copies are called 'Haj Khalili'.
Raj is the number of rows of knots per longitudinal gereh (6.25-6.95 cm).
Reg/raj: knots per gereh (about 2.75 inches).
Sales pages define raj as the number of knots in 7 cm across the width of the rug; Tabriz grades run from about 24 to 110 raj, most often 40-60.
Export weaving in Tabriz was first organized by Tabrizi investors and merchants, not foreign firms.
In 1913 'the weavers are in the employ of foreign companies who prescribe the character of workmanship' (Hawley describes his own day, so the two may refer to different periods).

rows.name: Kashan
rows.region: Kashan, north central Iran between Qom and Isfahan, and some 20 nearby villages (Jacobsen names Armaq, Alibad, Abuzaidabad, Fin, Nushabad); Aran and Natanz weave lesser or different grades.
rows.made_by: Home looms (one to four per house) and workshops working from paper cartoons; no factories in Jacobsen's day.
rows.date_note: Kashan's classical carpets are 16th-17th century; pile weaving nearly stopped after 1722 and revived about 1890-1900, first with imported merino yarn (see 'Manchester and Mohtasham Kashan'). Production continues.

structure.knot_note: Asymmetric (Hawley and May 'Sehna'; Stone 'asymmetric'). Lewis 1920 says 'Ghiordes'. Opening direction not stated by these sources.
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: 16-20 across x 16-24 down = 256-480. Lewis: 150-500. Jacobsen: about 14 x 14 (196), the best finer; village grades 8-10 each way (64-100). Stone: contemporary about 200.
structure.weft_color: fine, dyed blue (Hawley, May); rarely linen
structure.wefts_note: Two fine wefts per row, nearly hidden by the tightly packed knots (Hawley, May, Stone).
structure.pile_note: Very short, close-clipped, velvety wool (Hawley, May); early 20th-century rugs often of imported merino yarn with a silk-like sheen.
structure.sides: Tightly wound double overcasting in dark red, blue or brown wool (Hawley); Lewis: sometimes silk.
structure.ends: Lower end a narrow web; upper end a narrow web and short warp fringe (Hawley).
structure.handle: Very firm, thin and stiff when new (Hawley 'very firm'; Jacobsen: new Kashans harsh and stiff until washed).
structure.back: Very fine grain; warps hidden and the blue weft almost hidden (Hawley).

design.field: Floral medallion and corners (a diamond or pointed oval medallion with floral pendants), all-over floral or Shah Abbasi designs, prayer designs; some in Sarouk-style detached sprays for the American market.
design.border: Usually seven stripes; a fringe of small hooks often projects from the inner border into the field.
design.colors: Dark blue, red and yellowish brown with light blue and green; Jacobsen: after World War II nearly all red fields, few blue.
design.sizes: Commonly about 6.5 x 4.5 ft (dozar) and 7 x 10 or 9 x 12 ft; few 8 x 10 ft.

look_alikes.name: Sarouk
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Structure is nearly the same; Hawley says Kashan has shorter pile, firmer texture, more border stripes and sometimes linen warp; May calls Sarouk 'a slightly inferior grade of Kashan'. Count knots: Hawley's Kashan range starts where his Sarouk range is middling.

look_alikes.name: Qom (Qum)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Even dealers have trouble telling Qum from Kashan; Qum more often has all-over designs and silk.

look_alikes.name: Tabriz
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Tabriz has white or pink wefts and the symmetric knot; Kashan has blue wefts and the asymmetric knot.

rows.trade_use: 'Kashan' (Keshan) is used for rugs of the city and nearby villages and, loosely, as a mark of quality; 'Indo-Kashan' means an Indian rug in Kashan designs. Designer names (Dabir, Shad Sar, Tafazzoli, Madeh) are used for rugs to their cartoons. See also 'Manchester and Mohtasham Kashan' and 'Kashan silk'.
rows.what_it_tells: A thin, stiff, very finely knotted asymmetric rug on cotton with blue wefts, short velvety pile and a floral medallion design is typical of 20th-century Kashan.
rows.cautions: May says merchants take liberties with the name Kashan. Kashan-design rugs are made in Aran, Ardakan (Stone: coarser), India and elsewhere. Many early Kashans were chemically washed.

facts.text: Kashan was a major center of court carpet weaving in the Safavid period, but weaving nearly stopped after the Afghan invasion of 1722.
Kashan pile weaving revived about 1890-1900; Jacobsen says none had been woven there for some 200 years before 1900.
Hawley (1913) says woolen Kashans had only recently become generally known and were found in every market.
Kashan rugs are tied with the asymmetric knot on a cotton foundation with blue cotton wefts, two per row, and one warp of each pair buried.

Hawley's Kashan count is 16-20 knots per inch across and 16-24 down (256-480 per square inch); Lewis gives 150-500; Jacobsen gives about 14 x 14 per inch (196) for a typical mid-century Kashan and 8-10 each way for village grades; Stone gives about 200 for contemporary production.
Kashan wool is clipped very short and has a velvety surface.
Hawley says Kashans are sometimes described as a higher grade of Sarouk; May says Sarouks may be treated as a slightly inferior grade of Kashan.
facts.quote: Occasionally they are defined as a higher grade of Sarouks, on account of the striking resemblance in texture, colours, and designs

facts.text: Most Kashans that reached America before about 1930 were in Sarouk-like all-over floral designs; those for Europe kept traditional medallion designs, hence the trade term 'European type Kashan'.
Kashan rugs are woven from full-size paper cartoons.
Stone names Dabir Sanayeh, Shad Sar, Tafazzoli and Madeh as 20th-century Kashan weaver-designers whose names are used for rugs.
Over ninety per cent of Kashans sold in America by 1913 had been chemically washed to soften their colors.

'Kashan hand-woven carpet' is a registered geographical indication, nationally (Industrial Property Office 24 GI (6 Jul 2014)) and internationally (WIPO Lisbon register AO 951, 11 Oct 2014); the registered area is beneficiaries: Kashan rural carpet producers' cooperatives and the Kashan sellers' and producers' guilds.
facts.quote: (AO 951) فرش دستبافت كاشان / Kashan Handmade Carpet

says.text: Knot, Sehna [asymmetric].
Sehna.
about 200 asymmetric knots per square inch
Knot.—Ghiordes. Number vertically twelve to thirty-five; horizontally ten to twenty.
Kashan entry: weaving with Manchester-spun merino wool began at the beginning of the 20th century; Manchester Kashan entry: from about 1890.
None were made for 200 years until 1900.
Revived in the late 19th century by Mohtasham.
Warp generally cotton, rarely linen (type characteristics); the text says 'the warp is often linen'.
Cotton, frequently silk or linen.
Cotton foundation.

rows.name: Manchester Kashan and Mohtasham Kashan
rows.region: Kashan.
rows.made_by: Kashan home looms and workshops using imported merino wool yarn spun in Manchester, England.
rows.date_note: About 1890 to the early 1930s, ending with the Depression; Jacobsen: merino Kashans not made after 1930.

structure.knot_note: As for Kashan.
structure.kpsi_note: Not stated separately by any source; Hawley's Kashan range (256-480) describes rugs of exactly this period. Jacobsen says pre-1930 Kashans were about twice as fine as Sarouks.
structure.wefts_note: As for Kashan.
structure.pile_note: Imported merino wool spun in Manchester: very lustrous, so glossy that Jacobsen says it can be hard to tell from silk; clipped short to medium-short.
structure.sides: As for Kashan (double overcast in dark wool).
structure.ends: As for Kashan.
structure.handle: Firm, fine; the wool feels unusually soft and glossy.

design.field: Traditional medallion designs for Europe; Sarouk-style all-over floral designs for America from about 1915; prayer designs; some silk-inscribed pieces.
design.colors: Deep blue, red, ivory.
design.sizes: Dozar (about 6.5 x 4.5 ft) to 9 x 12 ft and larger.

look_alikes.name: Kashan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Later Kashans use local wool, which lacks the merino gloss; otherwise the structure is the same.

rows.trade_use: Dealers call any fine early-20th-century Kashan 'Mohtasham' or 'Manchester'; Stone thinks most rugs so attributed came from other workshops.
rows.what_it_tells: An early-20th-century Kashan with unusually glossy, soft wool fits the merino ('Manchester') period of about 1890-1930.
rows.cautions: 'Mohtasham' is a trade label, not a signature; only a few rugs actually carry the name.

facts.text: At the start of Kashan's revival, rugs were woven of Australian merino wool spun in Manchester, England.
Merino-wool Kashans were woven until about 1930, when the Depression ended the supply; local wool was used afterwards.
Jacobsen tells the trade story that a Kashan textile merchant overstocked with Manchester merino yarn had his wife weave a rug with it; Ghorbany names the merchant Mohammad-Hasan Mohtasham.

'Mohtasham' (Persian 'ceremonial', or a surname) is a trade term for high-quality late-19th- and early-20th-century Kashans; two silk prayer rugs and a wool rug dated 1905 carry the Mohtasham inscription, and most rugs so called probably came from other workshops.
Up to 1930 merino Kashans were the finest and costliest new Oriental rugs on the American market.
'Mohtasham Kashan' is used in the trade for fine Kashans of about the 1890s-1920s, including many that were not woven in Mohtasham's own workshops.
facts.quote: many carpets from Kashan are now called Mohtasham Kashan, even if they were not woven by his weaving centres

says.text: Supposed to be a weaver among the first to run a factory with Manchester wool; evidence is limited to a few inscribed rugs.
Mohammad-Hasan Mohtasham, a textile producer invited by Tabrizi merchants to revive Kashan weaving.
An unnamed Kashan textile merchant and his wife.

rows.name: Kashan silk rugs
rows.region: Kashan and its countryside, where silk is produced.
rows.made_by: Kashan workshops.
rows.date_note: Modern silk Kashans were being woven by 1911-1913; a famous 16th-century group of silk carpets is also attributed to Kashan, but those are classical court pieces.

structure.knot_note: Asymmetric as other Kashans (Hawley, Stone); Lewis gives 'Ghiordes' for all Kashans.
structure.kpsi_note: Lewis: 150-500 for Kashans, and his illustrated silk Kashan has 484 per square inch. No other source gives a separate count.
structure.wefts_note: Not stated separately; assumed as Kashan.
structure.pile_note: Silk pile, clipped short.
structure.sides: Overcast, sometimes with silk (Lewis).
structure.ends: Short web with loose warp threads at each end (Lewis).

design.field: Medallion, prayer and pictorial designs; Kashan classical-style hunting and animal designs.
design.colors: Reds, blues, ivory; sometimes with metal thread.
design.sizes: Mostly small rugs.

look_alikes.name: Qom (Qum)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Qom is the other main source of all-silk Persian rugs from the 1930s on, more often in all-over or compartment designs. Inscriptions or provenance may be needed.

look_alikes.name: Nain
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Nain silk rugs exist but most Nains are wool with silk outlines.

rows.trade_use: 'Silk Kashan' for silk rugs from Kashan; many silk rugs from Qom, Isfahan, Turkey, India and China are sold in Kashan designs.
rows.what_it_tells: A finely knotted, asymmetric all-silk Persian rug is consistent with Kashan, Qom, Isfahan or Nain; the name alone does not settle which.
rows.cautions: Silk-look rugs may be mercerized cotton or viscose (art silk); a burn or lab test separates them. Chinese and Turkish silk rugs copy Kashan designs.

facts.text: Raw silk was long brought to Kashan to be spun and dyed, and some was woven into rugs there.
facts.quote: it has been for a long time customary to take the raw silk from other places to be spun and dyed there

facts.text: Persian tradition and modern scholarship attribute many 16th-century silk carpets to Kashan; Walker counts about twenty with silk warp, weft and pile.
Lewis's illustrated silk Kashan has 484 knots per square inch.
Some silk rugs are woven in Kashan today.

museum_examples.title: Silk Kashan Carpet
museum_examples.shows: whole carpet; a classical silk carpet attributed to Kashan, the forerunner, not a modern silk Kashan

museum_examples.title: Silk Kashan Carpet
museum_examples.shows: whole carpet; classical silk Kashan group

museum_examples.title: Silk Kashan Carpet
museum_examples.shows: whole carpet; silk with metal-wrapped thread

rows.name: Isfahan
rows.region: Isfahan city and villages of the Isfahan area, central Iran.
rows.made_by: Home looms supplied by master weavers (ostad-kar) and workshops; Jacobsen counts about 2,000 home looms and no factories in the 1950s.
rows.date_note: Isfahan was the Safavid capital and court weaving center until 1722; modern commercial weaving began about 1920-1921 (Iranica xii; Stone; Jacobsen 'right after World War I'). Rugs called 'Ispahan' in older books are a different matter.

structure.knot_note: Asymmetric for the 20th-century revival (Stone). Hawley's 'modern Ispahans' of before 1913, a small and different group, are symmetric (Ghiordes).
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: post-World War II rugs up to 750. Jacobsen: about the same weave as contemporary Kashan or Kerman (roughly 200+). Hawley's pre-1913 'modern Ispahans': 6-9 x 8-14 = 48-126. Lewis (antique 'Ispahans'): 80-300.
structure.wefts_note: Not stated for the revival by these sources; Hawley's pre-1913 'Ispahans' cross once or twice.
structure.pile_note: Wool clipped very short; silk accents or all-silk in some later rugs (Stone). Jacobsen says inter-war rugs often used poor wool.
structure.sides: Not stated for the revival.
structure.ends: Not stated for the revival.
structure.handle: Thin and stiff (Jacobsen: too thin to stand New York chemical washing).

design.field: Safavid-style floral medallion designs, Shah Abbasi palmettes and arabesques; pictorial animal and tree-of-life designs; prayer designs.
design.colors: Inter-war rugs often ivory with bright yellows, greens and reds; dyes improved after World War II.
design.sizes: Mostly about 7 x 4.5 ft; some 7 x 10-11 ft; few larger.

look_alikes.name: Nain
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Nain often outlines motifs in ivory silk in a wool pile; otherwise both are fine asymmetric rugs in Isfahan-style designs.

look_alikes.name: Mashhad (Meshed)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: In the American trade 'Ispahan' was used for Mashhad Turkbaff carpets: those are thick, symmetric-knotted, about one-third as finely knotted, with cochineal-red fields.

rows.trade_use: Since the 19th century dealers use 'Ispahan' as a word of praise for many kinds of rug. In mid-20th-century America it usually meant a Mashhad Turkbaff carpet. 'Seirafian' and other workshop names are used for top Isfahan grades.
rows.what_it_tells: A thin, very finely knotted asymmetric rug with Safavid-style design, sometimes on silk warps, is typical of Isfahan work from the 1920s on.
rows.cautions: Old books' 'Ispahan' rugs are either 16th-17th-century classical carpets (many now thought to be from Herat) or unrelated 19th-century pieces; neither is the modern Isfahan.

facts.text: Commercial carpet weaving at Isfahan began about 1920-1921, aimed at European and American buyers.
Inter-war Isfahan rugs were finely woven but had poor dyes and often poor wool; after World War II dyes improved.
After World War II very fine Isfahan rugs in Safavid designs reached up to about 750 knots per square inch; some later rugs have silk warps or are all silk.
Modern Isfahans are tied with the asymmetric knot.
Isfahan rugs were too thin to be chemically washed in New York, so few reached America before World War II; most went to Tehran and Europe.
Dealers in Persia used 'Ispahan' as a term of praise for rugs regardless of origin.
facts.quote: even now Oriental dealers will often apply to rugs the term "Ispahan" as an epithet of superiority

facts.text: In the mid-20th-century American trade most rugs sold as 'Ispahan' were Mashhad Turkbaff carpets.
Stone names Emami, Sirafian and Hekmat Nejad as notable 20th-century Isfahan weaver-designers.

A 1310 SH (1931) questionnaire to Isfahan carpet factories asked owners for loom type (Turki, Kermani, Kashi or zamini, i.e. ground loom), warp type (cotton, wool, silk), dyes (natural and synthetic) and grades (a'la, motavasset, sost: best, middling, loose) priced by the gaz; most looms reported were the Kashi (Kashan) type and most warps cotton.
In 1310 SH (1931) the Isfahan government reported nearly 8,000 carpet looms in Isfahan and its districts to the Court Ministry.

'Isfahan hand-woven carpet' is a registered geographical indication, nationally (Industrial Property Office 1-GI (2 Jan 2010), the first number in the series) and internationally (WIPO Lisbon register AO 911, 27 Jan 2013); the registered area is the region of Isfahan.
facts.quote: (AO 911) فرش دستبافت اصفهان / Isfahan Handmade Carpet, Esfahan Handmade Carpet

facts.text: Fine modern Isfahan rugs are often woven on silk warps; a Persian study explains that in the dry climate of the Isfahan region thin cotton warps do not stand the tension of the loom, so silk warps are used, at a somewhat lower knot count.
facts.quote: در مناطق مرکزی مانند اصفهان به دلیل اقلیم خشک، چله های نازک پنبه ای ... مقاومت چندانی نداشته ... لذا باید از چله های ابریشم استفاده کرد (in central regions such as Isfahan, because of the dry climate, thin cotton warps do not hold up ... so silk warps must be used)

says.text: Modern Ispahans are few, symmetric-knotted, 48-126 knots per square inch, warps level, weft once or twice.
Saruks are 'the Ispahans of the present day'.
Rugs called Teheran and Ispahan are products of the village of Saruk and of Kirman.

rows.name: Nain
rows.region: Nain, a small town about 60 miles east of Isfahan, central Iran; 'emigrated' Nain-type weaving later spread to South Khorasan, Mazandaran, Shiraz and Isfahan.
rows.made_by: Home looms and workshops; the town turned from weaving wool cloth for cloaks ('aba') to carpets.
rows.date_note: From the 1930s; Jacobsen: just before World War II, with few rugs before the war. Production continues.

structure.knot_note: Asymmetric, tied singly on two warps in the original Nain weave (Babajamali, Persian 'farsi-ye tak-baft'); Jacobsen 1969 says Nains never contain jufti knots. Rugs woven elsewhere under the name shifted to jufti and other knots (Babajamali).
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: 200-800. Jacobsen 1962: carpets 250-400, small rugs 400-500, average about 22 x 22 per inch (484); Jacobsen 1969: 500-600 or more.
structure.wefts_note: Not stated by these sources.
structure.pile_note: Very fine wool clipped short, with motifs outlined in ivory silk; some all-silk rugs (Stone; Jacobsen 1969).
structure.sides: Not stated by these sources.
structure.ends: Not stated by these sources.
structure.handle: Thin, harsh and stiff when new (Jacobsen).

design.field: Isfahan-like and Safavid-style designs: Shah Abbasi palmettes, fine floral scrolls, medallions taken from the Ardabil carpet; ivory or light tan fields common.
design.border: More often red than blue, with buff or yellow minor stripes.
design.colors: Ivory, light tan, blue, soft rose; silk highlights in ivory.
design.sizes: Mostly 6.5 x 4.5 to 7 x 5 ft and 7 x 10 to 7.5 x 11 ft; few larger.

look_alikes.name: Isfahan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Ivory silk outlining in a wool pile is the Nain hallmark; designs are similar.

look_alikes.name: Qom (Qum)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Jacobsen says dealers can confuse Qum and Nain; Qum more often all-over or compartment designs, often all silk.

look_alikes.name: pakistani-persian-design
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Nain-design rugs from elsewhere in Iran and from abroad may use jufti knots and lower-grade wool.

rows.trade_use: Grades are sold as '4 la', '6 la', '9 la' (Persian la, 'layer'): dealers say the number refers to the plies in the warp yarn, lower numbers being finer; '12 la' is also met. Workshop names (Habibian, Mofidi) are used for top grades.
rows.what_it_tells: A very finely knotted asymmetric wool rug with ivory silk outlines in an Isfahan-style design is typical of Nain from the late 1930s on.
rows.cautions: The la grades are trade terms with inconsistent explanations, not a standard. Much 'Nain' is woven outside Nain.

facts.text: Nain turned to carpet weaving when its trade in hand-woven wool cloth for cloaks (aba) collapsed.
Densely knotted rugs have been woven in Nain since the 1930s, with few before World War II.
Nain rugs are knotted at about 200-800 asymmetric knots per square inch; Jacobsen gives an average of about 22 x 22 per inch.
Motifs in wool-pile Nains are outlined in ivory silk; some all-silk Nains are woven.
Nain designs follow Isfahan and Safavid models.
The original Nain weave uses single asymmetric knots; production moved to other places has changed to jofti knots, lower wool grades and chemical dyes.
Stone names Habibian and Mofidi as notable Nain weaver-designers.
Trade usage grades Nains as 4 la, 6 la and 9 la, lower numbers being finer.

Persian sources say Nain's carpet weaving began with Kerman-style carpets brought by a man named Shahdadi (late 13th century SH, before about 1921) and Arak-style carpets brought by Habibian, and boomed after the Second World War, when Nain's cloak (aba) weaving declined.

Since the 1340s SH (1960s) the white flowers of Nain rugs have been woven entirely in white silk, to compete with Isfahan and to soften strong colors; white silk is also woven along the edges of motifs.
Nain pile wool is mostly kork (fine wool) of yarn count 8 to 20, count 20 in fine pieces; warps are the Isfahan type, bought in Isfahan and Kashan.

Jufti, 'rubafi' and 'kamanshib' knots are called fraudulent knots in Iranian weaving; they spread into Nain-type rugs when production moved out of Nain, and are hard to detect because they show the same knot curve on the back.

'Nain hand-woven carpet' is a registered geographical indication, nationally (Industrial Property Office 25 GI (6 Jul 2014)) and internationally (WIPO Lisbon register AO 955, 11 Oct 2014); the registered area is the region of Nain.
facts.quote: (AO 955) فرش دستبافت نايين / Naein Handmade Carpet

says.text: One explanation: la is the number of plies in each warp yarn (e.g. 9 la = three strands each of three plies). Another: the number of threads per bundle of warp ends. Density figures for each grade differ from page to page.

rows.name: Qom (Qum)
rows.region: Qom, north central Iran, and (after 1948) a growing number of villages around it.
rows.made_by: Home looms (Jacobsen: about 1,000 looms, two per house); in the 1970s much weaving was organized by the municipality, which supplied materials and designs.
rows.date_note: Carpet production did not begin until about 1930; Jacobsen (1962) says weaving began 'some 20 years ago'. Production continues.

structure.knot_note: Asymmetric (Stone).
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: typically about 325 asymmetric knots per square inch for wool carpets. Silk rugs are often much finer; no source here gives a range.
structure.wefts_note: Not stated by these sources.
structure.pile_note: Wool on cotton foundations, or all silk (Stone).
structure.sides: Not stated.
structure.ends: Not stated.
structure.handle: Thin, fine (Jacobsen 1969: 'one of the thinner, finely woven types').

design.field: All-over designs more often than medallions: small vase-and-flower repeats (the 'Zell-i Sultan' design), boteh, tree of life, garden and panel (compartment) designs; also Kerman-like designs on ivory.
design.colors: Often ivory fields; many colorings.
design.sizes: Mostly about 4.5 x 7 ft and 7 x 10 ft.

look_alikes.name: Kashan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Qom rugs are close to Kashan in quality; all-over designs and silk point to Qom.

look_alikes.name: Nain
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Nain usually has ivory silk outlining in a wool pile.

rows.trade_use: 'Qum silk' or 'Ghom silk' for silk rugs from Qom; workshop names (Rashtizadeh, Arsalani, Archang) for top pieces.
rows.what_it_tells: A finely knotted asymmetric rug, often all silk or with an all-over vase or garden design, fits Qom work from the 1930s on.
rows.cautions: Silk Qom designs are copied in China, India and Turkey; check structure and fiber.

facts.text: Carpet production in Qom began in the 20th century, about 1930-1940.
Weaving spread to villages around Qom after 1948, when only eleven villages produced carpets; by 1966 about 36 per cent of households in the area wove carpets.
Qom rugs are close to Kashan rugs but use all-over designs more often than medallions.
Qom is noted for finely woven all-silk rugs, often in compartment designs; wool carpets are on cotton foundations.
Typical Qom wool carpets have about 325 asymmetric knots per square inch.
Many Qom rugs use an all-over small vase-and-flower design that dealers call 'Zell-i Sultan'.
Qom rugs were made mainly in European sizes (about 7 x 10 ft) and few reached America before the 1960s.

'Qom hand-woven carpet' is a registered geographical indication, nationally (Industrial Property Office 2-GI) and internationally (WIPO Lisbon register AO 913, 27 Jan 2013); the registered area is Qom township and the villages and towns of Qom province (Kahak, Ghanavat, Jafarieh, Khalajestan, Dastjerd, Salafchegan).
facts.quote: (AO 913) فرش دستبافت قم / Qom Handmade Carpet, Qum Handmade Carpet, Ghom Handmade Carpet

says.text: Carpet production did not begin until about 1930.
Weaving began in Qum 'some 20 years ago', i.e. about 1940.
In 1948 only eleven villages in the Qom area produced carpets, probably for local use.

rows.name: Kerman
rows.region: Kerman city, southeast Iran, and nearby villages (Mahan, Chatrud, Ravar and others); later also Zabol and other places trained by Kermani weavers.
rows.made_by: City home looms (two to four per house) and some twenty workshops, financed first by Kermani notables and merchants and from 1909 also by New York firms; designs drawn full size on paper by named designers.
rows.date_note: Kerman wove shawls more than carpets until the 1890s; in 1894 there were only about 100 carpet looms, and rapid commercialization began in 1895-1896. Stone: major production from about 1890; Jacobsen: export weaving from about 1870. Production continues.

structure.knot_note: Asymmetric (Hawley and May 'Sehna'; Lewis 'always Senna'; Stone; Iranica: the 'Persian' knot almost exclusively in urban workshops). The four-warp jofti knot spread in Kerman in the 1950s (Iranica Kerman; Jacobsen).
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: 11-20 x 11-20 = 121-400. Lewis: 80-480. Stone: 150-400. Kerman grades are quoted as warps per gereh / knots per gereh: 70/35, 80/40 (export standard), 90/45, 100/50 (Iranica xii; Jacobsen, who equates 80/40 with about 15 x 15 knots per inch, i.e. about 225).
structure.wefts_note: Hawley and May: two passes. Stone and Iranica: three wefts between rows (triple-wefted Kerman).
structure.pile_note: Fine, soft local wool and kork (down wool); short and silky in older pieces (Hawley), heavier in the American-market grades (Jacobsen).
structure.sides: Double overcasting in the same color as the outer edging, usually pink, sometimes green (Hawley).
structure.ends: Narrow web and short warp fringe at both ends (Hawley).
structure.handle: Very firm (Hawley); older and European grades thin, American grades thick.
structure.back: Moderately fine grain; warps hidden, weft partly visible (Hawley).

design.field: Naturalistic flowers (roses) in vases or bouquets, vase-and-lattice designs from the shawl tradition, medallions with open or covered fields, all-over, panel, prayer and pictorial designs; from the 1920s many medallion and broken-border designs; after World War II French-style florals.
design.border: Usually five stripes, the main one twice as wide; a narrow pinkish-red (sometimes moss-green) outer edging.
design.colors: Gray or ivory grounds with fawn, yellow, rose and blue; a very wide range of colors from Kerman's master dyers, including cochineal red.
design.sizes: Older rugs 5-7 ft; 20th-century production in all sizes up to 12 x 20 ft and larger.

look_alikes.name: 'Kermanshah' (old American trade name)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Many rugs sold in America as 'Kermanshah' are Kerman-type; Hawley's 'Kermanshahs' are coarser, with the weft conspicuous at the back.

look_alikes.name: Yazd
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Post-war Yazd copied Kerman designs and red open fields; Yazd avoided jufti knots; structure otherwise similar.

look_alikes.name: Mashhad (Meshed)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Mashhad medallion carpets resemble Kerman; look for jufti knots and heavy cable wefts at intervals on the back.

look_alikes.name: indo-persian
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Indian rugs in Kerman colors were made from the 1930s on; structure and wool differ.

rows.trade_use: 'Kerman' (or 'Kirman') covers city and village rugs in Kerman designs and many grades; 'Laver' or 'Lavar Kerman' is used for fine or older Kermans; 'Kermanshah' was an American trade name for Kerman-type rugs; designer names (Arjomand and others) are used for signed rugs.
rows.what_it_tells: An asymmetric, finely knotted rug on cotton with depressed warps, often three wefts per row and fine soft wool, in a naturalistic floral or medallion design with a narrow pink or green edging, is typical of Kerman.
rows.cautions: Kerman designs are copied widely (Yazd, India, Romania, China). Lewis's statement that Kermans were made by 'wandering tribes of Afghars' is wrong for city rugs: the Afshar tribal rugs of the Kerman region are a separate type.

facts.text: Kerman had a world-famous shawl industry in the 18th and 19th centuries, and many early Kerman carpet designs were borrowed from shawls.
In 1894 Kerman had only about 100 carpet looms; rapid commercialization began in 1895-1896, financed by Kermani notables and merchants.
Kerman carpet exports collapsed in 1904 and recovered after; by 1909 New York firms (Nearco Castelli & Brothers, Eastern Rug and Trading Co.) had agents in Kerman.
Kerman rugs are tied with the asymmetric knot on cotton warps with one warp of each pair buried.
facts.quote: Knot, Sehna. Knots to inch horizontally eleven to twenty; perpendicularly, eleven to twenty.

facts.text: Many Kerman rugs are triple-wefted.
Kerman fineness is expressed as warps per gereh over knots per gereh: 70/35, 80/40 (the export standard), 90/45 and 100/50.
Kerman wool includes a local down wool (kork) and the city's dyers used a very wide range of natural dyes.
Kerman borders often have a narrow outer edging of pink, sometimes green, and the sides are overcast in the same color.
The jofti (four-warp) knot was introduced in Kerman in the 1950s as a cost-cutting measure.
Mohammad Arjomand Kermani (born 1889/90) was one of the largest Kerman producers from the late Qajar into the Pahlavi period, and his rugs are signed.
Weaving conditions for children in Kerman's underground workshops led to Iran's first carpet labor regulations (1913, 1923).

'Kerman hand-woven carpet' is a registered geographical indication, nationally (Industrial Property Office 17 GI (22 Dec 2013)) and internationally (WIPO Lisbon register AO 953, 11 Oct 2014); the registered area is the region of Kerman.
facts.quote: (AO 953) فرش دستبافت كرمان / Kerman Handmade Carpet

facts.text: Kerman's carpet industry grew fast from the mid-1890s: Persian historians call about 1894-1925 the 'renaissance' (nowzayi) of Kerman carpets, when nearly half of the province's governors were themselves involved in carpet production, and local as well as foreign capital was invested.
facts.quote: دورة حدوداً سي ساله‌اي (از ۱۳۱۲ق/۱۸۹۴م تا ۱۳۴۴ق/۱۹۲۵م) كه نام «نوزايي» را در فرش كرمان به يدك مي‌كشد (the roughly thirty-year period, 1894 to 1925, that bears the name 'renaissance' in Kerman carpets)

facts.text: Kerman's carpet trade grew as its shawl weaving declined in the late 19th century.
facts.quote: با کسادی و رکود تدریجی شال‌بافی از اواخر این قرن، تولید و تجارت فرش رونق بالایی گرفته بود

facts.text: In the first decade of the 20th century New York-based firms set up in Kerman: Nearco Castelli & Brothers (an Italian merchant family with its head office in New York) opened a large trading office there, and American firms based in New York, with their main house at Sultanabad, kept agents in Kerman.
facts.quote: مرکز این شرکت در شهر نیویورک واقع بود ... او در دهۀ اول قرن ۲۰ با تأسیس دفتر تجاری بزرگی در شهر کرمان، شروع به سرمایه‌گذاری در صنعت فرش این منطقه نمود

says.text: A thread of weft crosses twice between every two rows of knots.
Crosses twice.
Three wefts between each row of knots; warps offset.
Triple-wefted carpets are produced today in the Kerman and Bijar areas.
Rapid commercialization in the 1890s; only about 100 looms in 1894.
Major rug production began in about 1890.
Kerman first started weaving rugs for export about 1870; shawls dominated before 1870.
By the wandering tribes of Afghars.
Urban carpets were woven in city workshops on vertical looms; tribal Afshar rugs are a separate production.
A city industry of long standing.

disagreements.about: number of carpet looms in Kerman in the 1890s

says.text: In 1894 Kerman had only about 100 carpet looms.

The province's looms rose from 220 in 1850 to 1,000 in the late 19th and early 20th century, about 3,000 in 1914 and 5,000 at the end of the Qajar period (it may count the province rather than the city).

rows.name: Lavar Kerman (Ravar)
rows.region: Ravar, a town north of Kerman; the trade name is also applied to Kerman-city rugs.
rows.made_by: A small community of carpet weavers in Kerman and Ravar who worked on commission in the Qajar period; later any fine Kerman.
rows.date_note: The oldest type of Kerman, made long before 1870. Stone: the term is applied to finer Kerman rugs whether or not woven in Ravar, so it is still used for 20th-century rugs. The 1850 start is an estimate from Jacobsen's wording.

structure.knot_note: As for Kerman.
structure.kpsi_note: No source gives a separate count; Stone's Kerman range (150-400) is used.
structure.wefts_note: As for Kerman.
structure.pile_note: Fine kork wool, short.
structure.sides: As for Kerman.
structure.ends: As for Kerman.
structure.handle: Thin and fine in older pieces.

design.field: Older Kerman designs: ivory fields with realistic vases of flowers, prayer designs with trees, shawl-derived patterns.
design.colors: Ivory, rose, soft blues and greens.
design.sizes: Mostly small and medium.

look_alikes.name: Kerman
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Nothing structural separates them; 'Lavar' is a dealer's grade or age label.

rows.trade_use: 'Laver' (a corruption of Ravar) is used by dealers for finer or older Kerman rugs, whether or not they were woven in Ravar.
rows.what_it_tells: A 'Lavar Kerman' label says a dealer judged the rug a fine or early Kerman; it does not prove the rug was made in Ravar.
rows.cautions: The name is applied loosely; treat it as a grade claim.

facts.text: Ravar is a town north of Kerman; 'Laver' or 'Lavar' is a corruption of its name.
In the Qajar period a small community of carpet weavers worked in Kerman city and in Ravar, mostly on commission.
The rug trade uses 'Laver' for finer-quality Kerman rugs whether or not they were made in Ravar.
Jacobsen describes 'Laver Kirmans' as the oldest type of Kirman, woven in Ravar.

says.text: Finer quality rugs from the Kerman area, whether or not woven in Ravar.
The oldest type of Kirman, made in the town of Ravar long before 1870.

rows.name: American-market Kerman (1920s-1950s)
rows.region: Kerman city and villages, often in factories owned or contracted by American importers.
rows.made_by: Kerman workshops and home looms working to importers' orders and paper cartoons.
rows.date_note: Classical designs for ten years after World War I; 1925-c.1937 Sarouk-style detached florals on rose or blue grounds, nearly all chemically washed and painted; after World War II ivory-ground pastel carpets for America. Iranica: the 1920s 'classic era'; French-inspired florals after World War II.

structure.knot_note: Asymmetric; jufti knots appear from the 1950s (Iranica Kerman).
structure.kpsi_note: Jacobsen: the common 80/40 grade is about 15 x 15 per inch (about 225); 70/35 coarser; 90/45 and 100/50 finer but thinner. Range here computed from those grades (70/35 about 170, 100/50 about 350 in Jacobsen's conversion) and rounded; not stated directly by any source.
structure.wefts_note: As for Kerman.
structure.pile_note: Thick, heavy pile for the American trade (Jacobsen; Iranica xii 'Americans prefer thick carpets').
structure.sides: As for Kerman.
structure.ends: As for Kerman.
structure.handle: Thick and heavy compared with European-market Kermans; edges of finely woven Kermans often curl under (Jacobsen 1969).

design.field: 1920s: classical medallions; c.1925-1937: detached floral sprays like American Sarouks; post-war: open ivory field with a floral medallion and 'broken' (Aubusson-style) border, or all-over French florals.
design.border: Often 'broken' borders that merge into the field.
design.colors: Post-war: ivory or cream with light blue and rose (pastel); 1925-1937: rose and blue grounds, usually painted.
design.sizes: 2 x 3 ft to 9 x 12 ft and many oversize carpets (10 x 14 to 12 x 20 ft and up).

look_alikes.name: American Sarouk (washed and painted)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: 1925-1937 Kermans copied American Sarouk designs; Kerman wool and tighter weave, often three wefts, separate them structurally.

look_alikes.name: indo-persian
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Indian pastel rugs in Kerman colors were made from the 1930s on.

rows.trade_use: Importers and dealers spoke of 'contract' (factory 80/40) and 'bazaar' (home-woven) quality Kermans.
rows.what_it_tells: A thick pastel ivory-ground Kerman with a broken border or French floral design fits post-World War II production for the American market; a rose or blue all-over floral Kerman with darker color on the front than the back fits the painted 1925-1937 type.
rows.cautions: Painted and heavily chemically washed Kermans of the 1920s-30s wear faster. Kerman-design rugs from India look similar.

facts.text: In the early 1900s most of Kerman's carpets were exported to America.
After World War I export production geared increasingly to the American market.
From about 1925 to 1937 many Kermans were woven in detached floral designs and rose or blue grounds like Sarouks, and most of these were chemically washed and painted.
After World War II Kerman production shifted toward French-inspired floral designs, and pastel ivory-ground Kermans became the main Persian supply for the American market.
American buyers preferred thick carpets with large plain light-colored backgrounds.
Some Kerman factories were owned by American importers in the 1950s.

rows.name: 'Kermanshah' (old American trade name)
rows.region: Disputed: Hawley places the type at Kermanshah in western Iran and 'workhouses of exporting companies'; Mumford says it was the Tabriz city type; Jacobsen says these rugs were made in Kerman.
rows.made_by: City workshops (Kerman or Tabriz, depending on the source).
rows.date_note: The name was common in the American trade from before 1900 to about 1940; Jacobsen says no rugs of this type were ever made in Kermanshah.

structure.knot_note: Hawley and May: Sehna (asymmetric).
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: 12-18 across x 11-18 down = 132-324.
structure.weft_color: white or pink, conspicuous at the back (Hawley)
structure.wefts_note: Two passes (Hawley; May).
structure.pile_note: Soft, medium length, floccy wool (Hawley).
structure.sides: Double overcasting in the color of the edging, usually red, sometimes blue (Hawley).
structure.ends: Lower end a narrow web with warp loops or short fringe; upper end narrow web and short fringe (Hawley).
structure.back: Moderately coarse grain with the weft showing (Hawley); May: medium coarse, medium loose.

design.field: Concentric or lobed medallions with pendants on an ivory or light rose field covered with dainty floral scrolls; prayer designs with Koranic verses.
design.border: Floral, often three stripes, with a narrow pink outer edging.
design.colors: Light rose, ivory, light blue, green and buff.
design.sizes: All sizes, small mats to large carpets.

look_alikes.name: Kerman
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Hawley separates them: his Kermans are finer with the weft hidden; his Kermanshahs coarser with the weft conspicuous.

look_alikes.name: Tabriz
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Tabriz is symmetric-knotted with harsher wool.

rows.trade_use: An old American trade name for Kerman-style rugs in pastel colors; not the Kurdish village rugs of the city of Kermanshah, which are symmetric-knotted.
rows.what_it_tells: An old 'Kermanshah' label usually means a Kerman-style city rug in soft colors, not a rug from Kermanshah.
rows.cautions: Three classic sources disagree about where these rugs were made; treat the name as a look, and check structure.

facts.text: Mumford says the Tabriz city type was sold in Western markets as 'Kermanshah', and that its model was the rug of Kirman; the confusion came from the similar names.
facts.quote: The type of carpet which has come to be known as representative of Tabriz bears the name of Kermanshah, generally, in Western markets.

facts.text: Jacobsen says rugs sold in America as 'Kirmanshah' were made in the Kerman district, and quotes H. G. Dwight (1917) that hardly any rugs were ever made in Kermanshah.
Hawley says most modern 'Kermanshahs' were made in the workhouses of exporting companies rather than in Kermanshah, and that over ninety per cent were chemically washed.
Stone describes the city of Kermanshah as a market for Kurdish village rugs with the symmetric knot, a different type from the trade-name 'Kermanshah'.
Rugs sold in the trade as 'Kermanshah' are tied with the asymmetric (Senneh) knot on cotton warps and wefts.
facts.quote: Knot.—Nearly always the Senna, seldom the Ghiordes. ... Warp.—Always cotton. Woof.—Always cotton, occasionally dyed brown.

facts.text: Lewis (1911) gives 8-12 knots per inch across and 8-16 down for modern 'Kermanshahs', which he works out as 64-192 per square inch; Hawley's count is higher (132-324).
facts.quote: Number vertically eight to sixteen; number horizontally eight to twelve; number to the square inch sixty-four to one hundred ninety-two.

facts.text: The city of Kermanshah itself wove few carpets; it served as a market for rugs woven in the surrounding Kurdish villages and mountains.
facts.quote: the finished carpets were sold at Sanandaj or Kermānšāh ... there were only twenty-three carpet-weaving establishments in the town of Kermānšāh

says.text: Kermanshah city and hills, but most modern ones in exporters' workhouses elsewhere.
Tabriz, after Kirman models.
Kerman district; 'no rugs of this type have ever been made in Kirmanshah'.
Treats Kermanshah as its own type: Sehna knot with a coarse weave and buried warps.
In the vicinity of Tabriz and of Sultanabad, under European supervision; no rugs are woven in the city of Kermanshah.
Marketed at Kermanshah but made near Tabriz or Sultanabad, tending to resemble Kirman rugs in color and design.
Modern rugs sold as Kermanshah are only exported from that caravan center; they are woven in Kirman.
The modern 'Kirman or Kermanshah' rug is made throughout the Kirman district; no rugs of value are made in Kermanshah (quoting Wigham).
64-192 knots per square inch.

rows.name: Yazd
rows.region: Yazd, central Iran between Isfahan and Kerman.
rows.made_by: City looms; Jacobsen says Yazd merchants imported designers and paper cartoons from Kerman after World War II.
rows.date_note: Hawley (1913): very few pile rugs then woven in Yazd. Jacobsen: few rugs until recent years; 300-400 carpets a year by about 1960. The 1920 start is an estimate for rugs readers may own.

structure.knot_note: Asymmetric (Stone). Jacobsen: one of the few towns where the jufti knot was not used.
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: about 100-200 asymmetric. Jacobsen: new Yazd 120-200.
structure.wefts_note: Not stated by these sources; assumed double-wefted like Kerman city rugs (unverified).
structure.pile_note: Medium to medium-short (Jacobsen).
structure.sides: Not stated.
structure.ends: Not stated.

design.field: Older rugs: Herati repeat, often on blue; post-war: Kerman-like medallion on an open cochineal-red field with a broken border.
design.border: Floral; broken borders after World War II.
design.colors: Red, blue and white; cochineal red fields after World War II.
design.sizes: Mostly 7 x 10 ft and up, commonly 8 x 11 to 11 x 16 ft.

look_alikes.name: Kerman
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Post-war Yazd copies Kerman designs.

look_alikes.name: Tabriz
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Pre-war Herati Yazd looks like Tabriz; Tabriz is symmetric-knotted.

rows.trade_use: Used for rugs of the city; Hawley noted the name was also applied to rugs made elsewhere.
rows.what_it_tells: A Kerman-like asymmetric carpet with a red open field, or an older Herati carpet, may be Yazd; structure alone does not separate it from Kerman.
rows.cautions: Hawley says the name Yazd was applied to products of other districts.

facts.text: In 1913 very few pile rugs were woven in Yazd, and the name was sometimes applied to rugs made elsewhere.
facts.quote: the name is sometimes applied to modern products made in other districts.

facts.text: Older Yazd rugs used the Herati design; later production uses medallion designs like those of Kerman.
Yazd rugs have about 100-200 asymmetric knots per square inch on cotton warps.
A Safavid-era traveler, Pedro Teixeira, judged the carpets of Yazd the best in Persia.
Yazd was formerly noted for silk rugs and felts.

'Yazd hand-woven carpet' is a registered geographical indication, nationally (Industrial Property Office 23 GI (6 Jul 2014)) and internationally (WIPO Lisbon register AO 957, 11 Oct 2014); the registered area is the region of Yazd.
facts.quote: (AO 957) فرش دستبافت يزد / Yazd Handmade Carpet

rows.name: Tehran
rows.region: Tehran and its surroundings; Tehran is mainly the country's rug market.
rows.made_by: City workshops (Stone names Hadj Muhammad Djafar and Farschi as early 20th-century weaver-designers).
rows.date_note: Hawley (1913) says Teherans 'were formerly made' in the capital; Stone dates notable designers to the early 20th century; Jacobsen (1962) saw few. The 1880 start is an estimate.

structure.knot_note: Stone: asymmetric. Hawley: Ghiordes (symmetric) with level warps, like his 'Iran' rugs.
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: 130-325. Hawley gives no count.
structure.wefts_note: Not stated.
structure.pile_note: Short clipped, dry and lusterless like Tabriz (Jacobsen).
structure.sides: Two-cord selvage (Hawley).
structure.ends: Not stated.

design.field: Herati or floral field two to three times as long as wide; floral and modern pictorial designs; interlaced tendrils, scrolls, the Mustaphi design.
design.colors: Rich reds and blues.
design.sizes: 6.5 x 4.5 ft and 7 x 10.5 ft.

look_alikes.name: Kashan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Jacobsen says Tehran rugs are hard to separate from fine Tabriz, Joshaghan or Kashan rugs.

rows.trade_use: Mumford (1902) found that rugs sold in America as 'Teheran' and 'Ispahan' were in fact from Saruk village and Kirman; the name was a market label.
rows.what_it_tells: A label 'Tehran' on an older rug is a trade name; on a 20th-century fine rug it may mean city work.
rows.cautions: The name has been used loosely since the 19th century.

facts.text: Hawley says rugs called Teheran were formerly made in the capital and were scarce by 1913.
facts.quote: The Teherans were formerly made in the present capital of Persia.

facts.text: Mumford believed the rugs sold in America as 'Teheran' and 'Ispahan' came mainly from the village of Saruk and from Kirman (Jacobsen repeats and doubts this).
facts.quote: I believe that all the fabrics called Teheran and Ispahan are the products of the village of Saruk in the Feraghan district

facts.text: Tehran is a major rug market; some floral and modern pictorial rugs are woven there at about 130-325 asymmetric knots per square inch on cotton.
Jacobsen found Tehran rugs fine with short pile and dry, lusterless wool like Tabriz, and rarely seen in America.
Tehran is a major rug market, and some rugs are also woven in and around the city.
Jacobsen counted some 2,000 retail rug stores in Tehran around 1960.

says.text: The knot is Ghiordes, each warp equally prominent at the back, warp and weft cotton.
Asymmetric knots at 130-325 per square inch.

disagreements.about: whether rugs were made in Tehran

says.text: Lists Teheran among Persian rug names as '(Market only)'.
'The Teherans were formerly made in the present capital of Persia.'
It is hard to say how long it has been since carpets in any number were made in the present or former capital; 'Teheran' rugs in Western shops were Saruk and Kirman work.
Made in and around the capital, though weaving there had slowed with modernization.

rows.name: Najafabad
rows.region: Najafabad, west of Isfahan, and its valley villages.
rows.made_by: Town and village weavers, formerly organized by master contractors (ostad-kar).
rows.date_note: No source gives a start date; 20th-century production.

structure.knot_note: Asymmetric (Stone).
structure.wefts_note: Not stated.
structure.pile_note: Not stated.
structure.sides: Not stated.
structure.ends: Not stated.

design.field: Medallion designs.
design.colors: Not stated.
design.sizes: Not stated.

look_alikes.name: Isfahan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Najafabad lies in the Isfahan area and uses similar medallion designs; sources give no structural test.

rows.trade_use: Sometimes sold under the Isfahan name.
rows.what_it_tells: Little: the name places a rug in the Isfahan area.
rows.cautions: Almost no documentation; treat as a gap.

facts.text: Najafabad is a source of medallion rugs with 120-475 asymmetric knots per square inch.
Weaving in the Najafabad valley was formerly organized by ostad-kars (master contractors).
A Persian study lists Najafabad among the towns of Isfahan province that now weave Nain-type rugs.
facts.quote: جدول ۲. تفکیک استان ها و شهرستان هایی که به تولید فرش نایین مبادرت کرده اند: ... خمینی شهر، نجف آباد، شاهین شهر ... (Table 2: provinces and towns that have taken up producing Nain carpets: Khomeinishahr, Najafabad, Shahinshahr ...)

facts.text: The Iran National Carpet Center lists Najafabad among places proposed for national registration as a carpet geographical indication (Isfahan province).
facts.quote: تودشک - میمه - فریدن - نجف‌آباد - گلپایگان (proposed for national registration)

rows.name: Ardabil (modern town rugs)
rows.region: Ardabil, Iranian Azerbaijan east of Tabriz, near the border with the Republic of Azerbaijan, and its villages.
rows.made_by: Town and village workshops; in 1972 about 5,500 weavers, 60 per cent men.
rows.date_note: A new type on the market only since 1950.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric (Stone; Jacobsen 'Ghiordes').
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: up to 160. Lower bound is an estimate; Jacobsen says they are not as finely woven as better old Caucasian rugs.
structure.wefts_note: Not stated.
structure.pile_note: Usually good wool; some 'dead' (skin) wool (Jacobsen).
structure.sides: Not stated.
structure.ends: Not stated.
structure.handle: Thin, like the thinner Caucasian rugs (Jacobsen).

design.field: Geometric Caucasian designs (Kuba, Shirvan, Daghestan types), usually on red or ivory fields.
design.colors: Red or ivory fields with blue, ivory, green and yellow.
design.sizes: About 2 x 4 ft to 8.5 x 11 ft; about half near 7 x 4.5 ft.

look_alikes.name: caucasian
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Old Caucasian rugs usually have wool foundations; Ardabil rugs are on cotton.

look_alikes.name: Ardabil design
look_alikes.how_to_tell: 'Ardabil' on a rug may instead mean the Ardabil-carpet design copied in Tabriz, Mashhad and elsewhere.

rows.trade_use: 'Ardebil rug' for the modern Caucasian-design rugs of Ardabil; 'Ardabil design' for the medallion of the 1539-40 Ardabil carpet, used everywhere.
rows.what_it_tells: A symmetric-knotted rug on cotton with Caucasian geometric designs fits Ardabil (or other Iranian Azerbaijan) production from 1950 on.
rows.cautions: Do not confuse with the classical Ardabil carpet or rugs in its design.

facts.text: Contemporary rugs of Ardabil use designs similar to Caucasian rugs, with symmetric knots on a cotton foundation.
Stone gives densities up to about 160 knots per square inch.
Ardabil rugs appeared on the Western market about 1950.
Ardabil-area carpet quality suffered from commercialization; in 1972 the industry employed about 5,500 weavers, 60 per cent of them men.
Ardabil hand-woven carpet is a registered geographical indication, nationally (Industrial Property Office no. 20 GI, 28 May 2014) and internationally (WIPO Lisbon register AO 948, 11 Oct 2014).
facts.quote: (AO 948) فرش دستبافت اردبيل / Ardabil Handmade Carpet

rows.name: Mashhad (Meshed)
rows.region: Mashhad, capital of Khorasan province, northeast Iran, and towns and villages up to about 100 miles around, which market their rugs there.
rows.made_by: City workshops (10-40 looms each in Jacobsen's day) founded largely by Tabrizi merchants and master weavers, and home looms; village grades from the wider district.
rows.date_note: Production in Mashhad began in the late 19th century. Persian sources date the revival to Azerbaijani (Tabrizi) entrepreneurs in the late Qajar period; Jacobsen says the Turkbaff workshops were set up about 1904. Production continues.

structure.knot_note: Two traditions: 'Turkbaff' (Persian torkbaf, 'Turkish-woven') workshop rugs with the symmetric knot, tied with a hook, introduced by Tabrizi entrepreneurs; and 'Farsibaff' ('Persian-woven') rugs with the asymmetric knot, often jufti (tied over four warps) in the cheaper grades. Hawley: generally Sehna, rarely Ghiordes; May: Ghiordes or Sehna.
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: 8-15 x 12-17 = 96-255. Lewis: 72-240. Jacobsen: Turkbaff 120-250 (older rugs more). The Amoghli workshop wove at 40-150 raj (Rahimpanah), which by the raj conversion (knots per about 7 cm) would be about 210 to over 3,000 kpsi at the top; the top figure is doubtful and is recorded as given.
structure.wefts_note: Double-wefted (Hawley, May, Stone); many modern rugs have a heavy cable weft every 4-8 inches that shows on the back (Stone).
structure.pile_note: Fine, silky wool of medium length (Hawley; May 'notably silky'); Jacobsen says many grades used lime-steeped wool, which wears fast.
structure.sides: Double overcasting in the color of the outer edging (Hawley).
structure.ends: Web and warp fringe at both ends (Hawley).
structure.handle: Turkbaff: thick, compact and heavy (Jacobsen). Farsibaff/jufti grades: looser and lighter.
structure.back: Slightly coarse grain (Hawley); periodic heavy wefts in many (Stone).

design.field: Large medallion and corners, often the Ardabil-carpet medallion; all-over Herati or Shah Abbasi designs (afshan); large elaborate boteh.
design.border: Elaborate, often more than five stripes, with a narrow outer edging.
design.colors: Deep cochineal red (often purplish, almost magenta) fields with blue medallions, corners and borders (Stone; Jacobsen; Heshmati Razavi 'laki' red).
design.sizes: Mostly large carpet sizes, nearly square in older pieces; 9 x 12 ft and larger.

look_alikes.name: Kerman
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Mashhad medallion carpets resemble Kerman and both use cochineal red; jufti knots and periodic heavy wefts on the back point to Khorasan.

look_alikes.name: Tabriz
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Turkbaff Mashhad carpets are made like Tabriz; the purplish cochineal field is the Mashhad sign.

look_alikes.name: Khorassan (older province rugs)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Old Khorassans have longer, unevenly clipped silky pile and the Khorassan border stripe; Hawley says Mesheds are shorter and more evenly clipped.

look_alikes.name: Isfahan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Many American 'Ispahans' are Mashhad Turkbaffs: thick and symmetric-knotted, unlike fine asymmetric Isfahan.

rows.trade_use: 'Turkbaff' (Turkibaff) for symmetric-knotted city workshop carpets; 'Meshed' or 'Khorassan' for asymmetric grades; American dealers sold Turkbaffs as 'Ispahan' (Jacobsen's 'Ispahan-Meshed'). 'Amoghli' names a celebrated early-20th-century Mashhad workshop.
rows.what_it_tells: A large carpet with a purplish-red field and blue medallion, either symmetric-knotted and thick (Turkbaff) or asymmetric with knots over four warps (jufti), fits Mashhad.
rows.cautions: Jufti knotting and lime-steeped wool make many cheaper grades wear thin (Jacobsen; Heshmati Razavi). Attributions to Amoghli are trade claims unless the rug is inscribed.

facts.text: Carpet production in Mashhad began (or revived) in the late 19th century, led by Azerbaijani (Tabrizi) merchants and weavers who set up workshops there in the late Qajar period.
Tabrizi entrepreneurs introduced 'Turkish' (symmetric-knot) workshop weaving in Mashhad; the trade calls these rugs Turkbaff, as opposed to Farsibaff (asymmetric).
Both the asymmetric (Persian) and the symmetric (Turkish) knot are in common use in Mashhad.
Many Khorasan rugs are tied with the jufti knot, an asymmetric knot tied over four warps instead of two, which uses less wool and lowers density and durability.
Turkbaff weavers tie knots with a hook, which makes jufti knotting impractical.
Mashhad carpets are typically double-wefted, and many have a heavy cable weft every 4 to 8 inches, visible on the back.
A deep cochineal red, often purplish, is the typical field color of Mashhad carpets.
Hawley says Mesheds are of the Khorassan type with the same silky nap, but shorter and more evenly clipped.
facts.quote: these rugs are of the Khorassan type, and have the same silky appearance of nap, though it is shorter and more evenly clipped.

facts.text: Weaving in Mashhad and other Khorasan towns is measured in a unit called moqat (mokata); Stone gives it as 16,000 knots.

The Amoghli (Amu-oghli) family, originally named Kohnamui, from a village near Osku in Azerbaijan, ran a celebrated Mashhad workshop in the early 20th century; Master Abd-al-Mohammad Amoghli wove mostly to commission, copying designs from books of classical carpets sent from England.
Amoghli carpets were woven at 40 to 150 raj.
Mesheds come almost only in large carpet sizes.
Abdolmohammad and Ali Khan Amoghli, Haj Ali Khamenei and Mohammad-Ebrahim Makhmalbaf are named as founders and revivers of contemporary Mashhad carpet weaving.

'Mashhad hand-woven carpet' is a registered geographical indication, nationally (Industrial Property Office 16 GI (22 Dec 2013)) and internationally (WIPO Lisbon register AO 954, 11 Oct 2014); the registered area is the region of Mashhad.
facts.quote: (AO 954) فرش دستبافت مشهد / Mashad Handmade Carpet, Mashhad Handmade Carpet

says.text: Generally Sehna, rarely Ghiordes.
Ghiordes or Sehna.
Usually the Senna, seldom the Ghiordes.
Some symmetric; most a jufti version of the asymmetric knot.
City Turkbaffs symmetric; district rugs asymmetric tied over four warps.
Tabriz businessmen set up looms in Meshed around 1904.
Tabrizis set up workshops in the late Qajar period.
Workshops of Amoghli, Makhmalbaf, Khamenei and Saber opened at the beginning of 'this century' (ambiguous: the 14th century AH began 1882/3; the 14th solar century in 1921).

rows.name: Khorassan (older province rugs)
rows.region: Khorasan province, northeast Iran: Mashhad district, Qain (Qainat), Birjand, Tun and other towns and villages.
rows.made_by: Town and village weavers across the province.
rows.date_note: Hawley (1913) says most Khorassans then seen were fifty or more years old; Ballard's example is 18th century; Jacobsen describes a thinner commercial 'Khorassan' type imported 1924-1940, after which the trade used 'Meshed' instead.

structure.knot_note: Hawley: Sehna, 'many are left-hand'. Stone: the Khurasan jufti knot is asymmetric and open to the left. May: Sehna (which separates Khorassan from Herat, tied symmetric).
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: 8-13 across x 12-20 down = 96-260. Lewis: 80-375. Ballard's 18th-century Khorassan rug: 45-70 (9-10 down x 5-7 across).
structure.wefts_note: The Khorassan hallmark: Hawley and May describe two wefts per row with three to five every six to eight rows; Lewis and Jacobsen describe several rows of knots with little or no weft between, then several wefts together, so the knots bunch in groups when the rug is folded.
structure.pile_note: Medium-length, silky, unevenly clipped wool (Hawley; May); Jacobsen: fine belly wool.
structure.sides: Double overcasting in the color of the edging (Hawley).
structure.ends: Narrow web and short warp fringe (Hawley); Lewis: fringe of loose warps.
structure.handle: Moderately firm (Hawley); older rugs soft and pliable (Lewis).
structure.back: Moderately fine grain with bands where extra wefts are packed (Hawley; Lewis).

design.field: Herati and large elongated boteh (pear) with smaller boteh leaning on them, medallions, vases; birds and animals in older pieces.
design.border: Wide; a characteristic main stripe of a heavy undulating vine with bird-head-like flowers (the 'Khorassan stripe', Hawley; May).
design.colors: Rose, wine, magenta or purple reds, blue and cream.
design.sizes: Mostly large, 5-12 ft; 7-15 x 10-25 ft.

look_alikes.name: herat
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Both have weft-grouping; Khorassan uses the asymmetric knot, Herat the symmetric.

look_alikes.name: Mashhad (Meshed)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Mashhad pile is shorter and more evenly clipped.

rows.trade_use: Before about 1940 'Khorassan' meant the thinner older type and 'Meshed' the thicker; Jacobsen treats the names as the same thing after that.
rows.what_it_tells: Bands of extra wefts at intervals on the back, silky uneven pile and magenta or purplish reds point to an older Khorassan rug.
rows.cautions: Cochineal-dyed wool steeped in lime wears poorly; many old Khorassans are worn.

facts.text: Khorassan rugs are tied with the asymmetric knot, many open to the left.
facts.quote: Knot, Sehna. Many are " left-hand."

facts.text: The characteristic Khorassan weave groups the rows of knots, with extra weft passes at intervals, so that bands are visible on the back and the knots part in groups when the rug is bent.
Khorassan pile is silky and unevenly clipped.
Magenta and purple shades, rare in other Persian rugs, are typical of Khorassans.
A main border stripe of a heavy undulating vine with bird-head-like flowers is so common in Khorassans that May calls it the Khorassan border stripe.
Khorassan boteh are elongated, often with two smaller boteh laid across them.
Hawley's count is 8-13 knots per inch across and 12-20 down; Lewis gives 80-375 per square inch; Ballard's 18th-century example has 45-70.
The geographer al-Maqdisi (10th century) already mentions carpets of Quhistan (Qainat) in Khorasan.
The Textile Museum describes classical (16th-17th-century) Khorasan carpets as usually knotted with asymmetric knots around four warps (jufti) rather than two, often offset row by row.

says.text: Weft crosses twice between two rows of knots, except every six or eight rows, where it crosses three or more times.
Twice, then at intervals three to five times.
Four or more rows of knots with no weft threads between, then several weft threads.
In old rugs a single weft between every three or four rows, then three or four weft lines; new rugs use one heavy coarse thread instead.

rows.name: Birjand
rows.region: Birjand, Qainat region of eastern Iran (South Khorasan), about 150 miles south of Mashhad.
rows.made_by: Factory and home weavers of Birjand and villages.
rows.date_note: Factory production from the beginning of the 20th century. Hawley (1913) speaks of earlier fine Birjands of 200-300 knots per square inch.

structure.knot_note: Jufti asymmetric knot tied over four warps (Stone; Jacobsen; Heshmati Razavi names jofti-bafi as the South Khorasan defect).
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: about 100 (jufti). Hawley: older Birjands 200-300. Older pieces denser (Stone).
structure.wefts_note: Not stated; Heshmati Razavi describes thick wefts and light beating used to hide jufti knotting.
structure.pile_note: Often poor wool steeped in lime before dyeing (Jacobsen).
structure.sides: Not stated.
structure.ends: Not stated.
