rows.name: Gorevan
rows.region: A village of the Heris district (Dehkhoda's c. 1950 gazetteer puts it about 28 km east of Ahar); the name is used for carpets from across the district.
rows.made_by: Heris-district village weavers (Azeri Turkish-speaking).
rows.kind: trade name (a name for a look, made in several places)
rows.date_note: Mumford (1902) says Tabriz shippers began invoicing Herez carpets as 'Gorevan' in the late 19th century; Hawley (1913) calls all Gorevans modern. The name stayed in use as a grade through the 20th century.

structure.knot_note: Ghiordes (symmetric) per Hawley, May and Kendrick & Tattersall; Lewis says usually Senna (asymmetric).
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: horizontally 6-8, perpendicularly 6-10 = 36-80. Lewis: 48-180. Jacobsen: in the coarsest grades over half the knots are jufti (tied over four warps).
structure.weft_color: Hawley: sometimes dyed blue; Kendrick & Tattersall: mostly dyed blue or brown; Lewis: sometimes dyed brown
structure.wefts_note: Hawley: coarse cotton weft crossing once, or frequently twice. May: twice.
structure.pile_note: Medium length (Hawley); coarse wool clipped short (Lewis); thick (Jacobsen).
structure.sides: Hawley: a two-cord double selvage. Lewis: usually overcast, as a rule with different colored wool.
structure.ends: Hawley: short warp fringe at both ends. May: end webs may be colored, 'a feature found in but few Persian rugs'.
structure.handle: Thick and coarse; Hawley calls the texture rather loose.
structure.back: Very coarse grain; warp rarely fully hidden (Hawley).

design.field: Concentric angular (stepped hexagonal) medallions with large corners; heavy, archaic angular leaves and flowers; figures often colored in two strongly contrasting halves.
design.border: Main stripe usually the turtle design.
design.colors: Dull brick red, terracotta, buff, dark blue, dull green, yellow, ivory; terracotta, apricot and blue; copper-red, dark blue and buff.
design.sizes: Carpet sizes, rarely small rugs; Hawley 10-16 ft long.

look_alikes.name: Heriz
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same district and design; Gorevan is the coarser grade name.

look_alikes.name: Serapi
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Serapis are often mistaken for Gorevans but are as a rule better woven, with lighter ivory or buff fields.

rows.trade_use: A quality name inside the Heriz family: Jacobsen says New York importers bought the cheaper Heriz grade as 'Gorevan' and retailers sold it as 'Heriz'; Stone says a very coarse rug in a Heriz pattern may be called Gorevan.
rows.what_it_tells: The name says the rug is from the Heris district and, in most trade use, that it is a coarser grade; it does not point to the village of Gorevan.
rows.cautions: The meaning has shifted: Mumford (1902) says the name was first used for Herez carpets and then for a new, finely woven Tabriz-style medallion type with an ivory ground; later authors use it for the coarse grade.

facts.text: Gorevan is the name of a small village in the Herez district.
Gorevans have concentric medallions and a turtle-pattern main border.
The knot is the symmetric (Ghiordes) knot and the warp is cotton.
Hawley gives 6-8 knots per inch across and 6-10 down (about 36-80 per square inch).
Gorevans come in carpet sizes and are rarely small rugs.
In the trade 'Gorevan' denotes a quality, the poorer grade of rugs sold as Heriz.
In 1954-60 many cheap Gorevans were woven with ready-dyed 'skin wool' bought in Tabriz and wore thin in a few years (Jacobsen).
Gorevan is listed as a proposed (not yet registered) carpet geographical indication, separate from Heris.

The internationally registered Heris appellation (WIPO Lisbon register AO 910, 2013) gives its area as 'Heris and its regions (Bakhshayesh, Guravan, Khajeh)', so Gorevan already falls inside the Heris registration.
facts.quote: Heris and its regions (Bakhshayesh, Guravan, Khajeh)

says.text: Ghiordes.
Ghiordes.
Usually the Senna, occasionally the Ghiordes.
First used by Tabriz shippers for Herez carpets; then for a new, finely woven medallion type of Tabriz drawing with an ivory ground.
A comparatively modern, moderately priced carpet of stout weave.
The lowest quality grade of Heriz.
Once, or frequently twice.
Twice.

rows.name: Mehriban (Heriz district)
rows.region: Mehraban village in the Heris district of East Azerbaijan. Not the same as the Mehraban district north of Hamadan (see Mehriban (Hamadan district)).
rows.made_by: Heris-district village weavers; from the 1940s-50s much of it contract weaving for importers.
rows.date_note: Jacobsen describes 'Mehrevan' contract-quality Heriz carpets reaching New York after World War II; the village is older.

structure.knot_note: As for Heriz (symmetric); no author gives a separate analysis.
structure.kpsi_note: No separate count found; Stone and Jacobsen rank it as a grade within the Heriz range.
structure.wefts_note: Not stated separately.
structure.pile_note: Thick, rather tightly woven (Jacobsen).

design.field: Geometric Heriz medallion designs with red fields, usually rosy or bluish reds rather than rust.
design.colors: Rosy red or deep bluish red fields.
design.sizes: Many sizes up to about 11 x 23 ft, including long narrow sizes made to importers' orders.

look_alikes.name: Heriz
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same family; Mehriban is a grade or village name within it.

look_alikes.name: Mehriban (Hamadan district)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A different place: Mehraban north of Hamadan weaves single-wefted village rugs, often with camel-colored fields.

rows.trade_use: 'Mehriban' or 'contract quality' was the trade's better grade of new Heriz in the 1940s-50s.
rows.what_it_tells: On an older American invoice the name points to a better-grade Heriz-district carpet; it does not by itself say Hamadan.
rows.cautions: Two different places share the name; Stone also ranks it differently in two entries.

facts.text: There are two places called Mehraban whose rugs reach the market: one in the Heris district and one in the Hamadan district.
Mehraban (East Azerbaijan) is a registered carpet geographical indication, listed with Heris, Bakhshayesh and Sarab.
Mehraban had about 600 looms in the late 1950s, second only to Heris town (Jacobsen).
The trade called Mehrevan carpets 'contract quality Herez'.
A Persian field study counts Mehraban among the coarse, symmetric-knotted rugs of the Heris area.

says.text: Mehriban entry: a grade of Heriz between Heriz and Gorevan in quality. Heriz entry: Mehraban and Serapi refer to the finer, more densely knotted rugs.
Mehrevans were among the best qualities of new Herez; some made in Herez town were better.

rows.name: Ahar
rows.region: Ahar, the market town of the Arasbaran region about 95 km northeast of Tabriz, and its villages (Khuniq, Cheshmeh-Vazan, Arpaliq, Zandabad, Qurchi-Kandi, Qarajeh).
rows.made_by: Village weavers of Ahar county (Azeri Turkish-speaking).
rows.date_note: Jacobsen says Heriz-type carpets marketed as 'Ahar' first appeared in 1958-59; village rugs of the county are older but less known in the West.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric (Stone; Persian field study).
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: about 65 per square inch. Persian field study: 15-22 raj (about 5.5-8 knots per inch across; vertical count not given).
structure.wefts_note: Stone: single-wefted Heriz-area rugs may be termed 'Ahar'.

design.field: Medallion and corner designs. Jacobsen: a large medallion, partly geometric with some curvilinear effect, on rose or red fields with large ivory corners.
design.colors: Red, rose or brick fields with much ivory.
design.sizes: Mostly about 9 x 12 ft when introduced.

look_alikes.name: Heriz
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Ahar carpets are a Heriz-family type; Stone treats 'Ahar' as a name for finer, more curvilinear or single-wefted Heriz-area rugs.

look_alikes.name: Karaja
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Qarajeh, whose small rugs are sold as Karaja, is itself a village of Ahar county (Persian field study).

rows.trade_use: From 1958-59 'Ahar' or 'Ahar Herez' was used for a superior grade of new Heriz-type carpet; Stone uses it as a designation of fine weave or curvilinear design in Heriz rugs.
rows.what_it_tells: A Heriz-type medallion carpet sold as Ahar is most likely from after the late 1950s.
rows.cautions: The trade's 'Ahar' (fine, curvilinear, from 1958) and the village rugs of Ahar county (coarse, geometric) described by a Persian field study are not the same thing.

facts.text: Ahar is a town of the Arasbaran region northeast of Tabriz; carpet and gelim weaving are among its main occupations.
Ahar village rugs use the symmetric knot.
Ahar village rugs are coarse (15-22 raj) with straight-line geometric drawing and are woven on vertical looms.
Contemporary Ahar rugs have medallions and spandrels on a cotton foundation at about 65 knots per square inch.
Heriz-type carpets sold as 'Ahar' first appeared in 1959 and were among the best new Heriz qualities.
Ahar is listed as a proposed carpet geographical indication.

says.text: A superior new Heriz type, close to a good Sarouk in quality, combining Tabriz curves with Heriz geometry.
Village rugs of Ahar county are coarse (15-22 raj) and geometric.
A designation of fine weave or curvilinear design in Heriz rugs; also single-wefted Heriz-area rugs.

rows.name: Bakshaish
rows.region: A village of the Heris district east of Tabriz (East Azerbaijan).
rows.made_by: Village weavers of the Heris district.
rows.date_note: Jacobsen describes old Bakshis of 1800-1900; a Negareh study (Mohammadi et al. 2016) traces weaving there to the Safavid period; since about 1900 the village has woven Heriz-type medallion carpets sold as Heriz or Gorevan.

structure.knot_note: Ballard's Bakshi rug and Stone: symmetric. Lewis: usually Senna, sometimes Ghiordes.
structure.kpsi_note: Ballard No. 4: Ghiordes, 9-10 vertical x 6 horizontal = 54-60. Lewis: 30-180.
structure.wefts_note: Not stated.
structure.pile_note: Ballard No. 4: long pile; Lewis: trimmed short.
structure.sides: Lewis: nearly always overcast with different colored yarns, occasionally finished flat.
structure.ends: Lewis: short fringe with loose warp threads at each end, occasionally knotted.
structure.handle: Ballard No. 4 is loosely woven with a long pile.

design.field: Older pieces: all-over Herati or angular palmette patterns in pale, faded blues, buffs and mauves; later: Heriz medallion designs. The Negareh study (Mohammadi et al. 2016) names three current designs, all medallion-and-corner.
design.border: Two narrow and one wide stripe, the wide one often with the Herati design.
design.colors: Old pieces pale blue, buff, mauve, faded magenta.
design.sizes: Old ones: runners about 3.5 ft wide and long narrow carpets 6 x 11 to 7 x 16 ft.

look_alikes.name: Heriz
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Modern Bakhshayesh carpets are sold as Heriz; the older all-over Herati or palmette pieces with pale colors are what collectors call Bakshaish (Jacobsen, Stone; Negareh study, Mohammadi et al. 2016).

look_alikes.name: Farahan (Feraghan)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Old Bakshis followed the small all-over Herati design of Feraghan rugs; Feraghans are asymmetric-knotted and finer.

rows.trade_use: Collectors use 'Bakshaish' for older Heriz-district pieces with all-over designs; new carpets woven there are sold as Heriz or Gorevan (Jacobsen; Negareh study, Mohammadi et al. 2016).
rows.what_it_tells: An older Heriz-district rug with an all-over angular design and soft, pale colors is the kind sold as Bakshaish.
rows.cautions: The name is applied loosely to old Heriz-area pieces; Mumford (1902) and Hawley (1913) describe the Bakshis of their day as hasty, poor weaving, the opposite of today's collector use.

facts.text: Bakhshayesh (Bakshis) is a weaving village of the Heris district east of Tabriz.
Because of Heris's fame, Bakhshayesh rugs are mostly sold as Heris rugs, though they have their own designs.
Older Bakshaish rugs used the Herati pattern; contemporary ones use the Heriz design.
A Ballard collection 'Bakshi rug' (catalogue No. 4) has Ghiordes knots at 54-60 per square inch, is loosely woven and has a long pile.
facts.quote: The rug is loosely woven and has a long pile. (Ballard catalogue, No. 4)

facts.text: Around 1880 a Sultanabad firm promoted weaving in Bakhshis; when quality fell the trade moved the name 'Herez' to other village work (Mumford's account).
Bakhshayesh is a registered carpet geographical indication.

says.text: Fifty miles southeast of Tabriz.
Southwest of Heriz.
The first day's stage east of Tabriz.
c. 1950: Bostanabad district of Tabriz county.
Usually Senna, sometimes Ghiordes.
Ghiordes (one rug).
Symmetric.
Those exported in his day were of little artistic value and carelessly woven.
Old Bakshis of 1800-1900 were rare and highly priced even 40 years before 1962.

rows.name: Serapi
rows.translit: Sarāb (the trade name 'Serapi' is not used in Persian)
rows.region: Heris district, East Azerbaijan. The name is said to come from Sarab (Sirab), a town between Tabriz and Ardabil, but the carpets sold as Serapi are Heriz-district work.
rows.made_by: Heris-district village weavers.
rows.kind: trade name (a name for a look, made in several places)
rows.date_note: Mumford (c. 1900) describes Serapi as a then-new Heriz-district type; Jacobsen says nothing was imported under the name after the 1930s. The trade still applies it to older Heriz carpets (Stone: some define a Serapi as a Heriz 100-200 years old).

structure.knot_note: Hawley: 'generally Sehna, frequently Ghiordes'; Lewis: usually Senna, the finest Senna; Mumford and Stone: symmetric (Turkish).
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: horizontally 6-10, perpendicularly 7-12 = 42-120. Lewis: 80-216.
structure.wefts_note: Hawley: coarse cotton weft crossing twice. Stone: single-wefted.
structure.pile_note: Medium length (Hawley); rather coarse but durable, generally clipped short (Lewis).
structure.sides: Hawley: a double selvage of two cords or double overcasting in figure-eight, usually red or buff. Lewis: nearly always overcast.
structure.ends: Hawley: lower end a narrow web and warp loops or short fringe; upper end a narrow web and fringe.
structure.back: Coarse grain; warp hidden; one warp of each pair much depressed or doubled under (Hawley).

design.field: Medallion with pendants and corners on an ivory, camel, light buff, light madder-red or light blue field, with more open ground and more floral detail than Gorevan; inscriptions occur.
design.border: Like Gorevan; three to five stripes.
design.colors: Light grounds (ivory, buff, camel, light red, light blue) with soft medium blues and coppery reds.
design.sizes: Hawley 10-18 ft, width 2/3-3/4 of length; Lewis 8-15 by 10-25 ft.

look_alikes.name: Heriz
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same district; trade usage reserves Serapi for older or finer pieces with lighter fields.

look_alikes.name: Gorevan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Large Serapis are often mistaken for Gorevans but are better woven, with lighter ivory or buff fields.

look_alikes.name: Sarab
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Rugs actually woven in Sarab are camel-ground runners, not carpets.

rows.trade_use: An American trade term for Heriz-district carpets of better or older quality; Jacobsen says no rugs ever arrived on invoices as Serapi and that dealers used it in place of Gorevan or Heriz.
rows.what_it_tells: 'Serapi' on a label says an older Heriz-district carpet with a light field; it is a market label, not a place of weaving.
rows.cautions: Not a place name a buyer can check; it is applied generously to older Heriz carpets. The Sarab town product is something else.

facts.text: The name Serapi is derived from Sarab (Sirab), between Tabriz and Ardabil.
facts.quote: The rugs known as Serapis are named after the village of Sirab in the mountainous district between Tabriz and Ardebil (Hawley 1922, p. 148)

facts.text: Serapi is a trade term used only in America.
No carpet-size rugs were made in Sarab itself; its looms were too narrow (Jacobsen).
Serapis have the medallion of the Heriz group with a light ivory, camel or buff field and often inscriptions.
Lewis calls the Serapi the best grade of the Herez products.
facts.quote: The best grade of the Herez products. (Lewis 1920, p. 177)

facts.text: Hawley gives 6-10 knots per inch across and 7-12 down (about 42-120 per square inch); Lewis 80-216.

says.text: Generally Sehna, frequently Ghiordes.
Usually the Senna.
Turkish.
Symmetric.
Twice.
Single-wefted.
In Sirab and the country farther east.
Sometimes in the Herez district, sometimes on Tabriz or Sultanabad looms.
All so-called Serapi carpets are Herez or Gorevan; none made in Serab.

rows.name: Karaja
rows.region: The village of Qarajeh and its neighbors north of the Heris district, between Tabriz and Ahar (a Persian field study places Qarajeh in Ahar county).
rows.made_by: Village weavers (Azeri Turkish-speaking).
rows.date_note: Jacobsen describes large numbers of new Karajas in the 1950s and a few prewar carpet sizes; earlier dating is not given by the sources.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric (Stone; Persian field study).
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: about 65-130 per square inch.
structure.wefts_note: Single weft (Jacobsen: 'Only one weft thread is used'; Stone: single-wefted). Stone: rugs of the same design that are double-wefted may be called Karadagh.
structure.pile_note: Clipped shorter than Heriz in small sizes (Jacobsen).

design.field: Two to four (usually three) hooked or stepped hexagonal medallions in a row on a red field, the center one blue, the end ones green, with small angular flowers between.
design.colors: Red, rose or brick fields; blue and green medallions; some runners with ivory fields.
design.sizes: Mats 2 x 2.8 ft, scatter rugs to about 6.4 x 4.10 ft, runners to 14 x 3 ft; a few carpets before World War II.

look_alikes.name: Karadagh
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Rugs of the Karadja design that are double-wefted may be called Karadagh; Jacobsen: weave differs but both are sold as Karaja.

look_alikes.name: Karaje (old-book name)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Old books' 'Karaje' is a Kurdish wool-warp runner from near Hamadan; Karaja has a cotton warp and geometric medallions.

look_alikes.name: Kazak
look_alikes.how_to_tell: 'the Kazaks of Persia'; Caucasian Kazaks have wool warps and red or wool wefts.

look_alikes.name: Hamadan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Also single-wefted on cotton; the row of hooked hexagon medallions points to Karaja.

rows.trade_use: Small rugs and runners of Heriz type from the Karaja villages were sold as Karaja or as Heriz.
rows.what_it_tells: A small rug or runner with a row of hooked hexagon medallions, a cotton warp and a single weft points to the Karaja villages north of Heriz.
rows.cautions: Do not confuse Karaja (Azerbaijan, cotton warp) with Karaje (old trade name for Kurdish runners) or with Karadagh (the mountain region).

facts.text: Karaja rugs are made in the village of Karaja (Qarajeh) and several nearby villages north of the Heriz district.
Karaja rugs have hooked (geometric) medallions in a row on a long format.
Karajas are single-wefted with the symmetric knot on a cotton foundation.
Stone gives about 65-130 knots per square inch.
A very dark, double-dyed indigo blue is characteristic of Bijar, Karaja and Karadagh carpets (Iranica).
Qarajeh is named among the main recent rug types of Azerbaijan and northwest Iran.

says.text: A village of Ahar county.
Within the Heris area.
The northern part of the Herez district.
Same design; Karadagh when double-wefted.
Weave differs; Jacoby (1952) calls Karadjia merely a dialect form of Karadagh; Jacobsen disagrees because Karaja is a town.

rows.name: Karadagh
rows.region: The Qaradagh (Arasbaran) mountains of northern Iranian Azerbaijan between Tabriz and the Aras river, bordering the Caucasian Karabagh.
rows.made_by: Mountain village and tribal weavers; Iranica notes Kurdish tribes of Qaradagh weaving work very like the Shahsavan's.
rows.date_note: Old books (1900-1922) describe Karadagh rugs; Jacobsen says none were imported under the name after about 1910 and the name passed to Karaja and, he thinks, to the new Ardabil rugs.

structure.knot_note: Ghiordes (Hawley, Lewis, May).
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: horizontally 7-11, perpendicularly 7-11 = 49-121. Lewis: 64-154. Kendrick & Tattersall plates: 50-100.
structure.weft_color: Natural brown or dyed wool (Lewis, Mumford); occasionally dyed (Hawley)
structure.wefts_note: Hawley, May: crosses twice. Lewis: usually extra weft threads.
structure.pile_note: Medium (Hawley); sometimes camel hair (Lewis).
structure.sides: Hawley: a double selvage of two or three cords; Lewis: usually selvaged, occasionally overcast; May: two- or three-cord double overcasting.
structure.ends: Hawley: narrow web and short fringe at both ends. Lewis and Mumford: one end selvaged and turned back, the other selvaged with loose warp fringe; selvage usually red.
structure.handle: Moderately firm (Hawley); Kendrick & Tattersall: pliable and soft.
structure.back: Rather coarse grain; warp shows and weft is prominent (Hawley).

design.field: Small repeating patterns: diagonal rows of conventional flowers, hexagons, Herati or Mina Khani-like lattices; sometimes pole medallions; Caucasian devices common.
design.border: Mechanical vines or Caucasian geometric borders; reciprocal trefoil guards.
design.colors: Blue or camel-hair yellow fields, sometimes rose; natural camel hair in the ground.
design.sizes: Hawley 5-9 ft long; Lewis 3-4 x 5-7 ft and runners 2.5 x 8-15 ft.

look_alikes.name: Karabagh
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Caucasian Karabagh rugs are similar; Hawley and Mumford say Karadagh designs keep more Persian floral character.

look_alikes.name: Karaja
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Karaja rugs have cotton warps and a single weft.

look_alikes.name: Kurdish village and tribal rugs (Persian Kurdistan)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kurdish rugs with Caucasian designs are incorrectly termed Karadagh.

rows.trade_use: An old-book and collector name; Kendrick & Tattersall say such rugs were also sold as Feraghan, Karabagh or Shiraz. Stone uses Karadagh for double-wefted rugs of Karadja design.
rows.what_it_tells: A wool-foundation, geometric northwest Persian rug that looks Caucasian may be what older books call Karadagh.
rows.cautions: The name is a guess for many geometric runners; attributions such as the Rijksmuseum's 'Karadagh (possibly)' show the doubt.

facts.text: Karadagh means 'black mountain(s)' and is a range in northern Azerbaijan between Tabriz and the Aras.
Karadagh rugs resemble the rugs of Karabagh across the Aras.
Karadagh warp and weft are wool, the knot Ghiordes, the weft crossing twice.
Hawley gives 7-11 knots per inch each way (about 49-121 per square inch); Lewis 64-154; Kendrick & Tattersall 50-100.
No rugs were imported under the name Karadagh for about fifty years before 1962 (Jacobsen).
Kurdish tribes of the Qaradagh region weave carpets very like Shahsavan work.

In Persian the region's older name is Qarajeh-dagh (قراجه‌داغ, also written قره‌جه‌داغ), now officially Arasbaran, a district of northern Azerbaijan drained by tributaries of the Aras; Dehkhoda's entry 'قره داغ' is a village near Mahabad.
facts.quote: ارسباران ... نام جدید بخشی است در شمال آذربایجان ... و آنرا پیشتر قراجه داغ میگفتند (Dehkhoda: 'Arasbaran ... the new name of a district in northern Azerbaijan ... formerly called Qarajeh-dagh')

facts.text: The village of Qarajeh (the Karaja of the trade) lies in Ahar county, the center of Arasbaran, i.e. inside old Qarajeh-dagh.

disagreements.about: what the name means in the trade

says.text: Double-wefted rugs of the Karadja design; Kurdish rugs with Caucasian designs are incorrectly called Karadagh.
Rugs of this kind were also sold as Feraghan, Karabagh or Shiraz.
Collectors used it as a guess for geometric runners.
Moderately firm.
Pliable and soft to the touch.
قراجه‌داغ / قره‌جه‌داغ (Qarajeh-dagh), now Arasbaran; قره‌داغ is a village near Mahabad.
Karadagh, 'black mountain(s)' (the table's قره‌داغ follows this reading; no Persian source for it).

museum_examples.title: Medaillonkleed, versierd met botehs tegen blauw fond en geometrische motieven en dierfiguren. Kersrode rand met s-vormige ranken en rozetten.
museum_examples.shows: one image (whole piece, front)
museum_examples.attribution: maker: anonymous, Karadagh (possibly); maker: anonymous, Koerdistan (possibly)
museum_examples.note: Production: Karadagh (possibly) / Kurdistan (possibly) - doubtful. Medallion rug with botehs, geometric motifs and animal figures; cherry-red border; probably cut down from a longer runner. 186 x 98 cm.

museum_examples.title: Oosters tapijt
museum_examples.shows: one image (whole piece, front)
museum_examples.attribution: maker: anonymous, Hamadan (possibly); maker: anonymous, Karadagh (possibly); maker: anonymous, Noordwest-Perzië (possibly); maker: anonymous, Zuid-Kaukasus (possibly)
museum_examples.note: Production: Hamadan (possibly) / Karadagh (possibly) / Northwest Persia (possibly) - doubtful. Runner of repeated lozenge medallions on dark blue; shortened. 210 x 90 cm.

rows.name: Sarab
rows.region: The town and district of Sarab between Tabriz and Ardabil, East Azerbaijan.
rows.made_by: Village and Shahsavan weavers of the Sarab district (Iranica: Shahsavan pieces from around Sarab).
rows.date_note: Jacobsen saw old, semi-antique and new Serab runners (about 100 old ones a year around 1960); no earlier date is given by the sources.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric (Stone).
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: about 50 per square inch. Jacobsen: slightly coarser than a Bijar.
structure.weft_color: Iranica: the Shahsavan used cotton for wefts
structure.wefts_note: Iranica: Sarab-area Shahsavan pieces usually have two weft shots after each row of knots (unlike single-wefted Hamadan camel-hair pieces).
structure.pile_note: Undyed camel hair or camel-colored wool in the field (Jacobsen, Stone, Iranica).
structure.handle: Thick and tightly woven, heavier than a Bijar (Jacobsen).

design.field: A row of repeating diamond or hexagon (often octagonal) medallions on a camel-colored field; the field around them may be filled with a lattice or short angled hatch lines.
design.border: Main border cream with blue, rose and green.
design.colors: Shades of undyed camel with red, green, blue and ivory.
design.sizes: Runners 5 x 3 ft to 14 x 3 ft, rarely larger; no carpet sizes.

look_alikes.name: Hamadan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Old 'Hamadan' camel-hair pieces look alike in color and design but have one weft per row; Sarab pieces usually two.

look_alikes.name: Serapi
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Despite the name, Serapi carpets are Heriz-district work, not Sarab runners.

rows.trade_use: 'Serab' in the trade means a camel-ground runner; 'Serapi' means a Heriz carpet.
rows.what_it_tells: A thick camel-ground runner with a row of medallions points to the Sarab district.
rows.cautions: The Saint Louis Art Museum's 'Serab Long Carpet' places Serab in Hamadan province; Sarab is in East Azerbaijan.

facts.text: Sarab weavers produce runners with repeating diamond or hexagon medallions on a camel-colored field.
Serab rugs come only in runner sizes and a few small rugs; no carpet sizes are made.
Shahsavan pieces from around Sarab use much undyed camel hair and usually have two weft shots after each knot row.
Stone gives about 50 symmetric knots per square inch on an all-wool or wool-and-cotton foundation.
Sarab is a registered national carpet geographical indication (East Azerbaijan).
The Shahsevan summer pastures lay in the Ardabil, Meshkin and Sarab districts.

says.text: Counts Sarab among the coarse rugs of the wider Heris area.
Registers Sarab separately from Heris.
Treats the Serab district as part of the Herez district but describes its rugs separately.

museum_examples.licence: Public Domain (Rights field on object page)
museum_examples.title: Serab Long Carpet
museum_examples.shows: one image (whole carpet)
museum_examples.attribution: Persian, Qājār dynasty; made in Serab, Hamadan province, Iran
museum_examples.note: Wool; 340.4 x 87.6 cm (runner/long carpet). DOUBTFUL PLACE: SLAM puts Serab in Hamadan province; Sarab town is in East Azerbaijan province (Hawley's 'Serab' camel-ground runners). Gift of Nellie Ballard White.

rows.name: Meshkin and Ardebil-area village rugs
rows.region: Meshkin Shahr, Ardabil and villages of Ardabil province near the Caucasian border; the Moghan plain.
rows.made_by: Village weavers, many of Shahsavan background; Persian sources say Shahsavan nomads carried Caucasian (Aran) designs across the Aras.
rows.date_note: The new Ardebil rug came on the market only after 1950; Meshkin rugs reached New York in the 1960s.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric (Stone; Jacobsen: Ghiordes).
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: Meshkin about 65; Ardabil up to 160.
structure.wefts_note: Stone: Meshkin double-wefted.
structure.pile_note: Jacobsen: usually good wool, though some with 'dead' (skin) wool.
structure.handle: Jacobsen: Ardebils thin like Kuba or Shirvan rugs; Meshkins heavier.

design.field: Copies of 19th-century Caucasian designs (Kuba, Shirvan, Kazak, Karabagh), red or ivory fields.
design.colors: Red or ivory fields with blue, ivory, green, canary.
design.sizes: From 2.5 x 4 ft to about 8.5 x 11 ft, a few 9 x 12 ft.

look_alikes.name: Kazak
look_alikes.how_to_tell: 19th-century Caucasian rugs have wool warps; these have cotton warps.

look_alikes.name: Ardabil (modern town rugs)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The persian_city topic covers town production of Ardabil; village rugs in Caucasian designs overlap with it.

look_alikes.name: Ardabil design
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Unrelated to the 16th-century Ardabil carpets.

rows.trade_use: 'Ardebil' for thin, cotton-warp rugs in Caucasian designs; 'Meshkin' for heavier ones.
rows.what_it_tells: A Caucasian-looking rug on a cotton foundation is likely a 20th-century northwest Persian copy such as Ardebil or Meshkin, not an old Caucasian rug.
rows.cautions: Sold in used-rug sales as 'collector's items' in the 1960s; they are post-1950 Persian rugs.

facts.text: Rugs of the Ardabil area employ Caucasian designs with symmetric knots on a cotton foundation.
The Ardebil rug in Caucasian designs is a new type that came on the market only after 1950.
Meshkin rugs have symmetric knots, are double-wefted on a cotton foundation at about 65 per square inch, and are similar to contemporary Ardabil rugs.
Meshkin rugs are heavy rugs in geometric designs copying Kazak, Karabagh and Kabistan rugs (Jacobsen 1969).
In 1972 the Ardabil carpet industry employed about 5,500 weavers, 60 percent of them men, with weaving shifting to villages.
Ardabil is a registered carpet geographical indication; Meshkin is proposed.
Meshkin Shahr, Ahar, the Moghan plain and the Aras banks are the present territory of the Shahsavan (renamed Ilsevan after the revolution).
Design frameworks, and even production methods, of Caucasian (Aran) rugs were carried across the Aras to Ardabil by Shahsavan nomads.
Ardabil hand-woven carpet is a registered geographical indication, nationally (Industrial Property Office no. 20 GI, 28 May 2014) and internationally (WIPO Lisbon register AO 948, 11 Oct 2014).
facts.quote: (AO 948) فرش دستبافت اردبيل / Ardabil Handmade Carpet, Ardebil Handmade Carpet

rows.name: Zanjan
rows.region: Zanjan and its villages (the old Khamseh district) between Tabriz and Tehran: Qoltuq, Bidgineh (Ijrud district), the Afshar villages, and Kurdish villages.
rows.made_by: Kurdish, Afshar and Shahsavan villagers.
rows.date_note: Mumford (1902) mentions a Zenjan dealer collecting Koultuk and Zenjan runners; Jacobsen describes coarse 'Zenjan' rugs until about 1958; Persian sources describe current production.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric (Stone; Mumford for Koultuk: Turkish; Persian article for Bidgineh: Turkish knot usual).
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: Khamseh-district small rugs 30-65; Qoltuq about 130. Bidgineh old pieces 20-40 raj, current 50-60 raj (about 7-14 and 18-22 knots per inch across).
structure.wefts_note: Stone: both single- and double-wefted rugs are woven around Zanjan; Qoltuq double-wefted; Khamseh-district small rugs single-wefted. Bidgineh: all double-wefted (Persian article). Mumford: Koultuk runners cotton warp, wool weft.
structure.ends: Mumford (Koultuk): one end plain selvage, the other selvage and loose ends.

design.field: Kurdish village designs; medallions with pendants and spandrels (Qoltuq); Bijar designs and colors in the fine double-wefted Afshar pieces (Persian article); coarse red-field medallion rugs.
design.sizes: One general size, about 6.5 x 3.5 ft, in the coarse grade.

look_alikes.name: Bidjar
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Fine double-wefted rugs of the Afshar villages near Zanjan follow Bijar designs and colors and sell well below Bijar prices (Persian article); Stone also notes Bijar imitations from Zanjan.

look_alikes.name: Mosul (trade name)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Coarse Zanjan scatter rugs were sold as 'Zenjan Mosuls'.

rows.trade_use: Coarse scatter rugs as 'Zenjan' or 'Zenjan Mosul'; finer pieces may be sold as Bijar.
rows.what_it_tells: A Bijar-looking rug that is lighter and cheaper may be Zanjan-area work.
rows.cautions: 'Khamseh' here is the old province around Zanjan, not the Khamseh confederacy of Fars.

facts.text: Zanjan is a source of Kurdish village rugs and of rugs woven in imitation of Bijars.
Both single-wefted and double-wefted rugs are woven around Zanjan, with the symmetric knot on a cotton foundation.
Bidgineh rugs are all double-wefted; old pieces were 20-40 raj, current ones 50-60 raj.
Qoltuq, southwest of Zanjan, is a Kurdish source of medallion rugs, double-wefted on cotton at about 130 knots per square inch.
Koultuk runners have a cotton warp, wool weft and the Turkish knot; a Zenjan dealer marketed them as Koultuk or Zenjan (Mumford).
Coarse Zenjan rugs of about 6.5 x 3.5 ft were marketed as 'Zenjan Mosuls' in Zenjan and Tabriz (Jacobsen).
Afshar groups have lived in Khamseh around Zanjan probably since Safavid times.
Qoltuq, Bidgineh and 'Khamseh Zanjan' are registered carpet geographical indications.

بیدگنه

rows.name: Shahsavan
rows.region: Northwest Iran: the Moghan plain, Ardabil, Meshkin, Sarab, Hashtrud, Mianeh, Khamseh (Zanjan), Bijar, Qazvin, Saveh and Varamin.
rows.made_by: Turkic-speaking Shahsavan tribes, nomadic and settled; women's domestic and dowry weaving.
rows.date_note: Museum bags date from about 1800 onward (Met 2015.490.24, about 1800-25); Iranica dates Shahsavan weaving to the 17th century. The trade recognized much 'Kurdish' or 'Caucasian' weaving as Shahsavan only in the 1970s.

structure.knot_note: Mostly flatweaves (soumak and tapestry); pile pieces rare (Stone). No source in hand states the pile knot.
structure.kpsi_note: No counts found.
structure.weft_color: Iranica: cotton used for wefts, occasionally warps
structure.wefts_note: Pile pieces from around Sarab usually have two wefts (Iranica).
structure.pile_note: Flatweave bags: soumak (weft wrapping) on wool warps, often with white cotton details (Met records).
structure.back: Iranica notes reverse soumak used as a ground weave particularly in Shahsevan flatweaves; Met records describe the backs of khorjin as weft-faced plain weave or slit tapestry.

design.field: Bold geometric medallions, hooked lozenges and stars on bags and bedding bags; designs close to Caucasian ones (Persian study).
design.sizes: Saddle bags about 20 in. square per half; bedding bags (mafrash) four-sided.

look_alikes.name: Soumak
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Some Shahsavan and Caucasian weavings are hard to tell apart, especially older ones from when the border was open (Persian study); Stone attributes soumak bags and mafrash to Kurdish weavers in the Caucasus and similar pieces to the Shahsavan in Iran.

look_alikes.name: Kurdish village and tribal rugs (Persian Kurdistan)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Much weaving sold as 'Kurdish' was later recognized as Shahsavan.

rows.trade_use: Used for soumak bags, mafrash panels and kilims from northwest Iran; pile rugs under the name are uncommon.
rows.what_it_tells: A soumak bag or bedding-bag panel from northwest Iran with bold geometric designs is the kind attributed to the Shahsavan.
rows.cautions: Attribution between Shahsavan, Kurdish and Caucasian work is often uncertain.

facts.text: The Shahsavan are a confederation of Turkish-speaking tribes of northwest Iran.
Shahsavan weavings are mainly flatweaves and flatwoven bags; pile carpets are rare.
The Shahsavan have made gelims, soumaks and knotted pile since the 17th century, with geometric designs.
Shahsevan weavers used cotton for wefts and occasionally for warps.
Reverse soumak appears as ground weave and decoration particularly in Shahsevan flatweaves.
Shahsevan mafrash (bedding bags) in Kurdistan are decorated only on the front sides; in Azerbaijan on all four sides.
In the 1970s the trade recognized that much 'Kurdish' or 'Caucasian' tribal weaving was Shahsevan.
Met Shahsevan saddle bags of about 1850-1880 are recorded as wool and cotton in soumak technique.
After the revolution the Shahsavan renamed themselves Ilsevan.
'Shahsavan' is proposed as a carpet geographical indication (East Azerbaijan).

After the 1979 revolution the Shahsevan were officially renamed Elsevan (Ilsevan), 'those who love the people (or tribe)'; the new name was not widely accepted, and by 1992 it was little used officially.
facts.quote: the Shahsevan were officially renamed Elsevan, 'those who love the people (or tribe),' but the new name was not widely accepted

says.text: After the revolution the Shahsavan renamed themselves Ilsevan.
They were 'officially renamed' by the new regime, which rejected anything to do with monarchy; the name was not widely accepted and was no longer widely used officially by 1992.

rows.name: Bidjar
rows.region: The town of Bijar and about forty villages around it in Kurdistan province (the old Garrus district); Bijar-type rugs are also woven by Afshar villages north of Bijar and near Zanjan.
rows.made_by: Kurdish townspeople and villagers (Bijar's population is predominantly Kurdish); Afshar villagers north of Bijar. Cottage industry without factories (Iranica, after Edwards).
rows.date_note: Old Bijars with wool warps reached the West in large numbers until about 1930; after World War II the foundation changed to cotton (Jacobsen; Persian article). Still woven.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric (Ghiordes) in every source.
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: horizontally 6-10, perpendicularly 8-12 = 48-120. Lewis: 48-120. Stone (later rugs): about 100-160. Persian article: 40-50 raj today (about 14.5-18 knots per inch across).
structure.weft_color: Old: wool, often dyed red (Hawley, Kendrick & Tattersall); later fine cotton
structure.wefts_note: Hawley and May: twice. Mumford: a heavy two-strand wool 'filling' laid straight across between the front and back wefts after every row, with a thin dyed weft. Stone: early rugs usually three wefts hammered down, one very heavy; later rugs two. Persian article: two wefts (one thick, one thin) plus a temporary rope-like weft ('ban pu') beaten down and then pulled out. Iranica: triple-wefted.
structure.pile_note: Medium length, heavy and lustrous (Hawley, Kendrick & Tattersall); camel hair partly in some (Hawley, May, Lewis).
structure.sides: Hawley: double overcasting in red or purple. Lewis: overcast.
structure.ends: Hawley: web, sometimes colored, or a narrow braided selvage; upper end web with loose fringe; web occasionally turned back and hemmed. Lewis and Mumford: one end's web often turned back and hemmed.
structure.handle: Very stiff and heavy; 'board-like' (Jacobsen); Persian name 'iron carpet'. Should be rolled, not folded (Lewis).
structure.back: Coarse grain; warps fully hidden because one of each pair lies under the other (Hawley, May); rows tightly packed.

design.field: Herati all over or with a small medallion and corners; open-field medallion and corners; Mina Khani; Shah Abbas; the 'Garrus' split-leaf arabesque; rose-cluster 'gol-farang' compartments; willow-and-cypress; samplers (vagireh).
design.border: Three stripes and often a plain outer edging.
design.colors: Red, blue, ivory, camel; a very dark double-dyed indigo; bright, strongly massed colors.
design.sizes: Old: about 7 x 4 ft most often, also carpets 8 x 12 to 11 x 18 ft and wide runners; Hawley 6-16 ft.

look_alikes.name: Kurdish village and tribal rugs (Persian Kurdistan)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: In Persian Kurdish rugs one warp of each pair is depressed at an acute angle; in Bijars it is doubled under at a right angle, so the rug is much stiffer.

look_alikes.name: Senneh
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Senneh rugs are thin, short-piled, single-wefted and soft-handled; Bijars are thick, stiff and double- or triple-wefted.

look_alikes.name: Zanjan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Afshar and Bidgineh villages near Zanjan weave fine double-wefted rugs in Bijar designs and colors, sold well below Bijar prices (Persian article; Stone).

look_alikes.name: Neyriz
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Bijars are much stouter than Niris and have one warp more completely doubled under; Niris end webs are much longer.

rows.trade_use: 'Bijar' covers the town and the surrounding villages; 'Kurdish Bijar' is used in the trade for village and tribal pieces of the area (the term itself was not found in the sources read).
rows.what_it_tells: A very stiff, heavy rug that will not fold easily, with symmetric knots and hidden warps, points to Bijar or a close imitation; a wool foundation suggests an older piece, cotton a later one.
rows.cautions: Bijar designs and the heavy build are copied nearby (Zanjan, Afshar villages) and in India; old books' names 'Sarakhs' and 'Lulé' refer to the same rugs.

facts.text: Bijar rugs use the symmetric (Ghiordes) knot.
One warp of each knot is doubled under the other, so the warps are fully offset and hidden at the back.
facts.quote: in Bijars one of the two threads of warp encircled by a knot is doubled under the other so as to be at right angles to that plane (Hawley 1922, p. 143)

facts.text: Old Bijars had wool warps; cotton has been used for the foundation since World War II.
Bijars are so stiff they should be rolled, not folded.
facts.quote: Many of them are so thick and heavy that they cannot be folded but must be rolled up. (Lewis 1920, p. 186)

facts.text: Kurdish rugs often have a heavy wool filling laid straight across between front and back wefts after every row, held by a thin dyed weft; Bijars show this method.
facts.quote: a coarse, heavy, two-strand wool yarn is passed straight across, between front and back weft-threads, after every row of knots, as filling. (Mumford 1902, p. 187)

facts.text: Bijar weavers today use two wefts per row (one thick, one thin) and pack each row with a temporary rope-like weft that is beaten down and pulled out.
Bijar carpets are known in Persian as the 'iron carpet'.
Hawley gives 6-10 knots per inch across and 8-12 down (about 48-120 per square inch); Stone gives 100-160 for later rugs; current Bijars are 40-50 raj.
Bijar is a town of Kurdistan surrounded by weaving villages; in 1976, 44 percent of the district's labor force worked in carpet weaving.
Bijar samplers (vagireh) are relatively common compared with other Persian areas.
Bijar kilims are slit-tapestry weaves; small ones resemble Senneh kilims.
Bijar is a registered carpet geographical indication (Kurdistan province).
A stylized willow-and-cypress (bid-majnun) design was woven in Bijar in the early 20th century and is thought to have its early base there.

says.text: Twice between rows.
Twice.
Early rugs usually three, one very heavy; later rugs two.
Bijar-area carpets are triple-wefted.
Two (thick and thin); a third, rope-like weft is used only to pack the row and is removed.

disagreements.about: who wove them / the name Sarakhs

says.text: Turkomans from Sarakhs are said to have settled near Bijar, hence the name 'Saraks' for Bijar rugs, though the rugs have no Turkoman features.
Sarakhs are the true 'Lulés', made by settlers from old Sarakhs around Bijar.
The population of the Bijar district is predominantly Kurdish.
40-50 raj (about 14.5-18 across per inch).

rows.name: Senneh
rows.region: The city of Sanandaj (Senneh), capital of Iranian Kurdistan (old Ardelan), and its villages.
rows.made_by: Kurdish weavers of Sanandaj and nearby villages; in the 19th century much of the finest work was made for the governors' households. In the 1970s most households around Sanandaj had small looms.
rows.date_note: Collectors prize pieces of about 1800-1900; current production is of lower quality.

structure.knot_note: Disputed. Hawley: 'Sehna, often Ghiordes'; Lewis and May: Senna (asymmetric) always; Stone and the Met record for 1971.200.9: symmetric. The 'Senna knot' trade name comes from the city, but Iranica warns that the knot names do not follow ethnicity or place.
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: horizontally 11-20, perpendicularly 12-24 = 132-480. Lewis: 100-960. May: often 400-500, antiques 700-800. Stone: up to 400. Jacobsen: old silk-warp 300-600, new cotton-warp 150-250.
structure.warp_color: white cotton (Kendrick & Tattersall); antique silk warps sometimes dyed in colored bands (Jacobsen, Stone)
structure.weft_color: white; occasionally wool, linen or silk (Hawley)
structure.wefts_note: A single fine weft crossing once between rows, so the white warps show at the back in a checkered (quincunx) pattern (Hawley, May, Stone). Kendrick & Tattersall: generally once, sometimes twice.
structure.pile_note: Clipped very short; knots not drawn tight, so the surface feels like a file (Hawley, Kendrick & Tattersall).
structure.sides: Hawley: a tightly wound double overcasting; Lewis: overcast with red cotton or silk.
structure.ends: Hawley: short web, with warp loops or short fringe. Lewis: narrow web at each end, often with one or two colored yarns through it. Jacobsen: silk warps in colored bands give a multicolored fringe.
structure.handle: Thin and firm; edges tend to curl (Lewis, Mumford, Kendrick & Tattersall).
structure.back: Fine grain but rough, file-like; warps level; single weft showing a checkered pattern (Hawley, May).

design.field: Small all-over Herati or boteh repeats; a field of plain color with a diamond or stepped medallion filled with Herati and matching corners; Gol-e Farang rose compartments (Gol-i-Mirza Ali); later 'Vekilli' designs.
design.border: Narrow borders, usually three stripes; main stripe red or yellow ground with rosettes or Herati.
design.colors: Dark blue, red, ivory with green, light blue and yellow, in small areas.
design.sizes: Usually small: 3-7 ft; old ones at most about 5 x 8 ft; also saddle bags and fine horse blankets.

look_alikes.name: Bidjar
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Bijars are heavy and stiff with long pile and two or three wefts; Sennehs are thin, short-piled and single-wefted.

look_alikes.name: Hamadan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Both have a single weft showing a checkered back, but the Hamadan weft is coarse and the knotting much coarser.

look_alikes.name: Farahan (Feraghan)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Sometimes confused through tone and pattern; Feraghans have two wefts and are coarser.

look_alikes.name: Senneh kilim
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Senneh kilims are flat-woven slit tapestry with no pile.

rows.trade_use: 'Senneh' is used for fine Kurdish rugs of Sanandaj; 'Senneh knot' became the trade name for the asymmetric knot. Jacobsen's 'Sena-Kurd' meant something else: finer Hamadan-district rugs.
rows.what_it_tells: A very thin, finely knotted rug with a file-like back, one fine cotton weft and short pile points to Senneh.
rows.cautions: Imitations were woven in Tabriz in Mumford's time; the knot named after Senneh is not necessarily the knot in a Senneh rug.

facts.text: Senneh rugs have a single weft between rows of knots, giving a checkered back.
Senneh rugs are among the most finely knotted Persian rugs; Hawley says 400 knots per square inch are not uncommon.
The pile is clipped very short and the knots are not drawn tight, so the surface feels like a file whichever way the hand is passed.
facts.quote: the yarn of the knots is not drawn tightly against the warp, so that in whatever direction the hand is rubbed the surface feels like a file. (Hawley 1922, p. 135)

facts.text: The warp is cotton; some antique pieces have silk warps, sometimes dyed in colored bands.
Senneh rugs are thin and tend to curl at the edges.
The Herati pattern, all-over botehs and diamond medallions are the usual designs.
The Met's late-19th-century carpet attributed to Senneh (1971.200.9) is recorded as cotton warp and weft with symmetrically knotted wool pile (record has no open image).
The Art Institute's Sehna prayer carpet of about 1894 (1948.163) is recorded with 'Persian' (Sehna) knots.
Senneh carpets were among those shown at the 1873 Vienna exhibition.
'Senneh' is a registered national and international carpet geographical indication (Kurdistan province).
Öztürk (2025) reports that the weavers of Senneh (Sanandaj, Kurdish 'Sine') generally tie the symmetric knot and use the asymmetric knot only rarely, for high-quality rugs.
Calling the asymmetric knot the 'Senneh knot' is a misnomer: the knot is not peculiar to Senneh, and Senneh's own fine rugs are described as symmetric-knotted.

says.text: Sehna, often Ghiordes.
Senna always.
Sehna.
Sehna.
Symmetric, up to 400 per square inch.
1971.200.9: symmetrically knotted.
1948.163: 'Persian' (Sehna) knots.
Each warp equally prominent at the back.
All warps level.
Warp on one level.
Single-wefted with offset warps.
Once.
Generally once, in some pieces twice.
Senneh weavers mostly use the symmetric knot, rarely the asymmetric.
The Sena of western Iran is an exception among western Persian rugs in using the Sena (asymmetric) knot (p. 159).

museum_examples.title: Oosters tapijt versierd met lotussen, palmetten, rozetbloemen en vogels
museum_examples.shows: one image (whole piece, front)
museum_examples.note: Production place: Senneh; date '1800' (single year as printed). Knotted wool runner; broken zigzag bands forming lozenges, very fine scattered lotus/palmette/bird field; description notes a section with lighter blue ground and pile worn to the knots in places.

rows.name: Senneh kilim
rows.region: Sanandaj and other places in Iranian Kurdistan (Stone: woven in other areas of Persian Kurdistan as well).
rows.made_by: Kurdish weavers of western Iran.
rows.date_note: Stone links the designs to Qajar patronage in the early 19th century; Jacobsen says none were imported in the 25 years before 1962.

structure.knot_note: Slit tapestry (kilim), no pile; eccentric (curving) wefts in fine pieces (Stone, Iranica).
structure.kpsi_note: No knots. Fineness is not given in knots; Stone calls them extremely finely woven.
structure.weft_color: Wool, with cotton or silk for highlights (Stone)
structure.wefts_note: Weft-faced tapestry; no knot rows.
structure.pile_note: No pile.
structure.handle: Thin, light and the same on both sides (Jacobsen).

design.field: Herati pattern, often filling a diamond medallion; all-over botehs; stripes of blossoms and vines; borders on all sides.
design.colors: Often light green and light red.
design.sizes: Typically about 4 x 5 ft.

rows.trade_use: Used for fine Kurdish slit-tapestry kilims with Persian floral designs.
rows.what_it_tells: A very fine, thin slit-tapestry kilim with Herati-filled medallions and borders on all sides is the Senneh type.
rows.cautions: Kilims in this style were woven across Persian Kurdistan, not only in Sanandaj.

facts.text: Senneh kilims are extremely fine single-piece slit tapestries with eccentric wefts, cotton warps in finer pieces, and borders on all sides.
Among Iranian gelims only Sanandaj gelims closely resemble Persian pile carpets in composition and design.
They were woven by Kurdish weavers in western Iran and look the same on both sides.
The Art Institute's Sehna rug 1948.165 is cotton and wool slit tapestry; the Met's 'Senneh' prayer rug 1970.302.8 is a cotton-warp, wool-weft tapestry weave.

rows.name: Kurdish village and tribal rugs (Persian Kurdistan)
rows.region: Western Iran: Kurdistan, Kermanshah and West Azerbaijan provinces, the Hamadan border country, and Kurdish settlements elsewhere (Khorasan, Kalardasht).
rows.made_by: Kurdish villagers and tribes (Sanjabi, Kolyai, Jaf, Herki, Shikak and others); generally settled, a few semi-nomadic.
rows.date_note: Old books describe 19th-century pieces; Kurdish runners were exported in large numbers in the early 20th century. Still woven.

structure.knot_note: Ghiordes (symmetric) in all sources.
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley (Persian Kurdistan): horizontally 7-10, perpendicularly 8-12 = 56-120. Lewis (Kurdistan proper): 36-80. Hawley's Western (Turkish) Kurdistan: 24-63.
structure.warp_color: brown or gray wool (Hawley: soft brown wool; Lewis: usually gray); later cotton (Stone)
structure.wefts_note: Hawley and May: usually twice, rarely once. Lewis: usually several weft threads between rows. Mumford: a heavy filling plus a thin weft.
structure.pile_note: Medium to long, heavy (Hawley, Lewis, Kendrick & Tattersall).
structure.sides: Heavy double overcasting in a dark color, often brown (Hawley, Lewis, Mumford).
structure.ends: Web crossed by a colored or parti-colored cord or a line of colored wool (Hawley, Lewis, Mumford); one end often turned back and hemmed (Lewis); warp ends looped and braided in many ways (Kendrick & Tattersall).
structure.handle: Very firm, stoutly woven; Kendrick & Tattersall say they can hardly be bent.

design.field: Mina Khani lattice on dark blue; Herati; all-over botehs; rows of flowering shrubs; lattices; medallions; Caucasian-like geometric designs.
design.colors: Dark blue grounds with shaded (abrash) changes; brown; reds, white, yellow.
design.sizes: Often runners and long narrow rugs; Hawley 6-12 ft.

look_alikes.name: Bidjar
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Bijar warps are doubled under at a right angle, giving a much stiffer rug; Kurdish warps are less depressed.

look_alikes.name: Mosul (trade name)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: In Mosuls every warp lies level; in Persian Kurdistans one warp of each pair is depressed.

look_alikes.name: Hamadan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Hamadans have cotton warps and a single coarse weft; Kurdish rugs wool warps and two wefts.

look_alikes.name: Karadagh
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kurdish rugs with Caucasian designs are sometimes wrongly called Karadagh.

look_alikes.name: East Anatolian Kurdish rugs
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kurdish rugs of Turkey are coarser (about 24-63 knots per square inch), browner, longer-piled, with both warps of each knot level.

rows.trade_use: 'Kurdistan' or 'Kurd' for Kurdish work not sold under a town name; Jacobsen says the working rule in his day was that a wool-warp rug not otherwise identified was called Kurdistan.
rows.what_it_tells: A heavy, wool-foundation rug with symmetric knots, shaded dark-blue grounds and Mina Khani or Herati patterns is typical of Persian Kurdish weaving.
rows.cautions: 'Kurdish' covers many tribes and structures; Stone says there are few overall characterizations. Many Shahsavan pieces were once sold as Kurdish.

facts.text: Kurdish village rugs of Iran are coarsely woven with the symmetric knot, usually on a wool foundation; later rugs may have cotton foundations.
The Mina Khani pattern on a dark blue ground is a characteristic Persian Kurdish design.
Kurdish weavers often shade the ground color from one end of the field to the other.
Hawley gives 7-10 knots per inch across and 8-12 down for Persian Kurdistans (about 56-120 per square inch); Lewis gives 36-80.
A colored line or cord across the end webs is a Kurdish mark.
facts.quote: Nearly always one or two lines of colored wool run through the selvage. This is a Kurdish characteristic and is a distinguishing feature. (Lewis 1920, p. 213)

facts.text: Kurdish rugs are stoutly woven and stiff.
facts.quote: The rugs are so stoutly woven that frequently they can hardly be bent. (Kendrick & Tattersall 1922, p. 178)

facts.text: The best-known Kurdish nomadic carpets are those of the Sanjabi and Kolyai.
Kermanshah traditional rugs belong to the Kurdish tribal and village group and often carry woven keepsake inscriptions with dates and names.
Kurdish saddle bags with all-over latch-hooked diamonds were imported in the thousands until about 1936 (Jacobsen).

says.text: Persian Kurdistan: one warp generally much depressed, sometimes level.
Generally all warps level, in some alternate depressed.
Warp on two levels only slightly separated.
Usually twice, rarely once.
Usually several weft threads between rows.
Twice; untypical pieces once.

rows.name: Koliai (Songhor)
rows.region: The Kolyai Kurdish tribal area around Sonqor (Songhor), Kermanshah province, about fifty miles west of Hamadan.
rows.made_by: Kolyai Kurds, nomadic and village.
rows.date_note: Stone distinguishes older wool-foundation rugs from newer cotton-foundation ones; no firm dates are given.

structure.knot_note: Not stated separately; Kurdish rugs of Iran use the symmetric knot (Stone).
structure.kpsi_note: No count found.
structure.wefts_note: Stone: newer rugs single-wefted on cotton; older rugs wool foundation.

design.field: Bright colors; the Takht-e Jamshid medallion (three narrow stacked hexagons) is common.
design.colors: Bright.

look_alikes.name: Hamadan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Newer Koliai rugs are single-wefted on cotton like Hamadan village rugs; the Takht-e Jamshid medallion and Kurdish colors point to Koliai.

rows.trade_use: Sold as Koliai, Songhor or simply as Kurdish/Hamadan.
rows.what_it_tells: A bright single-wefted Kurdish rug with a stacked-hexagon medallion points to the Kolyai of Songhor.
rows.cautions: Few sources; structure is single-sourced.

facts.text: The Kolyai are a Kurdish tribe of the Sonqor area and a major source of Kurdish rugs.
Newer Kolyai rugs have a cotton foundation and a single weft; older ones a wool foundation.
The Takht-e Jamshid design is common in Kolyai rugs.
'Songhor Kolyai' is a registered carpet geographical indication.

rows.name: Sauj Bulagh
rows.region: Mahabad (old Sauj Bulagh), the old Kurdish capital south of Lake Urmia, West Azerbaijan.
rows.made_by: Kurds of the Mahabad district.
rows.date_note: Jacobsen says none were imported under the name in the thirty years before 1962; old books describe 19th-century pieces.

structure.knot_note: Ghiordes (Hawley, Lewis, Mumford); symmetric (Stone).
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: horizontally 7-10, perpendicularly 8-12 = 56-120. Lewis: 48-88. Mumford: average 7-8 by 10-11 (about 70-88).
structure.wefts_note: Hawley: crosses twice.
structure.pile_note: Medium; yarns doubled, pile stands upright (Mumford, Lewis).
structure.sides: Hawley: a double selvage of two or three cords in blue, red or brown. Lewis: overcast like other Kurdish rugs.
structure.ends: Hawley: web with a parti-colored cord and warp fringe, often a braided selvage; upper web sometimes turned back and hemmed.
structure.handle: Very compact (Lewis, Mumford); Hawley: moderately loose.
structure.back: Slightly coarse grain; knots look uneven or serrated in alignment at the back (Hawley).

design.field: Herati; rows of flowering plants or potted flowers on blue; Gol-e Farang rose compartments; all-over Shah Abbas; Mina Khani (Hawley, Jacobsen, Persian study).
design.colors: Dark red and blue, ground shaded end to end; field more often blue.
design.sizes: Long narrow 'kellegi' carpets 6 x 12 to 8 x 18 ft; Hawley gives 6-7 ft.

look_alikes.name: Kurdish village and tribal rugs (Persian Kurdistan)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The closest and most difficult to tell apart.

look_alikes.name: Bidjar
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Bijars have warps doubled under and are much stiffer.

rows.trade_use: An old-book and collector name.
rows.what_it_tells: An older Kurdish long carpet with Persian floral designs and an uneven knot line at the back may be what old books call Souj Bulak.
rows.cautions: Stone's 'cotton foundation' versus the old books' wool warps may reflect a change over time.

facts.text: Sauj Bulagh (now Mahabad) is the old Kurdish capital south of Lake Urmia and a source of Kurdish rugs.
The knot is symmetric (Ghiordes) and the rugs are compactly woven of doubled yarns.
In a typical Suj-Bulak the knots look uneven or serrated in alignment at the back.
facts.quote: In a typical Suj-Bulak the alignment of knots at the back appears uneven or serrated. (Hawley 1922, p. 286)

facts.text: Hawley gives 7-10 knots per inch across and 8-12 down (about 56-120 per square inch); Lewis 48-88.
The rose-cluster 'Gol-e Farang' compartment design is found mainly in Suj Bulak, Bijar and Senneh rugs (Jacobsen).
Old examples of the Mina Khani design exist in Bijar and Savojbolagh rugs.

A Persian study of Savojbolagh rugs (Mokriyan region) counts them, with 'Mosul', among Kurdish rug types that are no longer made; it concludes that production stopped around the First World War, for reasons not known, and describes them as the best mid-priced Kurdish rugs of their day, dyed with natural dyes, now found mostly in European collections.

There are two Savojbolaghs in Persian: Savojbolagh-e Mokri, now Mahabad (the rug name), and Savojbolagh, a district west of Karaj near Tehran; today's Alborz-province Savojbolagh is among the places that weave Nain-type rugs.

says.text: Warp and weft wool.
Double wool yarn, sometimes half cotton.
Symmetric knot on a cotton foundation, red wefts.

rows.name: Quchan Kurdish rugs (Khorasan Kurds)
rows.region: Northern Khorasan: Quchan, Shirvan, Bojnurd, Esfarayen and Darreh Gaz.
rows.made_by: Kurds deported to Khorasan in the 17th century (Za'faranlu and others).
rows.date_note: No firm dates in the sources; still woven.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric (Stone; Persian field study).
structure.kpsi_note: No count found.
structure.wefts_note: Not stated.
structure.pile_note: Local wool, finer than that of western Kurdish rugs (Stone).

design.field: Traditional Kurdish polychrome geometric designs.
design.colors: Polychrome.

look_alikes.name: Baluch
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Rugs of the Quchan Kurds have been attributed to the Baluch; Baluch rugs use the asymmetric knot.

look_alikes.name: Kurdish village and tribal rugs (Persian Kurdistan)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same tradition; Khorasan Kurdish wool is finer and the market is Mashhad/Quchan.

rows.trade_use: Sold as Quchan, Kurdish or (wrongly) Baluch.
rows.what_it_tells: An all-wool, symmetric-knotted geometric rug from northeast Iran may be Khorasan Kurdish work.
rows.cautions: Few sources; often confused with Baluch work.

facts.text: The Quchan area is inhabited by Kurds descended from those deported from Kurdistan in the 17th century.
Quchan Kurdish rugs are all wool with the symmetric knot and traditional Kurdish designs.
Khorasan Kurds weave knotted Quchan carpets with polychrome geometric designs.
Khorasan Kurdish rugs were woven on horizontal looms; village weavers now use vertical looms.
North Khorasan Kurdish carpets are a registered geographical indication; 'Kordi Quchan' is proposed.
The 'Kordi' (Kurdish) hand-woven carpet of North Khorasan is a registered geographical indication (WIPO Lisbon register AO 1034, 28 Dec 2015; area: Bojnurd and Shirvan).
facts.quote: (AO 1034) فرش دستبافت کردی خراسان / Kordi Handmade Carpet of north Khorasan

rows.name: Mosul (trade name)
rows.region: Not made in Mosul: a trade name for coarse Kurdish and northwest Persian scatter rugs, first collected at Mosul (Iraq), later marketed through Hamadan; Jacobsen says most were from the Zanjan district.
rows.made_by: Kurdish and other village and tribal weavers of western Iran and the Iraq-Turkey border country.
rows.kind: trade name (a name for a look, made in several places)
rows.date_note: Used in Western books from about 1900 to the 1960s; Jacobsen says few were still imported in 1962.

structure.knot_note: Ghiordes (Hawley, Lewis, May).
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: horizontally 5-7, perpendicularly 7-9 = 35-63. Lewis: 36-80.
structure.warp_color: Lewis: coarse dark wool or goat hair, occasionally cotton
structure.weft_color: Hawley: red or orange; May: frequently blue
structure.wefts_note: Hawley and May: usually twice, sometimes once; Hawley: or two or three threads side by side.
structure.pile_note: Long, floppy, lustrous (Hawley); medium (Hawley TC).
structure.sides: Hawley: heavy double overcasting; a few two-cord selvages.
structure.ends: Hawley: lower end web; upper end web and fringe, sometimes braided or turned and hemmed.
structure.handle: Softer and more flexible than other Kurdistans (Kendrick & Tattersall); moderately firm (Hawley).
structure.back: Coarse grain; warps level; thick colored weft standing as high as the knots (Hawley).

design.field: No typical pattern: Caucasian stars and latch hooks, Kurdish all-over patterns, Bijar-like medallions, angular pears; often a camel-hair outer band.
design.border: Three stripes, often a plain outer edging.
design.colors: Yellows, browns and brownish reds.
design.sizes: About 6.5 x 3.5 ft; Hawley 6-10 ft.

look_alikes.name: Kurdish village and tribal rugs (Persian Kurdistan)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Mosul warps lie level; Persian Kurdistan warps are depressed. Kendrick & Tattersall: Mosuls are softer.

look_alikes.name: Hamadan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Jacobsen calls new Mosuls the poorest of the Hamadan-market rugs; Hamadans have cotton warps and a single weft.

rows.trade_use: A dealers' name; Jacobsen (quoting H. G. Dwight) says the only link with Mosul is that small Kurdish rugs were once collected there.
rows.what_it_tells: An old label or invoice reading 'Mosul' points to a coarse Kurdish or northwest Persian scatter rug, not to Iraq.
rows.cautions: Lewis files Mosul under Turkish rugs; other authors under Persian. The name says nothing reliable about origin.

facts.text: Mosul is a trade name; the rugs were not made in Mosul.
Mosul rugs have the Ghiordes knot with all warps level at the back.
facts.quote: it will usually be found that the warp lies on one level, and that the rugs are softer and more flexible than other Kurdistans. (Kendrick & Tattersall 1922, p. 179)

facts.text: Hawley gives 5-7 knots per inch across and 7-9 down (about 35-63 per square inch); Lewis 36-80.
Camel hair is often used, sometimes as a plain outer band.
By the early 20th century the Mosul trade had moved to Hamadan, and most 'Mosuls' were made north of Hamadan in the Zanjan district (Jacobsen).
Rijksmuseum Jaf Kurdish bags are described as 'Jaffi Kurdistan, formerly Mosul', showing the old trade use.
A Persian study lists 'Mosul' (موصل) with Savojbolagh as Kurdish rug types no longer produced and places it 'in Iraqi Kurdistan'.
Stone calls Mosul an obsolete trade name for Persian Kurdish rugs, and also a rug size of about 6½ x 3¼ ft, close to the size already in this row.
In Iraq itself, Stone names Erbil (not Mosul) as the market town for Kurdish rugs woven nearby by the Dizai, Girdi and Mantik tribes.
In Europe, rugs woven in the Hamadan district were long sold as 'Mosul' rugs, though no one knows how the name attached to them; today the name is used for a rug size.
facts.quote: قالیچه‌های بافت همدان در اروپا به نام قالیچة موصل (شهری در شمال عراق) معروف بودند. معلوم نیست چگونه این نام بر آن‌ها اطلاق شده است؛ اما امروزه با توجه به اندازة آن‌ها شناخته می‌شوند (after Edwards)

says.text: Frequently dyed red or orange.
Frequently dyed blue.
Turkish classification; made by Kurds around Lake Van.
Persian chapter; made by many peoples between Lake Van and western Persia.
Iranian; marketed in Hamadan, made mostly in the Zanjan district.
A Kurdish type of Iraqi Kurdistan, no longer made.
Iranian; marketed in Hamadan, made mostly in the Zanjan district.

museum_examples.shows: one image (bag face)

rows.name: Hamadan
rows.region: The city of Hamadan (ancient Ecbatana) and hundreds of villages within about 75 miles; the city is the market and the name covers the district's village rugs.
rows.made_by: Villagers of many backgrounds: Kurdish villages, Turkic-speaking villages such as Dargazin (Persian study), the Qaragözlü (Karagöz) tribe for the old camel-hair pieces, and Persian villages.
rows.kind: trade name (a name for a look, made in several places)
rows.date_note: Old camel-hair Hamadans were woven up to about 1900; Hamadan-market village rugs, runners and mats were imported in great numbers through the 20th century. Still woven.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric (Ghiordes) in all sources. Jacobsen: in rugs of the 1950s perhaps a quarter of the knots were jufti (tied over four warps).
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: horizontally 6-9, perpendicularly 8-12 = 48-108. Lewis: 49-100. Persian source (after Zhuleh): 15-25 raj (about 5.5-9 knots per inch across).
structure.weft_color: Hawley: generally cotton, frequently wool, coarse; Kendrick & Tattersall and Lewis: cotton, wool or camel hair; Jacobsen (1969): blue wefts in small 1950s Hamadans
structure.wefts_note: One thick weft between rows, so the white warps show at the back in a checkered (quincunx) pattern (Hawley, May, Kendrick & Tattersall, Stone, Persian source, Iranica). Exceptions: Hamadan-city 'Kasvin' rugs are double-wefted (Stone); Hawley's 'Irans' usually two wefts.
structure.pile_note: Old pieces largely camel hair (Hawley, May, Lewis, Kendrick & Tattersall); later mostly wool clipped short (Hawley).
structure.sides: Overcast, generally brown or red (Hawley).
structure.ends: Hawley: lower end a narrow web and warp loops; upper end a narrow web turned back and hemmed. Lewis: fringe at one end, hemmed web at the other.
structure.handle: Very firm (Hawley); medium thick to heavy (Jacobsen).
structure.back: Moderately coarse; the single thick weft and level white warps give a checkered back (Hawley).

design.field: Old type: a diamond or pole medallion with corners on a plain or faintly patterned camel or ivory field, inside a wide plain camel-hair outer band; the 'mirror' diaper. Later: Herati all over or with a small medallion, boteh, Sarouk-like sprays, by village (Jacobsen; Persian study).
design.border: Wide; three or four stripes plus a broad outer edging of camel hair as wide as half to two thirds of the border.
design.colors: Camel and ivory with red and blue (old); red fields with ivory or blue borders (1950s); blue fields common before 1948.
design.sizes: Mats 2 x 3 ft, scatter rugs, runners to 30 ft, some carpets; Hawley 3-24 ft.

look_alikes.name: Senneh
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Both are single-wefted with a checkered back, but Senneh's weft is fine and the knotting much finer; Hamadan's weft is coarse.

look_alikes.name: Karaje (old-book name)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Karaje (old-book Kurdish runners) are single-wefted like Hamadans but have wool warps and wool wefts.

look_alikes.name: Sarab
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Sarab camel-ground pieces look alike but usually have two wefts.

look_alikes.name: Mosul (trade name)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Mosuls have wool warps and usually two wefts.

look_alikes.name: Malayer
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Malayer rugs are single-wefted too but more densely knotted.

look_alikes.name: Karaja
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Karaja (Azerbaijan) is also single-wefted on cotton; its row of hooked hexagon medallions differs.

rows.trade_use: 'Hamadan' is a market name for rugs of hundreds of villages; better ones are sold under village names (Bibikabad, Ingeles, Borchalu, Hosseinabad, Dergazin, Kabutarahang). Jacobsen grouped the finer ones as 'Sena-Kurd'.
rows.what_it_tells: A single-wefted rug with symmetric knots on a cotton warp, showing a checkered back, points to the Hamadan district; the village name, if known, narrows it.
rows.cautions: Hamadan city's own 'Kasvin' rugs are double-wefted. Jacobsen warns that 1950s rugs used many jufti knots and some poor dyes, and that most pre-war Hamadans were chemically washed and painted. Indian and other copies exist.

facts.text: Hamadan rugs are single-wefted: one coarse weft between rows.
facts.quote: This lavish use of camel's hair, the broad encircling edging, the cotton warp, and a single thread of coarse weft passing once between two rows of knots, distinguish them from all other rugs. (Hawley 1922, p. 124)

facts.text: The warp is cotton and lies level.
The knot is symmetric (Ghiordes).
Hawley gives 6-9 knots per inch across and 8-12 down (about 48-108 per square inch); Lewis 49-100; a Persian source 15-25 raj.
Older Hamadans have much natural camel hair in the pile and a wide plain camel-hair outer band.
Most so-called Hamadan carpets with undyed camel hair were woven up to about 1900 by the Qaragözlü tribe, with cotton warps and wefts and one weft per row.
The Met's 19th-century Hamadan carpet fragment (23.211.8) is recorded as cotton warp and weft with symmetrically knotted camel-hair pile (record has no open image).
Hamadan village rugs are sold under the village's name (Injilas, Bibikabad, Dargazin, Kabudarahang, Borchalu), each with its own designs.
Hamadan villages weave on fixed upright looms with a single weft and level warps.
Many Hamadan-area villages are Kurdish.
Two thirds of the scatter rugs and ninety percent of the runners imported from Iran around 1960 came from the Hamadan district (Jacobsen).
Hamadan is a registered carpet geographical indication.
A Persian field survey gives Hamadan village rugs about 20-30 raj (knots per 7 cm across) and Hamadan town rugs 30-40.
facts.quote: رج‌شمار قالی همدان اغلب حدود ۲۰-۳۰ رج است؛ اما قالی شهری آن در رج‌شمار ۳۰-۴۰ تولید می‌شود

facts.text: Hamadan city was a market for Sarouk, Jowzan, Mehraban and Enjelas rugs.
facts.quote: شهر همدان بازار مناسبی برای عرضه و فروش فرش‌های ساروق، جوزان، مهربان و انجلاس بود (after Sur-Esrafil 1375)

facts.text: Double-wefted rugs with depressed warps are now also woven in Hamadan province alongside the traditional single-wefted kind; a 2010s field survey counted 190 double-wefted and 114 single-wefted rugs.
facts.quote: در قالی‌هایی که امروزه بافته می‌شوند، استفاده از دوپود با گرایش لول‌باف نیز دیده می‌شود

says.text: Real camel-hair antiques are very rare now and command vast prices; the moderns use camel hair and filik.
Moderately old Hamadans contain more camel hair than any other class.
Not more than one in twenty-five early Hamadans was camel tan; later writers copied Mumford.
Kasvin, the American trade name for rugs woven in Hamadan city, is double-wefted, unlike the single-wefted village rugs.
Kasvins are woven in Hamadan city and are like a modern Sarouk in weave and thickness.
15-25 raj (after Zhuleh), as already in the table.
Village rugs about 20-30 raj; town rugs 30-40.
6-9 knots per inch across (about 16-25 per 7 cm).
