rows.name: Hosseinabad
rows.region: A village near Hamadan (Jacobsen: about 30 miles southwest of the city; some made in the city).
rows.made_by: Hamadan-district villagers.
rows.date_note: Jacobsen knew only new rugs under this name (no semi-old or antique ones by 1962).

structure.knot_note: Symmetric, as Hamadan-area rugs (Stone, Hawley).
structure.kpsi_note: No count found.
structure.wefts_note: Single weft per row on a cotton foundation, as Hamadan-area village rugs generally (Stone; Persian article; Hawley for Hamadans); not stated specifically for this village by a second source.
structure.pile_note: Thick (Jacobsen).
structure.handle: Thick, medium to good tight weave (Jacobsen).

design.field: All-over small Herati on a rose to red field, often with a small blue or ivory center and corners.
design.border: Usually ivory with a conventional vine and pear design.
design.colors: Red field; ivory, light blue, pink, green, touches of navy, tan, canary.
design.sizes: Mostly about 7.5 x 4.5 ft; also smaller rugs, runners and some carpets.

look_alikes.name: Ingeles
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Both use Herati on red; Ingeles are rated the finer and also use small botehs.

look_alikes.name: Farahan (Feraghan)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Herati field like Feraghans; Feraghans are asymmetric-knotted and double-wefted.

rows.trade_use: A Hamadan village name used by importers; Jacobsen calls Husainabads the most typical new Hamadans.
rows.what_it_tells: A red Herati-field Hamadan scatter rug with an ivory border is typical of what was sold as Hosseinabad.
rows.cautions: 'Hosseinabad' is a common Iranian place name; the trade usage refers to the village near Hamadan.

facts.text: Hosseinabad is a village of the Hamadan area that weaves rugs with the Herati pattern.
Husainabads are typically red-field rugs with the small all-over Herati and ivory borders (Jacobsen).
Jacobsen knew no semi-old or antique rugs by this name before 1962.

rows.name: Ingeles
rows.region: A village about ten miles southeast of Hamadan (Stone; Jacobsen: a short distance south); the c. 1950 gazetteer puts it in the Simineh-rud district of Malayer county.
rows.made_by: Hamadan-district villagers.
rows.date_note: Jacobsen says the name was little known before about 1925; still woven.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric (Stone).
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: 130-160 per square inch.
structure.wefts_note: Single-wefted on cotton (Stone).
structure.pile_note: Heavy pile of good wool (Jacobsen).

design.field: Herati all over (in 6.5 x 4.5 ft rugs) or small botehs (smaller sizes and runners), sometimes with a small blue or ivory center and corners (Jacobsen, Stone, Persian study).
design.border: Turtle design in the main border.
design.colors: Deep blue-red field; blue or ivory border.
design.sizes: Scatter sizes and runners; very few carpets.

look_alikes.name: Hosseinabad
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Also Herati on red; Ingeles are finer and tighter.

look_alikes.name: Senneh
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Jacobsen and his teachers once grouped Ingeles among 'Sena-Kurds'; real Senneh rugs are much finer and thinner.

rows.trade_use: Sold under its own name since the 1920s-30s; earlier as Hamadan or 'Sena-Kurd'.
rows.what_it_tells: A fine, heavy Hamadan-district rug with Herati or small botehs on a deep red field may be Ingeles.
rows.cautions: Spellings vary widely (Injilas, Enjilas, Engeles).

facts.text: Ingeles (Injilas) is a village near Hamadan weaving single-wefted rugs with the symmetric knot on cotton, 130-160 knots per square inch.
Ingeles rugs use the Herati or small boteh designs.
Jacobsen rated Ingeles the best of the Hamadan-district village types, tightly woven with a heavy pile.
The c. 1950 gazetteer places Injilas in the Simineh-rud district of Malayer county.

says.text: About ten miles southeast of Hamadan.
A short distance south of Hamadan.
Simineh-rud district, Malayer county (c. 1950).

rows.name: Borchalu
rows.region: The Borchalu (Bozchelu) district near Hamadan, named after a Turkic tribe of the Hamadan region; a branch was deported by Shah Abbas to the Caucasus (Borjalou).
rows.made_by: Borchalu tribespeople and villagers.
rows.date_note: Sold as Hamadan or 'Sena-Kurd' until the name became known in the trade.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric (Stone).
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: about 65 per square inch.
structure.wefts_note: Single-wefted (Stone).
structure.pile_note: Heavy pile of excellent wool (Jacobsen).

design.field: Curvilinear floral medallion and corners, often on an ivory field; Persian study also lists Herati.
design.colors: Ivory, blue or rose fields; more green and canary than other Hamadans.
design.sizes: Mostly 6.5 x 4.5 ft and smaller; short runners; no carpets.

look_alikes.name: Hamadan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The only scatter rugs of the Hamadan area in a curvilinear floral design.

look_alikes.name: Borchalo Kazak
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Caucasian Borjalou Kazaks carry the same tribal name but are wool-foundation Caucasian rugs.

rows.trade_use: Sold under its own name from the mid-20th century.
rows.what_it_tells: A single-wefted Hamadan-area rug with a curvilinear floral medallion on ivory points to Borchalu.
rows.cautions: Not the same as the Caucasian Borjalou Kazak.

facts.text: Borchalu rugs have curvilinear floral medallions and are single-wefted with symmetric knots on cotton.
Iranians often spell the name Bozchelu.
Borjalou in the Caucasus was settled by Borchalu tribespeople deported from the Hamadan district in the 17th century (Stone).

Dehkhoda (from the Farhang-e joghrafiya'i-ye Iran) describes Bozchalu (بزچلو) as one of the three rural districts of Vafs, between Vafs, Shara and Farahan, with 45 villages and about 21,000 Turkish-speaking people; its center is Komijan and its main villages include Samqavar, Khosrowbeyg, Famarin and Esfandan; the women's craft is weaving rugs from cartoons.
facts.quote: صنایع دستی زنان قراء دهستان بزچلو قالیچه بافی با نقشه است ('the handicraft of the women of the Bozchalu villages is weaving rugs from cartoons')

facts.text: The district was once called Kohestan-e Dargazin and took the name of the Bozchalu tribe, which was moved there from Azerbaijan at the start of Safavid rule.

says.text: Entry: about 40 miles east of Hamadan; his own district table: 'a large area south of the city'.
A tribe of the Hamadan region (no direction given).
A rural district of Vafs with its center at Komijan, between Vafs, Shara and Farahan (now Markazi province, between Hamadan and Arak).
About 40 miles east of Hamadan (entry); 'a large area south of the city' (district table).
The Bozchalu tribe was moved into this district from Azerbaijan early in the Safavid period.
A branch of the Borchalu of the Hamadan region was deported to the Caucasus in the 17th century (Borjalou).

rows.name: Kabutarahang
rows.region: A town north-northwest of Hamadan and nearby villages (Jacobsen names Kahanabad, Famenin and Amirabad).
rows.made_by: Hamadan-district town and village weavers.
rows.date_note: The best-selling inexpensive Persian carpet in America in the later 1950s.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric (Stone); Jacobsen: many jufti knots by the late 1950s.
structure.kpsi_note: No count found; coarse (Stone).
structure.wefts_note: Single-wefted on cotton (Stone).
structure.pile_note: Long pile (Jacobsen).
structure.handle: Thick, heavy, coarse to average weave (Jacobsen).

design.field: A medallion with scattered floral sprays on a red field, or a diaper on a camel or ivory field; also Sarouk-like all-over florals.
design.colors: Bright red or ivory fields with green, blue, rose.
design.sizes: Carpet sizes only, 6 x 9 to 12 x 20 ft.

look_alikes.name: Gorevan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kabutarahang carpets replaced the cheap Gorevan as the best-selling inexpensive room-size carpet.

look_alikes.name: Hamadan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Also sold as Hamadan; the room-size format is unusual for the area.

rows.trade_use: Sold as Kabutarahang or as Hamadan.
rows.what_it_tells: A single-wefted Hamadan-area room-size carpet is likely Kabutarahang or Bibikabad.
rows.cautions: Jacobsen reports falling quality (jufti knots, skin wool) in the late 1950s.

facts.text: Kabutarahang, north of Hamadan, produces large single-wefted rugs on cotton with the symmetric knot.
Only carpet sizes are woven there (Jacobsen).
Designs: a red ground with a medallion and floral sprays, or a diaper on a camel-colored ground.
Dehkhoda (after Anandraj) calls Kabudarahang (کبودرآهنگ) one of the villages of Hamadan, home of the Haji-lu branch of the Qaraguzlu tribe.

rows.name: Nahavand
rows.region: Nahavand, south of Hamadan, and the villages between Nahavand and Oshvand.
rows.made_by: Village weavers related to Kurdish work.
rows.date_note: Iranica notes consistent quality over a long period; no start date given.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric (Stone).
structure.kpsi_note: No count found.
structure.wefts_note: Single-wefted (Stone; Iranica).

design.field: Large rugs with geometricized Sarouk designs; border sometimes penetrating the field; blue dominant.
design.colors: Blue grounds.
design.sizes: About 40 sq ft.

look_alikes.name: Sarouk
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Nahavand uses geometricized Sarouk designs but is single-wefted with symmetric knots.

rows.trade_use: A Hamadan-area village name.
rows.what_it_tells: A large, blue-ground, single-wefted rug with angular Sarouk-like drawing points to Nahavand.
rows.cautions: Few sources.

facts.text: Nahavand rugs are single-wefted, blue-dominant rugs of the Hamadan region.
Nahavand rugs use the symmetric knot on cotton and geometricized Sarouk designs (Stone).
Villages between Nahavand and Oshvand wove large blue-ground single-wefted rugs of about 40 sq ft related to Kurdish work (Iranica, Ford).
Nahavand is proposed as a carpet geographical indication (Hamadan province).
Nahavand rugs are mostly woven with one thick weft, though double wefts have spread recently; the knot may be symmetric or asymmetric, and zar-o-nim (about 1 x 1.5 m) and six-meter sizes are usual.
facts.quote: در شهرستان نهاوند، قالیچه‌ها اغلب با یک‌پود ضخیم بافته می‌شوند و امروزه دوپودبافی نیز رواج یافته است. در بافت آن‌ها از گره ترکی یا فارسی استفاده می‌شود

says.text: Symmetric knot on cotton.
Turkish (symmetric) or Persian (asymmetric) knot.

rows.name: Tuyserkan
rows.region: A town of Hamadan province south of Hamadan.
rows.made_by: Hamadan-district villagers.
rows.date_note: No dates in the sources.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric (Stone).
structure.kpsi_note: No count found.
structure.wefts_note: Single-wefted, a few double-wefted (Stone).

design.field: Geometric medallions with pendants and serrated medallion and corners on a dark blue field with geometricized florals.
design.colors: Dark blue field.

look_alikes.name: Hamadan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A double-wefted Tuyserkan can be mistaken for a non-Hamadan rug; Stone notes a few are double-wefted.

rows.trade_use: A Hamadan-area village name.
rows.what_it_tells: One of the few Hamadan-area names for which some double-wefted pieces are reported.
rows.cautions: Single source.

facts.text: Tuyserkan rugs have geometric medallions on a dark blue field and are single-wefted with a few double-wefted, symmetric knot on cotton.

Tuyserkan, on the southwest slopes of Mount Alvand, was one of the old 'Velayat-e Salas' (Malayer, Nahavand, Tuyserkan); carpets and rugs are among its crafts, made in three rural districts (Kerzan-rud, Khorram-rud and Qolqol-rud).
Tuyserkan rugs are single-wefted and coarse, mostly tied with the symmetric (Turkish) knot on a cotton foundation.
facts.quote: تویسرکان ... در بافت قالی آن اغلب از گره ترکی استفاده می‌شود. این قالی‌های تک‌پود و درشت‌باف، طرح‌های ساده‌ای دارند و حداکثر در ابعاد شش‌متری تولید می‌شوند

facts.text: Tuyserkan rugs have simple designs and are woven no larger than about six square meters.

rows.name: Mazlaghan
rows.region: An Azeri-speaking village about 58 km from Saveh on the old Saveh-Hamadan road (Persian study); similar rugs in Noberan and Kerdar. Sold as Hamadan-area rugs.
rows.made_by: Azeri Turkish-speaking villagers, weaving from memory (Persian study).
rows.date_note: Persian study: woven since old times; cotton wefts in the last hundred years.

structure.knot_note: Both knots used (Stone; Persian study).
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: typical 100 per square inch.
structure.wefts_note: Weft: wool formerly, cotton in the last century (Persian study, after Eschenbrenner). Weft count not stated.

design.field: A hexagonal medallion with spiked or stepped (lightning-like) outline and matching spandrels; open areas with geometricized blossoms.

look_alikes.name: Hamadan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The jagged 'lightning' medallion outline marks Mazlaghan, Noberan and Kerdar.

rows.trade_use: Sold as Mazlaghan or Hamadan.
rows.what_it_tells: A Hamadan-type rug with a jagged, spiked medallion outline points to Mazlaghan and nearby villages.
rows.cautions: The Persian study's structure facts are cited to a Western author (Eschenbrenner), so they are not independent of Western literature.

facts.text: Mazlaghan rugs have a spiked or stepped hexagon medallion with spandrels; similar rugs come from Noberan and Kerdar.
Mazlaghan rugs are woven with both symmetric and asymmetric knots.
Mazlaghan is an Azeri-speaking village near Saveh whose rugs are woven from memory.

says.text: Counted as a Hamadan-area rug; the village is near Saveh.
Listed under Markazi province (proposed).

rows.name: Dergezine
rows.region: A district and village about fifty miles north of Hamadan with some fifty weaving villages.
rows.made_by: Turkic-speaking villagers (Persian study).
rows.date_note: Iranica records silk carpets from Dargazin among Safavid gifts of 1567; the runners readers own are 20th-century.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric, as Hamadan-area rugs.
structure.kpsi_note: No count found.
structure.wefts_note: Single weft per row on a cotton foundation, as Hamadan-area village rugs generally (Stone; Persian article; Hawley for Hamadans); not stated specifically for this village by a second source.
structure.pile_note: Medium-heavy nap of good wool (Jacobsen).

design.field: Red or ivory fields with Sarouk-like floral sprays; Persian study lists saruqi, gol-boteh, dastgahi, tree, vase and medallion designs.
design.colors: Red or ivory fields with blue, green and ivory.
design.sizes: Mostly runners, including the longest stair runners (12-25 ft), and small mats.

look_alikes.name: Sarouk
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Dergezin runners copy Sarouk floral sprays but are single-wefted with symmetric knots (Jacobsen; Hamadan structure).

rows.trade_use: Sold as Dergezin or Hamadan.
rows.what_it_tells: A long Hamadan-area runner with Sarouk-like sprays is typical of Dergezine.
rows.cautions: Iranica's 'Dargazin in Khorasan' (CARPETS ix) refers to a different place (Darreh Gaz).

facts.text: Dargazin is the most productive rug district of Hamadan by volume and weaves many runners.
Dergezin rugs follow Sarouk-like floral designs on red or ivory fields.
Wool is still bought from the Shahsevan at Dargazin and blended with local wool.
Pictorial Hamadan rugs were mostly woven in Turkic-speaking villages such as Dargazin (Persian study after Tanavoli).
A Persian study cites historical documents that Shah Tahmasp gave a carpet woven at Dargazin to the Ottoman sultan Suleiman.
facts.quote: در مستندات تاریخی آمده است كه شاه طهماسب صفوی یك تخته قالی بافت درگزین را به پادشاه عثمانی، سلیمان، هدیه کرد

says.text: 'Dargazīn in Khorasan'.
'Dargazīn (or Darra-ye Gazīn), near Hamadān'.

rows.name: Bibikabad
rows.region: Bibikabad and Ainabad, about thirty miles northeast of Hamadan.
rows.made_by: Hamadan-district village weavers; Jacobsen distinguishes home ('bazaar') and supervised 'contract' qualities.
rows.date_note: Hawley (1913) mentions Bibikabad; Jacobsen describes large numbers in the 1950s.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric (Stone).
structure.kpsi_note: No count found.
structure.wefts_note: Single-wefted (Stone).
structure.pile_note: Very heavy nap (Jacobsen).

design.field: Small Herati field with a small central pendant and large corners; boteh.
design.border: Nine to eleven borders in large sizes.
design.colors: Red or light wine field with ivory and light blue.
design.sizes: Mostly carpet sizes, 6 x 9 ft and larger.

look_alikes.name: Kabutarahang
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Both are single-wefted Hamadan room-size carpets; Bibikabad typically has the Herati field with a small medallion.

rows.trade_use: Sold as Bibikabad (Ainabad rugs too); grouped by Jacobsen as 'Sena-Kurd'.
rows.what_it_tells: A single-wefted Hamadan room-size carpet with a Herati field and many borders points to Bibikabad.
rows.cautions: Hawley notes the town in passing; most detail is Jacobsen's.

facts.text: Bibikabad rugs often have boteh or Herati designs and are single-wefted with the symmetric knot.
Bibikabad and Ainabad weave the same type, sold as Bibikabad, mostly in carpet sizes (Jacobsen).
Bibikabad lies on the outskirts of the Kara-Geuz district northeast of Hamadan (Hawley).

rows.name: Mehriban (Hamadan district)
rows.region: A district beginning just north of Hamadan and extending about 40 miles northwest, with some 40 villages.
rows.made_by: Hamadan-district villagers.
rows.date_note: No dates in the sources.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric (Stone).
structure.kpsi_note: No count found.
structure.wefts_note: Single-wefted (Stone).

design.field: Often a medallion on a camel-colored field; many old village designs; Persian study lists dastgahi, afshan, goldani, Herati, medallion and tree designs.
design.colors: Indigo, madder red.
design.sizes: Mats to scatter sizes and runners.

look_alikes.name: Mehriban (Heriz district)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same name, different place: the Heriz-district Mehraban weaves Heriz carpets.

rows.trade_use: A Hamadan village-district name.
rows.what_it_tells: A single-wefted Hamadan-area rug, often camel-ground, sold as Mehriban.
rows.cautions: Check which Mehraban a label means.

facts.text: The Mehraban district north of Hamadan weaves single-wefted rugs with symmetric knots on cotton, often a medallion on a camel-colored field.
Jacobsen (1962) says Mehreban weavers kept vegetable dyes and had not taken up jufti knots.
A second Mehraban (Hamadan province) is proposed as a carpet geographical indication.

rows.name: Malayer
rows.region: The town and district of Malayer, south of Hamadan, halfway to Arak (about 100 weaving villages, Jacobsen).
rows.made_by: Village weavers; most Malayer rugs are village work (Persian study).
rows.date_note: Malayer was a major weaving area in the 1970s; collectors' Malayers are mostly late 19th to mid-20th century (Minneapolis dates one 'early 18th century', which is doubtful).

structure.knot_note: Symmetric (Stone).
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: about 25-130 per square inch.
structure.wefts_note: Stone: Malayer rugs single-wefted; Josan (Malayer district) double-wefted. Jacobsen: northern Malayer like Hamadans, southern like Sarouks.

design.field: Geometric medallions, Herati, Sarouk-like designs; local names mahi-herati, chahar-chang and 'pich-e Jowzan' (Stone, Persian study).
design.colors: Lac red (laki), white and navy grounds (Persian study).

look_alikes.name: Hamadan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Malayer rugs are single-wefted like Hamadans but more densely knotted.

look_alikes.name: Josan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Josan, in the Malayer district, is double-wefted and finer.

look_alikes.name: Sarouk
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Southern Malayer weaves Sarouk-like rugs ('Malayer Sarouk'), usually not as fine or heavy as Sarouks.

rows.trade_use: 'Malayer' or 'Malayer Sarouk'.
rows.what_it_tells: A Hamadan-structure rug that is finer than usual, often in Sarouk-like or Herati designs, points to Malayer.
rows.cautions: Borrowings from Arak and Bijar designs (Persian study) make design alone unreliable.

facts.text: Malayer rugs are single-wefted and more densely knotted than other Hamadan-area rugs, symmetric knot on cotton (Stone).
The northern Malayer district weaves Hamadan-like rugs, the southern Sarouk-like ones (Jacobsen).
Malayer is the most important carpet center of Hamadan province; its rugs borrow designs from Arak and Bijar.
Malayer was among the major carpet-making areas of Iran in the 1970s.

Malayer designs are mostly angular: the mahi ('fish', i.e. Herati) pattern, named with prefixes such as chahar, sag, rudbari, alamdar and herati, is typical of the single-weft areas; chahar-changh, pich-e Jowzan and shal-mahi are typical of the double-weft areas; panjeh-nabati and raised (barjasteh) patterns also occur, on lac red, white and navy grounds.
The town of Malayer was earlier called Dowlatabad, after its founder Prince Dowlatshah, a son of Fath-Ali Shah.

A Persian field survey describes Malayer county rugs as coarse, 20-30 raj, symmetric (Turkish) knot, cotton warps and wefts and wool pile; villages along the Malayer-Arak road weave double-wefted rugs.
facts.quote: در شهرستان ملایر نیز قالیچه‌های درشت‌باف با رج‌شمار ۲۰-۳۰ بافته می‌شود. گره این قالیچه‌ها ترکی است و تار و پود پنبه‌ای و پرز پشمی در آن‌ها به‌کار می‌رود

says.text: Single-wefted, and more densely knotted than other Hamadan-area rugs.
Coarse, 20-30 raj, the same count it gives for Hamadan village rugs generally; villages along the Malayer-Arak road are double-wefted.
Malayer has both single-weft and double-weft areas, with different design names in each.

museum_examples.shows: one image

rows.name: Josan
rows.region: A village in the Malayer district, southeast of Malayer (Stone; Jacobsen: about 60 miles south of Hamadan).
rows.made_by: Village weavers.
rows.date_note: Jacobsen saw mostly new Josans in the 1950s; designs follow early-20th-century (old) Sarouk medallion designs.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric (Stone).
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: about 200 per square inch.
structure.wefts_note: Double-wefted (Stone); Jacobsen: weave like Sarouks.
structure.handle: Thick, compact, finer than the average Sarouk (Jacobsen).

design.field: Old-style Sarouk medallion designs with intricate florals; red, rose, ivory or blue fields.
design.colors: Red or rose fields, some ivory, few blue.
design.sizes: Small sizes only: 2 x 3, 5 x 3.5, 6.5 x 4.5 ft; no runners or carpets.

look_alikes.name: Sarouk
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Josans have Sarouk designs but symmetric knots; Sarouks use the asymmetric knot.

rows.trade_use: 'Josan Sarouk' in the American trade.
rows.what_it_tells: A small, fine Sarouk-looking rug with symmetric knots and two wefts points to Josan.
rows.cautions: The Persian 'pich-e Jowzan' design name is used across Malayer.

facts.text: Josan rugs are similar to early-20th-century Sarouks in design but have symmetric knots.
Josans are double-wefted, about 200 symmetric knots per square inch, on cotton (Stone).
Josans were made only in small sizes (Jacobsen).
'Pich-e Jowzan' (the Jowzan scroll) is a characteristic Malayer design name.
Jowzan (Josan) is one of the villages along the Malayer-Arak road that weave double-wefted rugs, unlike the single-wefted rugs of Hamadan, Tuyserkan and Nahavand.
facts.quote: روستاهای در امتداد جادة ملایر-اراک بافته‌های دوپودی دارند که می‌توان به روستای جوزان اشاره کرد

rows.name: Viss
rows.region: A town near Hamadan. Exact location not settled by the sources read.
rows.made_by: Village weavers.
rows.date_note: No dates in the sources.

structure.knot_note: Not stated.
structure.kpsi_note: No count found.
structure.wefts_note: Single wefts on cotton (Stone).

design.field: Geometric designs on a red ground, often hooked diamond medallions alternating with hooked hexagons.
design.colors: Red ground.

look_alikes.name: Hamadan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same single-wefted structure; the alternating hooked diamond and hexagon medallions are the Viss mark.

rows.trade_use: A dealers' village name.
rows.what_it_tells: A single-wefted red-ground rug with alternating hooked medallions may be sold as Viss.
rows.cautions: Single source; a different Vist near Golpayegan also exists (research note), so the place is not settled.

facts.text: Vist (Viss, Wiss) near Hamadan is a source of single-wefted rugs on cotton with hooked diamond and hexagon medallions on a red ground.

A Persian field study places the memory-woven (zehni-baf) Vist rug in the central Isfahan region southwest of Khansar, woven by descendants of nomads from Hamadan who gave up nomadism about 400 years ago and settled in the present village of Vist.

The Vist design is fixed: it is repeated from rug to rug with very small changes, without any cartoon; the study measured 50 Vist rugs over 6 square meters and over 100 years old and found 16 one-dimensional proportion systems kept by the weavers from memory.
Zhuleh (quoted in the study) calls Vist the best-known rug of the south and southwest of Golpayegan.

A Persian field study gives the technical specification of the Vist rug: about 20 knots per 7 cm across (17 to 21), cotton warps of 12-ply yarn, cotton wefts of 7-ply yarn, two-ply wool pile, two wefts between rows, half-depressed warps (nim-lul), woven on upright looms without a hook.
facts.quote: فرش ويست، با متوسط رج شمار ۲۰ (بين ۱۷ تا ۲۱ گره در ۷ سانتي متر)، با چله هاي پنبه اي افشان ۱۲ لا پرز دولا پشمي و پود پنبه اي افشان ۷ لا ... دو پود و نيم لول (Vist rugs, average raj 20, 17-21 knots per 7 cm, 12-ply cotton warps, two-ply wool pile, 7-ply cotton weft ... two wefts and half-depressed)

facts.text: In Vist village itself the knot is symmetric (Turkish), with the asymmetric knot used at times in the last hundred years; the villages around Vist, whose rugs are called 'Khansari', use the asymmetric (Persian) knot.
facts.quote: گره بافت در روستاي ويست متقارن (ترکي) و روستاهاي اطراف ويست نامتقارن (فارسي) است (the knot in Vist village is symmetric, in the villages around it asymmetric)

facts.text: Genuine Vist rugs usually have three borders (two narrow, one wide); the Khansari rugs of the neighboring villages usually have five.
Our conversion: 17-21 knots per 7 cm is about 6.2-7.6 per inch, or roughly 38-58 knots per square inch if the knots are as tall as they are wide.

ویست

ویست (Vist).
Vist, Viss, Wiss (the table's ویس has no source).
A town near Hamadan.
The village of Vist, southwest of Khansar near Golpayegan (Isfahan province); the weavers' ancestors were nomads from Hamadan.

disagreements.note: Our reading: the Hamadan link in Stone may come from the weavers' origin; the round-1 research note about a Vist near Golpayegan now has a source.

says.text: Single-wefted, on cotton.
Two wefts (دو پود) between rows, cotton, with half-depressed warps (nim-lul).

rows.name: Karaje (old-book name)
rows.region: Tribes near Hamadan; Jacobsen: nomad Kurds about 50 miles north of Hamadan; Kendrick & Tattersall: Kurdistans made near Hamadan.
rows.made_by: Kurdish tribal weavers.
rows.kind: trade name (a name for a look, made in several places)
rows.date_note: None imported under the name for about 35 years before 1962; Hawley (1913) calls them almost always comparatively old.

structure.knot_note: Ghiordes (Hawley).
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: horizontally 6-12, perpendicularly 7-12 = 42-144.
structure.wefts_note: Single weft crossing once; in parts two to four thin threads laid side by side as one (Hawley, Kendrick & Tattersall, Jacobsen). Weft stands as high as the knots, giving an even back (Hawley).
structure.pile_note: Medium to fairly long, soft and lustrous (Hawley).
structure.sides: Heavy double overcasting (Hawley).
structure.ends: Lower end web and warp loops; upper end web and short fringe (Hawley).

design.field: Small sprigs in rows or in a trellis, or three or four large diamond medallions; Iranian floral character.
design.colors: Dark blue or plum and red.
design.sizes: Runners 8-14 ft long, width 3/8-1/2 of length.

look_alikes.name: Hamadan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Single weft like Hamadans, but wool warp and wool weft, more regular knot alignment and weft with some slack.

look_alikes.name: Karaja
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Karaja (Azerbaijan) is a different name: cotton warp, geometric medallions.

rows.trade_use: A name in books of about 1910-1925 for single-wefted Kurdish wool runners; Jacobsen says old dealers gave it to a certain kind of blue-field runner.
rows.what_it_tells: A single-wefted runner on a wool warp is the kind old books call Karaje.
rows.cautions: Easily confused with Karaja; Jacobsen thinks the authorities were not certain of the name.

facts.text: Karaje rugs have a single weft crossing once between rows.
facts.quote: As a rule, a single thread of weft crosses only once between two rows of knots (Hawley 1922, p. 143)

facts.text: Karajes have wool warps and wool wefts, unlike Hamadans.
Karajes are mostly runners.

rows.name: Bakhtiari
rows.region: The Chaharmahal and Bakhtiari region west of Isfahan (Shahr-e Kord, Saman, Shalamzar, Chaleshtar, Ben, Farsan, Qahfarrokh, Borujen, Boldaji, Babaheydar, Hafshejan, Ardal and others) and the Bakhtiari tribal territory of the Zagros.
rows.made_by: Mostly settled villagers of Chaharmahal, many not Bakhtiari tribe members (Stone, Jacobsen quoting Edwards); also Bakhtiari tribal weavers (a Lur people speaking an Iranian language).
rows.date_note: Bakhtiari rugs first reached America about 1924; inscribed rugs for Bakhtiari khans date from the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Still woven.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric in old and tribal pieces (Stone, Jacobsen, Met bag records); Jacobsen says some later village rugs use the asymmetric (Senna) knot.
structure.kpsi_note: No overall count in the sources read.
structure.wefts_note: Stone and Iranica (Ittig): tribal pieces double-wefted on wool, village (Chahar Mahal) pieces single-wefted on cotton. But Stone also calls Shahr-e Kord and Shalamzar rugs double-wefted and Feridan rugs single-wefted.
structure.pile_note: Thick in early pieces (Jacobsen).
structure.sides: Many village rugs have brown-black overcast edges (Stone).

design.field: The garden (kheshti, 'brick') design of square or lozenge panels each holding a flowering tree, vase, cypress, willow or mihrab; also medallion designs, vase designs, and long rugs with stripes of small botehs. Saman panels are diamond-shaped and abstract; Chaleshtar and Shahr-e Kord panels more naturalistic (Stone, Jacobsen; Negareh study, Aghadavoud Jolfaei & Barari 2014).
design.colors: Red, blue and ivory with more green, gold and yellow than most Persian rugs.
design.sizes: Old ones mostly about 6.5 x 4.5 ft, some to about 14 x 5 ft, runners.

look_alikes.name: Yalameh
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Yalameh rugs come from southeast of Chahar Mahal and use Qashqai, Lur and Khamseh motifs, usually stacked latch-hook diamonds rather than panels.

look_alikes.name: Varamin
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Small Veramin pillows were sold as Bakhtiari in the 1920s.

rows.trade_use: 'Bakhtiari' is used for rugs of the Chaharmahal villages, most often panel-design rugs; 'Bibibaf' (grandmother's weave) for particularly fine pieces.
rows.what_it_tells: A rug with a field of square garden panels holding trees and flowers points to Chaharmahal (Bakhtiari) village weaving.
rows.cautions: The trade name is a regional style name; weft count and foundation vary by village and period.

facts.text: Rugs marketed as Bakhtiari are woven mainly by villagers of Chahar Mahal, many of whom are not members of the Bakhtiari tribe.
The garden (kheshti) panel design is the best-known design of Chaharmahal and Bakhtiari.
Panels are drawn abstractly in Saman, Shalamzar and Ardal, more naturalistically in Chaleshtar and Shahr-e Kord.
Saman rugs are Bakhtiari panel-design rugs with diamond-shaped panels.
Double-wefted symmetric-knotted pieces on wool are classed as tribal, single-wefted pieces on cotton as village work.
Early Bakhtiari rugs used wool warps; most later ones cotton (Jacobsen).
Shahr-e Kord and Qahfarrokh had about 500 looms each, still horizontal (Jacobsen, after Edwards); Stone counts 2,297 weaving shops in Shahr-e Kord in the mid-1970s.
Late 19th- and early 20th-century Bakhtiari rugs often carry dated inscriptions to Bakhtiari khans.
'Bibibaf' carpets of fine weave are associated with Chahar Mahal and the Bakhtiari aristocracy.
Bakhtiari bags often combine soumak and pile; the Met's Bakhtiari khorjin and saddle cover are wool with symmetric knots.
Chaharmahal-Bakhtiari and 'Yalameh Borujen' are registered carpet geographical indications; Shahr-e Kord is proposed.
Carpet weaving was important in both the village and the nomadic economy of Chaharmahal.
'Chaharmahal and Bakhtiari' hand-woven carpet is a registered geographical indication (WIPO Lisbon register AO 1028, 28 Dec 2015); the registered area names the cities of Shahrekord, Saman and Kiar.
facts.quote: (AO 1028) فرش دستبافت چهارمحال و بختیاری / Chaharmahal and Bakhtiari Handmade Carpet

facts.text: The earliest dated Bakhtiari khan's carpet noted by Ian Bennett (Hali 44, 1989) is dated AH 1302 (1884-85).
facts.quote: The earliest dated carpet as noted by Ian Bennett is from AH 1302/1884-5 AD

says.text: Tribal: wool foundation, double weft; village: cotton foundation, single weft (wording not checked on page).
The Bakhtiari almost always used undyed cotton for warps and wefts.
Same tribal/village split as Ittig, but Shahr-e Kord and Shalamzar village rugs are double-wefted.
Old rugs Ghiordes only; some later village rugs Senna.
Symmetric.

disagreements.about: Shahr-e Kord as a geographical indication

says.text: Lists Chaharmahal and Bakhtiari as registered and Shahrekord separately as proposed for national registration.
The registered Chaharmahal and Bakhtiari appellation (AO 1028) already names Shahrekord, Saman and Kiar as its area.

rows.name: Joshaghan
rows.region: Joshaqan-e Qali, a small town in the mountains between Kashan and Isfahan, and nearby villages (Meymeh).
rows.made_by: Town and village weavers.
rows.date_note: Royal workshops under the Safavids; production stopped or dwindled in the mid-19th century (Hawley; Persian study: after an 1848 earthquake) and revived from the late 19th or early 20th century (Iranica; Persian study).

structure.knot_note: Hawley, Lewis, May, Kendrick & Tattersall: Ghiordes (symmetric). Stone: asymmetric, also for Meymeh.
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: horizontally 7-11, perpendicularly 8-13 = 56-143. Lewis: 64-400. Stone: 100-200. Jacobsen: new rugs after 1955 about 14 x 14 = 196; some post-war 8 x 8 = 64. Persian study: 2,000-5,000 knots per dm2 (about 129-323 per square inch).
structure.weft_color: Hawley: wool, sometimes red or brown, often natural; Kendrick & Tattersall: mostly red or brown
structure.wefts_note: Hawley: generally twice, sometimes three times. Kendrick & Tattersall: sometimes three shoots. May: twice.
structure.pile_note: Short to medium (Hawley); thick, soft and lustrous (Kendrick & Tattersall).
structure.sides: Double overcasting, generally brown or black (Hawley).
structure.ends: Web at lower end; web and fringe at upper (Hawley).

design.field: An all-over lattice of diamonds, each with a stiff angular flower spray, with or without a diamond center and corners; also Herati and guli hinnai.
design.colors: Red or deep blue fields.
design.sizes: Hawley 8-16 ft; Jacobsen from 5 x 3.5 to 10 x 14 ft.

look_alikes.name: Kashan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A 1967 government document shows Joshaqan rugs exported as 'Kashan' (Persian study).

rows.trade_use: Joshaghan design is widely copied elsewhere; old-book writers used the name loosely.
rows.what_it_tells: A rug with a lattice of small diamonds each holding a stiff flower spray is in the Joshaghan design, which may or may not mean Joshaghan.
rows.cautions: The design is copied in Bakhtiari, Indian and other rugs; structure reports disagree on the knot.

facts.text: Joshaghan rugs are known for an all-over lozenge pattern of geometricized flowers, used for about 200 years.
Joshaqan is a small town of the Kashan district.
Joshaqan was a Safavid royal weaving center whose carpets were royal gifts.
Hawley gives 7-11 knots per inch across and 8-13 down (about 56-143 per square inch).
Joshaqan rugs were exported under the name 'Kashan' in the 1960s (Persian study citing a 1967 document).
Joshaqan is a registered carpet geographical indication (Isfahan province).

rows.name: Yalameh
rows.region: Southeast of Chahar Mahal: Borujen and villages of Isfahan province (Aliabad, Dehaqan, Semirom, Shahreza and others).
rows.made_by: Settled Turkic villagers; Yalameh is a clan of the Amaleh tribe of the Qashqai (Persian study).
rows.date_note: Persian study: Qashqai Turkic nomads came to Borujen from about 1863 and Yalameh weaving flourished from then.

structure.knot_note: Persian study: Persian (asymmetric) knot, sometimes Turkish.
structure.kpsi_note: Persian studies: usually 20-30 raj (fine Aliabad 35-40) or 22-35 raj, about 7-11 knots per inch across.
structure.wefts_note: Double-wefted (Persian study).
structure.sides: Selvedges wrapped in two or three colors (Persian studies).

design.field: Three stacked latch-hook diamond medallions; Qashqai, Lur and Khamseh motifs; bright colors.
design.colors: Brighter than most southwest Persian rugs.
design.sizes: Many large sizes.

look_alikes.name: Qashqai
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Yalameh uses Qashqai motifs but is a settled village product with multicolor wrapped edges; often larger (Stone, Persian study).

rows.trade_use: A village-group name.
rows.what_it_tells: A bright rug with stacked latch-hooked diamonds and a two- or three-color edge wrap points to Yalameh.
rows.cautions: Structure from Persian field studies only.

facts.text: Yalameh rugs come from an area southeast of Chahar Mahal and use Qashqai, Lur and Khamseh motifs, typically three stacked latch-hook diamonds.
Yalameh rugs are woven on horizontal looms, double-wefted, with the asymmetric knot and sometimes the symmetric.
Yalameh selvedges are wrapped in two or three colors.
Yalameh of Aliabad (Isfahan) and of Borujen are registered carpet geographical indications.
Yalameh rugs of Borujen fall into three design groups: howzi ('pool'), shekarlu and bandi (compartment); the compartment form used in Yalameh rugs is qab-qabi (repeating frames).
Yalameh rugs are woven in six-meter (about 2 x 3 m), zar-o-nim (about 1 x 1.5 m), twelve-meter and runner sizes.

Colors are dark and light lac red (laki), dark navy, blue, yellow, cream, madder red, white, black and green, mostly from natural dyes; chemically dyed yarn has spread in recent years, and beige, brown, khaki, gray, yellow and orange have been added for new buyers' taste.

Until recently six Qashqai tribes had a large share in carpet weaving (Igdir, Safi-Khani, Rahimlu, Chegini, Shekarlu and Yalameh); the Yalameh people settled at the end of the 12th or start of the 13th century AH (about the 1780s) in their former summer pastures south of Isfahan.
Our conversion for the kpsi fill: 20 raj on a 7 cm count is about 53 knots per square inch and 40 raj on a 6.5 cm count about 244; the Persian studies do not say which gereh they use.

'Yalameh of Aliabad of Dehaghan' (Isfahan province) is a registered geographical indication, nationally (Intellectual Property Center 119 GI, 22 Apr 2018) and internationally (WIPO Lisbon register AO 1149, 14 May 2025).
facts.quote: (AO 1149) فرش دستبافت یلمه علی آباد دهاقان / Yalameh of Ali Abad of Dehaghan Handmade Carpet

says.text: 20-30 raj, fine Aliabad 35-40.

rows.name: Varamin
rows.region: The plain of Varamin southeast of Tehran.
rows.made_by: Kurdish, Turkic (Shahsavan, Afshar) and Lur (Hadavandi) settlers and tribes of the plain.
rows.date_note: Jacobsen saw Veramin pillows imported 1924-1930; Iranica and Stone describe later production.

structure.knot_note: Asymmetric (Stone; Met khorjin record).
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: 130-225 per square inch.
structure.wefts_note: Not stated.
structure.pile_note: Jacobsen: medium nap, silky.

design.field: Mina Khani lattice; Sariq-like guls and Memling guls on bags; S-motif main borders.

look_alikes.name: Bakhtiari
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Small Varamin pillows were sold as Bakhtiari.

rows.trade_use: Varamin for Mina Khani rugs and tribal bags of the Tehran plain.
rows.what_it_tells: A fine Mina Khani rug or a tribal bag with S-borders may be Varamin.
rows.cautions: Many tribes live in the area; attribution is broad.

facts.text: The Mina Khani design is particularly associated with Varamin.
Kurds, Turks and other tribes in the Varamin plain weave pile rugs and flatweaves.
Varamin pile weaving uses the asymmetric knot (Stone; the Met's Veramin khorjin half 2015.490.3 is asymmetrically knotted).
Some Varamin rugs are woven on cotton at 130-225 knots per square inch (Stone).
Varamin gelims have narrow weft-float bands forming S-shapes.
Varamin is a registered national and international carpet geographical indication.

rows.name: Luri
rows.region: The Lur tribal lands of the Zagros: Lorestan (Khorramabad), and Lur tribes of Fars (Mamasani, Boyer Ahmadi, Kuhgilu) and Isfahan province; Lurs also settled near Varamin.
rows.made_by: Lur tribes and villagers (an Iranian-speaking people; the Bakhtiari are also Lurs).
rows.date_note: No firm dates in the sources.

structure.knot_note: Some rugs symmetric, others asymmetric (Stone).
structure.kpsi_note: No count found.
structure.wefts_note: Not stated.

design.field: All-over hexagonal cells with geometricized Mina Khani blossoms, or diamond cells each with a tree of life; dark colors around Khorramabad.
design.colors: Dark.

look_alikes.name: Gabbeh (traditional)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Iranica says gabbehs are said to have originated in Lorestan; Lurs weave double-sided gabbehs.

look_alikes.name: Bakhtiari
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The Bakhtiari are a Lur people; their rugs are more often sold separately.

rows.trade_use: 'Luri' or 'Lori' for tribal rugs and bags of Lur groups, often sold through Shiraz or as 'Luri-Bakhtiari'.
rows.what_it_tells: A dark tribal rug with a Mina Khani-derived hexagon lattice from the Zagros may be Luri.
rows.cautions: Structure is poorly documented in the sources read.

facts.text: The Lurs are an Iranian-speaking people of the Zagros, partly still pastoral; the Bakhtiari belong to them.
Lur pile rugs often have hexagonal or diamond cell lattices with Mina Khani blossoms or trees of life (Stone).
Some Lur rugs use the symmetric knot, others the asymmetric (Stone).
Lur bags combine soumak, tapestry and pile; the Met's Luri bag of about 1900 is a soumak (sumak brocaded) wool and cotton bag.
The Lur and Bakhtiari obtain a black dye from acorn hulls.
'Lorestan' is a registered carpet geographical indication and 'Lori' (Fars) is proposed.

'Lorestan' hand-woven carpet is a registered geographical indication (WIPO Lisbon register AO 1033, 28 Dec 2015; area: Khorramabad, Kuhdasht, Azna, Aligudarz, Borujerd, Aleshtar, Nurabad, Dorud, Poldokhtar).
facts.quote: (AO 1033) فرش دستبافت لرستان / Lorestan Handmade Carpet

rows.name: Abadeh
rows.region: The town of Abadeh on the road between Isfahan and Shiraz (Fars).
rows.made_by: Town and village weavers.
rows.date_note: No dates in the sources read.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric (Stone).
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: 80-160 per square inch.
structure.wefts_note: Not stated.

design.field: Some copy Persian city designs; others copy local tribal (Qashqai) rugs.

look_alikes.name: Qashqai
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Abadeh rugs copy Qashqai designs on a cotton foundation with symmetric knots; Qashqai tribal rugs are all wool with asymmetric knots.

rows.trade_use: A town name.
rows.what_it_tells: A Qashqai-looking rug on a cotton foundation may be an Abadeh.
rows.cautions: Structure single-sourced.

facts.text: Abadeh lies between Isfahan and Shiraz; carpet and rug weaving are among its crafts.
Abadeh rugs have 80-160 symmetric knots per square inch on cotton, wefts sometimes blue (Stone).
Abadeh is proposed as a carpet geographical indication (Fars).

rows.name: Shiraz (market name)
rows.region: Fars province; Shiraz is the market city, and the name covers rugs made anywhere in Fars by the Qashqai, Khamseh, Lurs, Afshars and villagers.
rows.made_by: Fars tribes (Qashqai, Khamseh, Lur, Afshar) and village weavers; the city itself wove little.
rows.kind: trade name (a name for a look, made in several places)
rows.date_note: Old books describe 19th-century Shiraz rugs; Jacobsen says some 20,000 were made yearly around 1960. Still used.

structure.knot_note: Hawley: generally Sehna, frequently Ghiordes; Lewis: generally Senna; May and Kendrick & Tattersall: Sehna most common, Ghiordes also; Mumford: Ghiordes.
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: horizontally 7-12, perpendicularly 8-12 = 56-144. Lewis: 42-196. Jacobsen: choicest old 250-450, new 40-300.
structure.warp_color: white wool (Kendrick & Tattersall); some goat hair (Hawley, Lewis)
structure.weft_color: Often dyed red (Hawley, Kendrick & Tattersall) or pink (May)
structure.wefts_note: Hawley, May, Kendrick & Tattersall: twice. Lewis: frequently more than two.
structure.pile_note: Soft, lustrous, short to medium (Hawley); fleecy (May).
structure.sides: Heavy double overcasting in short lengths of two or more colors (barber-pole), often with small wool tufts at intervals (Hawley, May, Lewis, Kendrick & Tattersall, Mumford).
structure.ends: Broad striped webs, sometimes embroidered or crossed by colored cords; a checked (red, white and blue) band between pile and web; an extra band of pile beyond the border at each end (Hawley, Mumford, Jacobsen).
structure.handle: Loosely woven; tend not to lie flat (Hawley, Lewis, Kendrick & Tattersall); the best old pieces very pliable (Jacobsen).

design.field: Pole medallions of linked diamonds or hexagons; all-over angular botehs; diagonal stripes; latch-hooks; many small animals and birds.
design.border: Several narrow stripes including a barber-pole stripe and a vine with alternating red and blue oval flowers.
design.colors: Deep blue and red with small areas of ivory and yellow; a gray-green.
design.sizes: Hawley 5-9 ft; Jacobsen small to about 8 x 11 ft.

look_alikes.name: Shirvan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Geometric Shiraz rugs are mistaken for Caucasian Shirvans; Shiraz wefts are red-dyed wool and sides are barber-pole wrapped with tufts.

look_alikes.name: Neyriz
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Niris webs are flatly woven in stripes; Shiraz webs embroidered and crossed by cords.

look_alikes.name: Qashqai
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Qashqai rugs are the finest group sold as Shiraz.

look_alikes.name: Afshar
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Some Afshar rugs are sold as Shiraz.

rows.trade_use: 'Shiraz' = any Fars tribal or village rug; 'Mecca' or 'Mecca Shiraz' was a dealers' name, usually for Qashqai rugs, based on the pilgrimage story.
rows.what_it_tells: Barber-pole side wrapping with tufts, striped end webs and red-dyed wool wefts point to Fars; the market name does not say which tribe.
rows.cautions: 'Mecca' implies nothing about origin. Hawley contradicts himself on Shiraz weft (red wool in the type analysis, frequently cotton in the Niris text).

facts.text: The term 'Shiraz' is used for rugs made anywhere in Fars; Shiraz is the market.
Shiraz sides are overcast in short lengths of different colors, often with tufts of wool.
facts.quote: The sides are overcast with heavy strands of wool varied like a barber-pole at regular intervals (Hawley 1922, p. 117)

facts.text: Shiraz warps are wool and wefts wool, often dyed red or pink, crossing twice.
Hawley gives 7-12 knots per inch across and 8-12 down (about 56-144 per square inch); Lewis 42-196.
Shiraz rugs are loosely woven and often do not lie flat.
'Mecca' as a rug name is a dealers' fiction tied to the pilgrimage.
In 1956 rug-making was more important in the villages and tribes around Shiraz than in the city's workshops.
Ninety percent of Shiraz rugs still had wool warps around 1960 (Jacobsen).

says.text: Generally Sehna, frequently Ghiordes.
Generally the Senna.
Ghiordes.
Sehna most common, Ghiordes also.
AIC 1986.1351 (Shiraz area, 1875-1900): Ghiordes knots.
Shiraz prayer rug No. 5: Ghiordes.
Type analysis: wool, frequently red. Niris text: Shiraz weft frequently of cotton.
Wool dyed pink.
Red wool.

rows.name: Qashqai
rows.region: Fars province, north and west of Shiraz (Firuzabad, Semirom and the migration routes); Kashkuli groups around Kamehr, Kakan and Ardakan.
rows.made_by: The Qashqai confederacy of Turkic-speaking tribes (Amaleh, Darashuri, Farsimadan, Kashkuli Bozorg and Kuchek, Shish Boluki and others), nomadic and settled.
rows.date_note: Jacobsen dates his finest example to 1850-1890; still woven, now often for foreign markets.

structure.knot_note: Asymmetric, open to the left (Stone). Kashkuli also asymmetric (Stone).
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: about 70-170. Jacobsen: 120-250, a few older pieces finer.
structure.weft_color: Madder-dyed red (Stone; Kashkuli: usually red); ruby-red silk wefts only in exceptional pieces (Iranica)
structure.wefts_note: Double wefts (Stone).
structure.pile_note: Short to medium (Jacobsen).
structure.sides: Barber-pole wrapping (Stone).
structure.ends: Plain weave with brocade at the ends (Stone); the domino-like 'Qashqai frieze' border at the ends of many pieces (Stone).
structure.handle: Tightly woven, more so than other Shiraz (Jacobsen).
structure.back: Kashkuli: warps offset (Stone; degree not stated).

design.field: The Qashqai medallion (a hexagon or diamond with four hooks inside a hooked diamond); fields of small scattered blossoms, animals, birds and figures; botehs; Herati; Kashkuli Millefleurs prayer designs; 'yek-sar-nazem'; lion rugs (Stone, Jacobsen, Persian studies, Iranica).
design.border: Many; eight-pointed stars, serrated leaf and cup.
design.colors: Blue or wine fields with much ivory.
design.sizes: Small to about 7 x 10 ft.

look_alikes.name: Khamseh
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Khamseh yarns are more coarsely spun and designs often scatter chickens and animals; Stone notes both knots among Khamseh groups.

look_alikes.name: Abadeh
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Abadeh copies Qashqai designs on cotton with symmetric knots.

look_alikes.name: Gabbeh (traditional)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Qashqai also weave gabbehs: coarse, long pile, many wefts.

rows.trade_use: Sold as Shiraz, as 'Mecca Shiraz' in old America, as Kashkai in London; 'Kashkuli' for the most finely knotted Qashqai rugs.
rows.what_it_tells: A finely knotted all-wool Fars rug with red wefts, barber-pole edges and the hooked Qashqai medallion points to Qashqai weaving.
rows.cautions: Settled-village Qashqai rugs on cotton are coarser and market-driven; after land reform factory yarn and chemical dyes spread (Persian study).

facts.text: The Qashqai are a confederacy of Turkic-speaking tribes of Fars and its largest weaving group.
Qashqai rugs use the asymmetric knot with two red-dyed wefts.
Jacobsen gives 120-250 knots per square inch; Stone 70-170.
Nomadic Qashqai rugs are all wool; settled-village ones often have cotton warps.
Ruby-red silk wefts appear only in exceptional Qashqai and Khamseh pieces.
The Kashkuli are Qashqai tribes; their finely knotted rugs use the asymmetric knot, red wefts and offset warps, many woven in Firuzabad (Stone).
The 'yek-sar-nazem' design was formerly specific to the Qashqai and their Kashkuli clan.
The Met's Qashqai khorjin half (about 1875) has asymmetrically knotted wool pile on wool warp and weft.
Qashqai is a registered carpet geographical indication; Kashkuli is proposed.
Qashqai weavers make many bag forms (mafrash, khorjin, chanteh, juval, tobreh, salt bags); the mafrash is woven in a complementary-weft technique.
After forced settlement, land reform and tribal schooling, factory-made yarn and chemical dyes reached the Qashqai and commercial production grew.
Most surviving lion rugs are Bakhtiari and Qashqai work of the 19th and 20th centuries.
'Qashqai hand-woven carpet of Fars' is a registered geographical indication (WIPO Lisbon register AO 1030, 28 Dec 2015).
facts.quote: (AO 1030) فرش دستبافت قشقایی فارس / Qashqaie Handmade Carpet of Fars

facts.text: Since the tribes were settled, many Fars nomadic rugs, including those of the Kashkuli clan, are woven for producers to market-led, often computer-drawn cartoons that the producers supply, replacing weaving from memory.
facts.quote: نقشه کامپیوتری ... توسط عشایر اسکان یافته طایفه کشکولی ساکن در شهر فیروزآباد ... بافته شده است (a computer-drawn cartoon ... woven by settled nomads of the Kashkuli clan living in Firuzabad)

facts.text: Qashqai weavers make many bag forms: khorjin (double saddlebag), juval, chanteh, mafrash (bedding bag), tobreh, water-pipe bags, Koran bags and salt bags (namakdan).
facts.quote: خورجین، جوال، چنته، مفرش، توبره، قلیان‌دان، اُکاش، قرآن‌دان، نمکدان (khorjin, juval, chanteh, mafrash, tobreh, qalyan-dan, okash, Koran-dan, salt bag)

facts.text: In the Qashqai dialect the symmetric knot is called kora ilma and the asymmetric knot yurma ilma, and the weft is called tab.
facts.quote: در گویش قشقایی به‌آن کورا ایلما (گره متقارن یا ترکی) و یورما ایلما (گره نامتقارن یا فارسی) گفته می‌شود

says.text: The mafrash is woven in a complementary-weft technique (as in the table).

Sozani (weft-wrapping) is the technique most used for juvals, khorjins, chantehs and mafrashes (quoting Rahmani & Ashouri 1385), and mafrashes were formerly also woven in dowrechin (reverse wrapping).

rows.name: Khamseh
rows.region: Fars province, east of the Qashqai; not the Khamseh district around Zanjan.
rows.made_by: The Khamseh confederacy: Arab (the largest weaving group; Jabbareh clans), Basseri, Baharlu, Aynallu and Nafar tribes.
rows.date_note: The confederacy was formed in 1861-62 and disbanded in the 1960s.

structure.knot_note: Stone: Arab and Basseri asymmetric; Baharlu both. AIC's Khamseh carpet (c. 1890): Turkish (Ghiordes) knots.
structure.kpsi_note: No count found.
structure.wefts_note: Not stated; ruby silk wefts in exceptional pieces (Iranica).
structure.pile_note: Shaggy pile in Arab rugs (Stone); yarns more coarsely spun than Qashqai (Stone).

design.field: All-over geometric florets and animals scattered at random; columns of compartments with stylized chickens (Stone; AIC label).

look_alikes.name: Qashqai
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Khamseh yarns are coarser and drawing looser; many birds and animals.

rows.trade_use: Sold as Shiraz or Khamseh.
rows.what_it_tells: A loosely drawn Fars tribal rug with many chickens and animals may be Khamseh.
rows.cautions: Two different Khamsehs: the Fars confederacy and the old Zanjan province.

facts.text: The Khamseh confederacy (Arab, Basseri, Baharlu, Aynallu, Nafar) was formed in the 1860s as a counterweight to the Qashqai.
The Arab tribe is the largest Khamseh weaving group (Stone); its weaving clans are Jabbareh Arabs and the pile khorjin is its most common bag.
Khamseh designs often scatter geometric florets and animals over the field.
'Khamseh Fars' and 'Arab' are proposed geographical indications; 'Khamseh Zanjan' (northwest) is a separate registered one.

'Khamseh of Zanjan' (northwest Iran) is a registered geographical indication (WIPO Lisbon register AO 1143, 31 Oct 2025; area: Ijrud, Garmab and Khodabandeh), separate from the Khamseh tribal confederacy of Fars.
facts.quote: (AO 1143) فرش دستبافت خمسه زنجان / Khamseh Handmade Carpet of Zanjan

says.text: Arab and Basseri: asymmetric; Baharlu: both.
AIC 2014.1172 Khamseh carpet: Turkish (Ghiordes) knots.
Fars entry: two tribal groups, about 70,000 people; Shiraz entry: three tribes, about 30,000.

rows.name: Gabbeh (traditional)
rows.region: Southwest Iran (Fars, the Qashqai and Lur territories, Lorestan) and also Khurasan; Iranica: Kurdish, Lori-speaking and Qashqai tribes of the Zagros.
rows.made_by: Qashqai, Lur, Bakhtiari and other tribal weavers, for their own use.
rows.date_note: First mentioned in a mid-16th-century farman; most surviving gabbehs are 20th-century, a few probably 19th. Woven for home use until Western demand in the 1980s (see Gabbeh (modern export, from the 1980s)). Mumford (1902) describes plain-field Shiraz 'comforters' of the same build.

structure.knot_note: Both, sometimes in the same rug (Stone; Iranica).
structure.kpsi_note: Mumford's plain-field Shiraz 'comforters' (gabbeh-type): 18-20 per square inch. Iranica: low knot density. No other counts found.
structure.wefts_note: Many wefts between rows: four to six (Stone); six or eight (Mumford, for the Shiraz 'comforters').
structure.pile_note: Long and shaggy, lying flat because of the many wefts (Mumford; Iranica).
structure.sides: Mumford: Shiraz-type tufted overcasting.
structure.ends: Ends folded over and hemmed off the loom (Stone); Mumford: checked colored band at the ends.

design.field: Open fields of plain color or simple geometric patterns, sometimes naive people, animals and flowers; undyed wool in 'Shouli' gabbehs; lions in 'gabba-ye shiri'.
design.colors: Bright, often synthetic dyes; undyed natural wool in Shouli gabbehs.
design.sizes: About 90 x 150 cm or larger; 4.5 x 7 ft.

look_alikes.name: Gabbeh (modern export, from the 1980s)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Post-1980s commercial gabbehs are made for sale, often with modern abstract designs; traditional ones are domestic pieces.

look_alikes.name: Luri
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Lurs weave gabbehs with pile on both sides ('gabbeh patuee') used as blankets.

rows.trade_use: Gabbeh = a coarse, long-piled, plain-field tribal rug.
rows.what_it_tells: A thick, long-piled rug with a mostly plain field, few knots and many wefts is a gabbeh-type tribal piece.
rows.cautions: Large carpets with elaborate motifs are sometimes mislabeled gabbeh. The Met's 'Gabbeh' (22.100.66, Ballard collection) is an older example.

facts.text: A gabbeh is a coarse pile rug with long pile, low knot density and many weft rows between the knot rows.
facts.quote: after each row of knots there are six or eight threads of dyed weft, causing the pile, which is long, to lie flat. (Mumford 1902, p. 214)

facts.text: Gabbehs were woven for domestic use and not for the market until recently.
Symmetric and asymmetric knots may occur in the same gabbeh.
Gabbeh is also called khersak; Dehkhoda defines gabbeh as khersak, a long-piled carpet.
The first known reference to gabba is a farman of Shah Tahmasp (mid-16th century).
Undyed-wool gabbehs are known in the trade as Shouli gabbehs (Stone).
The Met's 'Gabbeh' of the late 19th century (22.100.66) is all wool with symmetrically knotted pile.
'Gabbeh' is a registered national and international carpet geographical indication (Fars).
Lion rugs are called gabba-ye shiri ('lion gabbeh').

says.text: Undyed-wool gabbehs are called Shouli-Gabbehs in the trade, after the town of Shul Sanger near Shiraz.
Shul is 'a village on the edge of the Bushehr province which was reputed to produce the best gabbas'; it does not say that undyed gabbehs are named after it.

rows.name: Gabbeh (modern export, from the 1980s)
rows.region: Fars (Qashqai and other weavers working for foreign markets) and, as copies, India and other countries.
rows.made_by: Qashqai and other Fars weavers for the export market; copies by commercial weavers elsewhere.
rows.date_note: Western demand from the 1980s led to commercial production; Makhmalbaf's film 'Gabbeh' (1996) added to the fashion.

structure.knot_note: As traditional gabbehs (Iranica).
structure.kpsi_note: No counts found.
structure.wefts_note: Many wefts per row, as in traditional gabbehs (Iranica; not separately measured).
structure.pile_note: Long pile.

design.field: Open color fields with small figures, trees and animals, as in traditional gabbehs; no design study of export gabbehs was found in the sources read.
design.colors: Copies are often made with synthetic dyes.

look_alikes.name: Gabbeh (traditional)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Traditional gabbehs were domestic pieces; modern ones were made to sell and many are copies made outside Iran.

rows.trade_use: 'Gabbeh' as a style name for any long-piled, open-field rug, Persian or not.
rows.what_it_tells: A gabbeh-style rug is most likely from 1980 or later and may not be Persian.
rows.cautions: Indian and other copies use the name; origin needs other evidence.

facts.text: Since the 1980s Western demand has led to commercial gabbeh production, including copies in India and elsewhere, often with synthetic dyes; some Qashqai weavers now work only for foreign markets.
Makhmalbaf's 1996 film 'Gabbeh' gave further impetus to the fashion.
Stone (2013), writing of gabbehs generally, says most are very brightly colored with synthetic dyes.

Gabbehs were long neglected by the tribes themselves; from about the 1980s-90s outside demand turned them into a commercial product, with merchants, large producers and companies commissioning and investing in new gabbehs.
facts.quote: تقریباً تا سه دهه گذشته گبه با بی توجهی ... عشایر مواجه بود ... سفارش دهندگان و تولیدکنندگان عمده ای نیز ... تولید گبه را آغاز نمودند (until about three decades ago the gabbeh was neglected ... orderers and large producers also began producing gabbehs)

facts.text: The first article on gabbehs appeared in Hali in 1983 (1362 SH) and the first book on them in 1989 (1368 SH).
facts.quote: نخستین مقاله در سال (۱۳۶۲) درباره ی گبه در مجله هالی درج گردید و در سال (۱۳۶۸) نخستین کتاب درباره ی گبه منتشر شد

rows.name: Neyriz
rows.region: The town of Neyriz and the area around Lake Neyriz (Bakhtegan), east of Shiraz, Fars.
rows.made_by: Hill-country weavers around the lake; Afshar and other tribal rugs are collected there.
rows.date_note: Old books describe 19th-century Niris; Jacobsen says no new rugs under the name for 30 years before 1962; Stone describes a minor current production.

structure.knot_note: Hawley, Lewis, Mumford, Kendrick & Tattersall: Ghiordes; May: as Shiraz (Sehna or Ghiordes); Stone (current): asymmetric.
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: horizontally 6-11, perpendicularly 7-15 = 42-165. Lewis: 40-96. Stone: 65-100.
structure.wefts_note: Twice (Hawley).
structure.pile_note: Medium (Hawley).
structure.sides: Heavy double overcasting in barber-pole or short lengths of colors (Hawley).
structure.ends: Broad web of colored stripes, one row of knots and loose fringe (Hawley); webs flatly woven in stripes, not embroidered (Hawley, Jacobsen).
structure.handle: Firmer than Shiraz (Hawley, Mumford); Jacobsen likens the back to a Bijar.
structure.back: Slightly coarse grain; warp noticeable, weft conspicuous (Hawley).

design.field: Large jewel-like botehs in rows on dark blue or ivory; sometimes lattice; tree-of-life medallion in later pieces.
design.colors: Copper or burnt orange and a sharp green; madder red.

look_alikes.name: Shiraz (market name)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Niris webs are flat-striped and the rug firmer, with one warp depressed.

look_alikes.name: Afshar
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Neyriz is a collection point for Afshar rugs.

rows.trade_use: 'Laristan' in old British trade.
rows.what_it_tells: A firm Fars rug with large botehs and flat-striped end webs is what old books call Niris.
rows.cautions: Lewis treats Niris, Laristan and Luristan as one name; Luristan is a different region.

facts.text: Niris rugs take their name from Lake Niris east of Shiraz and resemble Shiraz rugs.
Niris end webs are flatly woven in stripes of color, unlike the embroidered Shiraz webs.
facts.quote: those of the Shiraz are embroidered and crossed with one or more parti-coloured cords, whilst those of Niris pieces are, as a rule, flatly woven in stripes of different colours. (Hawley 1922, p. 119)

facts.text: Niris rugs are firmer than Shiraz, with one warp depressed.
Old Niris rugs use the Ghiordes knot on wool.
English dealers grouped Niris rugs under the name Laristan.

says.text: Ghiordes; wool warp and red wool weft.
Current production: 65-100 asymmetric knots per square inch on cotton.
Synonyms: Laristan, Luristan.
Laristan only.

rows.name: Afshar
rows.region: Mainly Kerman province: Sirjan, Shahr-e Babak, Baft, Rabor and west Jiroft, with Sirjan as market (Persian study); Afshar groups also live north of Bijar, near Zanjan, at Takab and Lake Urmia, and in Fars.
rows.made_by: Turkic Afshar tribes, nomadic and village (in Kerman also the Buchakchi, per Jacobsen).
rows.date_note: Old pieces have wool foundations; 20th-century ones often cotton (Stone; Iranica: cotton replaced wool after 1948 in the Kerman tribal area).

structure.knot_note: Jacobsen: village rugs Persian knot, tribal rugs Turkish knot. Iranica (Kerman): Turkish knot typical of tribal work. Stone does not state.
structure.kpsi_note: No count in the sources read.
structure.weft_color: Stone: pink or orange; Sirjan: blue cotton; Iranica: early pieces red wool
structure.wefts_note: Sirjan rugs double-wefted (Stone).
structure.pile_note: Medium to short (Jacobsen).

design.field: Floral central medallion with floral spandrels and opposed vases; diamond lattices of blossoms; botehs; the 'hen' design; geometricized over time.
design.colors: Red and blue with green, ivory and canary.
design.sizes: Mostly squarish, about 6.5 x 4.5 ft.

rows.what_it_tells: A squarish south Persian rug with a floral medallion and opposed vases, or a blossom lattice, with offset warps, points to Afshar weaving.
rows.cautions: 'Afshar' in Hawley (1913) means the Afshars of Lake Urmia in the northwest, a different group.

facts.text: The largest Afshar weaving group lives south of Kerman; Sirjan is a market for their rugs.
Afshar rugs are squarish; a common design is a floral medallion with opposed vases.
Old Afshar pile rugs have wool foundations and red, pink or orange wefts; later ones often cotton.
In Kerman the Turkish knot is typical of tribal production (Iranica); Jacobsen says Afshar village rugs use the Persian knot and tribal ones the Turkish.
Sirjan rugs are double-wefted with blue cotton wefts (Stone).
Sirjan Afshars weave fine soumak (weft-wrapped) rugs and bags.
Shahr-e Babak is a registered carpet geographical indication; Afshar Kerman and Sirjan are proposed.

Shahr-e Babak hand-woven carpet is a registered geographical indication, nationally (Intellectual Property Center 123 GI, 6 May 2018) and internationally (WIPO Lisbon register AO 1456, 21 May 2025); the registered area is Meymand village in Shahr-e Babak county.

The largest group is south of Kerman.
Pink or orange wefts; Sirjan: blue cotton.
Early pieces red wool wefts; elsewhere says Afshar used cotton for wefts.

rows.name: Baluch
rows.region: Khorasan (Iran) and western Afghanistan (Herat area), also Sistan; Iranica: not, as often assumed, Makran. Marketed in Mashhad, Herat and formerly Bokhara.
rows.made_by: Baluch tribes and other Khorasan groups weaving in the Baluch tradition (Timuri, Kurd, Arab, Brahui, Jamshidi, Barbari) whose rugs are sold as Baluch.
rows.date_note: Old books (1900-1922) describe 19th-century pieces; Afghan production continues, including 'war rugs' from 1979.

structure.knot_note: Asymmetric (Sehna) in Hawley, Lewis, Iranica, Stone (mostly; a very few symmetric) and museum records. Iranica: open to the left; a Persian source says 'inclined to the right'.
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: horizontally 6-9, perpendicularly 7-10 = 42-90. Lewis: 30-120. Kendrick & Tattersall: 50-65. Persian source: up to 1,600 knots per dm2 (about 103 per square inch), exceptionally 3,000 (about 194).
structure.warp_color: light-colored wool (Iranica); white wool in one Kendrick & Tattersall plate
structure.weft_color: Dark brown (Iranica, Lewis); black (Kendrick & Tattersall); coarse and wiry (Hawley)
structure.wefts_note: Two shoots (Hawley, Kendrick & Tattersall, Stone, Iranica). Persian source: old Sistan-Baluchestan prayer rugs mostly one thick wool weft. Iranica notes Edwards claimed all Baluch rugs single-wefted.
structure.pile_note: Lustrous, medium (Hawley); camel hair in some fields (Hawley, Lewis, Jacobsen).
structure.sides: Heavy goat-hair selvage of three or four cords, dark brown or black, up to 2 cm wide (Hawley, Iranica, Persian source).
structure.ends: Broad flat-woven ends, often striped or with weft-substitution patterning (Hawley, Lewis, Stone).

design.field: All-over gul-like octagons or lozenges, Mina Khani lattices, botehs, Herati variants; prayer rugs with a rectangular niche, often camel-hair field with a tree of life.
design.border: Three or four stripes; latch-hooks, reciprocal trefoils.
design.colors: Dark madder red, purplish blue, dark brown, with small sharp areas of ivory.
design.sizes: Mostly 5 x 3 to 6 x 3.5 ft; Hawley 4.5-6 ft.

look_alikes.how_to_tell: Old books classified Baluch with Turkoman rugs; Kendrick & Tattersall and Lewis note the dark blue led to the wrong name 'Blue Bokhara'.

rows.trade_use: 'Baluch' covers rugs of several Khorasan and Afghan groups; Jacobsen bought many as Afghans exported from Afghanistan.
rows.what_it_tells: A small, dark, floppy rug with asymmetric knots, a dark goat-hair edge and long flat-woven ends points to Baluch-type weaving of Khorasan or western Afghanistan; the country often cannot be told from the rug.
rows.cautions: Museum records split on country (Cleveland and Saint Louis: Iran; Rijksmuseum: Afghanistan or Iran; Met: Central Asia). Most Baluch rugs in 1920s America were chemically washed.

facts.text: Baluch pile rugs are woven by the Baluch of Khorasan in Iran and of Afghanistan, not mainly in Baluchistan proper.
Baluch rugs use the asymmetric knot.
Baluch wefts are dark wool, two shoots per row.
A heavy dark goat-hair selvage is typical.
Hawley gives 6-9 knots per inch across and 7-10 down (about 42-90 per square inch); Lewis 30-120.
Baluch rugs have long flat-woven ends.
Baluch prayer rugs often have a camel-hair field with a tree of life; Iranica says the camel color is undyed camel hair.
Before World War II Baluch rugs had wool warps; by 1960 many had cotton warps (Jacobsen).
Timuri, Kurd, Arab, Brahui, Jamshidi and Barbari groups in Khorasan also weave rugs sold as Baluch.
Ballard's 19th-century Beluchistan mat (No. 103) has Sehna knots; the OCR of the count is damaged (it reads '1 34-163' per square inch, '14-13' vertical by 11 horizontal), probably about 154-165.

says.text: Asymmetric, open to the left.

Two sinuous brown shoots; disputes Edwards, who said all are single-wefted.
Old Sistan-Baluchestan prayer rugs mostly one thick wool weft.
Cleveland 1961.385 and SLAM 110:1930, 1837:1981: Iran (Khorasan/Mashhad); Rijksmuseum BK-1975-259: Afghanistan or East Iran (possibly).
Met 22.100.12: 'Central Asia, Baluchistan'.
