rows.name: Kazak
rows.country: Azerbaijan, Armenia, Georgia (the old Kazak district of Transcaucasia)
rows.region: South-central Transcaucasia: the Kazak district and the country around Tiflis (Tbilisi), Lake Sevan and Erivan (Yerevan), north of the Araxes and south of the Kura; Hawley places the weavers on the plateau between Lake Gotcha (Sevan) and Mount Ararat; Lewis places them in the Erivan district near Ararat. Named village and design groups: Fachralo, Lori-Pambak, Borchalo (Bordjalou), Karachov, Sewan, Shikli, Lambalo, Star, Pinwheel and others.
rows.made_by: Village weavers of the region, who included Armenians, Azerbaijani Turks (Hawley's 'Tartars') and others; Hawley names Armenians, Tartars and 'the native people' in the district. Attribution of particular groups to Armenian or Azerbaijani weavers is disputed.
rows.date_note: Rugs readers are likely to own under this name were mostly woven between about 1850 and 1930. Stone's averages describe nineteenth-century rugs; Jacobsen (1962, p. 48) says few good Caucasian rugs were made after about 1915, and later rugs in the same designs came from Soviet state production (see Soviet-era Caucasian rugs ('Russian rugs')). The earliest Kazaks in museums are dated by them to the first half of the nineteenth century (Cleveland 1989.473, 1800-1850).

structure.knot_note: Symmetric (Turkish, Ghiordes) knot in every source (Hawley, Lewis 1911, Stone).
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: 'Knots to inch horizontally six to nine; perpendicularly, seven to ten' = 42-90. Lewis 1911: 36-120. Stone: 'about 40 to 60' (average about 60 for Kazaks, p. 61). Ballard 1924 records one Kazak at 63.
structure.warp_color: natural (undyed) wool; Cleveland's Kazak record: undyed wool warp
structure.weft_color: usually dyed red or brown (Hawley); 'for most rugs, wefts are dyed red or pink' (Stone); Jacobsen: 'a fine, red woolen weft thread'
structure.wefts_note: The sources disagree: Hawley says a weft generally crosses only twice, occasionally three or four times; Lewis 1911 says usually four or more; Stone says two to eight, varying within one rug. Many wefts push the pile to lie flat and open up the rows (Lewis's knot photograph shows 6 x 9 knots with wide spacing).
structure.pile_note: Long, lustrous, 'almost shaggy' (Hawley); Lewis: the many wefts make the pile lie so the side of the yarn shows.
structure.sides: A double overcasting attached figure-eight fashion, or a double selvage of three to five cords (Hawley); 'usually a wide selvage in colored wool. Occasionally overcast' (Lewis).
structure.ends: Lower end: a red or brown web and warp loops, or a braided selvage and fringe; upper end: red or brown web, sometimes a braided selvage or rows of knots, and warp fringe (Hawley). Lewis: a short colored selvage at each end, one sometimes turned back and hemmed; knotted or braided fringe.
structure.handle: Stout, thick and heavy yet soft (Hawley 'texture, stout'; Lewis 'thick and heavy though soft').
structure.back: Very coarse grain; the warps lie side by side (level), so both loops of each knot show equally (Hawley).
structure.spin: Not given for Kazaks in the sources at hand. Stone notes that many Zakatala (north-west Azerbaijan) rugs use S-spun, Z-plied yarn, the reverse of the usual Caucasian and Anatolian Z-spun yarn.

design.field: Large bold geometric medallions or octagons, often two to four in a column, or a field split into three panels; star, cross, shield and 'sunburst' medallions; many small fillers (eight-pointed stars, hooked lozenges, S-forms, small animals and people). Prayer rugs have a small square or tent-shaped niche.
design.border: Usually one dominant main border (crab, 'tarantula', wine-glass, latch-hook) between reciprocal sawtooth or trefoil guards.
design.colors: Strong reds, greens and yellows with blue, white and brown; 'a liberal amount of green is almost invariably present'. Natural dyes in older pieces; anilines in some later ones.
design.sizes: Mostly 4-6 ft x 5-8 ft, often nearly square (Lewis, Hawley 5-12 ft long, width a third to three quarters of length); Stone gives an average area of about 33 sq ft; Jacobsen: most 5 x 4, 7 x 4.5, 8 x 4.5 ft.

look_alikes.name: Kars
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kars rugs from north-east Turkey copy Kazak designs on the same all-wool foundation; Stone says Kars reds tend to burgundy rather than the Kazak brick red. Look for Turkish design elements and newer wool; structure alone may not separate them.

look_alikes.name: Gendje
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Gendje rugs are more oblong, shorter in pile and looser, with many (four to eight) wefts giving a beaded back.

look_alikes.name: Karabagh
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Karabagh rugs often have one warp of each pair depressed and often show Persian floral elements.

look_alikes.name: Soviet-era Caucasian rugs ('Russian rugs')
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Soviet-era 'Kazaks' (from about 1929) may have cotton warps and tend to be evenly woven and bright.

look_alikes.name: Yağcıbedir
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Turkish village copies, including copies of the Eagle Kazak made in the Yağcıbedir area, are dark blue and red with plaited warp ends.

rows.trade_use: 'Kazak' is used in the trade for almost any coarse, long-piled, boldly geometric south Caucasian rug, and today also for new rugs in Kazak designs woven in Turkey, Iran, Afghanistan and Pakistan.
rows.what_it_tells: A rug that matches this type (all wool, symmetric knots, level warps, red wefts, long glossy pile, big geometric medallions) points to the south-central Caucasus, most likely nineteenth or early twentieth century.
rows.cautions: The name has been used loosely since at least Hawley's day: 'many inferior rugs of other tribes have been sold as Kazaks'. Turkish (Kars, Yağcıbedir), Persian and modern Afghan/Pakistani rugs are woven in Kazak designs. Village sub-names (Fachralo, Lori-Pambak and others) are design labels, not proof of village origin.

facts.text: Kazak rugs are woven with the symmetric (Ghiordes) knot on an all-wool foundation.
facts.quote: Knot, Ghiordes. Knots to inch horizontally six to nine; perpendicularly, seven to ten.

facts.text: Kazaks are coarsely knotted: about 40 to 60 symmetric knots per square inch on average (Stone), 42-90 (Hawley), 36-120 and 'fewer than any of the other Caucasian fabrics' (Lewis 1911).
facts.quote: number to square inch thirty-six to one hundred twenty. Fewer than any of the other Caucasian fabrics.

facts.text: The wefts are wool and usually dyed red (or brown/pink).
facts.quote: Weft, wool, of coarse diameter, usually dyed red or brown.

facts.text: Kazak pile is long and lustrous; only the Tcherkess rugs rival them in length of pile.
facts.quote: Only the Tcherkess vie with them in the length of the nap

facts.text: Green is used more freely in Kazaks than in most other Caucasian rugs.
facts.quote: They have bright, rich colours, of which a liberal amount of green is almost invariably present

facts.text: The Kazak region lies north of the Araxes and south of the Kura and includes Tiflis and Erivan; Stone says the average Kazak covers about 33 square feet.
Stone's named Kazak design groups include Borjalou, Fachralo, Karachov, Lambalo, Lori Pambak, Pinwheel, Sevan, Shield, Shikli, Star and Tree Kazaks.
Echmiadzin, Erivan, Dilijan and Shamshadin (Shamshadnee) are places whose nineteenth-century rugs are classified as Kazaks.
The Azerbaijani state's 2010 UNESCO nomination lists the Kazakh region (Gedebek, Geranboy, Kazakh, Shamkir, Tovuz) among Azerbaijan's carpet regions.
Jacobsen (1962) says new Kazaks woven under the Soviet five-year plans began using cotton warps, which allows finer weaving.

The 'sunburst' medallion is found on some Kazaks; Hawley calls it characteristic of Tcherkess rugs, Jacobsen says such rugs are really Kazaks, and Stone classes the design (Chelaberd, Eagle Kazak) under Karabagh.
Azerbaijani scholars extend the Kazak group well beyond the Kazakh district: north to Tiflis (Lambalı, Muganlı, Karayazı, Borçalı, Kaçağan) and south-west along the shore of Lake Sevan (Göyçe).
facts.quote: "'Kazak' adı ile bir çok bölgeye yayılmış halılarımız" ('our rugs spread over many districts under the name Kazak')

facts.text: Isaev's 1929-31 survey divides the Kazak group into Kazak proper (the Dashsalahly, Salahly and Akstafa clusters), Tauz, and Borchalo-Karayaz in Georgia (with Lembalo and Karachop), and lists the carpets of Lori, Pambak, Ijevan-Shamshadin and Zangezur as a separate 'Armenian' group.

Under early Soviet direction, weaving in Armenia and western Azerbaijan was moved from the coarse, thick-yarn, long-piled Kazak type toward the finer, short-piled Kuba-Shirvan type, and new Kazaks became finer than old ones.

Sixteen dated Kazak, Lori-Pambak and Akstafa-design rugs (1886 to 1938, most from 1904-1929) in one catalogue have all-wool foundations of Z-spun, S-plied yarn, symmetric knots of about 36-64 per square inch, and usually two (sometimes one to four) wefts between rows.

says.text: A thread of weft generally crosses only twice between every two rows of knots, but occasionally three or four times.
A characteristic feature is the number of weft threads between each row of knots, usually four or more.
From two to eight wefts between rows of knots, varying within the same rug.
Derives the name from Cossack settlers ('Kazaks'), the word meaning 'marauder' to the Tartars.
'A corruption of the word Cossack'; woven by 'Cossack nomads'.
Most rug books derive the name from 'Cossacks', 'which is not the case at all'.
Says the Kazak district also held 'Armenians, Tartars, and the native people'.
Rugs with Armenian inscriptions come mostly from the Caucasus, Caucasian rugs with Western (AD) dates are probably Armenian, and Echmiadzin and Erivan rugs are classified as Kazaks.
Azerbaijan's UNESCO nomination counts the Kazakh region as one of the regions of the Azerbaijani carpet.
Woven in western Azerbaijan and in towns and villages of northern Armenia and southern Georgia; the weavers 'probably mostly Azerbaijanian Turks', though Armenians and Georgians also took part.
The majority of rugs called Kazak come from the Lake Sevan region of Armenia (Lori-Pembak, Karachoph, Gendje); their dated rugs carry Armenian inscriptions.
'Kazakh' (Gardman), 'Borchalu' (Gugark) and 'Lembalu' are distorted names given to Armenian rugs; Isaev named Armenians and Lezgins as the indigenous holders of the highest weaving forms.
Kazak and Borçalı rugs are Karapapak (Terekeme) Turkish rugs of the Azerbaijani Gence-Kazah group.

facts.text: Fachralo rugs are classed as Kazaks; many have a medallion made of a horizontal rectangle laid over a lozenge (a ten-sided figure), the prayer format is common, density averages about 64 symmetric knots per square inch and area about 23 square feet (Stone, p. 106).

Fachralo rugs are often prayer rugs with a single large medallion.
In Borçalı the Fachralo design is called 'Kurbağalı' or 'Kurbağaoğlu' (the frog) for its medallion with arms.

structure.wefts_note: As for Kazaks generally; Stone gives two to eight wefts in Kazaks.

rows.what_it_tells: The design points to the Kazak group; the village name is an attribution by design, not a certificate of where the rug was made.

facts.text: The Lori Pambak motif is a large octagonal medallion filled with two pairs of opposed calyxes joined at the base; Stone says it evolved from an Anatolian medallion, is still used by Turkish and Kurdish weavers around Kars, and that nineteenth-century Kazaks with it average about 64 knots per square inch and 23 square feet (Stone, p. 178).
Lori and Pambak (Bambaki) appear as weaving districts in Isaev's 1929-31 survey, which lists villages for each (Lori: Ardvi, Bert, Ledzhan, Agarak; Bambaki: Shokh, Uzunlyar, Akhpat, Dseg).
Two dated Lori-Pambak Kazaks (1914; 1919-1938) are all wool with symmetric knots of about 36 and 56 per square inch and two wefts.

says.text: Lori and Pambak belong to the group of 'Armenian carpets', not to the Kazak group.
Loru-Pembek is a production center of the (Azerbaijani) Kazakh group, on the territory of the Republic of Armenia.
Lori-Pembak Kazaks are Armenian rugs of the Sevan region; their examples carry Armenian dates.

facts.text: Borjalou rugs are classed as Kazaks; they often have broad zigzag borders with latch hooks on both sides, are the most coarsely knotted Kazak design type (about 52 knots per square inch), average about 35 square feet, about half have red wefts, and blue-wefted examples are later (Stone, p. 52).
The name Borchalo comes from the Borchalu, a Turkic tribe settled in the district by Shah Abbas I in the early seventeenth century.
Borchalo rugs are heavy and long-piled: Kerimov gives 30x30 to 35x35 knots per 10 cm (about 58-79 per square inch), pile 8-12 mm, in medium and large sizes (100 x 150 to 180 x 300 cm).
facts.quote: "30x30 ile 35x35 arasında değişmektedir"

facts.text: Azerbaijani scholarship (Kerimov, Muradov) names five Borchalo compositions: Çobankərə, Qurbağalı, Ziynətnişan (Zeyvənişan) and two called Lembəli.
One Borchalo pattern is called 'tamgaly' or 'damgalı' (with brands or tribal marks).

says.text: The most coarsely knotted Kazak design type, about 52 knots per square inch.
30x30 to 35x35 knots per 10 cm (about 58-79 per square inch), citing Kerimov.
Borchalo rugs are Karapapak (Terekeme) Turkish rugs; Borçalı was split between Armenia and Georgia in 1918-1920.
'Borchalu' is a distorted name for Armenian rugs of the historic Armenian district of Gugark.

facts.text: Karachov rugs are classed as Kazaks and have a large central octagon with two rectangles above and two below (a 2-1-2 layout), a design Stone thinks is Turkish in origin; they average about 39 square feet and 60 knots per square inch (Stone, p. 149).
The Karachov layout is a large central octagon or square with four smaller square medallions around it, two above and two below.
facts.quote: "four small corner medallions to balance a large square or cruciform central one" (Gregorian)

facts.text: Weavers call the Karachov design 'yaşıllı' ('the green one'), because the ground is dark blue and often green.
facts.quote: "yerli dokumacılar bu halılara 'yaşıllı' adı vermişler" ('local weavers named these rugs yaşıllı')

facts.text: Karachov rugs come from a cluster of villages in Georgia south of Tiflis (Tüller, Lembəli, Muğanlı), counted in the Borchalo-Karayaz part of the Kazak group.

says.text: Karachop center (Tiullyar, Lembalo) in the Borchalo-Karayaz cluster, Georgia.
Karachoph is a village near Lake Sevan in Armenia.
The design is thought to be Turkish in origin.

The central medallion suggests the floor plan of a traditional Armenian church.

facts.text: Sevan (Sewan, Shield) Kazaks have field medallions in various cruciform shapes; the design is also found in rugs attributed to Kuba and Shirvan; Kazak examples average 58 knots per square inch and 34 square feet, are all wool, and about 70 percent have red wefts (Stone, p. 256).
The Art Institute of Chicago catalogues a 'Sewan Kazak Rug' of about 1875 as wool pile on a wool foundation.
Stone also uses the name 'Shield Kazak' for a different design: an all-over pattern of diagonally arranged shield-shaped motifs, also found in some Shirvans (p. 260).

says.text: 'The boldest and most primitive' Kazaks are from the Sevan district; most rugs called Kazak come from the Lake Sevan region of Armenia.

rows.name: Karabagh
rows.country: Azerbaijan (the region also has an Armenian population and is claimed in Armenian tradition as Artsakh)
rows.region: The mountainous Karabagh region south-east of Lake Sevan and north of the Araxes, in the south of the former Elisavetpol (Ganja) province; capital and rug market Shusha. Design groups: Chelaberd (Eagle), Chondzoresk (Cloudband), Kasim Ushag, Lampa, Goradis, and Persian-style Herati and boteh carpets.
rows.made_by: Village and town weavers of Karabagh, both Armenian and Azerbaijani (attribution of particular groups is disputed). Hawley also mentions 'desert tribes' around Shusha.
rows.date_note: Rugs readers are likely to own under this name were mostly woven between about 1850 and 1930. Stone's averages describe nineteenth-century rugs; Jacobsen (1962, p. 48) says few good Caucasian rugs were made after about 1915, and later rugs in the same designs came from Soviet state production (see Soviet-era Caucasian rugs ('Russian rugs')). Hawley (1913) describes then-current Karabaghs as coarse and poorly dyed and contrasts them with pieces 'woven half a century ago'.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric knot (Hawley, Lewis, Stone).
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: horizontally six to ten, perpendicularly seven to ten = 42-100. Lewis 1911: 30-120. Stone: average about 65.
structure.wefts_note: Hawley: two wefts of medium or coarse wool; Lewis: 'generally several strands between each row of knots'.
structure.pile_note: Short to medium (Hawley) or 'long, heavy wool or camels' hair' (Lewis).
structure.sides: Generally a double selvage of two or three cords in lengths of different colors; sometimes a double overcasting attached figure-eight fashion (Hawley). Lewis: antiques usually selvaged, moderns overcast in colored wool.
structure.ends: Lower end: web and warp loops, or braided selvage, rows of knots and fringe; upper end: a web, often turned back and hemmed (Hawley, Lewis).
structure.handle: Loose (Hawley); Lewis: coarsely woven and carelessly knotted.
structure.back: Coarse grain; one warp of each pair depressed below the other (Hawley).

design.field: Very varied: Persian-derived floral designs (Herati, boteh, roses) and Caucasian medallion designs (Chelaberd 'Eagle', Chondzoresk 'Cloudband', Kasim Ushag, Lampa). Prayer rugs occasionally have stepped niches.
design.border: Often one Persian-style and one Caucasian stripe together; crab and running-vine borders.
design.colors: Red, blue, yellow and white; Stone notes cochineal in Shusha rugs.
design.sizes: Often long: Stone says Karabaghs are typically the largest Caucasian rugs, averaging about 41 square feet in a long format; Hawley says older sedjadehs are often nearly twice as long as wide.

look_alikes.name: Kazak
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kazaks have level warps and heavier, stouter weave; Hawley says Karabaghs have one warp of each pair depressed and are looser and lighter.

look_alikes.name: Gendje
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Gendje rugs have many wefts and a beaded back; Karabaghs usually two.

look_alikes.name: Shusha
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Hawley says Shusha rugs are stouter, with one warp doubled beneath the other rather than merely depressed.

rows.trade_use: Used for south-east Caucasian rugs of Karabagh, including the Chelaberd ('Eagle Kazak') and Chondzoresk ('Cloudband Kazak') groups that the trade often calls Kazaks. Hawley notes many were taken to Tabriz for sale; Persian 'Karadagh' rugs from across the Araxes are similar.
rows.what_it_tells: A coarse, symmetric-knotted all-wool rug with a depressed warp, a long format and Persian-influenced floral or Eagle/Cloudband medallion designs points to Karabagh.
rows.cautions: Stone and others note the Karabagh/Kazak boundary in trade names is blurred ('Eagle Kazak' is a Karabagh design). Persian Karadagh and Heriz-area rugs use similar designs.

facts.text: Karabagh rugs are coarsely woven with the symmetric knot, averaging about 65 knots per square inch (Stone); Hawley gives 42-100 and Lewis 30-120.
facts.quote: Knot, Ghiordes. Knots to inch horizontally six to ten; perpendicularly, seven to ten.

facts.text: In Karabagh rugs one warp of each pair is depressed below the other, unlike Kazaks.
facts.quote: one of the two threads encircled by a knot is depressed

facts.text: Karabagh rugs tend to be the largest Caucasian rugs, in a long format averaging about 41 square feet.
Shusha is the capital and rug market of Karabagh.
facts.quote: Shusha, capital of Karabagh

facts.text: One end of a Karabagh is often finished with a web turned back and hemmed.
facts.quote: Short webs, one of which is generally turned back and hemmed.

facts.text: Karabagh lies just across the Araxes from Persia, and Hawley says many of its rugs were taken to Tabriz.
Much of nineteenth-century Shusha production is thought to have been woven by Armenians (Stone); the Azerbaijani UNESCO nomination counts Karabagh, with Shusha, among Azerbaijan's carpet regions.
Azerbaijani museum scholarship gives Karabagh pile rugs 30x30 to 40x40 knots per 10 cm (90,000-160,000 per square meter, about 58-103 per square inch).
facts.quote: "Karabağ halılarının ilme sıklığı 30x30'dan 40x40'a kadardır"

facts.text: Isaev's 1929-31 survey divides Karabagh into Shusha city, the villages of Nagorno-Karabakh, the 'Kurdistan' villages (Muradkhanly, Kasim-Ushagy, Kubatly), Khanlyg, Jebrail (Jebrail, Goradiz, Bahmanly) and the lowland near the Kura.

says.text: A thread of weft crosses twice between every two rows of knots.
Generally several strands between each row of knots.
Much of the rug production of Shusha in nineteenth-century Karabagh is thought to have been woven by Armenians.
The Azerbaijani nomination lists the Karabagh region (Bard, Jebrail, Agdam, Fizuli and Shusha) as a region of the Azerbaijani carpet.
Most people of Karabagh remained Armenian; the 'Dragon', 'Cloudband' and 'Eagle' rugs, which Armenians call vishapagorg, are a typically Armenian form of Karabagh weaving.

Isaev (1932) wrote that the valuable rugs of the Karabagh Armenians were known on the world market as 'armenian carpets'; Babenchikov (1948) called Shusha the largest center, where the best Armenian weavers worked.
Reports the dispute: Azerbaijan regards the Karabagh carpet as its own, Armenia and Karabagh as Armenian.
Karabagh is one of the groups of Azerbaijani carpets (Azerbaijan Carpet Museum view).

facts.text: Chelaberd ('Eagle', 'Sunburst', 'Adler' Kazak) rugs are nineteenth-century Karabagh rugs with a lozenge medallion with parallel radiating arms and outward-facing hooked brackets above and below; the design is thought to derive from Dragon carpets, and seventeenth-century Caucasian carpets show this medallion; they average about 60 knots per square inch and 35 square feet, with an all-wool foundation (Stone, p. 66).
Hawley called rugs with these 'sunburst' medallions Tcherkess (Circassian) rugs: tawny-red fields, long pile, very firm weave, two wefts (sometimes four to six), a heavy braided selvage at the ends.
facts.quote: diamond-shaped figures sometimes called "sun bursts," that are often regarded as crude copies of the Russian coat of arms

facts.text: Lewis (1911) calls the 'Palace' or 'Sunburst' field design common in Kazaks (and Shirvans) and says the Russian coat of arms is common in Kazak designs.
Jacobsen says the 'Sunburst' design 'which some collectors call Tcherkess' is really a Kazak.
The Eagle (Chelaberd) design, long sold as a Kazak, is now classed with Karabagh rugs.
facts.quote: "the well-known Eagle and Cloudband Kazakh patterns are now claimed for Karabagh" (Britannica)

facts.text: Armenian writers treat the Eagle design as one family of vishapagorg (Վիշապագորգ, 'dragon carpet') and point to many examples with Armenian inscriptions.

says.text: Tcherkess (Circassian) rugs, distinct from Kazaks though constantly mistaken for them; the medallions derived from Armenian rugs of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries.
The sunburst rugs some collectors call Tcherkess are really Kazaks.
Chelaberd is a Karabagh design; 'Eagle Kazak' is a trade name; the design is thought to derive from Dragon carpets.
'Chalaberd' is a distortion of Jraberd (Ջրաբերդ), a district of Artsakh (Karabagh).
The design is the Karabakh-school 'Berde' carpet, popularly called 'Çelebi' and in Europe 'Kartal' (eagle).
One of the 'new definitive names' coined in the Caucasus; the Eagle Kazakh pattern is now claimed for Karabagh.

facts.text: Chondzoresk ('Cloudband Kazak') rugs have one or more medallions containing motifs like cloudbands; mean density 58 knots per square inch; the smallest Karabagh rugs, averaging 33 square feet (Stone, p. 71).
The Cloudband design, once classed as a Kazak, is now attributed to Karabagh.
facts.quote: "once called 'cloudband' and until recently was considered a member of the Kazak family" (Gregorian)

facts.text: Khndzoresk ('Khdozoresk') in Zangezur was a carpet-weaving village in Isaev's 1929-31 survey, listed in his group of Armenian carpets.

Five cloudband rugs (four dated, 1898-1918) are all wool with Z-spun, S-plied yarn, two wefts, and about 42-81 knots per square inch; Armenians count the design as a vishapagorg (dragon carpet), its 'dragons' drawn like stylized roosters in confronted pairs.

facts.text: Lampa is a nineteenth-century Karabagh design with eight-lobed medallions alternating with flattened rectangular medallions in a column; these rugs have the longest format of Karabagh rugs (length about 3.7 times width) and about 60 knots per square inch (Stone, p. 172).
Lampa (Lempe, Azerbaijani Lamba) rugs often have cotton in the warp or weft, especially early ones, and pairs of large confronted birds beside the medallions.
facts.quote: "The use of cotton for warp and/or weft is a feature of many early 'Lempe' rugs."

facts.text: Lampa (Lamba) is counted among the principal compositions of the Karabagh group in Azerbaijani classification, and Kerimov places these rugs in the Shusha region.

Goradiz (Horadiz) is a village of the Jebrail district of southern Karabagh, named as a weaving village in Isaev's 1929-31 survey.

says.text: A staggered, angular comet-shaped motif that may derive from the boteh.
The 1932 approved design from Goradiz village is a gyaba 'with stylized pictorial scorpions'.
Karabagh masters formerly called the 'Buynuz' (horn) carpets 'Horadiz'.

rows.name: Shusha
rows.region: The town of Shusha, capital of Karabagh, and its suburbs; a market for the surrounding villages.
rows.made_by: Town and village weavers; Stone says much of Shusha's nineteenth-century production is thought to have been woven by Armenians; large rugs were woven on commission.
rows.date_note: Stone describes nineteenth-century production; Hawley (1913) knew Shushas as a current import 'sold under several names'.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric knot (Hawley).
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: horizontally seven to twelve, perpendicularly six to eleven = 42-132.
structure.wefts_note: Hawley: two wefts of medium wool.
structure.pile_note: medium
structure.sides: Double selvage of two or three cords, often attached figure-eight fashion (Hawley).
structure.ends: Lower end: narrow web and warp loops; upper end: a web sometimes turned back and hemmed, and fringe (Hawley).
structure.handle: Moderately firm; stouter than other Karabaghs (Hawley).
structure.back: Slightly coarse grain; one warp of each pair is doubled beneath the other, whereas in the rugs of the surrounding tribes it is only depressed (Hawley).

design.field: Persian-derived designs: boteh, mina khani and Herati; also Karabagh medallion designs.
design.colors: Dark blue, red and brown with green and yellow; cochineal reds in many.
design.sizes: 4-9 ft long; large rugs on commission.

look_alikes.name: Karabagh
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Shushas have one warp doubled beneath the other and richer, more subdued colors; village Karabaghs have it only depressed.

rows.trade_use: Rarely used as a trade name today; such rugs are usually sold as Karabagh.
rows.what_it_tells: A Karabagh-type rug with a deeply depressed warp and finer, stouter weave in Persian floral designs is consistent with Shusha town work.
rows.cautions: Hawley says Shusha rugs were sold under several names; the attribution of Shusha production to Armenian or Azerbaijani weavers is contested.

facts.text: Shusha rugs have one warp of each pair doubled beneath the other, unlike the merely depressed warps of the surrounding rugs.
facts.quote: One thread of warp to each knot is doubled beneath the other, whereas in the rugs of the desert tribes it is only depressed.

facts.text: Shusha was noted for high-quality, large production in the nineteenth century, including large rugs woven on commission, with boteh, mina khani and Herati designs and cochineal dye.
Shusha is the capital of Karabagh.
Stone says Dragon carpets, first thought to come from Kuba, are now believed to have originated in Shusha (p. 93).
Shusha's town carpets were large, specially commissioned pieces, unlike Karabagh country rugs.
Dragon carpets were attributed to Kuba in the first half of the twentieth century; later scholars moved them to the Karabagh area.
facts.quote: "now thought to have originated somewhere in the Karabagh or Genje region" (Britannica)

says.text: Much of the rug production of Shusha in nineteenth-century Karabagh is thought to have been woven by Armenians.
Lists Shusha among the localities of the Karabagh region of the Azerbaijani carpet (noting its weavers are 'now relocated to Baku').
Now believed to have originated in Shusha.
Somewhere in the Karabagh or Genje region.
An older Britannica entry still calls them 'the most numerous group of the Kuba carpets'.
Azerbaijani view: woven in the Kuba, Shirvan and Karabagh centers of northern Azerbaijan; Kerimov classes them as 'Hatayi' compositions; the authors report that Wright and Wertime argue for Tabriz.
Armenians call these patterns vishapagorg; the Armenian claim to have originated them 'has been argued over the years'.
Cites Babenchikov (1948): Shusha was the largest center of fine carpets, where the best Armenian weavers worked.
Shusha city is listed as the first subarea of the Karabagh group, with no ethnic attribution.

museum_examples.title: Dragon Carpet
museum_examples.shows: Museum record: present-day Azerbaijan; wool, symmetric knots. A classical Dragon carpet (the group Stone says is now believed to come from Shusha); not a nineteenth-century Shusha rug. Image: front.

rows.name: Gendje
rows.region: The city and former khanate of Ganja (Elisavetpol under Russia, Kirovabad under Soviet rule) and the country around it between the Kazak district and Karabagh; Hawley says the rugs were marketed at the yearly fair of Elisavetpol.
rows.made_by: Village and semi-nomadic weavers 'of mixed origin'; Lewis records a claim that they were woven by a nomad tribe called Genghis.
rows.date_note: Rugs readers are likely to own under this name were mostly woven between about 1850 and 1930. Stone's averages describe nineteenth-century rugs; Jacobsen (1962, p. 48) says few good Caucasian rugs were made after about 1915, and later rugs in the same designs came from Soviet state production (see Soviet-era Caucasian rugs ('Russian rugs')).

structure.knot_note: Symmetric knot (Hawley, Lewis).
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: horizontally six to eight, perpendicularly six to nine = 36-72. Lewis 1911: 30-80. Stone: about 57.
structure.warp_color: brown wool, occasionally goat hair (Hawley); 'a three-strand thread of brown wool or goats' hair' (Lewis)
structure.weft_color: usually dyed red (Hawley); gray or brown, frequently dyed (Lewis)
structure.wefts_note: Hawley: generally three and often six or eight wefts between rows, so the weft band can be up to four times as wide as a row of knots and looks beaded.
structure.pile_note: medium length (Hawley), 'rather long' (Lewis)
structure.sides: Double selvage of two to four cords (Hawley); selvaged or overcast with colored wool (Lewis).
structure.ends: Lower end: a web, usually red, and warp loops; upper end: a web often with a braided selvage, and fringe (Hawley).
structure.back: Coarse grain with conspicuous bead-like bands of weft between the knot rows (Hawley).

design.field: No single design: diagonal stripes (often with boteh), lattices, all-over Memling guls, hooked lozenges and tarantula figures, much ivory.
design.colors: Often much ivory, otherwise like Karabagh.
design.sizes: 5-9 ft long, oblong; average about 31 sq ft, longer format than Kazaks.

look_alikes.name: Kazak
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Gendjes are more oblong, shorter in pile and less stoutly woven, with four to eight wefts between rows, against generally two in Kazaks.

rows.trade_use: Used for coarse south Caucasian rugs between Kazak and Karabagh, especially with diagonal stripes.
rows.what_it_tells: A loose, Kazak-like rug with many wefts showing as beaded bands on the back points to the Gendje group.
rows.cautions: 'There is no characteristic pattern'; Jacobsen calls the name one most dealers cannot define.

facts.text: Gendje rugs resemble Kazaks but are more oblong, shorter in pile and less stoutly woven, with four to eight wefts between rows of knots.
facts.quote: in these rugs a thread of weft crosses from four to eight times between two rows of knots, which are not firmly pressed down

facts.text: Gendje rugs have several wefts between rows and are coarsely woven.

Nineteenth-century Genje rugs are similar to Kazaks, may have a longer format, often show diagonal stripes with botehs, Memling guls or lattices, average about 57 knots per square inch and 31 square feet.
Ganja became Elisavetpol under Russia and Kirovabad under Soviet rule, and has reverted to Ganja.
Gendje rugs are often long, narrower rugs than Kazaks, and show features of both Kazak and Karabagh rugs.
Gendje designs are most often octagons, stars or three geometric medallions on the long axis, in blue, dark blue and madder red; old Gendjes are all wool, newer ones have cotton foundations.

says.text: Authorities differ: some say the name should be Guenja, the ancient name of Elizabethpol; others that Genghis is the name of a nomad tribe near Elizabethpol.
The name comes from Ganja (Gengha), the city where the nomads' rugs were marketed.
Named after the city and khanate of Genje.
Four to eight wefts between rows of knots.
Six Gendje rugs dated from 1858 on have two or three weft shots, Z-spun S-plied wool, 36-81 knots per square inch.

rows.name: Moghan
rows.region: The Moghan plain south-east of the Caucasus range, bordering Iran and Talish.
rows.made_by: Village and formerly semi-nomadic weavers of the plain (Stone names no group; the Shahsavan of Iranian Moghan are a separate weaving group).
rows.date_note: Rugs readers are likely to own under this name were mostly woven between about 1850 and 1930. Stone's averages describe nineteenth-century rugs; Jacobsen (1962, p. 48) says few good Caucasian rugs were made after about 1915, and later rugs in the same designs came from Soviet state production (see Soviet-era Caucasian rugs ('Russian rugs')).

structure.knot_note: Symmetric knot (Stone).
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: typically about 72 knots per square inch.
structure.wefts_note: Not given for this group; two or more wefts is the Caucasian norm (Stone, p. 61).
structure.sides: not recorded in the sources at hand
structure.ends: not recorded in the sources at hand

design.field: Memling guls in rows or hooked medallions.
design.sizes: About 33 sq ft, about twice as long as wide.

look_alikes.name: Talish
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Talish rugs are long with empty or near-empty fields; Moghans have rows of Memling guls.

look_alikes.name: Gendje
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Gendjes also use Memling guls but are looser with many wefts.

rows.trade_use: A collector's attribution for south-east Caucasian rugs with Memling guls.
rows.what_it_tells: Rows of hooked Memling guls on a long-format symmetric-knotted rug point to Moghan or neighboring groups.
rows.cautions: Single source for this group's structure.

facts.text: Moghan rugs usually have Memling guls or hooked medallions, about 72 knots per square inch, average about 33 square feet, and are about twice as long as wide.
Two dated Moghan rugs (1900, 1928) with repeated rows of gul-like medallions are all wool, with 56-64 symmetric knots per square inch and two or three wefts.
Kendrick & Tattersall (1922) list 'Moghan' and 'Talish' among names the trade gave to Shirvan carpets.
facts.quote: "Carpets of this kind are known in the trade also as Moghan, Talish, Daghestan"

says.text: 'So-called Mughan carpets' are made in Karadon village, Salyan area (lowland Shirvan).
Places the Moghan district on the southern (Iranian) side of the Araxes and calls their Moghan rugs 'from Dasht-i-Moghan'.

rows.name: Talish
rows.region: The Talish area of the south-eastern Caucasus on the Caspian, bordering Iran; Lenkoran (Lankaran) was the capital of the khanate.
rows.made_by: Village weavers of Talish (Stone names no group).
rows.date_note: Rugs readers are likely to own under this name were mostly woven between about 1850 and 1930. Stone's averages describe nineteenth-century rugs; Jacobsen (1962, p. 48) says few good Caucasian rugs were made after about 1915, and later rugs in the same designs came from Soviet state production (see Soviet-era Caucasian rugs ('Russian rugs')).

structure.knot_note: Symmetric knot (Stone).
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: about 83 for Talish rugs; about 69 for Talish rugs with the Lenkoran medallion.
structure.wefts_note: Not given; see Caucasian norm.
structure.pile_note: short (Jacobsen puts Talish among the thin, short-piled Caucasian rugs)
structure.sides: not recorded in the sources at hand
structure.ends: not recorded in the sources at hand

design.field: Long format; many have empty or almost empty fields (often blue), others the Lenkoran medallion; main border of a large blossom alternating with four small florets.
design.border: Large blossom alternating with four florets.
design.sizes: About 30 sq ft, shape ratio about 2.2.

look_alikes.name: Moghan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Moghans have rows of Memling guls; Talish fields are often plain.

rows.trade_use: Collector's name for long south-east Caucasian rugs with open fields or Lenkoran medallions; Stone notes 'Lambalo' Kazaks have similar designs.
rows.what_it_tells: A long rug with a plain field and the blossom-and-floret border points to Talish.
rows.cautions: Structural detail rests on one source; Jacobsen says few dealers could define the name in his day.

facts.text: Talish rugs tend to have a long format, many with empty fields; Lenkoran is the major city; many have a main border of a large blossom alternating with four florets; density about 83 knots per square inch, area about 30 square feet, shape ratio about 2.24.
Jacobsen groups Talish with the thin, finely woven, short-piled Caucasian rugs.
The Lenkoran medallion may be a geometricized calyx or derived from a dragon motif; Talish rugs with it average about 69 knots per square inch; it also appears on Kazak and Karabagh rugs.
Talish rugs are long and narrow, and many have a plain dark blue field.
facts.quote: "Talysh rugs may have a perfectly plain field of dark blue" (Britannica)

facts.text: Isaev's 1929-31 survey places Talish weaving in Lenkoran district, naming the villages Assaly, Adzhiismailly, Seidbazar, Dzheferly, Astanly and Zokup.

says.text: 'Talish' was also a trade name given to Shirvan carpets (plates 120B-126).
Talish is an independent branch, woven in Lenkoran district.

rows.name: Shirvan
other_names: Shemakha (old books, for pile rugs of the Shemakha area)
rows.region: The former khanate of Shirvan in the central-eastern Caucasus, south of Daghestan and Kuba, from the Caspian to the Kur, capital Shemakha; marketed at Baku. Named groups: Marasali, Bijov, Akstafa, Chajli, Afshan.
rows.made_by: Village weavers of Shirvan; Lewis (1911) says 'Lesgie tribes'.
rows.date_note: Rugs readers are likely to own under this name were mostly woven between about 1850 and 1930. Stone's averages describe nineteenth-century rugs; Jacobsen (1962, p. 48) says few good Caucasian rugs were made after about 1915, and later rugs in the same designs came from Soviet state production (see Soviet-era Caucasian rugs ('Russian rugs')).

structure.knot_note: Symmetric knot (Hawley, Lewis, Stone).
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: horizontally seven to twelve, perpendicularly eight to twelve = 56-144. Lewis 1911: 30-108. Stone: typically about 113.
structure.warp_color: white or gray wool, sometimes brown; occasionally cotton or goat hair (Lewis)
structure.wefts_note: Hawley: two wefts, generally wool, occasionally cotton; Stone: wool warps with cotton or wool wefts; Lewis notes some wefts of cotton and wool strands twisted together, which makes the rug pucker when wet.
structure.pile_note: short or medium
structure.sides: Generally a weft selvage of two or three cords or a double selvage, occasionally a double overcasting (Hawley); overcast or selvaged (Lewis).
structure.ends: A web, one or more rows of knots and a warp fringe (Hawley); 'an extra large fringe of loose or knotted warp threads' (Lewis).

design.field: Small-scale geometric fields: rows of stylized flowers, lattices, medallions and stars like Daghestan designs; a 'pole medallion' of linked octagonal compartments; many prayer rugs with a lattice or rows of blossoms.
design.border: Three to five stripes; the serrated leaf and wine-glass border is 'almost typical'; carnation guards.
design.colors: Blue, red, ivory; wide range including ivory fields.
design.sizes: 4-6 ft long; average about 28 sq ft.

look_alikes.name: Daghestan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Hawley says Daghestans are more finely and evenly woven with shorter pile and more regular knots; Lewis says Daghestans always have wool warps.

look_alikes.name: Kuba
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kubas usually have blue selvages and blue herringbone-woven ends and are finer.

look_alikes.name: Baku
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Bakus have dull light blue and tan colors and large rectangular botehs.

rows.trade_use: One of the most used Caucasian trade names; applied broadly to finely knotted, short-piled east Caucasian rugs with small geometric designs. Persian Ardebil and Meshkin rugs are woven in Shirvan designs.
rows.what_it_tells: A short-piled, symmetric-knotted rug with wool warps, wool or cotton wefts and small-scale geometric or prayer designs points to the east Caucasus.
rows.cautions: Jacobsen and Stone both say the Daghestan / Shirvan / Kuba boundary often cannot be fixed for a particular rug. Iranian Ardebil rugs copy these designs.

facts.text: Shirvan rugs are symmetric-knotted on wool warps, with wool or cotton wefts.
facts.quote: Warp, wool; each of the two threads encircled by a knot is equally prominent at back. Weft, generally wool, occasionally cotton

facts.text: Nineteenth-century Shirvan rugs average about 113 knots per square inch and 28 square feet (Stone); Hawley gives 56-144.
Stone's named Shirvan design types are Afshan, Akstafa, Bijov, Chajli and Marasali.
The serrated-leaf and wine-glass border is so common in Shirvans that Hawley calls it almost typical of them.
Jacobsen says it is often impossible to decide between Daghestan, Shirvan, Kubistan or Kuba for a particular rug.
Pile rugs of the Shemakha area were sometimes sold by dealers as 'Royal Daghestans' (Hawley).

Rugs of the eastern Caucasus (Daghestan, Kuba, Shirvan) are often hard to assign to one group; small Shirvans share field designs and borders, and one type of Shirvan prayer rug was long sold as a Daghestan.

says.text: 56-144 knots per square inch (horizontally seven to twelve, perpendicularly eight to twelve).
30-108 knots per square inch.
Typically about 113 knots per square inch.
Akstafa and Chajli are Shirvan design types.
Akstafa and Chaily are clusters of the Kazak group (Kazak proper), not Shirvan.
Illustrates a 'Shirvan rug of the Akstafa type'.

rows.name: Marasali
rows.region: A village south of Shemakha in Shirvan; the Azerbaijani UNESCO nomination lists Maraza among Shirvan-region localities.
rows.made_by: Village weavers of Shirvan.
rows.date_note: Stone's figures describe nineteenth-century rugs of this design. Rugs readers are likely to own under this name were mostly woven between about 1850 and 1930. Stone's averages describe nineteenth-century rugs; Jacobsen (1962, p. 48) says few good Caucasian rugs were made after about 1915, and later rugs in the same designs came from Soviet state production (see Soviet-era Caucasian rugs ('Russian rugs')).

structure.knot_note: Symmetric knot (Stone).
structure.kpsi_note: No figure for this group; Shirvan average about 113 (Stone).
structure.wefts_note: As for Shirvan rugs.
structure.pile_note: short
structure.sides: as for Shirvan: cord selvages or overcasting
structure.ends: as for Shirvan: web, knots and fringe

design.field: Prayer rugs with an all-over field of large, many-colored botehs, often on a dark ground.
design.colors: See Shirvan

look_alikes.name: Shirvan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A design group within Shirvan; structure is the same.

rows.trade_use: 'Marasali' is a design label for a Shirvan rug.
rows.what_it_tells: The design points to Shirvan.
rows.cautions: Design names are attributions by design; the same designs appear in rugs given to other groups and in later copies.

facts.text: Nineteenth-century prayer rugs with large colorful botehs are attributed to Marasali, a village south of Shemakha (Stone, p. 186).
The Azerbaijani UNESCO nomination (2010) lists Maraza among the localities of the Shirvan carpet region.

museum_examples.shows: Museum record: Azerbaijan, Shirvan; wool warp, weft and pile, symmetric knots; a dated prayer rug. Image: front, whole rug.

rows.name: Bidjov
rows.region: A town near Shemakha.
rows.made_by: Village weavers of Shirvan.
rows.date_note: Stone's figures describe nineteenth-century rugs of this design. Rugs readers are likely to own under this name were mostly woven between about 1850 and 1930. Stone's averages describe nineteenth-century rugs; Jacobsen (1962, p. 48) says few good Caucasian rugs were made after about 1915, and later rugs in the same designs came from Soviet state production (see Soviet-era Caucasian rugs ('Russian rugs')).

structure.knot_note: Symmetric knot (Stone).
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: averaging 94 knots per square inch.
structure.wefts_note: As for Shirvan rugs.
structure.pile_note: short
structure.sides: as for Shirvan: cord selvages or overcasting
structure.ends: as for Shirvan: web, knots and fringe

design.field: Vertical rows of nested hooked brackets and large flower heads.
design.colors: See Shirvan
design.sizes: The largest Shirvans

look_alikes.name: Shirvan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A design group within Shirvan; structure is the same.

rows.trade_use: 'Bidjov' is a design label for a Shirvan rug.
rows.what_it_tells: The design points to Shirvan.
rows.cautions: Design names are attributions by design; the same designs appear in rugs given to other groups and in later copies.

facts.text: Bijov is a Shirvan design of a vertical arrangement of nested bracketing elements; Bijov rugs are the most coarsely woven Shirvans (about 94 knots per square inch), the largest Shirvans, and woven on an all-wool foundation (Stone, p. 49).
Bidjov (Bico) is a weaving village of the hilly Akhsu part of Shirvan, and Bijov is counted among the Shirvan rug types.

rows.name: Akstafa
rows.region: The town and river Akstafa in the Transcaucasus (now north-west Azerbaijan); the design is classed under Shirvan.
rows.made_by: Village weavers of Shirvan.
rows.date_note: Stone's figures describe nineteenth-century rugs of this design. Rugs readers are likely to own under this name were mostly woven between about 1850 and 1930. Stone's averages describe nineteenth-century rugs; Jacobsen (1962, p. 48) says few good Caucasian rugs were made after about 1915, and later rugs in the same designs came from Soviet state production (see Soviet-era Caucasian rugs ('Russian rugs')).

structure.knot_note: Symmetric knot (Stone).
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: about 107 knots per square inch.
structure.wefts_note: As for Shirvan rugs.
structure.pile_note: short
structure.sides: as for Shirvan: cord selvages or overcasting
structure.ends: as for Shirvan: web, knots and fringe

design.field: Large stepped medallions in a column flanked by big geometric 'peacock' birds with fanned tails; often a long rug.
design.colors: See Shirvan
design.sizes: About 34 sq ft

look_alikes.name: Shirvan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A design group within Shirvan; structure is the same.

rows.trade_use: 'Akstafa' is a design label for a Shirvan rug.
rows.what_it_tells: The design points to Shirvan.
rows.cautions: Design names are attributions by design; the same designs appear in rugs given to other groups and in later copies.

facts.text: The Akstafa peacock is a geometricized bird with an elaborate tail found on Shirvan and Turkish rugs; Akstafa-design Shirvans average about 107 knots per square inch and 34 square feet, with wool warps and cotton or wool wefts (Stone, p. 21).
The Akstafa design is recognized by stylized birds (peacocks) flanking or at the base of its medallions.
facts.quote: "eight-sided medallions flanked by stylized peacocks" (Gregorian)

facts.text: Akstafa-design rugs were woven in many parts of the Caucasus, and variations occur in north-west Iran (Ardebil, Meshkin).

says.text: A Shirvan design type.
Akstafa is a cluster of the Kazak group (Dagkesaman, Poily and other villages).
Their Akstafa-design rug is 'clearly Kazak' in weave.

rows.name: Chajli
rows.region: Attributed to Shirvan; the Azerbaijani UNESCO nomination lists Chaily among localities of the Ganja region.
rows.made_by: Village weavers of Shirvan.
rows.date_note: Stone's figures describe nineteenth-century rugs of this design. Rugs readers are likely to own under this name were mostly woven between about 1850 and 1930. Stone's averages describe nineteenth-century rugs; Jacobsen (1962, p. 48) says few good Caucasian rugs were made after about 1915, and later rugs in the same designs came from Soviet state production (see Soviet-era Caucasian rugs ('Russian rugs')).

structure.knot_note: Symmetric knot (Stone).
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: about 100 knots per square inch.
structure.wefts_note: As for Shirvan rugs.
structure.pile_note: short
structure.sides: as for Shirvan: cord selvages or overcasting
structure.ends: as for Shirvan: web, knots and fringe

design.field: Three or more large clipped-octagon medallions in a column, alternating light and dark.
design.colors: See Shirvan
design.sizes: About 40 sq ft

look_alikes.name: Shirvan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A design group within Shirvan; structure is the same.

rows.trade_use: 'Chajli' is a design label for a Shirvan rug.
rows.what_it_tells: The design points to Shirvan.
rows.cautions: Design names are attributions by design; the same designs appear in rugs given to other groups and in later copies.

facts.text: Chajli rugs are nineteenth-century Shirvans with three or more large octagonal medallions (often like clipped rectangles) in alternating light and dark colors; about 100 knots per square inch; average 40 square feet; wefts cotton or wool (Stone, p. 64).
The Azerbaijani UNESCO nomination lists Chaily among the localities of the Ganja region.

says.text: A group attributed to Shirvan.
Chaily is listed as a locality of the Ganja region.

rows.name: Baku
rows.region: Baku and the Apsheron (Absheron) peninsula on the Caspian; the name covers rugs of Baku, Khila (Chila), Surakhany and Salyan.
rows.made_by: Village weavers of the Apsheron peninsula.
rows.date_note: Rugs readers are likely to own under this name were mostly woven between about 1850 and 1930. Stone's averages describe nineteenth-century rugs; Jacobsen (1962, p. 48) says few good Caucasian rugs were made after about 1915, and later rugs in the same designs came from Soviet state production (see Soviet-era Caucasian rugs ('Russian rugs')).

structure.knot_note: Symmetric knot (Hawley, Lewis, Stone).
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: horizontally six to nine, perpendicularly seven to eleven = 42-99. Lewis 1911: 64-192. Stone: average 84 (88 for Chila).
structure.warp_color: Lewis: cotton or wool, frequently camel hair
structure.weft_color: Stone: usually white, but blue- and red-wefted examples occur
structure.wefts_note: Hawley: weft usually cotton, sometimes wool; Stone: slightly more often cotton-wefted (52%) than wool-wefted (45%).
structure.pile_note: short (Hawley, Lewis); Lewis adds 'more or less camels' or goats' hair'.
structure.sides: A weft overcasting or a narrow weft selvage (Hawley); usually overcast (Lewis).
structure.ends: A web, one or more rows of knots and a fringe (Hawley); Lewis says a small streak of camel hair is usually thrown across one end, a characteristic Baku feature.

design.field: Large, very rectangular botehs in rows, often round a star-shaped central medallion with radiating rays; quarter-medallion corners; mechanically drawn birds; Chila rugs have an all-over boteh field with stepped spandrels and a stepped central medallion.
design.border: Three to five stripes, at least one geometric.
design.colors: Subdued light blue, tan, pale yellow, black and natural browns; turquoise blue and earth tones.
design.sizes: 6-9 ft long; average 35 sq ft.

look_alikes.name: Shirvan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Baku colors are duller (light blue, tan, natural brown) and the botehs larger and more rectangular.

rows.trade_use: Used for Apsheron rugs, especially the large-boteh 'Chila' and Surakhany types.

rows.region: The town and former khanate of Kuba, south of Derbend in the north-eastern Caucasus, and its villages: Konaghend, Perepedil, Chichi, Seichur (Zeikhur), Zejwa (Zeyva), Karagashli, Alpan and others (Stone; the UNESCO nomination lists Gonahkend, Afurja, Erfi, Zeyva, Syrt-Chichi and Pirebedil).

structure.knot_note: Symmetric knot (all sources).
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley 'Kuba': horizontally six to nine, perpendicularly seven to thirteen = 42-117; Hawley 'Kabistan': seven to twelve x eight to sixteen = 56-192; Lewis 1911 'Kabistan': 80-224. Stone: average about 115 (Kuba rugs are the finest Caucasians on average: 114, p. 61); Perepedil about 167.
structure.wefts_note: Hawley: two wefts, occasionally three; Kabistan wefts wool or cotton (Hawley), usually cotton (Lewis); Mumford: Kabistan weft and sometimes warp of cotton cord.
structure.pile_note: short to medium, closely clipped
structure.sides: A blue double selvage of two or three cords (Hawley 'Kuba'); Kabistans overcast or with a two-cord weft selvage, often in cotton (Hawley, Lewis, Mumford).
structure.ends: A narrow blue web of 'herring-bone' weave, a knotted selvage or several rows of knots, and a short warp fringe (Hawley 'Kuba'); Kabistan lower end often a fine braided selvage and warp loops (Hawley).
structure.handle: Slightly loose to moderately firm; thin and supple.
structure.back: Moderately fine to medium grain; neat rows.

design.field: Small, densely filled geometric fields and all-over repeats: honeycombs (Konaghend), ram's horns (Perepedil), rosette rows with the Chichi border, Seichur crosses and roses, dented-quadrilateral 'palmettes' (Karagashli), cruciform shields (Zejwa); also large floral Kubas and rayed-star medallions; 'Kufic' borders.
design.border: Kufesque and running-dog borders common; the beautiful Cufic-derived stripe on cream ground (Hawley, Kabistan).
design.colors: Blue, red, sable brown and yellow.
design.sizes: Small: average about 27 sq ft; 4-9 ft long.

rows.trade_use: 'Kuba' is the trade and scholarly name today; 'Kabistan' was the older trade name for the same rugs and Stone says it is no longer used. Iranian Ardebil rugs are woven in Kuba designs.
rows.what_it_tells: A small, finely knotted, short-piled symmetric-knotted rug with blue selvages and herringbone ends and a densely filled geometric field points to Kuba.
rows.cautions: The Kuba / Shirvan / Daghestan boundary is often uncertain. 'Dragon carpets' were once attributed to Kuba; Stone says that is being reconsidered.

facts.text: The name Kabistan is a corruption of Kuba/Kubistan; Mumford was told in Batum and Tiflis that 'Kabistan' rugs come from the Kuba district.
facts.quote: No. That's one of your American inventions. Those rugs come from Kuba, down in the southeastern part of Daghestan.

facts.text: Stone says 'Kabistan' is of controversial origin, names no real place, has no certain structural or design features, and is no longer used.
Nineteenth-century Kuba rugs are small and comparatively finely knotted: average about 115 knots per square inch and 27 square feet (Stone).
Kuba rugs often have blue end webs of herringbone weave and blue cord selvages.
facts.quote: Both ends, a narrow blue web of "herring-bone" weave, a knotted selvage or several rows of knots, and short warp fringe.

facts.text: Kabistans may be overcast or have a selvage made with the (often cotton) weft, while Daghestan selvages are of extra colored wool.
facts.quote: Kabistans are overcast at the side, or if selvaged the selvage is made with the cotton weft, while the Daghestan selvage is of fine, extra, colored wool yarn

facts.text: Soviet-controlled weaving of about 1929-1938 produced 'Kubistans' finer than old ones, on cotton (or linen) warps for the first time.
The Azerbaijani UNESCO nomination lists Gonahkend, Afurja, Erfi, Zeyva, Syrt-Chichi and Pirebedil as localities of the Kuba region.

Azerbaijani classification splits the Kuba region into mountain, foothill and plain zones: mountain villages such as Konakkend and Afurja, foothill villages such as Pirəbədil, Zeyvə and Çiçi, and plain villages such as the Qaraqaşlı villages.
From the Soviet period on, Kuba rugs have often been woven on cotton warps and wefts with wool pile.
facts.quote: "Çözgü ve atkı da pamuk, düğüm de ise yün tercih edilir" ('cotton is preferred for warp and weft, wool for the knots')

facts.text: Azerbaijan's first large carpet workshop opened in 1933 in Konakkend (Kuba), with a carpet vocational school from 1934 whose teaching was led by Latif Kerimov.

says.text: Kabistans are a variety of Daghestans from the south of the province, distinguishable only by strict analysis; Kuba is a separate class.
Kabistan is an error for Kubistan; the rugs come from the Kuba district.
There is no such place as Kabistan and no certain features; the attribution is no longer used.
Kuba 42-117; Kabistan 56-192.
Kabistan 80-224.
Average about 115.
Azerbaijani classification counts rugs woven in Daghestan, especially Derbent, in the Kuba group (citing Kerimov 1961).
Treats Derbent-district rugs as Daghestan rugs that share many designs with Kuba district through mutual influence.

rows.region: The mountainous north-east Caucasus on the Caspian, including Derbend and the old 'Lesghistan'; Hawley says the trade name was given to rugs from several parts of the province.
rows.made_by: Village weavers of Daghestan's many peoples; Stone names Avars, Dargins, Kumyks, Lezgins (Kurins) and Tabasarans in connection with Daghestan weaving.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric knot (all sources).
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: horizontally seven to twelve, perpendicularly eight to fifteen = 56-180. Lewis 1911: 80-210. Mumford: 64-144.
structure.warp_color: gray wool (Mumford); dark brown or natural in old rugs, white or gray in later ones; some later warps of cotton and wool plied together, which puckers the rug when wet (Lewis)
structure.weft_color: white or gray wool in old rugs; nearly always cotton in later ones (Lewis)
structure.wefts_note: Hawley: two wefts of medium wool.
structure.pile_note: short, fine
structure.sides: A selvage of two to four cords, sometimes overcast (Hawley); a fine colored selvage of extra wool (Mumford).
structure.ends: A web, one or more rows of knots and loose fringe, occasionally a narrow braided selvage (Hawley); a narrow woven selvage and a knotted fringe (Mumford).
structure.back: Fine grain; very even rows; the warp shows at the back (Hawley).

design.field: Small, closely packed geometric figures 'compared to mosaic work': lattices, all-over repeats, Lesghi star medallions; many prayer rugs with a lattice or all-over field and a small arch.

design.colors: Blue, red and ivory with green and yellow.
design.sizes: 5-10 ft long; small.

rows.trade_use: Used for finely knotted north-east Caucasian rugs, especially prayer rugs with lattices; Persian Ardebil rugs are woven in 'Daghestan' designs.
rows.what_it_tells: A fine, short-piled, all-wool symmetric-knotted rug with a lattice or mosaic-like field and a small arch points to Daghestan or its neighbors.
rows.cautions: Hawley says Daghestan and Kabistan (Kuba) rugs are often indistinguishable; Jacobsen says the same of Daghestan, Shirvan and Kuba.

facts.text: Daghestan rugs are tied with the symmetric knot on wool warps and wefts (older pieces).
facts.quote: Genuine Daghestans are made, warp, weft and pile, of the best wool, and are tied with the Ghiordes knot.

facts.text: Later Daghestans may have cotton wefts or warps of mixed cotton and wool.
facts.quote: In the moderns nearly always cotton. In the antiques usually white or gray wool or a mixture of the two.

facts.text: Nineteenth-century Daghestan rugs are small and usually have a lattice, an all-over pattern or Lesghi star medallions; many are prayer rugs (Stone, p. 84).
Hawley says the province's isolation slowed the arrival of aniline dyes and new designs.
Much of the weaving sold as Daghestan or Derbend was done in southern Daghestan, in villages around Orta-Stal and Kasumkent and in the Akhty, Mikrakh and Tabasaran districts.
Daghestan rugs are more often all wool than Kuba rugs, favor blue over red, often have blue wool edges, and many have ribbed backs.
Akhty and Mikrakh pile rugs are the densest of southern Daghestan, about 211,600 knots per square meter (about 137 per square inch).

rows.name: Derbend
rows.region: The walled Caspian city of Derbend and the mountain districts that marketed rugs there.
rows.made_by: 'Tartar and Turkoman inhabitants' and mountain villagers.
rows.date_note: Hawley and Mumford describe the Derbends of their day (1900s-1910s) as coarse market rugs; old pieces were already rare.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric knot (Hawley, Lewis).
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: horizontally five to nine, perpendicularly six to twelve = 30-108. Lewis 1911: 40-120.
structure.warp_color: generally wool, occasionally cotton (Hawley); brown wool or goat hair (Lewis, Mumford)
structure.wefts_note: Hawley: twice, often both twice and three times in the same rug, rarely once with a coarse weft; Lewis: usually more than two.
structure.pile_note: medium length; soft, thick, lustrous (Lewis)
structure.sides: A double selvage of two or three cords, or a double overcasting (Hawley); generally overcast (Lewis).
structure.ends: A web, often a knotted selvage, and fringe; sometimes a wide reddish-brown web like Yomud Turkmen rugs (Hawley, Mumford: usually four rows of knots in the end selvage).

design.field: Copies of Daghestan designs on a larger scale: large stars or hooked diamonds repeated across a blue or red field; old pieces with botehs or lattices.
design.colors: Blue, white, red and lavish yellow.
design.sizes: Slightly larger than Daghestans.

look_alikes.name: Daghestan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Derbends are coarser and heavier with longer pile and sometimes goat-hair warps; Stone says the trade uses 'Derbend' for a lower-density Daghestan.

rows.trade_use: In the trade 'Derbend' may suggest a Daghestan rug of lower knot density.
rows.what_it_tells: A coarse, longer-piled rug in Daghestan designs, perhaps with a goat-hair warp, points to the Derbend market.
rows.cautions: A market name, not a design school.

facts.text: Derbend rugs are coarser, heavier, longer-piled copies of Daghestan designs.
facts.quote: The regulation rug of the Derbend variety is merely a copy of the Daghestan, but upon a heavier scale.

facts.text: Some Derbends have goat-hair warps and a wide end web like Turkmen rugs.
facts.quote: the warp is of brown goat's hair, and at each end is a reddish brown web like what may be seen in the rugs of Yomud tribes

facts.text: Stone says 'Derbend' in the trade may suggest a Daghestan rug of lower knot density.
Derbend is a trade label taken from a major collecting point; Derbent-district rugs share many designs with Kuba rugs, such as a lattice with flowers in each compartment.

rows.name: Lesghi (Lesghi star rugs)
rows.region: The Lesghian tribes of the high Daghestan mountains east of Kazbek. Stone: the Lesghi star design is especially associated with nineteenth-century Daghestan rugs, but is also used in Shahsavan flatweaves, east Anatolian rugs and other Caucasian rugs.
rows.made_by: Mountain village weavers of Daghestan (Hawley's 'Lesghians'). Stone calls the Lesghis 'Turkic' and includes Avars, Dargins, Kumyks and Kurins; of these only the Kumyks speak a Turkic language, so that word should not be repeated.
rows.date_note: Rugs readers are likely to own under this name were mostly woven between about 1850 and 1930. Stone's averages describe nineteenth-century rugs; Jacobsen (1962, p. 48) says few good Caucasian rugs were made after about 1915, and later rugs in the same designs came from Soviet state production (see Soviet-era Caucasian rugs ('Russian rugs')).

structure.knot_note: Symmetric knot (Hawley).
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley 'Lesghian': horizontally six to nine, perpendicularly six to eleven = 36-99. Stone: Daghestan rugs with the Lesghi star about 99.
structure.wefts_note: Hawley: two wefts of medium wool.
structure.pile_note: medium
structure.sides: An added selvage, usually wool, occasionally cotton, of two to four cords (Hawley).
structure.ends: A web, two or three rows of knots and a warp fringe, sometimes a braided selvage (Hawley).
structure.back: Slightly coarse; one warp of each pair depressed or doubled under the other (Hawley), unusual in the Caucasus.

design.field: One or more large eight-pointed stepped stars with arrow-like arms (the Lesghi star), with octagons, stars and S-forms.
design.colors: Blue and yellow generally, often red and brown.
design.sizes: About 33 sq ft, shape ratio about 2.

look_alikes.name: Daghestan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Stone files Lesghi-star rugs as a Daghestan design; Hawley's Lesghians have depressed warps, unusual in Daghestan rugs.

look_alikes.name: Shirvan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The star also appears on rugs attributed to Shirvan.

rows.trade_use: 'Lesghi' is used for rugs with the Lesghi star whatever their origin.
rows.what_it_tells: The Lesghi star points to the east Caucasus, Daghestan especially, but the motif is also used outside the Caucasus.
rows.cautions: The motif alone does not fix origin.

facts.text: The Lesghi star is an eight-pointed stepped star with four radiating arrows; Daghestan rugs with it average about 99 knots per square inch and 33 square feet (Stone, p. 175).
Hawley says Lesghian rugs have brown wool warp and weft and, unusually for the Caucasus except Shusha, one warp of each pair almost doubled beneath the other.
facts.quote: as is rarely the case with any other Caucasian rugs excepting the Shushas, one of the two threads of warp encircled by a knot is often almost doubled beneath the other.

facts.text: The Lesghi star is a stepped medallion made of a diagonal cross laid over an upright cross, often with arrowheads at the ends of the diagonal arms.
facts.quote: "a diagonal cross superimposed on an equilateral cross ... within a stepped medallion" (Gregorian)

says.text: Especially associated with nineteenth-century Daghestan rugs.
'Traditionally associated with the Kuba district', 'more typical of the Shemakha district'; many inscribed Armenian examples from Kars, Gendje and Iranian Azerbaijan.
The eight-pointed star medallion of the Kuba-group 'Zeyvə' composition is the one some sources call the 'Lezgi star' (citing Kerimov 1983 and Görgünay-Kırzıoğlu).

rows.name: Soumak
rows.country: Azerbaijan and the Caucasus generally (also Iran, Anatolia)
rows.region: The name is thought to derive from Shemakha in Shirvan; large Caucasian soumaks were woven throughout the Caucasus, many in Kuba.
rows.made_by: Village weavers; Stone says soumaks are woven by Kumyks and Lesghians in Daghestan, and that soumak bags are attributed to Kurdish weavers in the Caucasus and Shahsavan in Iran.
rows.date_note: Jacobsen (1962) says none had been made since about 1925 or imported since about 1932; Soviet-era and modern soumaks exist.

structure.knot_note: No pile: a weft-wrapping flatweave (soumak) in which colored wefts wrap groups of warps (e.g. forward over four, back under two) between plain ground wefts; plain, countered (herringbone) or reverse soumak (Stone). Hawley calls it a 'flat stitch'.
structure.kpsi_note: Not a knotted rug. Hawley gives 'knots' (wrapping stitches) to the inch horizontally eight to fourteen, perpendicularly six to sixteen.
structure.wefts_note: Hawley: a ground weft crosses twice between rows of wrapping in old rugs, and between every second and third row in modern ones.
structure.pile_note: No pile. The back is covered with loose cut ends of the colored yarns, which is why the trade called them 'Kashmirs' (Hawley, Lewis).
structure.sides: Generally a double selvage of several cords, occasionally overcast (Hawley).
structure.ends: Narrow web, one or more rows of knots and fringe; sometimes a heavy added selvage (Hawley).
structure.back: Shaggy with loose yarn ends; the face is flat and slightly ribbed with a herringbone look in countered soumak.

design.field: Three or four large hexagonal-diamond medallions in a column with flattened octagons, many small fillers; dragon soumaks and large S-forms (sileh); bags and animal trappings.
design.border: Running latch-hook outer stripe almost typical.
design.colors: Red, blue and later brown; an orange-yellow rare in other Caucasian rugs.
design.sizes: 5.5-12 ft long; rugs 6 x 4 to 9 x 12 ft.

look_alikes.name: Kuba
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kuba and Shemakha pile rugs share the soumak finish of sides and ends; check for pile.

rows.trade_use: 'Soumak' is both the name of the weave and a trade name for Caucasian rugs made with it; modern soumaks are made in Iran, India and Afghanistan.
rows.what_it_tells: A pileless rug with a back of loose yarn ends is a soumak (weft-wrapped) weaving; Caucasian soumaks with large diamond medallions are typically nineteenth century.
rows.cautions: 'Soumak' names a technique used in many regions; the Caucasian label must come from design and materials.

facts.text: Soumak is a flatweave in which wefts wrap groups of warps, producing a flat face and a back covered in loose yarn ends.
facts.quote: ends of yarn hang loosely at the back, as is the case with the beautiful shawls of the noted valley of India.

facts.text: The name 'soumak' is thought to derive from the town of Shemakha in the south-east Caucasus.
facts.quote: By a corruption of the name of the city, their fabrics are called Soumaks

facts.text: Soumaks were also sold as 'Kashmirs' because of their shawl-like back.
facts.quote: Sometimes called Kashmir from the resemblance of the under side to that of Cashmere shawls.

facts.text: Hawley thought the cross-incised diamond medallions derived from very old Armenian rugs and reports a claim that the earlier weavers were Christian.
Jacobsen (1962) says no Caucasian soumaks had been made since about 1925 or imported since about 1932.
Soumaks were woven by the Lezgins of southern Daghestan (Kasumkent district) and of the neighboring Lezgin villages of northern Azerbaijan.
Large Caucasian soumaks usually have a column of large diamond medallions, usually three and up to five.
In the Azerbaijani classification flat-woven floor covers are called palaz; among them are kilim, zili, cecim (cicim), şedde, verni and sumak.

says.text: Woven by the Shemakha tribes (Shirvan).
Large soumaks were woven throughout the Caucasus, many of them from Kuba; regional attribution of Caucasian flatweaves is problematic.

disagreements.about: ground wefts between rows of wrapping

says.text: A weft crosses and recrosses between each row of stitches in old soumaks, and between each second and third row in new ones (p. 47).
In a Salyan-type soumak at the Nakhchivan State Carpet Museum, pattern yarns wrap the warps in pairs and no weft is put in between.
Weft-wrapped Persian flatweaves may have a ground weft between rows of wrapping, or none.
