rows.name: Karastan
rows.region: Leaksville, Rockingham County, North Carolina (later sources name the plant as Eden, NC); production moved to northwest Georgia from 2019.
rows.made_by: Marshall Field & Company's mills; later Fieldcrest Mills; Mohawk Industries from 1993.
rows.date_note: First Karastan off the loom April 8, 1928. Wool rug weaving in North Carolina ended between 2019 and 2021 (sources differ). The Karastan name continues on synthetic Mohawk products.

structure.knot_note: No knots. Woven on spool Axminster power looms that Eugene Clark began modifying for Marshall Field in 1926 so that the pile yarn was pulled through to the back.
structure.kpsi_note: Not knotted, so knots per square inch do not apply. The power-loom trade counts pitch (pile ends in 27 inches of width) and rows or wires per inch (Stone pp. 114, 238, 306; CRI Carpet Primer).
structure.pile_note: Wool (worsted wool per the 2021 New York Times report, seen only in excerpts). Up to 50 colors.
structure.sides: Not described in the sources read.
structure.ends: Not described in the sources read.
structure.back: The pattern shows through on the back, made to look hand-knotted on both sides (NC DNCR); no knot bumps.

design.field: Reproductions of Persian and other oriental designs, sold under design names such as Kirman (the 717 Kirman of 1937 had 50 colors).
design.colors: Up to 50 colors.

look_alikes.name: hand-knotted
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The pattern shows on the back, but there are no knots: parting the pile shows no knot loop around the lengthwise threads (Jacobsen 1969; NC DNCR).

look_alikes.name: Axminster rug in an oriental design
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A Karastan is an Axminster; the brand is told by its label and design numbers.

rows.trade_use: 'Karastan' is a brand, not a place. Design names such as 'Kirman 717' are pattern names.
rows.what_it_tells: An American machine-woven wool rug made in North Carolina between 1928 and about 2019-2021, in a design copied from an oriental rug.
rows.cautions: 'Karastan' sounds like a weaving region but is an invented place-like name (Stone p. 239). Because the back shows the pattern, a Karastan can be taken for hand-knotted; part the pile to look for knots. Karastan also made tufted and nylon carpet from the 1960s (Floor Focus), and Mohawk sells synthetic Karastan products after 2021, so the name alone does not date a piece.

facts.text: The first Karastan rug came off the loom on April 8, 1928.
Karastans were made by Marshall Field & Company at its Rockingham County, North Carolina mill (Leaksville; later sources say Eden).
The loom was a spool Axminster power loom that Marshall Field's engineers began modifying in 1926; Floor Focus says the Axminster equipment was bought in England.
Eugene Clark's modification pulled the pile yarn through to the back, allowing up to 50 colors and a hand-knotted look on both sides.
The trade press called them 'Mystery Rugs'; after more than five million people walked on a Kirman-design Karastan at the 1933-34 Chicago World's Fair they were sold as 'Wonder Rugs'.
The 717 Kirman design, introduced in 1937 with 50 colors, stayed the best seller for about 50 years.
Mohawk Industries bought Karastan from Fieldcrest in 1993.
Karastan added tufted carpet in the 1960s and its first nylon broadloom in 1967.
Rug-name lists include 'Karastan' as a name made to sound like a place.
In 1969 Jacobsen named Karastan, with Bigelow and Cabin Crafts, among the American makers of machine-made rugs in oriental designs.

disagreements.about: date_to (end of wool rug weaving in North Carolina)

says.text: The Eden Karastan plant closed in 2021 (93 years after 1928).

Excerpts of the 2021 New York Times report say the Axminster looms made the wool rug until 2019, when Mohawk closed that department; a 2019 Floor Daily item (excerpt only) says rug production moved to northwest Georgia from October 2019.
1935: Marshall Field merged its 24 textile mills into one operation, Fieldcrest; 1953: Fieldcrest spun off.
1953: Marshall Field sold its mill operations to Amoskeag, which formed Fieldcrest Mills, Inc.
Eugene Clark began modifying the spool Axminster loom in 1926.
Gives no year for the loom; headline dates the mill's innovation 'since 1929'.

rows.name: A. & M. Karagheusian (Gulistan)
rows.country: United States (with an operation at Tianjin, China)
rows.region: Freehold, Monmouth County, New Jersey (weaving); Roselle Park NJ (spinning, 1923); Tianjin (Tientsin), China (1925).
rows.made_by: Armenian-American brothers Arshag and Mihran Karagheusian's mills.
rows.date_note: First carpets off the Freehold looms in 1905; the Gulistan rug was introduced in 1928; oriental carpet production stopped in 1953 and the Freehold mill closed in 1964 (Baptista, NCSU).

structure.knot_note: No knots: the Freehold mill was equipped with Brussels and Wilton power looms bought in Kidderminster, England.
structure.kpsi_note: Not knotted, so knots per square inch do not apply. The power-loom trade counts pitch (pile ends in 27 inches of width) and rows or wires per inch (Stone pp. 114, 238, 306; CRI Carpet Primer).
structure.pile_note: The Gulistan rug was sold on its silk-like sheen (Baptista, NCSU); how the sheen was made was not described.
structure.sides: Not described in the sources read.
structure.ends: Not described in the sources read.
structure.back: Not described in the sources read.

design.field: Persian-style designs (Gulistan).

look_alikes.name: gulistan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Older books use 'Gulistan' for hand-knotted rugs: a Persian type near Kashan and a grade of Oushak rugs from Turkey (Mumford; Lewis; Rug Primer). A machine-woven rug with no knots is the American Gulistan.

look_alikes.name: Wilton rug in an oriental design
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Karagheusian made Wilton and Brussels weaves; the label tells the maker.

rows.trade_use: 'Gulistan' was Karagheusian's brand from 1928 and survives as the name of Gulistan Carpet, Inc.
rows.what_it_tells: An American machine-woven rug from Freehold NJ, 1905-1953, or a later Gulistan carpet.
rows.cautions: The firm also imported oriental rugs (from 1899) and was one of the American firms in the hand-knotted export rug trade at Tianjin, China (Stone p. 68), so a Karagheusian connection does not by itself mean machine-made. 'Gulistan' (Persian for rose garden) was a trade name for hand-knotted Persian and Turkish rugs long before 1928.

facts.text: Arshag and Mihran Karagheusian, Armenian brothers from Turkey, were importing oriental rugs in America by about 1899-1903.

In 1904 the brothers set up a carpet mill in a former shirt factory in Freehold, New Jersey, with 60 Brussels and Wilton power looms bought in Kidderminster, England; the first carpets came off the looms in 1905.
Karagheusian introduced the Gulistan rug in 1928, a Persian-style rug with a silk-like sheen.
Karagheusian had an operation at Tianjin (Tientsin), China, from 1925, and is listed among the American firms in Tianjin's export rug industry.
Oriental carpet production stopped in 1953; J. P. Stevens bought the company in 1964 and the Freehold mill closed that year.
Older books use 'Gulistan' for hand-knotted rugs: Hawley for a Persian type made near Kashan, and Mumford, Lewis and The Rug Primer for a fine grade of Oushak (Usak) rugs from western Turkey.
facts.quote: Gulistan is the Persian name for a flower garden

rows.name: Bigelow (Bigelow Carpet Co.; Bigelow-Sanford)
rows.region: Clinton, Massachusetts; Thompsonville (Enfield), Connecticut; Amsterdam, New York (Sanford); later Southern plants.
rows.made_by: Power-loom carpet mills founded on Erastus B. Bigelow's inventions.
rows.date_note: Brussels carpet on Bigelow's looms from 1849 at Clinton. Bigelow-Hartford 1914-1929; Bigelow-Sanford from 1929 (one archive says 1924); the Thompsonville plant closed in 1971. When Bigelow's oriental-design rugs began and ended was not found.

structure.knot_note: No knots; Bigelow's looms wove ingrain (flat), Brussels, Wilton, tapestry and velvet carpeting.
structure.kpsi_note: Not knotted, so knots per square inch do not apply. The power-loom trade counts pitch (pile ends in 27 inches of width) and rows or wires per inch (Stone pp. 114, 238, 306; CRI Carpet Primer).
structure.back: Not described in the sources read.

look_alikes.name: Wilton rug in an oriental design
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Bigelow made Wilton and other power-loom weaves; the label names the maker.

rows.trade_use: Brand name of carpets and rugs.
rows.what_it_tells: An American machine-made carpet or rug; the company name on the label (Bigelow Carpet, Bigelow-Hartford, Bigelow-Sanford) narrows the date.
rows.cautions: Name changes help date a label: Bigelow-Hartford (1914-1929), Bigelow-Sanford (from 1929).

facts.text: Erastus Brigham Bigelow (1814-1879) invented power looms for carpets, including ingrain, Brussels, Wilton, tapestry and velvet carpeting, and his looms greatly increased carpet production from the 1840s.

Bigelow had power looms for ingrain carpet by 1842, patented the first Brussels power loom in 1847 and a tapestry Brussels loom in 1850, and took six patents for pile and cut-pile carpet looms in 1851-57.
In 1849 Erastus and his brother Horatio began weaving Brussels carpet on his looms at Clinton, Massachusetts; they incorporated as the Bigelow Carpet Company in 1854.
The company was Bigelow-Hartford from 1914 to 1929 and Bigelow-Sanford from 1929; the Thompsonville, Connecticut plant (carpet making there since 1828) closed in 1971.
In 1969 Jacobsen named Bigelow among the American makers of machine-made rugs in oriental designs.
Mohawk bought 'Karastan Bigelow' from Fieldcrest Cannon in 1993.

says.text: Bigelow-Hartford period 1914-1929; Bigelow-Sanford period 1929-1971.
Search excerpt of Cornell's Bigelow-Hartford Carpet Company Records finding aid: merged in 1924 with Stephen Sanford & Sons of Amsterdam NY to become Bigelow-Sanford (page not opened; 403).

disagreements.about: dates of Bigelow's Brussels and Wilton looms

says.text: First Brussels power loom patented 1847; pile and cut-pile looms 1851-57.
Search excerpt: developed his power loom for Brussels and Wilton carpets from 1845 to 1851.

rows.name: Mohawk Carpet Mills
rows.region: Amsterdam, New York; after the 1960s the South (Georgia).
rows.made_by: Mohawk Carpet Mills, formed by merger in 1920.
rows.date_note: The Mohawk name dates from the 1920 merger; the Shuttleworth mill (from 1878) and McCleary, Wallin & Crouse were earlier. Mohasco from 1956. Manufacturing in Amsterdam ended by the end of the 1960s.

structure.knot_note: No knots; Mohawk offered Wilton, Axminster, velvet and chenille weaves (Gale).
structure.kpsi_note: Not knotted, so knots per square inch do not apply. The power-loom trade counts pitch (pile ends in 27 inches of width) and rows or wires per inch (Stone pp. 114, 238, 306; CRI Carpet Primer).
structure.back: Not described in the sources read.

design.field: Mohawk's oriental-design lines were not identified in the sources read (the 1908 Shuttleworth 'Karnak' pattern is named, without a description).

look_alikes.name: Wilton rug in an oriental design
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Check the label and the weave (Wilton or Axminster back).

rows.trade_use: Brand of a large US carpet maker; the modern Mohawk Industries also owns Karastan.
rows.what_it_tells: An American machine-woven rug, from Amsterdam NY between 1920 and the 1960s if the label says Mohawk Carpet Mills.
rows.cautions: Mohawk Industries today sells many kinds of rugs, including tufted and printed ones; the old Mohawk Carpet Mills label and a woven back point to the Amsterdam years.

facts.text: The Shuttleworth family began weaving carpets at Amsterdam, New York in 1878 with 14 used Wilton looms shipped from Britain, and incorporated as Shuttleworth Brothers Company in 1902.
Mohawk Carpet Mills was formed in 1920 by the merger of Shuttleworth Brothers Company and McCleary, Wallin & Crouse, both of Amsterdam NY.
Mohawk Carpet Mills offered Wilton, Axminster, velvet and chenille weaves.
Mohawk merged with Alexander Smith, Inc. in 1956 to form Mohasco Industries.
Carpet manufacturing by Mohawk in Amsterdam ended by the end of the 1960s.
Mohawk bought Karastan in 1993.

rows.name: Whittall rugs (Anglo-Persian and others)
rows.region: Worcester, Massachusetts (South Worcester; Whittall Mills off Brussels Street); a Palmer MA mill from 1891.
rows.made_by: Matthew J. Whittall's mill, from 1906 the trust M. J. Whittall Associates.
rows.date_note: Manufacturing began in 1880 on Wilton and Brussels looms (period sources via CBHL). Ads of 1911-12 promoted the woven name on the back. When the Anglo-Persian line began and when the mill closed were not settled.

structure.knot_note: No knots; Whittall's mill wove Wilton and Brussels carpet.
structure.kpsi_note: Not knotted, so knots per square inch do not apply. The power-loom trade counts pitch (pile ends in 27 inches of width) and rows or wires per inch (Stone pp. 114, 238, 306; CRI Carpet Primer).
structure.back: 1911-12 ads said the name 'Whittall's' was woven into the back of every rug; an auction listing reports 'Whittalls Anglo Persian' marked on the back of one rug.

design.field: Persian and Chinese-style designs (the 1913 catalogue is titled 'Oriental Art in Whittall Rugs').

look_alikes.name: Wilton rug in an oriental design
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Look for the woven Whittall name on the back.

rows.trade_use: 'Anglo-Persian' was a Whittall line name; it does not mean the rug was made in England or Persia.
rows.what_it_tells: An American machine-woven (Wilton-type) rug from Worcester, Massachusetts, early to mid 20th century.
rows.cautions: 'Anglo-Persian' sounds like an origin but is a line name.

facts.text: Matthew J. Whittall began making carpets on his own account in 1880 in South Worcester, Massachusetts, with machinery for Wilton and Brussels carpets; in 1906 the business passed to the trust M. J. Whittall Associates.
Whittall advertisements of 1911 and 1912 told buyers to look for the name 'Whittall's' woven into the back of the rug.
Whittall Mills in Worcester was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on March 5, 1980.

disagreements.about: number of looms at the start (1880)

says.text: Hurd (1889): seven looms.
Textile World obituary (1922) and Isaiah Thomas Lodge tribute (1928): eight looms.

rows.name: Couristan
rows.country: United States (importer and distributor; rugs made in Belgium and elsewhere)
rows.region: New York City (company); manufacture abroad.
rows.made_by: Founded by the Couri brothers; machine-made rugs from mills abroad (Belgium named).
rows.date_note: Founded 1926 as an importer of handmade Persian rugs; machine-made rugs from 1964 (company text).

look_alikes.name: Modern power-loomed rug in an oriental design (Belgium, Egypt, Turkey)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Couristan's Belgian machine-made rugs belong to this group; check the back and label.

rows.trade_use: Brand on imported rugs of several kinds: hand-knotted (early imports), machine-woven (Wilton, Axminster), hand-tufted, hand-loomed and printed.
rows.what_it_tells: A Couristan label alone does not tell how the rug was made; the back and the label's words do.
rows.cautions: The same brand has sold hand-knotted, machine-woven, hand-tufted and printed rugs.

facts.text: Couristan was founded in New York City in 1926 by the brothers Basil J., Aleer J. and George J. Couri as an importer of handmade Persian rugs.
Couristan began selling machine-made rugs in 1964, naming Belgium for its 100% wool machine-made rugs; it also sells hand-tufted, hand-loomed, digitally printed and Axminster products.

rows.name: Egyptian silk and wool hand-knotted rugs (Saqiyet Abu Shaara)
rows.native: سجاد ساقية أبو شعرة / السجاد الحرير اليدوي
rows.translit: sajjād Sāqiyat Abū Shaʿra / al-sajjād al-ḥarīr al-yadawī ('hand-made silk carpet')
rows.region: Saqiyet Abu Shaara (ساقية أبو شعرة), a village of Menoufia governorate in the Nile Delta north of Cairo.
rows.made_by: Village families on home looms and in small workshops: men, women and children, including young girls (Al-Ittihad 2010); about 3,000-4,000 villagers in 2018 (Al-Borsa).
rows.date_note: Al-Borsa (2018) dates the village's carpet craft to 1955, when villagers trained on looms in the Darrasa district of Cairo; production began with wool and kilims and grew to silk. Exports nearly stopped after 2011.

structure.knot_note: Not given in the sources read.
structure.kpsi_note: No knot count found for this village. Stone's Egyptian notation (knots per cm across x along, e.g. '4 x 5') may be what sellers use; not confirmed here.
structure.pile_note: Silk, wool, and wool with silk highlights (Al-Borsa 2018; Al-Ittihad 2010).

design.field: Made to order: natural (floral) or geometric designs, letters, or words such as a Qur'anic verse or a line of poetry, chosen by the customer or trader (Al-Ittihad 2010).

look_alikes.name: Kashan silk rugs
look_alikes.how_to_tell: No source read gives a structural difference between Egyptian and Persian silk rugs; the label ('Made in Egypt') or the seller's papers are the main clue.

rows.trade_use: Sold in Egypt and exported to Europe, America and the Gulf as hand-made Egyptian silk or wool rugs, often through Egyptian middlemen; Al-Ittihad (2010) says the village aims to compete with Iranian carpets.
rows.what_it_tells: A hand-knotted silk or silk-accented rug bought in Egypt or labeled Egyptian is consistent with Nile Delta village production of 1955 or later.
rows.cautions: Press sources only; no structure, knot count or open-licence museum example found. Before the 1950s most rugs sold in Cairo were imported, so an older 'rug from Cairo' is usually not Egyptian.

facts.text: Carpet making in Saqiyet Abu Shaara dates from 1955, when villagers trained on looms in Cairo's Darrasa district and brought the skill home.
facts.quote: «عندما بدأ أهالي القرية عام 1955 التدريب على الأنوال في منطقة الدراسة بالقاهرة»

facts.text: The village weaves silk and wool pile rugs (and kilims); Al-Borsa adds wool rugs with silk highlights.
facts.quote: «من الحرير والصوف والكليم» (of silk, wool and kilim; Al-Ittihad 2010)

facts.text: Designs are chosen by the customer or trader and can include Qur'anic verses or lines of poetry.
Whole families weave, including girls; a 14-year-old was reported weaving five hours a day in 2010.
Most of the output was exported to Europe and America (2010); exports nearly stopped after 2011 (2018).
Looms were financed in part through the state Productive Families Project and Social Fund loans of up to 5,000 Egyptian pounds.
facts.quote: «مشروع الأسر المنتجة» (the Productive Families Project)

facts.text: The village is in Menoufia governorate (a governor of Menoufia inspected its hand-carpet workshops).

search_names: Egyptian silk and wool hand-knotted rugs

rows.name: Egyptian kilims and tapestries (Fuwwa, Bani Adi, Assiut, Harraniya)
rows.translit: kilīm / al-kilīm al-ʿadawī ('Bani Adi kilim') / nasīj al-Ḥarrāniyya ('Harraniya weaving')
rows.region: Fuwwa (Kafr el-Sheikh, Nile Delta); Bani Adiyat village, Manfalut district, Assiut (Upper Egypt); Asyut; Helwan, south of Cairo; Harraniya village on the Saqqara road, Giza.
rows.made_by: Fuwwa: family workshops (about 3,000 workers in 2023). Bani Adi: women at home on household looms. Harraniya: villagers of all ages trained in the art school of Ramses Wissa Wassef.
rows.date_note: Fuwwa's weaving trade is dated to 1812 or 1822 by Egyptian press; Bani Adi kilim weaving was 'more than 100 years' old in 2017; Harraniya's tapestry school dates from 1952 or the 1950s (Youm7). The pieces readers meet are mostly modern.

structure.knot_note: Flat-woven: kilims and tapestries, no pile. Stone calls Bani Adi rugs tapestry-woven.
structure.pile_note: No pile. Bani Adi: pure natural wool with no other thread added (Youm7 2017). Fuwwa: wool and cotton, also linen and chenille (Youm7 2023). Harraniya: cotton and wool with plant dyes grown in the village (Youm7 2023).

design.field: Fuwwa: rural scenes, pyramids and Sphinx, mosques, Qur'anic verses. Bani Adi and Helwan: geometric designs in natural colors. Assiut ('assyuti'): traditional designs in bright colors. Harraniya: naive pictures of village life, animals and buildings, usually hung on a wall.

look_alikes.name: Egyptian hand-knotted rugs, including Mamluk-design rugs
look_alikes.how_to_tell: These have no pile; Egyptian hand-knotted rugs do.

rows.trade_use: Sold to tourists in Egypt and exported to Europe and the US; 'Harrania' and 'Wissa Wassef' name pictorial tapestries usually hung on a wall.
rows.what_it_tells: A flat-woven Egyptian piece with village scenes points to Harraniya-style tapestry; a geometric all-wool kilim to Upper Egypt (Bani Adi, Assiut) or Helwan; pictorial or verse designs in mixed fibers to Fuwwa.
rows.cautions: Dates rest on Egyptian newspapers (weak sources). No open-licence museum example found. 'Assyuti' and 'helwan' are Stone's terms; Egyptian press calls the Bani Adi kilim «الكليم العدوي».

facts.text: Fuwwa in Kafr el-Sheikh is a center of hand-woven kilims, with designs that include rural scenes, the pyramids, mosques and Qur'anic verses.

The Bani Adi kilim (al-kilim al-'adawi) is made in Bani Adiyat village, Manfalut district, Assiut, of pure natural wool, by women at home on household looms; the craft was said in 2017 to be over a century old.
facts.quote: «من الصوف الطبيعى غير المضاف إليه أى خيوط أو مواد أخرى» (natural wool with no other thread or material added; Youm7 2017)

facts.text: Harraniya pieces are tapestries woven in an art school founded near Cairo by Ramses Wissa Wassef, showing naive scenes of village life.

disagreements.about: date the Fuwwa weaving trade began

says.text: Spread from 1812.
Established in 1822.

rows.name: Kairouan rugs (Tunisian knotted carpets), including the alloucha
rows.translit: zarbiyyat al-Qayrawān / al-zarbiyya al-qayrawāniyya ('the Kairouan carpet')
rows.region: Kairouan, central Tunisia, and the surrounding area; knotted carpets are now woven in every region of Tunisia (ONAT); Bizerte weaves imitations of Kairouan styles.
rows.made_by: Women, at home, in organized workshops and by subcontracting (Stone; Al-Ittihad 2019).
rows.date_note: ONAT and the Tunisian tourist office repeat a legend that Kamla, daughter of Muhammad al-Shawush, the Ottoman-era governor of Kairouan, introduced the Anatolian-style knotted carpet in 1830; ONAT itself says carpet weaving there is older than the story, and Stone dates the earliest Kairouan rugs (prayer rugs) to the early 19th century.

structure.knot_note: 'Turkish knot', woven on horizontal looms (Stone); 'nœud de Ghiordes', locally 'ghorza' (WMC 2009; probably Arabic غرزة, 'stitch': our reading).
structure.kpsi_note: No official count read. A 2024 travel guide says Tunisian carpets are most often 20, 30 or 40 knots per square centimeter (about 130, 195 and 260 per square inch); not confirmed by ONAT.
structure.wefts_note: Stone: all-wool carpets.
structure.pile_note: Short pile (Stone); wool natural or dyed (ONAT; Al-Ittihad 2019).

design.field: A rectangular field with a large central medallion, often with pointed or stepped ends, among geometricized flowers, framed by borders of parallel bands (Stone; ONAT; ONTT). Early 19th-century pieces were prayer rugs with opposed niches and red mihrabs, some with Kufic-style borders.
design.border: Several parallel bands with floral or geometric motifs (ONAT; ONTT).
design.colors: Either a bright red main color, or the natural wool colors (white, beige, brown, gray: the alloucha) (ONTT; Stone).

look_alikes.name: Rabat rugs (Moroccan urban carpets)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Both copy Anatolian models; Rabat rugs are long and narrow with a small field inside many borders, while Kairouan rugs center a large medallion in a framed field (Stone; ONTT).

look_alikes.name: Anatolian village rug
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kairouan designs come from Anatolian ones (Stone; ONAT); an ONAT stamp or lead seal on the back is the practical clue.

rows.trade_use: 'Zarbia' (زربية) is the Tunisian word for a knotted pile carpet; 'alloucha' names the undyed natural-color type. Inspected carpets carry ONAT's stamp, a paper label with a lead seal (see label ONAT stamp: paper label with a lead seal (Office National de l'Artisanat Tunisien / الديوان الوطني للصناعات التقليدية)).
rows.what_it_tells: A medallion rug with a framed field in red or in undyed wool colors, with a Tunisian ONAT label or lead seal, points to Kairouan-type Tunisian production.
rows.cautions: The 1830 founding story is a legend in the sources. Knot grades rest on a travel guide. No open-licence museum example found. The Arabic spelling علوشة for 'alloucha' was not seen in a source.

facts.text: Tunisian tradition credits Kamla, daughter of the Ottoman-era governor of Kairouan, with introducing the Anatolian-style knotted carpet there in 1830, but ONAT says the weaving is older than this legend.
facts.quote: «وتروي الأسطورة، أن ‹كاملة› إبنة محمد الشاوش والي القيروان من أصل تركي هي أول من أدخلت للمدينة سنة 1830 صناعة الزربية ذات العقد» (ONAT)

facts.text: Kairouan carpets are knotted with the symmetric (Turkish, Ghiordes) knot.
The classic Kairouan carpet has a large central medallion among flowers inside a frame of parallel bands; designs come from Anatolian models.
facts.quote: A Kairouan carpet is the one that most closely resembles oriental carpets. (ONTT)

facts.text: Kairouan carpets come either with a bright red main color or in the natural colors of the wool; the undyed type, in white, beige, brown and gray, is called alloucha.
Kairouan carpets are all wool with a short pile.
Early 19th-century Kairouan rugs were prayer rugs with opposed niches, red inside the mihrabs, some with Kufic-style borders.
Carpets brought to Kairouan's stamp house for inspection fell from about 12,000 pieces (18,440 m²) in 2010 to 3,500 pieces (9,698 m²) in 2020.
Machine-made carpets are also produced in Tunisia.

disagreements.about: when knotted carpet weaving began at Kairouan

says.text: The 1830 Kamla story is a legend; weaving predates it.
Introduced in 1830 by Kamla, 'selon la légende'.
Kairouan carpets were part of the tribute sent to Damascus and Baghdad under the Aghlabids (800-909).
The earliest Kairouan rugs described are early 19th-century prayer rugs.

rows.name: Tunisian flatweaves: mergoum and kilim
rows.region: Throughout Tunisia (ONAT); a travel guide says mergoums are made mostly in the interior and the south; ONAT names the Gafsa kilim and the Bou Saïd mergoum.
rows.made_by: Tribal and village women on horizontal and vertical looms.
rows.date_note: No dating found.

structure.knot_note: Kilims are wool bands of single colors (ONAT); the mergoum is another woolen weave used as a floor rug (ONAT; Stone lists Tunisian flatweaves). The tourist office calls both 'short pile rugs'.
structure.pile_note: No pile, per ONAT and Stone.

design.field: Parallel bands, at first plain stripes; later pieces add diamonds, triangles, chevrons and small stylized animals (Stone; ONTT). Kilims also serve as wall hangings and blankets (ONAT; Stone).
design.colors: Plant-dye reds, dark blue, brown and orange (ONTT).

look_alikes.name: Anatolian or Caucasian kilim
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Not settled by the sources read.

rows.trade_use: Sold as 'mergoum' or 'kilim' beside Kairouan pile carpets; cheaper kilims may mix wool with other fibers (travel text).
rows.what_it_tells: A Tunisian flatweave with bands of motifs in wool is a mergoum or kilim, not a Kairouan pile carpet.
rows.cautions: Sources disagree on whether the mergoum has pile.

facts.text: Tunisia is known for its floor coverings: the knotted zarbiya, the mergoum and the kilim.
facts.quote: «إشتهرت تونس بالمفروشات مثل الزربية و المرقوم والكليم» (ONAT)

facts.text: Tunisian kilims are woven in parallel bands of single colors and used as wall hangings or floor rugs.

says.text: 'Klims' and 'mergoums' are short pile rugs.
The mergoum is another kind of woolen weave used as a floor rug, listed apart from the knotted zarbiya.
Treats Tunisian kilims and related pieces as flatweaves.

rows.name: Algerian rugs (Djebel Amour, Guergour, Kalâa and others)
rows.translit: zarbiyya / zarābī Jabal ʿAmūr ('Djebel Amour rugs')
rows.region: Sétif, noted for rug production; Guergour; Kalâa des Beni-Rached south of Oran; Djebel Amour around Aflou, Laghouat province, about 400 km south of Algiers (Oman Daily 2017).
rows.made_by: Traditionally men (reggema) wove pile rugs with women assisting; today women design and weave. At Djebel Amour women weave while men traditionally worked out the geometry (Oman Daily).
rows.date_note: No dated sequence found.

structure.knot_note: Pile rugs are all wool with the symmetric knot (Stone). Qtif and tanchra have uncut looped pile (Stone).
structure.wefts_note: Kalâa: seven to ten wefts between rows of knots (Stone).
structure.ends: Frach and Kalâa carpets have wide flat-woven ends (Stone).

design.field: Kalâa: long vertical octagonal compartments (early rugs, Stone). Djebel Amour: geometric designs.
design.colors: Djebel Amour: white, red and black, later also green and yellow, from natural dyes (Oman Daily).
design.sizes: Djebel Amour: about 3 x 2 m up to 10 x 5 m (Oman Daily).

look_alikes.name: Middle Atlas pile rugs (incl. the ivory 'Beni Ourain' type)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Stone says Algerian rugs are similar to those of Morocco and Tunisia; no structural test found.

rows.what_it_tells: An all-wool, symmetrically knotted North African rug with wide flat-woven ends or a long-compartment design is consistent with Algerian weaving.
rows.cautions: Mostly one book plus one news report; Algerian sources were not otherwise reached.

facts.text: Algerian pile rugs are all wool with the symmetric knot; Sétif is noted for rug production.
Djebel Amour rugs come from the Aflou area of Laghouat province, are of wool dyed with natural colors, mainly white, red and black, and take three women about three months each.
facts.quote: «المعروفة بمنطقة آفلو بولاية الأغواط (400 كم جنوب الجزائر)» (known in the Aflou area of Laghouat province, 400 km south of Algiers)

museum_examples.title: Tent Hanging or Coverlet (Djerbi)
museum_examples.shows: museum's primary image; possibly Laghouat, Algeria; a flat-woven (tapestry and plain weave) hanging, not a pile rug

rows.name: Bedouin weaving of Arabia (Al Sadu)
rows.country: Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Qatar (UNESCO); also woven in the UAE, Oman, Jordan, Syria and Egypt (UNESCO nomination)
rows.region: Saudi Arabia: Tabuk and Al-Jouf in the north, Al-Qassim in the center and the Eastern Province (UNESCO nomination; Saudipedia names Al-Jouf). Kuwait: women of the Ajman, Mutair, Awazim, Rashaida and Shammar tribes.
rows.made_by: Bedouin women; men shear and clean the wool and may sell the pieces. Stone: some Bedouin men weave, but most weavers are women.
rows.date_note: A living craft, listed by UNESCO for Saudi Arabia and Kuwait in 2020 and extended to Qatar in 2025. No dating guide found.

structure.knot_note: Warp-faced plain weave on a ground loom (UNESCO; Stone); weft twining for decorative stripes and to strengthen edges (Stone).
structure.pile_note: No pile. Sheep's wool (Saudipedia: the white Naimi breed), camel hair and goat hair; commercial cotton yarn in recent work (UNESCO; Saudipedia).

design.field: Geometric bands of stripes, dots, squares and triangles in rhythmic repetition; diamonds, checks and animal brands (wasm); camels (Saudipedia).
design.colors: Bright reds and oranges with the natural colors of the fibers; plant dyes before chemical dyes.

look_alikes.name: other Middle Eastern warp-faced weaving (Jordan, Syria, Egypt)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: UNESCO says the same weaving is done in those countries; 'sadu' alone does not show which.

rows.trade_use: Sold through cooperatives such as Kuwait's Al Sadu Weaving Cooperative Society (1991, at Sadu House); recent sales include small items such as bookmarks rather than rugs.
rows.what_it_tells: A tightly woven, warp-faced flatweave in wool, camel or goat hair with bright red and orange geometric bands points to Bedouin weaving of Arabia.
rows.cautions: Recent pieces may use commercial cotton or synthetic yarn instead of hand-spun wool.

facts.text: Al Sadu is a warp-faced plain weave woven by Bedouin women on a ground loom.
Weavers use sheep's wool, camel hair and goat hair; before chemical dyes, wool was used undyed or dyed with plants such as cactus, pomegranate and onion.
facts.quote: «وبر الإبل» ... «شعر الماعز» (camel hair ... goat hair; Saudipedia)

facts.text: Designs are geometric (stripes, dots, squares, triangles), in bright colors such as red and orange.
Sadu furnishes the tent (bayt al-sha'r) and household: storage bags, cushions, rugs and dividing curtains.
UNESCO inscribed 'Traditional weaving of Al Sadu' for Saudi Arabia and Kuwait in 2020 and extended it to Qatar in 2025.
Kuwait's Al Sadu Weaving Cooperative Society, owned by the weavers, was founded in 1991 and works from Sadu House.
facts.quote: «الجمعية تأسست عام 1991» (Al-Rai 2022)

facts.text: Weavers increasingly use commercial cotton thread, which is easier on the hands, and now sell small items such as bookmarks more than rugs.

rows.name: Mamluk and Cairene carpets (design)
rows.region: Originals: Cairo (Pope 1926; Met; Art Institute of Chicago 'possibly Cairo'); some groups called 'Mamluk' are attributed to Damascus, Anatolia or the Maghreb. Later rugs in the design: Egypt and elsewhere (see Egyptian hand-knotted rugs, including Mamluk-design rugs).
rows.made_by: Originals: Cairo workshops under the Mamluk sultans and, after 1517, under Ottoman rule.
rows.date_note: Originals: late 15th to early 16th century (geometric Mamluk) and 16th to 17th century (Ottoman floral designs woven in Cairo). Dates here are for later rugs in the design; Egypt's knotted production restarted in the 1950s.

structure.knot_note: Originals: asymmetric knot (Stone; Met; AIC records 'Persian (Sehna)' knots). Copies use their own center's structure.
structure.pile_note: Originals: all wool, S-spun (most rugs are Z-spun), red from lac (Stone); one all-silk Mamluk carpet is in Vienna (Stone).

design.field: Originals: one or more large octagonal or round medallions built of small geometric units (stars, small conical trees) in a field of geometric ornament, with a border of long cartouches and rosettes. Later 'compartment' or 'chessboard' designs repeat octagons linked by radiating lines. After 1517 Cairo also wove curving Ottoman floral designs.
design.border: Long cartouches alternating with small rosettes.
design.colors: A limited palette: red with blue, green and yellow (Stone; Pope: blue, green, ruby and gold).

look_alikes.name: Egyptian hand-knotted rugs, including Mamluk-design rugs
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Classical originals are all wool, S-spun, with lac red; a later rug in the design shows modern dyes and its own center's foundation.

rows.trade_use: 'Mamluk' on a modern rug names the design, wherever the rug was made.
rows.what_it_tells: The name identifies a design family; it says nothing about where or when a later rug was made.
rows.cautions: Old books call these 'Damascus' carpets. Many rugs called Mamluk are of uncertain origin.

facts.text: These carpets were once published as Damascus, Syrian, Syracuse, Asia Minor, Moroccan or Hispano-Moresque; Friedrich Sarre's research showed they were woven in Cairo from the 15th to the 17th century.
facts.quote: They have been published as Damascus, Syrian, Syracuse, Asia Minor, Morocco and Hispano Moresque. (Pope 1926)

facts.text: Mamluk and Cairene carpets were woven in Cairo between the late 15th and the 17th century.
The originals are all wool and use the asymmetric knot.
Their yarn is S-spun, unlike the Z-spun yarn of most rugs, and their red is from lac.
Pope traced the designs to Cairo's mosaic fountains, Coptic textiles and the borders of 15th-century book covers.
facts.quote: The long cartouche and rosette patterns are taken from the borders of book covers, particularly those of the fifteenth century. (Pope 1926)

facts.text: After the Ottoman conquest of 1517, Cairo workshops went on weaving geometric Mamluk designs and also wove Ottoman floral designs.

says.text: Sarre showed 'to the satisfaction of most scholars' that they are from Cairo.
Many so-called Mamluk rugs are of problematic origin; one group is attributed to the Maghreb, and para-Mamluk rugs to Cairo, Damascus or Anatolia.
AIC 1950.1365: 'Egypt, possibly Cairo'.

dates.title: Dates, signatures and words woven into rugs

numerals.name: Arabic-Indic digits (the digits of the Arab world and the Ottoman Empire; often called 'Arabic numerals' in old rug books)
numerals.codepoints: U+0660 ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT ZERO, U+0661 ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT ONE, U+0662 ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT TWO, U+0663 ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT THREE, U+0664 ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT FOUR, U+0665 ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT FIVE, U+0666 ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT SIX, U+0667 ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT SEVEN, U+0668 ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT EIGHT, U+0669 ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT NINE
numerals.used_on: Ottoman and Anatolian rugs until Turkey made Western digits compulsory in official use (1 June 1929); Muslim-woven Caucasian rugs; Arab-world pieces. Iranian weavers mostly used the Persian forms (next entry), but woven digits mix forms, so the shape of a 4, 5 or 6 is a hint, not proof, of where a rug was made.

woven_forms.0: ٠ a dot. Woven, it is one knot or a tiny diamond of knots, easy to miss or to take for a stray knot.
woven_forms.2: ٢ an upright with one hook at the top right, like a Latin r.
woven_forms.3: ٣ an upright with two small teeth at the top: a 2 with an extra tooth.
woven_forms.4: ٤ Arabic form: shaped like a backward 3 (an epsilon ε).
woven_forms.5: ٥ Arabic form: a small circle or loop, which a Western reader takes for a zero.
woven_forms.6: ٦ Arabic form: a hook with a downstroke, like a backward Western 7 or a small 'L' turned over.
woven_forms.9: ٩ a loop on a stem, much like a Western 9.
woven_forms.general: Knotted on a grid, curves become steps, so teeth and hooks blur. Ripley (1904) advises counting the knots that make each stroke to recover the shape.

confusions.example: Met 22.100.3: the Met's 1923 catalogue printed 1323; the Met now reads 1223. V&A T.25-1983: the last digit read as 2 or 3 (1202 or 1283).
V&A T.25-1983: third digit read as 0 or 8 (1202 or 1283).
Met 22.100.61: read 1110 in 1921, 1210 today; the 1923 catalogue says the date 'appears to have been altered by restoration'.
Poldi Pezzoli hunting carpet: 'the second digit ... can be read either 2 or 4' (929 or 949).

confusions.pair: 7 and 8 when upside down (V and Λ)
confusions.example: Inferred from the shapes only: turning a date upside down swaps ٧ and ٨. No source read reports a case.

confusions.pair: 5 read as 0 by Western readers (٥ is a circle; ٠ is a dot)
confusions.example: Inferred from the shapes; no source read reports a case.

numerals.mirrored: Dates can appear reversed (mirror image) when a weaver copied an inscription from the back of another rug (Stone, 'mirror writing'), and some dates are woven upside down (Gregorian 1987 on Armenian-inscribed rugs). Hawley and Lewis advise reading a worn date from the back, where the order of digits runs the other way. No source gives a count of how common mirrored dates are.

facts.text: Dates woven in these digits on rugs are usually years of the Muslim lunar (Hijri) calendar.
Numbers are read from left to right (largest place first), as in Western usage, even though the words around them run right to left.
Old rug books print tables of these digits and note that woven forms vary ('numerous modifications').
facts.note: Jacobsen copies Hawley's text; the OCR of every table is garbled, so shapes here are described from the Unicode reference glyphs.

facts.text: Unicode encodes the Arabic-Indic digits at U+0660–U+0669, separate from the Persian/Urdu (Eastern) set.

numerals.name: Persian (Eastern Arabic-Indic, 'extended') digits
numerals.codepoints: U+06F0 EXTENDED ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT ZERO, U+06F1 EXTENDED ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT ONE, U+06F2 EXTENDED ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT TWO, U+06F3 EXTENDED ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT THREE, U+06F4 EXTENDED ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT FOUR, U+06F5 EXTENDED ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT FIVE, U+06F6 EXTENDED ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT SIX, U+06F7 EXTENDED ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT SEVEN, U+06F8 EXTENDED ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT EIGHT, U+06F9 EXTENDED ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT NINE
numerals.used_on: Iranian rugs (Persian), and the Persian/Urdu-writing world: Afghanistan, Pakistan and India per Unicode. On rugs: Persian city, village and tribal rugs dated in the lunar (AH) or, from 1911/1925, the solar (SH) year.

woven_forms.0: ۰ a dot, as in the Arabic set.
woven_forms.2: ۲ an upright with one hook at the top right.
woven_forms.3: ۳ an upright with two teeth at the top.
woven_forms.4: ۴ Persian form: an upright with a small double curl on its upper left; unlike the Arabic ٤.
woven_forms.5: ۵ Persian form: a pointed loop, like an upside-down heart, narrow at the top; it can be read as a 0 or an o.
woven_forms.6: ۶ Persian form: a small head with a tail swept down to the left; unlike the Arabic ٦.
woven_forms.7: ۷ a V (some local hands differ, per Unicode).
woven_forms.general: As with the Arabic set, knotting turns curves into steps. Persian and Arabic forms of 4, 5 and 6 can appear on the same rug.

confusions.pair: last digit of the Ardabil date
confusions.example: Printed 942 by Pope (1926, with '1539') and read 946 by the V&A and LACMA; Stone gives '1535 or 1540, according to inscriptions'.
Same shapes and same risks as the Arabic set; see the museum cases there.
Inferred from the shapes; no source read reports a case.

numerals.mirrored: As for the Arabic set: mirror writing when copied from the back (Stone); read from the back in reverse order when the front is worn (Hawley, Lewis).

facts.text: Unicode encodes a separate set of digits for Persian, Sindhi and Urdu (U+06F0–U+06F9), used in Afghanistan, India, Iran and Pakistan.
The Persian/Urdu forms of four, five, six and seven differ from the Arabic forms, and four, six and seven vary a good deal between places.
The Ardabil carpet's date is woven in these digits after the word سنه ('year'): «سنه ۹۴۶».

numerals.name: Western (European) digits 0–9
numerals.codepoints: U+0030 DIGIT ZERO, U+0031 DIGIT ONE, U+0032 DIGIT TWO, U+0033 DIGIT THREE, U+0034 DIGIT FOUR, U+0035 DIGIT FIVE, U+0036 DIGIT SIX, U+0037 DIGIT SEVEN, U+0038 DIGIT EIGHT, U+0039 DIGIT NINE
numerals.used_on: Armenian-inscribed Caucasian, Anatolian and Persian rugs (about 1800–1930s), Turkish rugs after the 1928–29 reforms, Soviet-era rugs, some Muslim-woven Caucasian rugs (with Hijri years), Harvard's Marasali prayer rug '1908', and modern export rugs.

woven_forms.general: Ordinary shapes, but weavers wove digits reversed, upside down, doubled, dropped or scrambled; day and month are often put between the century and the year (e.g. '19 11/7 27' for 7 Nov 1927).

confusions.example: '1992' woven for 1929 on a pictorial Karabagh rug.
A Kazak with 'Ya Huseyn' and the year 1333 in Western digits = AH 1333 (Nov 1914–Nov 1915), not AD 1333.

numerals.mirrored: Gregorian (1987) shows several Armenian-inscribed rugs with dates reversed or upside down (e.g. Plate 12, '1919' and '1329' both reversed).

facts.text: In a few cases the first or last numeral is doubled or omitted, and dates can be reversed or upside down.
Turkey made international (Western) numerals compulsory in official writing from 1 June 1929 (Law 1288 of 20 May 1928).
English rug books use 'Arabic numerals' for both Western digits and Arabic-script digits; check which is meant.

numerals.name: Armenian letter-numerals (capital letters with number values)
numerals.used_on: Armenian-era dates on 17th-century inscribed rugs; some AD years on 20th-century Caucasian rugs; manuscript colophons and gravestones
numerals.woven_forms: Written largest first and added: ՌՃԻԹ = 1000+100+20+9 = 1129. A point or stroke may follow (ՌԾԶ.). Hundreds can be written as multiplier + Ճ (ՌԲՃ եւ Կ = 1000 + 2×100 + 60 = 1260, a manuscript note). The thousands letter may be left off (a '106' read as 1706 on a ceramic).
numerals.confusions: Ի (20) vs Խ (40): the Gohar readings 1129 and 1149 differ by exactly this letter; Ghazaryan says one letter is 'sometimes confused' with another (letters lost in our OCR copy, so the pair is our inference from the arithmetic). Ռ (1000) vs Ո (600): Riegl's 651 against 1051 on the three-apsed carpet differs by exactly this letter (same inference).

facts.text: The W3C 'armenian' counter style maps 1000 to U+054C and 1 to U+0531, additive, range 1-9999.
Stone prints a table 'Armenian alphabet with numerical equivalents' for reading rug dates.
ՌԾԶ = 1056 (Armenian era) = 1607 in a dated colophon.

calendars.label: Muslim lunar (Hijri) year: AH; Persian 'qamari' (ه.ق); the usual era of woven dates before the 20th century
calendars.how_to_convert: EXACT (tabular arithmetic): AH year N begins on Julian Day JD = 1948439.5 + 354×(N−1) + floor((3 + 11×N)/30) and ends the day before year N+1 begins; turn the JD into a calendar date (Julian calendar before 15 Oct 1582, Gregorian after). Year 1 began Friday 16 July 622 (Julian). Each AH year has 354 or 355 days, so it is about 11 days shorter than a solar year and almost always straddles two AD years: write the result as a range, e.g. AH 1300 = 12 Nov 1882 – 1 Nov 1883 ('1882/83'). Real dates set by sighting the new moon can differ from the tabular ones by a day or two. QUICK ESTIMATE (old rug books): AD ≈ AH − AH/33.7 + 622 (Hawley, Stone; Jacobsen copies Hawley) or AH − AH/33 + 622 (Lewis). These land in or next to the right AD year but cannot show the straddle; use them only as a check.
worked: 946: JD of 1 Muharram 946 → 19 May 1539; year ends 7 May 1540 → '1539/40' (V&A and LACMA: 1539–40).
1247: Hawley's example: 1247 − 37 + 622 = 1832; exact range 12 Jun 1831 – 30 May 1832.
1331: Lewis's example: 1331 − 40 + 622 = 1913; exact range 11 Dec 1912 – 29 Nov 1913.
calendars.when_used: Dated rugs from the 16th century (Ardabil, AH 946) through the 20th: Persian rugs before the 1925 calendar law and often after it for religious or traditional wording; Ottoman/Anatolian prayer rugs (Ladik, Ghiordes, Kula; AH 1110–1300s); Muslim-woven Caucasian rugs (Daghestan, Shirvan, Kazak; AH 1212–1333 in the examples). Turkey's 1925 law kept the Hijri calendar for religious use.
calendars.tells_apart: On an Iranian rug a number from about 1290 to 1405 can be AH or SH, and the two readings are 38–41 years apart (AH 1300 = 1882/83; SH 1300 = 1921/22; AH 1350 = 1931/32; SH 1350 = 1971/72). A number at or below 1289 is AH, because the solar Hijri count was not in official use before 1911. A number above the current SH year (1405 in 2026) but within the AH range is AH. Lunar month names (Muharram, Rajab, Ramadan…) point to AH. On an Ottoman rug of about 1840–1925, AH and Rumi years for the same date differ by 0–3. Sources resolve the rest by style, dyes and structure, not by the number.

facts.text: The tabular Islamic calendar starts on Friday 16 July 622 (Julian), JD 1948439.5, with alternating 30- and 29-day months and 11 leap years in a 30-year cycle.
For religious purposes Muslim months begin with the first sighting of the new crescent, so real dates can differ from tabular dates.
facts.note: Met 57.5: the Met gives 14 Rajab 1280 as 26 Dec 1863; the tabular arithmetic gives 25 Dec 1863.

facts.text: Dates woven in Arabic-script digits on rugs are Hijri (Muslim) years, reckoned from the Hijra of 622.
The lunar year gains about one year on the solar year every 33.7 years; subtract 1/33.7 of the AH year and add 622.
facts.note: Jacobsen 1962/1969 copies Hawley's wording and example; not independent.

facts.text: A bare AH year covers parts of two AD years; museums write ranges such as '1210 AH/1795/96 CE' and '1287 AH (1870/71)'.
Hijri years were also written in Western digits on some Caucasian rugs (Kazak, '1333' = 1914/15, with 'Ya Huseyn').
Turkey's Law 698 (26 Dec 1925) made the Gregorian year official from 1 Jan 1926 and kept the Hijri lunar calendar for religious use.

says.text: says the Muslim year is 'thirty-three days less than ours' (an error; his 1/33 rule is still close)
lunar year gains about a year every 33.7 years (i.e. about 11 days a year)
354- or 355-day years
A.D. 1568 (wrong by about 28 years)
A.D. 1553 (wrong)
prints the year as 942 'i.e. 1539 A.D.' (942 = 1535/36, so the two do not match)
'1535 or 1540, according to inscriptions'
1298 AH catalogued as 1880 (AH 1298 began 4 Dec 1880, so nearly all of it fell in 1881)
AH 1322 catalogued as 1905 (AH 1322 ran 18 Mar 1904 – 7 Mar 1905)

disagreements.note: Catalogues pick either the starting or the ending AD year; neither is wrong, but a reader should see the range.

calendars.label: Iranian solar Hijri year: SH; Persian 'shamsi' or 'khorshidi' (ه.ش)
calendars.how_to_convert: SH year + 621 = AD year from 1 Farvardin (about 21 March) to 31 December; SH + 622 from 1 January to the end of Esfand (about 20 March). A bare SH year N therefore runs from about 21 March (N+621) to about 20 March (N+622). Months: Farvardin, Ordibehesht, Khordad, Tir, Mordad, Shahrivar (31 days each), Mehr, Aban, Azar, Dey, Bahman (30), Esfand (29, 30 in leap years). From 1911 to 1925 the same year count was used with zodiac month names (Hamal = Aries … Hut = Pisces).
worked: SH 1304 began 21 Mar 1925, so 11 Farvardin 1304 = 31 Mar 1925.
calendars.when_used: Iran's official accounting year from the General Accounts Law of 21 Safar 1329 = 2 Hut 1289 (21 Feb 1911); with Persian month names by the law of 11 Farvardin 1304 (31 Mar 1925), effective from Nowruz 1304. On rugs: Iranian rugs woven from the 1920s on may carry SH years (13xx, then 14xx from March 2021). No museum record with a woven SH date was found for this file.
calendars.tells_apart: See ah-lunar: 1290–1405 on an Iranian rug is ambiguous (38–41 years apart). Persian month names (Farvardin … Esfand) beside the year point to SH after 1925, but V&A 390-1880 shows the Persian month Khordad beside a year the V&A reads as AH (1277 = 1860/61), so a Persian month name alone is not proof. Zodiac month names point to the 1911–1925 accounting usage or to almanacs.

facts.text: The solar Hijri year with zodiac months became the official accounting calendar by Article 3 of the General Accounts Law, 21 Safar 1329 = 2 Hut 1289 SH (21 Feb 1911).
facts.note: 21 Safar 1329 = 21 Feb 1911 by the tabular arithmetic, which agrees.

facts.text: The law converting the zodiac months to Persian month names was approved on 11 Farvardin 1304 (31 March 1925), effective from Nowruz 1304.
facts.note: The 1925 year is confirmed by fourmilab_calendar; the exact day rests on Hamshahri plus the arithmetic. Encyclopaedia Iranica 'Calendars' and the University of Tehran Calendar Center pages could not be opened (403 / redirect).

facts.text: The modern Persian calendar was adopted in 1925.
The year begins at the vernal (March) equinox.
The first six months have 31 days, the next five 30, and the last 29 (30 in a leap year).
The era is counted from the Prophet's Hijra from Mecca to Medina, the same starting point as the lunar AH count.

The Persian text of the law of 11 Farvardin 1304 makes the yearly official date, from Nowruz 1304, count from the Hijra, begin the year on the first day of spring, keep 'the true solar year', and name the months Farvardin to Esfand (six of 31 days, five of 30, Esfand 29, or 30 in leap years).
facts.quote: الف - مبدأ تاریخ: سال هجرت حضرت خاتم‌النبیین ... ب - آغاز سال: روز اول بهار. ج - سال: کماکان شمسی حقیقی. ('a. era: the year of the Hijra of the Prophet ...; b. start of the year: the first day of spring; c. the year: as before, the true solar year')

facts.text: Article 2 of the same law abolished the Khata-Ighur (Turkic-Uighur twelve-animal) year names used in earlier almanacs.
facts.quote: ترتیب سال شماری ختاوایغور که در تقویم‌های سابق معمول بوده از تاریخ تصویب این قانون منسوخ خواهد بود ('the Khata-Ighur year count used in former almanacs is abolished from the date of this law')

facts.text: The Majlis passed it at a night sitting whose record is headed 'night of Tuesday 11 Farvardin 1304, corresponding to 6 Ramadan 1343' (31 March 1925).
The law spells the fifth month امرداد (Amordad); the 1978 reprint and later usage write مرداد (Mordad). A woven month name may use either spelling.
In 1329 AH/1911 the parliament made official the Jalali solar year with zodiac month names (Hamal to Hut) and twelve-animal year names; it remained in use until 1925.

The solar Hijri era is reckoned from 1 Farvardin of the year of the Hijra, 119 days before 1 Muharram AH 1; Iranica gives that day as 19 March 622 (Julian) and notes Taqizadeh's 17 March 622, apparently the date the 1925 calendar commission used.

disagreements.about: when Iran 'adopted' the solar Hijri year

says.text: official for state accounts from 1911 (zodiac months); Persian month names and the full official calendar from Nowruz 1304 (1925)
adopted in 1925

disagreements.note: Two steps, not a conflict: the SH year count existed officially from 1911.

calendars.label: Iranian imperial (shahanshahi) year, March 1976 to August 1978
calendars.how_to_convert: Imperial year − 1180 = SH year; so 2535 = SH 1355 (21 Mar 1976 – 20 Mar 1977), 2536 = SH 1356 (1977/78), 2537 = SH 1357 (1978/79, until the count was dropped in late summer 1978).
calendars.when_used: Iran's official year count from March 1976 to late August or early September 1978. No source read shows it woven on a rug.
calendars.tells_apart: A woven 2535–2537 (in Persian digits) on an Iranian rug would fit this count; no other calendar on Iranian rugs gives a number in the 2500s.

facts.text: The imperial count replaced the SH year in March 1976 (year 1355 became 2535) and was abandoned in 1978.
facts.note: Only Persian and English Wikipedia were readable; they cite the University of Tehran Calendar Center and Gheissari (2010), neither of which could be opened. The two Wikipedias disagree on the start day (20 or 24 Esfand 1354) and the end day (5 or 11 Shahrivar 1357).

facts.text: On 24 Esfand 1354 (14 March 1976) the Majles approved a new era counted from the supposed accession of Cyrus the Great (559 BC); 21 March 1976 became Nowruz of the year 2535 shahanshahi. The Persian month names were kept unchanged, and official documents were dated by the new count.

On 5 Shahrivar 1357 (27 August 1978) the government went back to the solar Hijri count: the Prime Minister's circular to all ministries, agencies and state companies declared the law of 11 Farvardin 1304 still in force, reprinted it, and ordered it applied in all correspondence and documents.
facts.quote: نظر به‌اینکه قانون مصوب یازدهم فروردین ماه ۱۳۰۴ شمسی ... بقوت خود باقی است ('whereas the law passed on 11 Farvardin 1304 SH ... remains in force')

facts.text: The imperial year is the solar Hijri year plus 1180 (2535 = 1355); the circular of 1978 was printed under the heading 'The imperial year has changed'.

says.text: Approved 24 Esfand 1354 (printed '14 March 1975'); in force from Nowruz 2535 (21 March 1976); dropped 5 Shahrivar 1357 (27 August 1978).
The circular restoring the 1304 law was issued 'today', 5 Shahrivar 1357.

disagreements.note: The table's existing note reports that Persian and English Wikipedia give 20 or 24 Esfand 1354 for the start and 5 or 11 Shahrivar 1357 for the end; the two sources read here agree on 24 Esfand and 5 Shahrivar. The 'unverified' flag on this calendar can be cleared.

calendars.label: Ottoman Rumi (fiscal, 'malî') year
calendars.how_to_convert: Up to Rumi 1332 (early 1917): the year began on 1 March and the days ran on the Julian calendar. For March-December add 584; for January and February add 585. Rumi 1 March = Gregorian 13 March in the 1800s and 14 March in the 1900s. By 1925 the year was the same as AD minus 584 for December, and the day numbers matched Gregorian ones (31 Kânunuevvel 1341 was followed by 1 Kânunusani 1926). Unverified here: the 1917 law that dropped 13 days (the day after 15 Şubat 1332 became 1 Mart 1333) and the move of New Year to 1 January from 1918 (Rumi 1334), after which +584 works all year.
calendars.when_used: Ottoman state finance and official documents: the malî year from a 1677 ferman (TDV), with TDV's worked examples from malî 1256 (= 1840); ended 31 Dec 1925 (Law 698). We found no source documenting Rumi years woven on rugs.
calendars.tells_apart: Between 1840 and 1926 a Rumi year runs 0 to 3 below the Hijri year for the same date (1840: Rumi 1256 = AH 1256; 1900: Rumi 1316 vs AH 1317/18; 1925: Rumi 1341 vs AH 1343/44). Month names Mart ... Şubat, Teşrinievvel, Kânunuevvel, Kânunusani mark a Rumi date in writing. No rug in the sources read is documented with a Rumi year.

facts.text: Julian-type 365.25-day calendars are called 'Rûmî takvim' in Turkish; the Ottoman malî year began on 1 March.
Rumi 1 March = 13 March (Gregorian) in the 1800s, 14 March in the 1900s.
Malî 1256 began on 1 March 1840 (Julian) = 9 Muharram 1256, so 1256 + 584 = 1840.

Law no. 698 (accepted 26 Dec 1925, Resmî Gazete 2 Jan 1926 no. 260): the day after 31 Kânunuevvel 1341 is 1 Kânunusani 1926; the international year count becomes official; the Hijri lunar calendar stays for religious use.
Rumi + 584 holds for December 1925 (1341) and March 1840 (1256): the two official sources agree on the same 584-year offset 85 years apart.

says.text: By the old rule tying the malî number to the Hijri year, 1288 'disappeared' (a 'sıvış yılı'); the same text calls 1 March 1872 '1 Mart 1288'.
December 1341 = December 1925, which with TDV's 1256 = 1840 leaves no room for a dropped year between 1840 and 1925.

calendars.label: Christian (Gregorian, AD) year in Western digits or, rarely, in Armenian letters
calendars.how_to_convert: Read the year as written. On Armenian-inscribed rugs, the day and month often sit between the century and the year ('19 11/7 27' = 7 Nov 1927; '18 3/10 89' = 10 Mar 1889). Before 1918 a day-and-month date from the Russian Empire was probably in the Julian calendar (Old Style), 12 days behind in the 1800s and 13 in the 1900s (not confirmed in a source read).
calendars.when_used: Armenian-inscribed Caucasian, Anatolian and Persian rugs (dated examples 1810–1938 in the Gregorian collection; Karabagh rugs of 1810–1898 in Kouymjian); Turkish rugs after the 1926–1929 reforms; Soviet-era rugs (e.g. a 1929 pictorial Karabagh); Harvard 1977.166 ('1908' three times).
calendars.tells_apart: A 4-digit Western number from 1700 to today. A Western-digit number in the 1100s–1300s on a Caucasian or Persian rug is a Hijri year written in Western digits, not an AD year (Ibrahimov's Kazak '1333'). A Western date does not by itself show an Armenian weaver.

facts.text: Law 698 (accepted 26 Dec 1925; Official Gazette 2 Jan 1926 no. 260) made the international year count official in Turkey from 1 Jan 1926: the day after 31 Kânunuevvel 1341 became 1 Kânunusani 1926.
Law 1288 (20 May 1928) made Western numerals compulsory in official writing from 1 June 1929; Law 1353 (1 Nov 1928) adopted the Latin alphabet.
Turkish rugs were often dated in Western style after Atatürk's reforms.
Dates on Armenian-inscribed rugs are often followed by ԹՎ ('year') or ԱՄԻ ('in the year').
Kouymjian's captions give Armenian-inscribed Karabagh rugs dated 26 June 1810, 1815, 1866, 1877, 8 June 1884, 6 April 1888 and 1898 (AD).
facts.note: Several are Gregorian Collection rugs, so not fully independent of gregorian_1987.

facts.text: A Gregorian date is a year counted from the birth of Christ as adjusted by Pope Gregory in 1582, as distinct from Islamic dates.

disagreements.about: does a Western-digit date point to an Armenian weaver?

says.text: Caucasian rugs with western dates are 'probably Armenian in origin'.
a western-style date is not enough, since Turkish rugs were dated in western style after Atatürk's reforms.
Hijri years in Western digits appear on Muslim-inscribed Kazaks sold as Armenian.

calendars.label: Armenian era (Great Armenian Era) year written in Armenian letters
calendars.how_to_convert: Add up the letter values (see numerals.armenian_letters), then add 551. The Armenian year had 365 days and no leap day, so its New Year slid back through the Julian calendar about one day every four years (by our calculation from a 552 epoch: early October in the 1670s, late September around 1700, end of August around 1810). A bare Armenian year therefore straddles two AD years: +551 gives the AD year that holds most of it, and the last months of the AD year before belong to the same Armenian year. When a Julian month is named, add 551 (Khachikian, followed by Grigoryan).
calendars.when_used: On the oldest inscribed Armenian rugs: the 'three-apsed' carpet (Armenian era 1051 = 1602) and the Gohar carpet (1129 or 1149 = 1680 or 1700). Later inscribed rugs (1800s-1930s) mostly give the AD year (see ad_western_digits_armenian), but some AD years are written with Armenian letters (see ad_in_armenian_letters).
calendars.tells_apart: Armenian capital letters, not digits, usually led by Ռ (1000). If letters + 551 lands in the future (e.g. ՌՋԻԸ = 1928, +551 = 2479), the weaver wrote the AD year in letters: read it without adding 551.

facts.text: Dates on Armenian rugs often appear in letter form; convert by summing the letter values and adding 551.

Kendrick & Tattersall read the Gohar inscription's date as Armenian 1129 = AD 1679; Ghazaryan gives the same inscription as 1680. Armenian year 1129 ran from about 3 Oct 1679 to 1 Oct 1680 (Julian), so both fit one reading.
Armenian-era 1051 + 551 = 1602 (the 'three-apsed' carpet).
In manuscript colophons the date is introduced by the word թվական ('year'), e.g. 'ի թվականիս հայոց ՌԾԶ' (in the Armenian year 1056 = 1607), December ԻԳ (23).

Some editors add 550 instead of 551 for dates between about 18 October and 31 December in the early 1600s, because the Armenian year then began in October; Khachikian argued +551 still applies when Julian months are named.
The day the Armenian era began (by our calculation 11 July 552, Julian) is not confirmed in a source read; the +551 rule is (Stone, Ghazaryan, Grigoryan).
facts.note: Year ranges given in this file assume the 552 epoch and a 365-day year with no leap day.

disagreements.about: +550 or +551 for the last months of the AD year

says.text: Hakobyan & Hovhannisyan add 550 for 18 Oct-31 Dec in 1604-1607; Khachikian (followed by Grigoryan) adds 551 whenever Julian month names are used.

calendars.label: AD year written with Armenian letter-numerals (no 551 added)
calendars.how_to_convert: Sum the letter values; the result is already the AD year.
calendars.when_used: Early 1900s Caucasian rugs; Gregorian's Plate 87 (Moghan, dated 1928) writes the year first in ornate Armenian numerals, then the same AD year in western digits.
calendars.tells_apart: Letter sum of 1800-1950 with Ռ (1000) + Պ (800) or Ջ (900). Adding 551 would give a year after 2350.

facts.text: On a rug dated 1928 the date is written in ornate Armenian numerals first, followed by the same Christian-calendar year in western digits.
The History Museum of Armenia describes dating on Armenian-inscribed carpets as 'often made in Armenian letters or in Arab figures' (it does not say which era the letters count from).

calendars.label: Chinese reign title with a 60-year cycle (ganzhi) year; Mongolian and Tibetan forms name an element-color and an animal
calendars.how_to_convert: 1) Find the reign's span (Qianlong 乾隆 1736–1795; Jiaqing 嘉慶 1796–1820; Daoguang 道光 1821–1850; Xianfeng 咸豐 1851–1861; Tongzhi 同治 1862–1874; Guangxu 光緒 1875–1908; Xuantong 宣統 1909–1911). 2) The cyclical sign repeats every 60 years. Stem = (AD − 4) mod 10 in 甲乙丙丁戊己庚辛壬癸; branch = (AD − 4) mod 12 in 子丑寅卯辰巳午未申酉戌亥. 3) Take the one AD year inside the reign that has the sign. Mongolian/Tibetan wording such as 'year of the blue hen' gives the element-color (blue/green = wood = 甲 or 乙; the female animal = the odd stem 乙) and the animal (hen/rooster = 酉).
worked: 乙酉 (yi-you): 1765, 1825, 1885. In Qianlong only 1765 (Qianlong 30); in Guangxu only 1885 (Guangxu 11).
'Year of the blue hen' in Guangxu (Mongolian 'Badaraghultu Tore') = 乙酉 = 1885.
calendars.when_used: Inscribed temple pillar rugs and hangings (Chinese, Mongolian, Tibetan). The V&A's pair of pillar rugs carries a Chinese Qianlong yi-you date and a Mongolian Guangxu 'blue hen' date. No reign mark (年製) woven into a Chinese pile carpet was verified (see words).
calendars.tells_apart: Chinese characters for a reign name plus two cyclical characters; or a Mongolian/Tibetan line naming a color and an animal year.

facts.text: A Chinese inscription on V&A pillar rug T.238-1928 gives the yi-you year of Qianlong, i.e. 1765; the museum dates the rug 1885 and calls the Chinese date a weaving error.
The Mongolian inscription on its pair, T.239-1928, names the year of the blue hen in the reign of Badaraghultu Tore (Guangxu), which the V&A gives as 1885.
Reign-plus-cyclical dating appears on other Qing textiles (AIC 1907.322, a Daoist vestment: the guichou year of Qianlong, i.e. 1793).
facts.note: Not a rug; shows the formula.

disagreements.about: which date on the V&A pillar-rug pair is right

says.text: Chinese date = 1765, called a weaving error
Mongolian date = 1885, used for both rugs

words.script: Arabic script (Arabic word used in Persian and Ottoman Turkish)
words.meaning: year
words.where_on_rug: just before, or above, the digits of the year; often at the end of a maker's line

Dates are woven in numbers 'above a word denoting year'.
V&A 390-1880 is woven 'Ta'rikh-e hashtom-e Khordad saneh 1277' (date of 8 Khordad, year 1277).

words.where_on_rug: not documented on a rug

Mumford (1902) records a Kirman rug inscribed 'Amli Kirman, made at Kirman' (= عمل کرمان).

facts.text: Recorded as 體和殿御用 (Tihedian yuyong) on a silk-and-metal-thread five-dragon carpet catalogued as '19th century'.
The Palace Museum says the hall was rebuilt as a through-hall and named 体和殿 in the Guangxu reign. A carpet inscribed for it therefore cannot have been made for that hall before Guangxu.

words.meaning: Hall of Martial Valor, which flanks the three great halls on the west
words.where_on_rug: top edge

facts.text: Recorded as 武英殿備用 on a silk 'landscape' carpet catalogued as Qing, 19th century.

words.native: 天壇 (characters not given by the source)
words.meaning: Temple of Heaven, Beijing
words.where_on_rug: in a cartouche

facts.text: A silk and gold metal-thread dragon carpet, which the auction house called 'signed' and 'Ningxia', had a cartouche inscription said to show it was made for imperial use in the Temple of Heaven. It was catalogued as Qing, 19th century. The wording is not given.

words.meaning: 'mark' or 'inscription'. Chinese catalogues write 《景仁宮御用》款 to mean 'with the mark Jingren gong yuyong'
words.where_on_rug: not on the rug; it is used in catalogue titles

facts.text: Sotheby's Chinese lot titles quote carpet inscriptions as 《…》款.

words.meaning: 'laid for use' (on a floor or platform)
words.where_on_rug: unknown

facts.text: No source read records 铺用 woven into a carpet. The phrase appears only in Chinese descriptive prose about where carpets were laid.

words.native: 年製 (simplified 年制), e.g. 大清乾隆年製
words.meaning: reign mark, 'made in the … years'
words.kind: reign mark (NOT verified on Chinese pile carpets)
words.where_on_rug: unknown

facts.text: None of the inscribed palace carpets in the auction texts read has a reign mark; their inscriptions give only the hall and the use.
Kendrick (1922), Stone (2013) and Hackmack (1921) do not mention reign marks or cyclical dates woven into Chinese rugs.

words.meaning: long life; comes in a round form (圓壽) and a long form (長壽), and is also used as a general good wish
words.kind: auspicious character (ornament, not a mark or date)
words.where_on_rug: central medallion, corners, repeated in borders, often with five bats around it

facts.text: Various forms of the long-life character are used as ornament in Chinese carpets.
Five bats around shou (wu fu peng shou) stand for the five blessings.

words.meaning: happiness, good fortune
words.where_on_rug: field or border

facts.text: Used, sometimes in stylized form, in Chinese rugs.

words.meaning: happiness; the doubled form means wedded happiness
words.where_on_rug: field

facts.text: Xi is sometimes used in Chinese rug designs, and a pair suggests wedded happiness.

words.meaning: monk (a fully ordained monk)
words.where_on_rug: temple and pillar rugs; position not stated by AIC

facts.text: Recorded in the inscription on AIC 1997.895, translated as 'donated by the monk Trinlay'. The Tibetan script here is converted from the museum's Wylie transliteration.

words.meaning: offer or donate; '’bul lo' means 'is offered' or 'donated'
words.where_on_rug: a line of Tibetan across the top of temple hangings and rugs

facts.text: Tibetan inscriptions on Chinese and Tibetan temple carpets record an offering by a named person, often a monk or teacher.

words.meaning: 'by command of': opens a commission line naming a ruler or patron, e.g. «حسب‌الامر مبارک بندگان اعلیحضرت همایونی رضاشاه پهلوی شاهنشاه ایران» ('by the blessed command of His Imperial Majesty Reza Shah Pahlavi, Shahanshah of Iran').
words.where_on_rug: In a cartouche in the main border; on the Amoghli carpet for Reza Shah it sits in the middle of the main border just above the maker's cartouche.

facts.text: An Amoghli carpet ordered by Reza Shah carries «حسب‌الامر مبارک بندگان اعلیحضرت همایونی رضاشاه پهلوی شاهنشاه ایران» in navy on a cream cartouche, with the maker's mark «مشهد عبدالمحمد عمواغلی» in the inner guard below.

words.meaning: An abjad number standing for a first name: 110 = علی ('Ali': ʿ 70 + l 30 + y 10). Ali Khan Amoghli wrote it beside the family name to tell his rugs from his brother's. (after a family name, e.g. «عمواوغلی ۱۱۰»)
words.where_on_rug: Inside the maker's cartouche, top center of the uppermost narrow guard border (Amoghli practice).

facts.text: Ali Khan Amoghli used «عمواوغلی ۱۱۰», the abjad value of his name 'Ali' beside the family name, to distinguish his mark from Abdolmohammad's plain «عمواوغلی».
facts.note: The abjad sum ع(70)+ل(30)+ی(10)=110 is our check.

facts.text: Not every Ali Khan piece has the number: ordinary rugs kept by his daughter read only «عمواوغلی».

words.meaning: 'hand-woven carpet'. The Iranian national standard ISIRI 1460 (Farhang-e farsh-e dastbaf, the handmade-carpet glossary) defines it as a floor covering every stage of whose making is done by a person, the wefts laid and the knots woven by hand.
words.where_on_rug: Iranian tags, certificates (shenasnameh) and export papers; not woven.

facts.text: ISIRI 1460 defines a hand-woven carpet as a floor covering all of whose production stages are carried out by a human agent and which is wefted and woven by hand.
facts.quote: فرش دست‌باف، کفپوشی است که كليه مراحل تولید آن توسط عامل انساني انجام شود و با دست، پوددهي و بافته شود ('a hand-woven carpet is a floor covering all of whose production stages are done by a human agent and which is wefted and woven by hand')
facts.note: Quoted from the standard by Maleki; the standard itself was not reached.

words.meaning: 'aniline dye', the usual Qajar and Pahlavi Persian name for synthetic dyes; set against rang-e giahi ('vegetable dye') or rang-e sabet-e nabati ('fast vegetable dye').
words.where_on_rug: Not woven; used in Persian documents and books about dyes.

facts.text: Persian texts from 1892 to the present call synthetic dyes rang-e jowhari.
facts.note: feuvrier_tr_eqbal is a Persian translation of a French memoir; the term is the translator's (Abbas Eqbal), not Feuvrier's.

words.meaning: 'ply': the number of single strands twisted into a yarn (warp, weft or pile), as in 'cotton warp 9 la'; on Nain tags '6 la', '9 la'.
words.where_on_rug: Tags and sellers' descriptions.

facts.text: Iranian textbooks and studies write yarns as 'n la' for pile wool, cotton warps and silk warps alike.

words.translit: zarbiyya, pl. zarābī (French spellings zerbia, zarbia)
words.meaning: knotted pile carpet, in Tunisia, Algeria and Morocco; in Egypt and the Levant the usual word is سجاد/سجادة (sajjād/sajjāda) (pl. زرابي)
words.kind: rug-type word (on labels, stamps and in documents; not usually woven)
words.where_on_rug: not woven; seen on labels, shop signs and official texts

facts.text: ONAT (Tunisia) uses الزربية for the knotted carpet, beside مرقوم and كليم for flatweaves; Moroccan decree titles use الزرابي المغربية for Moroccan carpets.

words.translit: qaṭīfa / qṭīf (Stone: qtifa, qtif; Tunisian tourist office: gtif)
words.meaning: pile, plush; in Morocco the knotted pile of a rug, and in Tunisia and Algeria a thick-pile rug
words.where_on_rug: not woven

facts.text: A Moroccan Arabic article says Beni Ouarain wool is prepared «لإنتاج العقدة والقطيفة» (to make the knot and the pile); ONAT lists قطيف among Tunisian floor coverings; the Tunisian tourist office calls 'gtifs' thick, bright carpets of the south.

words.meaning: the (state) stamp / the seal / 'stamped carpets' (not 'printed carpets': in Moroccan and Tunisian official Arabic مطبوع here means bearing the state stamp)
words.where_on_rug: on the stamp or label on the back, and in official texts about it

facts.text: Tunisian sources speak of دار الطابع (the stamp house), الختم (the seal) and الإنتاج المطبوع (stamped production); Moroccan decree titles speak of a fee on الزرابي المطبوعة, which French texts render as 'tapis estampillés'.

words.meaning: There is no god but God: the first half of the profession of faith (shahada), whose second half is محمد رسول الله (see that entry)
words.where_on_rug: Holt reports it on a rug in Berlin; the source does not say where on the rug

facts.text: Holt (1901) records a rug in Berlin's Industrial Museum inscribed 'There is no Deity but God, and Mahomet is His Prophet'.
Stone says the shahada is often calligraphed on mosques and on textiles and other objects, sometimes so stylized it is barely legible.

words.meaning: God is greatest
words.where_on_rug: not stated by the source

facts.text: Holt (1901) records a rug inscribed 'God is greatest! He is great!'

words.meaning: Everything perishes except His face (God's): from the last verse of Sura 28 (al-Qasas)
words.where_on_rug: not stated by the source

facts.text: Holt (1901) records this line from the Koran on a Persian silk rug ('All perisheth but His face').

words.native: اللهم صل على محمد المصطفى وعلي المرتضى وفاطمة الزهراء ...
words.translit: Allāhumma ṣalli ʿalā Muḥammad al-Muṣṭafā wa ʿAlī al-Murtaḍā wa Fāṭima al-Zahrāʾ ...
words.meaning: 'O God, bless Muhammad the chosen, Ali the elect, Fatima the radiant...', a Shi'i blessing that goes on to name the Twelve Imams through the awaited Mahdi (blessing on the Prophet, Fatima and the Twelve Imams)
words.kind: Shi'i blessing (salawat on the Fourteen Infallibles)
words.where_on_rug: cartouches of the outer border of a 16th-century Persian prayer rug (Hawley)

facts.text: Hawley (1913) translates the inscription in the upper border cartouches of the Bardini-Altman prayer rug (then at the Met) as blessings on Muhammad, Ali, Fatima and the Imams by name, ending with the Mahdi; he calls it verses from the Koran, but the names show it is a Shi'i blessing, not Qur'anic text.
facts.note: The Arabic opening is our rendering from Hawley's English; the source gives no Arabic text.

words.meaning: In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate: the formula that opens every sura but one and begins most Muslim writings
words.where_on_rug: not documented on a rug in the sources read

facts.text: Lewis (1914) gives the opening sura, which begins 'In the name of God, the compassionate...', as the prayer most often said on a prayer rug; he does not say it is woven.

words.script: Arabic letters (with Western digits as printed in the source)
words.meaning: 'Corona' / 'Covid-19'
words.kind: modern word woven as ornament (dates a rug to 2020 or later)
words.where_on_rug: woven into the decoration of a Beni Ouarain rug (place on the rug not stated)

facts.text: A 2021 report from Taza describes a Beni Ouarain rug whose decoration includes the words كورونا and كوفيد19, showing that Moroccan village weavers weave current words into rugs.

words.meaning: the digit forms used in much of North Africa, unlike the Arabic-Indic digits (٠١٢٣…) of the Arab East (European digits; called 'Arabic numerals' in the Maghreb)
words.where_on_rug: dates and numbers on Maghreb rugs (expected, not verified on a rug)

facts.text: Unicode notes that European digits are used even in many Arabic-speaking countries of North Africa, while Arabic-Indic digits are used in most of the Arab world. So a woven number on a Moroccan, Algerian or Tunisian rug may well be in Western digits; no dated Maghreb rug was found to confirm it.

signatures.who: named in the maker's line of both Ardabil carpets; LACMA calls him 'probably the designer who prepared the patterns and oversaw the project'
signatures.place: signature says 'of Kashan'; where the carpets were woven is disputed (LACMA: possibly Tabriz)

signatures.cautions: Many later copies of the Ardabil design exist (Jacobsen: 'a number of wonderful copies ... during the past 50 years'); a copy may reproduce the inscription. Old books convert the date wrongly (1553, 1568) or print 942.

facts.text: Both Ardabil carpets are signed and dated; the inscriptions differ slightly in letter ligatures.
The line reads 'the work of the servant of the threshold, Maqsud of Kashan, in the year 946'.
Copies of the Ardabil design were woven in the 20th century.

V&A T.128-1928, a Kerman pictorial carpet, is dated 1327 AH (1909); its record names an Ustad ʿAli as maker (same carpet probable, not confirmed).

signatures.who: workshop owner, producer and designer
signatures.what_it_tells: The form of the signature helps date the rug: «عمل محمد ابن جعفر» before 1927–28; «محمد ارجمند کرمانی», «ارجمند کرمانی» or «فابریک ارجمند کرمانی» after.
signatures.cautions: Most signed pieces were commissions and may also carry the patron's mark. Do not confuse «محمد ابن جعفر» with other men of that name (Stone lists a 'Hadj Muhammad Djafar' of Tehran).

facts.text: Stone lists Arjomand among Kerman weaver-designers.
Known as Mohammad ebn Jafar until he took the surname Arjomand in 1306–1307 SH (1927–28); died 1347 SH (1968).
His woven signatures read «عمل محمد ابن جعفر», «محمد ارجمند کرمانی», «ارجمند کرمانی» and «فابریک ارجمند کرمانی»; 16 of 20 signed carpets studied were commissions.
