labels.title: Labels, brands, country names and import rules on rugs

rows.text: MADE IN ___ / PRODUCT OF ___ (US country-of-origin marking)
rows.meaning: US customs law requires most imported goods to be marked with the English name of the country where they were made. On rugs this shows up as a stamp on the back, a sewn cloth label, or a paper or cloth tag.
rows.date_note: The McKinley Tariff (approved Oct. 1, 1890; marking section in force March 1, 1891) reached only goods usually marked anyway. The Tariff Act of 1922 (Sept. 21, 1922) made every article that could be marked without harm carry its country of origin in English words. The 1930 Act's section 304, rewritten in 1938, is today's 19 U.S.C. 1304. Since the 1938 rewrite, goods made more than twenty years before import do not need marking.
rows.what_it_tells: An origin label names the country where the rug was made, and shows it was imported into the US, or labeled for sale here, at some point after the rules began. It does not date the weaving. A missing label tells you very little: items more than twenty years old can come in unmarked, tags are often cut off, used rugs are not relabeled, and rugs brought home by travelers or as household goods may never have had one.
rows.cautions: A label dates from when it was attached, not when the rug was woven. Tags are easy to cut off and can end up on the wrong rug. A name on a label can be a design or trade name (Kashan, Bokhara, Persian) rather than the country. When a label names another country or place that could mislead, US rules require the real country to appear nearby with 'Made in' or 'Product of'. Customs accepts variant spellings (e.g., 'Italie', 'Brasil'), so an old-looking spelling is not a date by itself.

facts.text: Section 6 of the 1890 McKinley Tariff, in force March 1, 1891, required country-of-origin marking in English only for foreign goods 'such as are usually or ordinarily marked, stamped, branded, or labeled', and for their packages.
The Tariff Act of 1922 required every imported article that could be marked without injury to be marked in legible English words with its country of origin.
facts.quote: every article imported into the United States, which is capable of being marked, stamped, branded, or labeled, without injury, at the time of its manufacture or production, shall be marked, stamped, branded, or labeled, in legible English words

facts.text: The Customs Administrative Act of 1938 (June 25, 1938) rewrote section 304 of the Tariff Act of 1930: an imported article must show 'the English name of the country of origin' to an ultimate purchaser in the US. This is today's 19 U.S.C. 1304.
Articles produced more than twenty years before import into the US are excepted from origin marking. The exception appears in the 1938 text and in the current statute and regulations.
facts.quote: Such article was produced more than twenty years prior to its importation into the United States

facts.text: Carpets, rugs and floor coverings are not on the 'J-list' of goods excepted from origin marking (19 CFR 134.33).
Customs accepts abbreviations and variant spellings that clearly show the English name of the country (examples: 'Gt. Britain', 'Brasil', 'Italie').

If an imported article carries the name of a country or place other than where it was made, and that could mislead the buyer, the real country of origin must appear in close proximity, preceded by 'Made in', 'Product of' or similar words (19 CFR 134.46, current wording from 1997).
For Native American-style rugs made abroad, a sewn-in label counts as an acceptably permanent origin marking (19 CFR 134.43(d)).

Since the Textile Fiber Products Identification Act took effect (March 3, 1960), imported textile products, floor coverings included, must also carry a label naming the country where they were processed or manufactured.

rows.text: Textile Fiber Products Identification Act labels (fiber content, country, RN or company name)
rows.meaning: The US federal law that requires new textile products sold in the US, including rugs, to carry a label giving fiber content, the country of origin, and the company responsible (by name or FTC registered number).
rows.date_note: Enacted Sept. 2, 1958; the act and the FTC's first rules took effect March 3, 1960. Goods acquired before that date in the same form were excepted. The Wool Products Labeling Act of 1939 has never applied to carpets, rugs or mats.
rows.what_it_tells: A full US-style fiber label (for example '100% Wool Pile', a country, and an RN number) was made for a rug offered new in the US on or after March 3, 1960. It does not show when the rug was woven, and it may have been sewn on by the importer.
rows.cautions: Used rugs that are clearly secondhand do not need these labels, so a rug sold at an estate sale may have lost or never had one. Backings and pads are exempt, so the fiber line describes the pile only. Before 1960 some sellers labeled fiber voluntarily; no source checked shows how common that was.

facts.text: The Textile Fiber Products Identification Act was approved September 2, 1958 and took effect eighteen months later; the FTC made its rules effective March 3, 1960.
facts.quote: the following rules and regulations under the Textile Fiber Products Identification Act are hereby promulgated and made effective as of March 3, 1960.

facts.text: The act defines 'household textile articles' to include floor coverings, and the FTC rules list floor coverings (rugs, carpets and mats) among covered products.
The Wool Products Labeling Act does not apply to carpets, rugs, mats or upholsteries, so wool rugs are labeled under the Textile Act instead.
facts.quote: None of the provisions of this subchapter shall be construed to apply to the manufacture, delivery for shipment, shipment, sale, or offering for sale any carpets, rugs, mats, or upholsteries

facts.text: The Wool Products Labeling Act was passed Oct. 14, 1940 (cited as 'of 1939') and took effect nine months later.

The required label must show each fiber of 5 percent or more by its generic name and percentage, the manufacturer's name or FTC registered number, and, for imports, the country where processed or manufactured.
Backings of floor coverings, and pads or cushions used under them, are exempt from the act.
Secondhand household textile articles that are clearly secondhand or marked as such are excluded from the labeling rules, unless a fiber claim is made.
The FTC excepted textile products acquired before March 3, 1960 and sold on or after that date in the same basic form.
A 1984 amendment (in force late December 1984) added the requirement that products made in the US be identified as such.
Hand-woven Navajo rugs carrying the Indian Arts and Crafts Board 'Certificate of Genuineness' are excluded from the labeling rules.
In the early 1960s a rug dealer described the rule as requiring a tag stating the pile content on all rugs sold in the US, domestic and Oriental, but not the warp and weft.

variants: Textile Fiber Products Identification Act labels

rows.text: Iranian-origin carpets: US import bans and openings
rows.meaning: Several times since 1980 the US has banned imports of goods from Iran, Persian rugs included, and twice it has made a specific exception for carpets. These windows limit when a rug labeled 'Iran' could have been imported new into the US.
rows.date_note: Banned April 17, 1980 to Jan. 19, 1981 (hostage crisis). Banned again from Oct. 29, 1987. Carpets allowed again from April 28, 2000. Banned from Sept. 29, 2010 (CISADA). Allowed from Jan. 21, 2016 (JCPOA). Banned after 11:59 p.m. EDT Aug. 6, 2018, and still banned as of the sources read (Nov. 2026).
rows.what_it_tells: A rug bought new in the US with an 'Iran' import label most likely came in before April 1980, between January 1981 and October 1987, between April 2000 and September 2010, or between January 2016 and August 2018.
rows.cautions: Imports outside these windows did happen legally. Rugs shipped directly from Iran before Oct. 29, 1987 could still enter. Household goods and personal effects were licensed separately. An Iranian rug bought in a third country was still 'Iranian-origin' under the rules, and from 2010 OFAC said carpets transshipped through Iran counted as Iranian-origin too. The regulations also limited US persons' dealings in Iranian-origin goods abroad (the 2000 license gives as an example that a US person living abroad may now buy or sell an Iranian carpet); this entry does not cover the rules for reselling a rug already in the US. Without paperwork these windows are only a guide.

facts.text: Executive Order 12211 of April 17, 1980 banned, effective immediately, the direct or indirect import of Iranian goods or services into the US, except materials for news publication or broadcast.
facts.quote: Effective immediately, the direct or indirect import from Iran into the United States of Iranian goods or services, other than materials imported for news publication or news broadcast dissemination.

facts.text: Executive Order 12282 of January 19, 1981, issued to carry out the Algiers declarations on releasing the hostages, revoked the prohibitions of EO 12205, EO 12211 and Proclamation 4702, effective immediately.

Executive Order 12613 of October 29, 1987 banned imports of goods and services of Iranian origin from 12:01 p.m. EST that day. Exceptions: Iranian news materials, petroleum products refined from Iranian crude in a third country, and articles imported directly from Iran that had been exported from Iran before the order took effect.
facts.quote: no goods or services of Iranian origin may be imported into the United States, including its territories and possessions, after the effective date of this Order.

facts.text: Following Secretary of State Albright's announcement of March 17, 2000, OFAC issued a general license, effective April 28, 2000, allowing imports from Iran or a third country of Iranian-origin carpets, other textile floor coverings, and carpets used as wall hangings (HTS chapter 57 or 9706.00.0060).

Under CISADA (signed July 1, 2010), OFAC revoked the carpet and foodstuff general licenses effective Sept. 29, 2010; such goods had to be entered for consumption before that date. The general license for Iranian-origin household goods and personal effects stayed in force.
OFAC treats goods that 'have entered into Iranian commerce' as Iranian-origin, so carpets of third-country origin transshipped through Iran were caught by the 2010 revocation.
To carry out the JCPOA, OFAC re-authorized imports of Iranian-origin carpets and foodstuffs from Iran or a third country by a general license effective Jan. 21, 2016.

After the President's May 8, 2018 decision to leave the JCPOA, OFAC narrowed the carpet license to winding down transactions through 11:59 p.m. eastern daylight time on Aug. 6, 2018; no further transactions were authorized after that.
Executive Order 13846 of Aug. 6, 2018 reimposed broader Iran sanctions; it does not itself mention carpets.
A reference on rugs lists the US embargo on Iranian imports among the causes of reduced Iranian rug production after 1979.

variants: Iranian-origin carpets: US import bans and openings

rows.meaning: 'Persia' was the usual English name for Iran until 1935, when the Iranian government asked foreign governments to use 'Iran'.
rows.date_note: US origin marking began in 1891 for goods usually marked, and covered all markable imports from 1922. The US State Department used 'Iran' officially from March 22, 1935. A 'Persia' label most naturally belongs to the years before that. The end date is soft: old stock and old habits kept the word in use, and no source checked shows when US Customs stopped accepting 'Persia'.
rows.what_it_tells: A label reading 'Persia' points to a label made while 'Persia' was the country's usual English name, generally before 1935. The rug itself may be older than the label.
rows.cautions: 'Persian' on a tag can be a design or trade word, not a country: rugs from India, Pakistan, China and Romania are sold in 'Persian designs'. The word 'Persia' stayed in use after 1935, and rug books of the 1960s still say 'Persian rug'. Labels can be moved, copied or added later. A missing label means nothing by itself (see the US marking rule).

facts.text: In 1935 the Iranian government asked the foreign governments it had relations with to call the country 'Iran' instead of 'Persia'.
The request went out as a circular from Iran's Ministry of Foreign Affairs to the foreign embassies in Tehran.
The US Department of State put the name 'Iran' into official use on March 22, 1935 (Department of State Press Releases, March 23, 1935, p. 181).
facts.quote: On March 22, 1935, the name “Iran” came into official use for the country known up to that time as “Persia”

facts.text: US diplomatic papers addressed the American minister 'in Persia' in March 1935 and 'in Iran' by June 1935.
'Persia' continued in use after 1935 in historical, cultural and trade contexts; a 1962 American dealer's guide still classifies rugs as 'Iran (Persia)' and calls them Persian rugs.

says.text: The name 'Iran' came into official US use on March 22, 1935.
Gives only the year: in 1935 Reza Shah asked western diplomats to say 'Iran'.
Gives only the year 1935, with no day.

rows.text: MADE IN IRAN (also 'Product of Iran', 'Imported from Iran', 'Handmade in Iran', 'IRAN')
rows.meaning: The rug was labeled as made in Iran, the country's name in English since 1935.
rows.date_note: The English name 'Iran' came into US official use on March 22, 1935. For rugs imported new into the US, the import-ban windows narrow the dates further (see 'Iranian-origin carpets: US import bans').
rows.what_it_tells: The label was made in 1935 or later. A US import label on a rug bought new in the US most likely means import before April 1980, January 1981 to October 1987, April 2000 to September 2010, or January 2016 to August 2018. Under the Textile Act a fiber label for a rug sold new in the US from 1960 on must also name the country.
rows.cautions: 'Iran' on the label names where the rug was made, not its design: a 'Kashan' made in India must say 'Made in India'. During the bans, rugs could still come in as personal effects or household goods, or be bought abroad. Wording such as 'Imported from' or 'Handmade in' is the seller's choice; no source checked gives these wordings any separate meaning.

facts.text: The name 'Iran' came into US official use on March 22, 1935; the Iranian request dates from 1935.
US law requires the English name of the country of origin on imported articles, so an Iranian rug imported for sale is marked 'Iran'.
Imported textile products sold new in the US since March 3, 1960, floor coverings included, must name the country where they were processed or manufactured.

US imports of Iranian-origin goods, carpets included, were banned April 17, 1980 to Jan. 19, 1981 and from Oct. 29, 1987; carpets were licensed April 28, 2000 to Sept. 29, 2010 and Jan. 21, 2016 to Aug. 6, 2018.

rows.text: MADE IN USSR / MADE IN U.S.S.R.
rows.meaning: Made in the Soviet Union, which included the Caucasus republics (Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia) and the Central Asian republics (Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan and others) where Caucasian and Turkmen rugs were woven.
rows.date_note: The Soviet Union existed from 1922 until December 1991 (Gorbachev resigned Dec. 25, 1991). The 1922 start is not double-sourced here. US imports were small: AMTORG sent old and new rugs in the late 1920s and 1930s; a 1962 dealer reported none imported in 1952 and only a handful of new Soviet Caucasian rugs in 1960; a 1969 dealer guide says none were imported.
rows.what_it_tells: A 'USSR' label points to a rug labeled between 1922 and 1991, most likely Caucasian or Turkmen work from a Soviet weaving cooperative or factory.
rows.cautions: No source checked shows an actual 'Made in USSR' label on a rug, or what Soviet export labels looked like. After 1991 rugs from the same places are labeled with the new countries' names. US duty on Soviet goods was higher after 1951, which kept imports small.

facts.text: The Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991; Gorbachev resigned as Soviet president on Dec. 25, 1991.
AMTORG, the Soviet trading company in the US, exported old Caucasian and Turkmen rugs to the US from 1926 to about 1930, and 'five-year plan rugs' after 1931.
Rug-weaving cooperatives were set up in Soviet Russia in the 1920s to weave rugs for export.
A US dealer wrote that no Caucasian rugs were being imported in 1952, and that new Soviet-made Caucasian rugs first appeared in New York in 1960, in small numbers.

The Trade Agreements Extension Act of 1951 withdrew trade-agreement tariff cuts from imports from the USSR and areas under communist control; a dealer reported that the new Soviet rugs of 1960 paid at least 45% duty against 22.5% for most rug countries.
A 1969 dealer guide lists the Caucasus and Turkestan as Soviet states with no rugs imported to the US at that time.

rows.text: MADE IN CHINA (also 'CHINA', 'Made in People's Republic of China')
rows.meaning: Made in China. The US barred Chinese goods from late 1950 until June 10, 1971.
rows.date_note: Chinese rugs were made for export from the late 1800s. A 1962 dealer says no new Chinese rugs were imported directly from China for about 25 years. US Foreign Assets Control Regulations of December 1950 cut off trade, and Treasury allowed imports of mainland Chinese goods again from June 10, 1971.
rows.what_it_tells: A US import label 'China' on a rug bought new in the US points to import before the end of 1950 or after June 10, 1971. Chinese rugs in American homes from 1950 to 1971 were mostly older pieces bought before the embargo.
rows.cautions: 'Chinese' rugs sold in the US from 1950 to 1971 were mostly Chinese designs made in Japan, India or Taiwan. A design is not an origin. No source checked shows how US Customs treated 'PRC' or 'People's Republic of China' on labels, or the labeling of Taiwan-made rugs.

facts.text: The US was the largest importer of Chinese rugs in the early twentieth century, with the peak of production and shipment in 1925.
Chinese rug production fell sharply after the Japanese invasion in the 1930s.
Treasury's Foreign Assets Control Regulations (published Dec. 19, 1950) designated China as a blocked country effective Dec. 17, 1950, with North Korea.

A 1962 dealer guide says no new Chinese rugs had been imported directly from China in about 25 years. A few came 1946-48 by way of Hong Kong, Panama and Hawaii, and 'nothing made in China can be imported' into the US.

By a general license (31 CFR 500.547) effective June 10, 1971, Treasury allowed imports of 'merchandise of mainland Chinese origin and merchandise of Chinese type', except goods originating in North Korea or North Vietnam.
facts.quote: import into the United States on or after June 10, 1971, merchandise of mainland Chinese origin and merchandise of Chinese type

facts.text: Large-scale commercial rug production in China did not resume until the 1960s.
A 1969 dealer guide says Chinese rugs, like Russian ones, lacked most-favored-nation treatment, so the duty would be 45% against 18% for Indian rugs.

rows.meaning: Made in Japan. Japan produced two different rug trades that reached the US: cotton and jute rugs around 1900, and hand-knotted wool rugs in Chinese and French designs from about 1950.
rows.date_note: In the early 1900s 'modern Japanese rugs' of cotton or jute were widely used in American summer homes. A dealer dates Japan's hand-knotted wool Oriental rugs (Imperial, Peking, Fuigi Royal) from about 1950; by 1969 rising costs had nearly stopped their import.
rows.what_it_tells: On a wool-pile, hand-knotted rug in Chinese, Savonnerie or Aubusson design, 'Made in Japan' points to about 1950 to the late 1960s. On a cotton or jute rug it can be much earlier.
rows.cautions: No source checked confirms whether rugs exported from 1947 to 1952 were labeled 'Made in Occupied Japan'. The trade names (Imperial, Peking) were also used for rugs from other countries.

facts.text: In the early 1900s Japanese rugs had cotton or jute pile, and they were widely used in American summer homes.
facts.quote: The modern Japanese rugs are made of cotton or jute, and are used extensively in the United States in summer homes.

facts.text: Japan began weaving hand-knotted wool Oriental rugs about 1950, in Savonnerie, Aubusson and Chinese designs, and most went to America.
By 1969 rising Japanese costs had almost stopped imports of Japanese rugs in Chinese design.

disagreements.about: when Japan began making rugs for the US

says.text: Modern Japanese rugs of cotton or jute were already used extensively in the US in 1901.
Japan began weaving Oriental rugs about 1950 (he means hand-knotted wool-pile rugs).

rows.text: MADE IN INDIA / HAND KNOTTED IN INDIA
rows.meaning: Made in India. Indian rugs for the US have copied Persian, Chinese, Turkmen, Savonnerie and Aubusson designs.
rows.date_note: India's name gives no date window. Production rose sharply in the 1950s. A dealer says the Persian-design types of 1920-1940 (Indo-Sarouk, Indo-Kirman, Laristan) had stopped by the early 1960s.
rows.what_it_tells: The label names the country where the rug was made, whatever its design name. In the 1960s Indian rugs for the US were sold with tags stating the pile content.
rows.cautions: Indian rugs often carry Persian place names as design names. 'Hand knotted' is the seller's claim; no source checked gives it a legal meaning on rug labels.

facts.text: Indian rug production increased significantly in the 1950s; contemporary Indian rugs copy Chinese, Persian, Turkmen, Aubusson and Savonnerie designs.
A dealer says Indian types made 1920-1940 such as Indo-Sarouk, Indo-Kirman and Laristan were no longer made by the early 1960s, and the Indo-Kirman stopped about 1945.
1960s dealer guides say tags on Indian rugs had to state the pile content, e.g., 100% wool or 70% wool and 30% jute.

rows.meaning: Made in Pakistan, a country since 1947. Its export rugs were long mostly 'Bokhara' (Turkmen-design) rugs, with Persian designs later.
rows.date_note: Pakistan became independent in 1947, so a 'Pakistan' label cannot be earlier. By the early 1960s American dealers were selling Pakistani rugs.
rows.what_it_tells: The label was made in 1947 or later.
rows.cautions: 'Bokhara' and 'Royal Bokhara' on a tag are design names, not places of origin. Tags may show Pakistani knot-count notation such as '16/18'. No source checked covers 'West Pakistan' labels before 1971.

facts.text: Pakistan became independent in 1947 with the partition of India.
Nearly all contemporary Pakistani pile rugs are made for export, long mostly in Turkmen ('Bokhara') designs, with Persian copies later.
By 1962 a dealer listed Pakistan among countries that had begun weaving Oriental rugs; by 1969 Pakistani 'Bokhara' rugs, called Mori in Pakistan, came in Lahore and Karachi qualities.

rows.meaning: Made in Afghanistan, mostly by Turkmen and Baluch weavers in Turkmen-type designs.
rows.date_note: The name gives no date window. Exports rose in the 1970s; war from 1979 disrupted production.
rows.what_it_tells: The label names the country of manufacture. It does not separate Turkmen, Baluch or other groups.
rows.cautions: Afghan rugs were long sold as 'Afghan Bokhara' or under Turkmen tribal names. No source checked gives any date meaning to Afghan label wording.

facts.text: Rug exports from Afghanistan increased in the 1970s with large-scale production of lower-quality rugs; the Soviet occupation (Dec. 1979 to Feb. 1989) and later wars disrupted production.
A 1962 dealer guide says rugs from Afghanistan were known in the trade as 'Afghans' or 'Afghan Bokharas', and lists Afghanistan among countries that had entered the rug-weaving field.
Turkmen tribes (Ersari, Tekke, Yomud, Sariq), most of whom moved to Afghanistan in the 1920s, weave much of its pile production in Turkmen gul and geometric designs.

rows.meaning: Made in Nepal, usually Tibetan-style rugs woven by Tibetan refugees and their workshops.
rows.date_note: Tibetan refugees arrived in Nepal in 1959-1960 and began weaving there.
rows.what_it_tells: A rug labeled Nepal is most likely Tibetan-style work from after 1959.
rows.cautions: Importers may call these rugs 'Tibetan' although they were woven in Nepal.

facts.text: Tibetan carpets are woven in Nepal by refugees from Tibet who arrived in 1959 and 1960; importers may describe them as 'Tibetan'.

rows.text: MADE IN ROMANIA / MADE IN ROUMANIA
rows.meaning: Made in Romania, usually by cooperatives weaving Persian, Turkish and Caucasian designs on steel looms in set quality grades.
rows.date_note: Export pile-rug weaving began about 1950. A US dealer was seeing Romanian rugs by 1969. Exports grew after US tariffs were lowered in 1975.
rows.what_it_tells: A 'Romania' label with a grade name (Milcov, Olt, Bucharest and others) is typical of export rugs of the 1960s and later.
rows.cautions: 'Roumania' is an older English spelling; Customs accepts variant spellings, so the spelling alone does not date the label. Romanian workshops of the 1920s and 1930s wove close copies of Caucasian and Turkish rugs.

facts.text: Significant Romanian pile-rug weaving for export began about 1950 and increased with the lowering of US tariffs in 1975; rugs are woven by cooperatives on steel-frame looms in set grades.
A 1969 dealer guide reports handmade rugs from 'Roumania' reaching the US, with government export subsidies.
In the 1920s and 1930s Romanian workshops wove fine copies of Caucasian and Turkish pile rugs.

rows.meaning: Made in Greece. Knotted pile rugs were woven there by refugee weavers from Turkey after the 1922 war, in workshops partly backed by American firms.
rows.date_note: Both sources start the trade after the Greco-Turkish war ended in 1922. They disagree on the end date: about 1931-32 (Jacobsen) or the Second World War (Stone). 1940 is used here as the outer bound
rows.what_it_tells: A Greek-made knotted rug in Turkish ('Sparta') designs is typical of the 1920s and 1930s.
rows.cautions: Greek rugs were sold in the US under many trade names, often 'Sparta', and used the same designs as Turkish carpets of the time.

facts.text: Knotted carpet weaving in Greece began with refugee weavers from Turkey after the Greco-Turkish war ended in 1922.
A dealer says American interests set up small factories at Piraeus among Armenian refugees, and around Salonika, and the rugs were sold in America under many trade names, generally as 'Sparta' rugs.

says.text: Made only 1923-1931 (p. 20); 'up to about 1932' (p. 91); none made commercially in 1962.
Knotted pile carpets were woven in Athens and Corinth up to the Second World War.

rows.meaning: Made in Turkey (Anatolia or the European part around Istanbul).
rows.date_note: The English name 'Turkey' was used before and after the republic was founded in 1923, so the name gives no date window. A source notes production declined from 1923 to the 1950s.
rows.what_it_tells: The label names the country of manufacture only.
rows.cautions: Woven inscriptions are a better clue than labels: Turkey adopted the Latin alphabet on Dec. 1, 1928, and this was soon reflected in rug inscriptions.

facts.text: Turkish rug production declined from the founding of the republic in 1923 until the 1950s.
Turkey adopted the Latin alphabet on Dec. 1, 1928, and the change was soon reflected in rug inscriptions.

rows.meaning: Made in Belgium, a large producer of power-loomed (machine-made) rugs in Oriental designs.
rows.date_note: Belgian machine-made copies were sold in the US by the 1960s and are still made.
rows.what_it_tells: On a rug in an Oriental design, 'Made in Belgium' is typical of a machine-made copy, not a hand-knotted rug.
rows.cautions: Check the back as well: the label can be missing or wrong. Machine-made copies also came from the US, France, England and Italy.

facts.text: Belgium has a large production of power-loomed carpets, most imitating hand-knotted Near Eastern designs.
By 1969 machine-made rugs in oriental designs were being imported from Belgium, France, England and Italy, as well as made in the US.
Polypropylene is used in some Belgian Wilton (power-loomed) rugs.

rows.meaning: 'Maroc' is French for Morocco; the label marks Moroccan rugs.
rows.date_note: One source says Moroccan rugs have been labeled this way since 1919.
rows.what_it_tells: A 'Maroc' or 'M.A.R.O.C.' label points to a Moroccan rug labeled in 1919 or later.
rows.cautions: Single source. No source checked describes the label's form (stamp or seal) or who issued it.

facts.text: Since 1919, Moroccan rugs have been labeled 'M.A.R.O.C.' or 'Maroc'.
A dahir of 22 May 1919 set up a state stamp (estampille) on Moroccan carpets, to guarantee their origin, quality and 'native' character; this confirms Stone's 1919 date.
facts.quote: « 1919 : Premier dahir instituant l'estampille de l'Etat sur les tapis marocains garantissant leur origine, leur qualité et leur type. » (Rahel 2021)

facts.text: The stamp was run by the protectorate's Office des industries d'art indigènes (founded 1918, renamed Service des arts indigènes in 1920), headed by Prosper Ricard from 1920 to 1935.
Inspectors refused the stamp to carpets they judged garish or badly dyed; in Marrakesh the program combined workshop visits, advice and close checks on dyes.
facts.quote: « ...des tapis criards et mal teints, que nous refusions inexorablement à l'estampillage. » (Mammeri, quoted by Rateau)

facts.text: Later texts: a 1921 amendment; a 1934 dahir extending the state stamp to other craft products; a 1947 dahir; and a 1974 text on the stamp guaranteeing origin, quality and Moroccan authenticity.

The text in force for carpets is Decree 2.73.116 of 23 April 1974, applying the dahir of 13 October 1947 to Moroccan carpets of craft and manufactured production. It was amended by Decree 2.22.729 (December 2022), and a separate 2022 decree (2.22.727) abolished the fee paid when the stamp is applied. In Moroccan legal Arabic, stamped carpets are «الزرابي المطبوعة».
Since the 2000s Morocco has moved from state inspection to producers' self-control and collective labels.

disagreements.about: what kind of text the 1974 rule is

says.text: '1974: Dahir instituant l'estampille de l'Etat...' (calls it a dahir).
Décret n° 2.73.116 of 23 April 1974, applying the dahir of 13 October 1947 to Moroccan carpets (a decree applying the 1947 dahir).
Labeled 'M.A.R.O.C.' or 'Maroc' since 1919.
Describes a state stamp (estampillage) from 1919 but not its wording; no source read shows the stamp's text.

rows.meaning: The name of the Ottoman, later Turkish state carpet factory at Hereke, near Istanbul, woven into the rug as a mark.
rows.date_note: Court workshops opened at Hereke about 1843 and rug weaving began in 1864. The inscription's position and style have changed. It is currently in Latin capitals in the top left border; Turkey adopted the Latin alphabet in 1928.
rows.what_it_tells: A woven 'Hereke' is the factory's mark. Its script and position may help narrow the date (Ottoman script before the 1928 alphabet change, Latin capitals later), but no source checked gives a dated sequence of styles.
rows.cautions: 'Hereke' is also used loosely in the trade for fine Turkish silk rugs from other workshops. A woven name can be copied. One source says wool Herekes may be called 'Tokat'.

facts.text: Rugs produced at the Hereke National Manufactory have the inscription 'Hereke' woven into the border; the location and style have varied, and currently it is in Latin capitals in the top left border.
Court weaving workshops were set up at Hereke about 1843, and rug weaving began in 1864.

Hereke began as an Ottoman court workshop (one dealer says established and subsidized by the Sultan), and it wove copies of classic Persian designs and of Gordes prayer-rug designs, much of it in silk.

disagreements.about: whether Hereke kept producing after the early twentieth century

says.text: None made in thirty years; good ones probably made not later than 1914.
Production continued after World War II, with fine Bursa-silk rugs still woven at Hereke.

rows.meaning: A number issued by the US Federal Trade Commission to a US company that makes, imports or sells textile products. It can be printed on the fiber label instead of the company name.
rows.date_note: Registered identification numbers were part of the FTC's original Textile Act rules, effective March 3, 1960. The FTC keeps an online RN database.
rows.what_it_tells: An RN on a rug label shows the label was made for the US market under the Textile Act (1960 or later). Looking the number up in the FTC database (rn.ftc.gov) names the US company responsible for the label: usually the importer or seller, not the weaver.
rows.cautions: An RN identifies a US company, not where or when the rug was woven. No source checked gives the years in which particular numbers were issued.

facts.text: The Textile Act lets the label show either the manufacturer's name or an identification number issued and registered by the FTC.
RNs are issued to qualified persons residing in the US and may only be used by the firm they were issued to.
Registered identification numbers appear in the FTC's original 1959 Textile Act rules, effective March 3, 1960.
The FTC's RN database is available on the FTC website.

rows.meaning: Used in US advertising and on labels for machine-made rugs that copy Oriental patterns, as against hand-knotted 'Oriental rugs'.
rows.date_note: A 1962 dealer says the government had recently begun requiring machine-made American copies to be advertised as 'Oriental Designs' instead of the older 'American Oriental Rugs'. The FTC rule or order behind this was not found.
rows.what_it_tells: 'Oriental Design' on a label or in an old ad points to a machine-made rug, usually American or European, not a hand-knotted one.
rows.cautions: Single source for the rule (one dealer author, two books). Older machine-made copies may be labeled 'American Oriental' or carry a mill brand. The 1922 US tariff already named power-loomed rugs 'of oriental weave or weaves'.

facts.text: A US dealer wrote in 1962 that the Federal Government requires machine-made American copies to be designated and advertised as 'Oriental Designs' instead of the old 'American Oriental Rugs', and that a real Oriental rug must be hand knotted.
The same author wrote in 1969 that the FTC requires advertisements to say 'Oriental Design' and not 'Oriental Rugs', but that many stores still ran misleading ads.
The Tariff Act of 1922 (par. 1116) taxed hand-made Oriental carpets and 'carpets and rugs of oriental weave or weaves, produced on a power-driven loom' at the same 55 percent rate.
facts.quote: Oriental, Axminster, Savonnerie, Aubusson, and other carpets and rugs, not made on a power-driven loom; carpets and rugs of oriental weave or weaves, produced on a power-driven loom

rows.text: INDO-KASHAN, INDO-PERSIAN, INDO-SAROUK, INDO-KIRMAN, INDO-TABRIZ (and other 'Indo-' names)
rows.meaning: 'Indo-' means woven in India in the design of another region: an Indo-Kashan is an Indian rug in a Kashan design.
rows.date_note: A dealer names Indo-Sarouk and Indo-Kirman as types made 1920-1940; the Indo-Kirman stopped about 1945. The prefix is still in trade use.
rows.what_it_tells: The rug was made in India; the second part of the name is a design, not a place of origin.
rows.cautions: Under US marking rules, a label naming a foreign place that is not the real origin (such as Kashan) must also show the true country ('Made in India') close by. Rugs whose 'Indo-' tag is lost are easily mistaken for Persian.

facts.text: The prefix 'Indo-' indicates a rug woven in India with a design characteristic of some other region, e.g., Indo-Persian or Indo-Chinese.
Indo-Sarouk, Indo-Kirman, Indo-Feraghan and Indo-Ispahan were Indian rugs in Persian designs sold before World War II; a dealer says the Indo-Kirman stopped about 1945.

When an import carries the name of a foreign place other than its true origin in a way that could mislead, the real country must appear nearby preceded by 'Made in', 'Product of' or similar (19 CFR 134.46).

rows.meaning: A trade name for Turkmen rugs, especially Tekke rugs, and for rugs in Tekke-style designs made elsewhere (Pakistan, Afghanistan, Iran). 'Royal' alone is a vague trade word suggesting quality.
rows.date_note: The name was in American use for Tekke rugs by the early twentieth century. From the 1950s-60s it was also used for Pakistani rugs in Tekke design.
rows.what_it_tells: A 'Bokhara' tag names a design family, not a city of origin. Most rugs sold under the name were not made in or near Bukhara.
rows.cautions: Sources disagree on how fixed the meaning is. 'Royal' carries no defined grade.

facts.text: Mid-twentieth-century rug books use 'Royal Bokhara' as the name of a fine Turkmen (Central Asian) rug type.
The name is tied to the Tekke: one dealer calls Royal Bokhara the old name of the Tekke rug and design, and a lexicon says it may refer to Tekke main carpets.
Pakistani rugs in the Tekke ('Royal Bokhara') design are called Mori in Pakistan and came in Lahore and Karachi qualities.
'Royal' is an indefinite trade term suggesting high quality in rugs.

says.text: A supposedly superior grade of Turkmen rug or rug with Turkmen designs; 'The meaning is indefinite'; may refer to Tekke main carpets.
Treats 'Royal Bokhara' as simply the old name of the Tekke rug and design.

rows.meaning: A Chinese rug trade grade: 90-line knot density, 5/8-inch pile, closed back.
rows.date_note: Used for contemporary (post-1960s) Chinese export rugs; no source gives a start date.
rows.what_it_tells: A 'Super' grade tag on a Chinese rug states its line count (90 knots per foot weftwise), pile height and closed back. It points to the contemporary Chinese export trade.
rows.cautions: Single source. 'Super' is a common sales word in other contexts and means nothing fixed outside the Chinese line system.

facts.text: The Chinese rug trade designation 'Super' means a 90-line rug with 5/8-inch pile height and a closed back; woolen carpets are made in 70, 80, 90 and 120-line qualities.
'Line count' is the number of knots in one foot weftwise.

rows.text: MILCOV, OLT, HARMON, POSTAVARUL, MURES, BRASOV, BRAILA, BUCHAREST (BUCURESTI), BRAN, DORNA (Romanian grade names)
rows.meaning: Quality grades for Romanian export rugs, named after places and rivers. Each stands for a set foundation and knot density.
rows.date_note: Grades belong to the cooperative export production that began about 1950 and grew after 1975.
rows.what_it_tells: A grade name on a tag identifies a Romanian export rug and its intended knot density: Milcov 194 (cotton foundation), Olt 160 (cotton), Postavarul 155 (wool), Harmon 130 (wool), Mures 129 (cotton, Persian designs), Brasov about 100 (wool), Braila about 100 (cotton), Bucharest about 70 (cotton), Bran about 60 (wool), Dorna 25 (cotton) knots per square inch.
rows.cautions: Single source. Knot densities are nominal grade figures, not counts of a particular rug. Several grade names are also city names.

facts.text: Romanian rugs are woven in grades named Braila, Bran, Brasov, Bucuresti, Dorna, Harmon, Milcov, Mures, Olt and Postavarul; knot density runs 25-200 per square inch by grade.

Milcov is the highest commercial grade on a cotton foundation (194 kpsi); Olt cotton foundation 160; Postavarul wool foundation 155; Harmon wool 130; Mures cotton 129, Persian designs; Brasov wool about 100; Braila cotton about 100; Bucharest cotton about 70; Bran wool about 60; Dorna cotton 25.

variants: MILCOV, OLT, HARMON, POSTAVARUL, MURES, BRASOV, BRAILA, BUCHAREST , BRAN, DORNA

rows.meaning: Quality numbers printed on tags or used in the trade to state knot density. India and Pakistan use different systems.
rows.date_note: In use in the contemporary trade; a dealer cites '80-40' Kirman as a 1960s contract quality.
rows.what_it_tells: Indian numbers count knots in nine-inch spans: the first number is horizontal knots per 9 inches divided by 10, the second vertical knots per 9 inches divided by 2 (7/52 = about 90 knots per square inch). Pakistani numbers are knots per inch horizontal/vertical (11/22 = 242). See the knot-count converter for full rules.
rows.cautions: The same-looking pair means different things in different countries. Numbers are nominal grades, not counts of the rug in hand.

facts.text: Indian knot counts are shown as two numbers separated by a slash, based on nine-inch spans (7/52 = 70 x 104 per 81 sq in = about 90 kpsi); common counts are 4/30, 5/40, 7/52, 9/60 and 12/60.
Pakistani knot densities are written as knots per horizontal inch / knots per vertical inch (11/22 = 242 kpsi); 'doubles' means the vertical count is twice the horizontal.
A 1969 dealer guide refers to the 'contract-quality 80-40 Kirman' of Iran.

rows.text: 100% WOOL PILE (also 'PILE: 100% WOOL', 'FACE—100% WOOL', 'OUTER SURFACE—100% WOOL', '70% WOOL 30% JUTE')
rows.meaning: A US-style fiber-content statement for a floor covering. It describes only the pile (face), because backings are exempt from the Textile Act.
rows.date_note: Required on new rugs sold in the US from March 3, 1960 under the Textile Fiber Products Identification Act. The FTC's 1959 rules gave 'Outer Surface—100% Wool' as an example.
rows.what_it_tells: A sewn label in this form points to a rug offered new in the US on or after March 3, 1960. A dealer of the 1960s says tags on Indian rugs had to show pile composition, e.g., 100% wool or 70% wool and 30% jute.
rows.cautions: It describes the pile, not the warp and weft. It does not prove hand knotting or age. Fibers under 5 percent are listed only as 'other fiber'. Percentages may vary by up to 3 percent of total fiber weight.

facts.text: For floor coverings with exempt backings, fillings or paddings, the fiber disclosure must show that it relates only to the face, pile or outer surface (16 CFR 303.11, in the FTC's rules since 1959).
facts.quote: the disclosure shall be made in such manner as to indicate that it relates only to the face, pile, or outer surface of the floor covering and not to the backing, filling, or padding.

facts.text: Pile fabrics may be labeled with the face and the back separately, for example '100% Nylon Pile 100% Cotton Back'.
1960s dealer guides say tags on Indian rugs had to show pile composition (100% wool, or 70% wool and 30% jute) and that most Indian rugs for America had 100% wool pile.
Fibers present at 5 percent or less of total fiber weight must be shown only as 'other fiber' or 'other fibers' (with exceptions for fibers with a clear functional purpose).
A labeled percentage may deviate by up to 3 percent of the total fiber weight.

rows.text: SILK / ART SILK / ARTIFICIAL SILK / FLOSS / MERCERIZED COTTON / IPEKLI / 'TURKISH SILK'
rows.meaning: 'Silk' should mean real silk. 'Art silk' and 'artificial silk' are trade terms for imitation silk: rayon (viscose) or mercerized cotton. 'Floss', 'ipekli' (Turkish 'silken') and 'Turkish silk' are trade words for mercerized cotton polished to look like silk.
rows.date_note: Mercerized-cotton imitations of silk rugs were already common in the early twentieth century (Hawley 1913/1922; Lewis 1920).
rows.what_it_tells: 'Art silk', 'floss' or 'ipekli' on a tag means the shiny pile is not silk. Under US rules a fiber label must use generic names such as 'silk', 'rayon' or 'cotton'.
rows.cautions: 'Silk' on a seller's tag is a claim, not proof. Some sellers use 'silk' loosely for any shiny fiber. US rules forbid words that imply a fiber that is not present.

facts.text: 'Art silk' is a trade term for artificial silk or mercerized cotton.
Mercerized cotton was used for the pile in some districts of Asia Minor and Persia, and imitation silk rugs of mercerized cotton were numerous by about 1920.
facts.quote: It is easy to go astray in the purchase of silk rugs on account of the numerous mercerized and wool silk imitations

facts.text: 'Floss' is mercerized cotton polished to look like silk, sometimes called 'Turkish silk'; 'ipekli' (Turkish 'silken') means carpets with mercerized cotton pile.
Mercerized cotton is cotton treated with alkali under pressure to increase its strength and gloss.

US fiber labels must use generic fiber names such as 'cotton', 'rayon', 'silk', and words or near-spellings that imply a fiber not present may not be used to suggest it is present (16 CFR 303.6, 303.18).

rows.text: RAYON / VISCOSE / LYOCELL / BAMBOO / BAMBOO SILK / 'RAYON MADE FROM BAMBOO'
rows.meaning: Rayon and viscose are names for the same manufactured fiber made from regenerated cellulose; lyocell is a related type. 'Bamboo' and 'bamboo silk' rugs are almost always rayon (viscose) made from bamboo pulp.
rows.date_note: Since 1998-2000 US rules accept the ISO generic fiber names, in which 'viscose' is the name for this fiber. The FTC acted against 'bamboo' labeling of rayon in 2009 and warned 78 retailers in 2010.
rows.what_it_tells: A label reading rayon, viscose or bamboo silk means the shiny pile is a manufactured cellulose fiber, not silk, and points to modern production. A compliant US label for bamboo-based rayon says 'rayon' or 'rayon made from bamboo'.
rows.cautions: 'Bamboo silk' is a marketing name, not a fiber. 'Banana silk' and similar names were not checked against any source.

facts.text: US rules define rayon as a manufactured fiber of regenerated cellulose; 'lyocell' may be used for cellulose fiber precipitated from an organic solution without substitution.

The FTC says most if not all 'bamboo' textiles are really rayon and should be labeled with the generic name, e.g., 'rayon' or 'rayon made from bamboo'; a product may be called bamboo only if made directly of bamboo fiber.
In 2009 the FTC announced four enforcement actions over 'bamboo' used in place of 'rayon', and in 2010 it sent warning letters to 78 retailers.

The FTC incorporated the ISO 2076 generic fiber names into its rules in 1998 (1989 edition) and from Dec. 1, 2000 (1999 edition). In the ISO list 'viscose' is the existing name, and the 2010 revision added 'rayon' as an alternate.

rows.meaning: Synthetic fibers. Olefin is the US generic name for fibers of at least 85 percent ethylene, propylene or other olefin units, which includes polypropylene.
rows.date_note: Nylon was already a US generic fiber name in the FTC's 1959 rules. No source checked dates synthetic piles in Oriental-design rugs.
rows.what_it_tells: A synthetic pile is typical of power-loomed or tufted rugs; one source names polypropylene in tufted Chinese rugs and in some Belgian Wiltons.
rows.cautions: Synthetic fibers can be blended with wool; read the percentages.

facts.text: Olefin is a manufactured fiber of at least 85 percent by weight ethylene, propylene or other olefin units (16 CFR 303.7(m)).
Polypropylene is used in tufted Chinese rugs and in some Belgian Wilton weaves; olefin fibers are used mainly in loop-pile rugs.
Nylon was defined as a generic fiber name in the FTC's original 1959 Textile Act rules.

rows.meaning: Jute is a coarse plant fiber. On labels it appears either as part of the pile (cheaper rugs) or as the backing of tufted and machine-made rugs.
rows.date_note: Dealers of the 1960s describe cheaper Indian rugs with part-jute pile; jute and cotton piles were also used in Japanese rugs around 1900.
rows.what_it_tells: Jute in the pile marks a cheaper grade. A jute backing is usual on tufted and machine-made rugs; the backing is exempt from the US fiber label, so it may not be listed.
rows.cautions: The US label lists the pile; a backing need not be declared.

facts.text: 1960s dealer guides say some cheaper Indian rugs had jute in the pile, up to half in 1962 and typically 30% by 1969, and that the tag had to state it.
The cheapest Pakistani grades may have jute wefts.
Backings of floor coverings are exempt from the Textile Act's labeling requirements.
In the early 1900s Japanese rugs sold in the US had cotton or jute pile.

rows.meaning: 'Kork' (Turkish) is the underhair of a goat or the fine belly wool of a sheep. It is used in the trade for a soft, high-grade wool.
rows.date_note: No date significance found.
rows.what_it_tells: A 'kork wool' tag claims a fine, soft wool pile.
rows.cautions: Single source for the definition. The spelling 'kurk' and how sellers use it were not confirmed in any source checked. It is a quality claim and cannot be checked by eye.

facts.text: Kork (Turkish) is the underhair of a goat or the fine belly wool of a sheep.

rows.meaning: Kashan rugs woven from Australian merino wool spun in Manchester, England. 'Manchester' means merino wool processed in Manchester.
rows.date_note: Woven from about 1890 or the early twentieth century until the early 1930s, when the Depression ended the trade and local wool took over (one source, two entries).
rows.what_it_tells: A rug sold as a 'Manchester Kashan' is claimed to be a Kashan of about 1890-1930s with imported merino wool pile.
rows.cautions: Single source. It is a trade attribution, usually made by feel and sheen, not a label the weavers applied.

facts.text: At the beginning of the twentieth century, Kashan weaving used Australian merino wool spun in Manchester; these 'Manchester' Kashans were woven until the early 1930s, after which local wools were used.
'Manchester' is Merino wool processed in Manchester, England; Australian Merino is used in some rugs from Iran, Pakistan, China and India.

says.text: Entry 'Manchester Kashan' (p. 184): woven about 1890 to 1930.
Entry 'Kashan' (p. 151): began at the beginning of the twentieth century and continued until the early 1930s.

rows.text: RUGMARK / GOODWEAVE (certification label with a code)
rows.meaning: A label from a nonprofit certification scheme, founded by Kailash Satyarthi in 1994, meant to show that no child, forced or bonded labor was used in making the rug. It began as RUGMARK and is now GoodWeave.
rows.date_note: GoodWeave gives its founding year as 1994. A 'Rugmark Foundation-USA' was active in Washington by March 1999. The date of the first labeled rugs and the date of the RUGMARK-to-GoodWeave name change were not confirmed in sources checked.
rows.what_it_tells: A RUGMARK or GoodWeave label points to a rug made in 1994 or later by a licensed producer, in practice in South Asia (GoodWeave today has programs in India, Nepal and Bangladesh). A 'RUGMARK' label is likely older than a 'GoodWeave' one, but no source checked gives the changeover year.
rows.cautions: It is a labor-certification label, not a mark of quality, fiber or hand knotting. Each GoodWeave label has a unique code that can be traced to the licensed producer; checking the code is the way to test a label, since labels can be removed or reused.

facts.text: Kailash Satyarthi founded Rugmark, now known as GoodWeave, as a voluntary labeling scheme to monitor and certify that carpets under the label were made without child labor.
GoodWeave says it was founded in 1994 by Kailash Satyarthi.

A representative of the 'Rugmark Foundation--USA' sat on the US Treasury Advisory Committee on International Child Labor Enforcement, listed in March 1999 alongside the Oriental Rug Importers Association.

Each GoodWeave label has a unique code that can be traced back to the licensed producer; certification requires no child labor, no forced or bonded labor, and documented workplace conditions, checked by unannounced inspections.
GoodWeave now runs programs in India, Nepal and Bangladesh and has expanded beyond rugs into other goods.

rows.text: (no label) US ban on convict-made imports: jail-made rugs
rows.meaning: Since 1890 US law has barred goods made wholly or partly by convict labor in a foreign country from entering the United States. Indian jail carpets (Agra, Lahore and others) fell under it.
rows.date_note: Tariff Act of 1890 (McKinley Tariff) sec. 51; carried on in the tariffs of 1913 and 1922 and in sec. 307 of the Tariff Act of 1930 (19 U.S.C. 1307), still in force (now also forced labor).
rows.what_it_tells: A 19th- or early 20th-century Indian jail carpet in the US probably did not arrive new through US customs as a declared jail product; it may have come by way of Britain or with a later owner. The rule itself is not a mark on the rug.
rows.cautions: Holt (1901) and Langton (1905) say the law kept jail carpets off the American market, but how strictly it was enforced against rugs was not found. Mumford (1902) says the jail output went mainly to England.

facts.text: Section 51 of the Tariff Act of 1890 barred from entry all goods made wholly or partly by convict labor in any foreign country.
facts.quote: shall not be entitled to entry at any of the ports of the United States, and the importation thereof is hereby prohibited
facts.note: Primary law; one instrument.

facts.text: The same rule is now sec. 307 of the Tariff Act of 1930 (19 U.S.C. 1307), with similar provisions in the tariffs of 1913 and 1922; it now also covers forced and indentured labor.
facts.note: Primary law; one instrument.

facts.text: Books of 1901-1905 say US law kept Indian jail-made carpets out of the American market; Holt says many more Agra rugs would otherwise have been imported.
facts.quote: These carpets are prohibited by law from the American market.

variants: US ban on convict-made imports: jail-made rugs

rows.text: شناسنامه فرش دستباف (shenasnameh-ye farsh-e dastbaf, 'hand-woven carpet ID certificate')
rows.meaning: An Iranian identity document for a hand-woven carpet: a booklet, sheet, tag, or electronic code with a valid digital signature, recording the rug's technical and artistic features.
rows.date_note: The textbook shows a certificate registered for an Iranian carpet town in 1397 SH (2018); when such certificates began was not found.
rows.what_it_tells: A shenasnameh states what the seller or producer declares about the rug (type, place, materials, knot, raj, size); it is a document, not proof.
rows.cautions: A certificate can be separated from its rug or copied; check the rug against what it states. Its purpose, per the textbook, is to protect Iranian identity and prevent counterfeiting by rival countries, so it is a trade instrument.

facts.text: Iranian textbooks describe the carpet shenasnameh as an official or unofficial document in booklet, sheet, label or electronic-code form, with a valid signature and digital approval, used for workshop archives, attached to the sales invoice, for packing lists and tax declarations, and for museum labels.
Its stated aims are to preserve the Iranian identity of hand-woven carpets, prevent counterfeiting by competing countries and reassure buyers.

rows.text: ONAT stamp: paper label with a lead seal (Office National de l'Artisanat Tunisien / الديوان الوطني للصناعات التقليدية)
rows.meaning: The Tunisian handicrafts office inspects carpets and stamps those that pass. In Kairouan the inspection is done at the 'stamp house' (dar al-tabaa, دار الطابع), which checks quality and wool density, records the measurements and attaches the stamp: a paper label and a piece of lead.
rows.date_note: ONAT was created by Law no. 133 of 14 October 1959 (as the Office national de l'artisanat), with technical control of craft products for export among its duties. When the carpet stamp itself began was not found.
rows.what_it_tells: A paper label with a lead seal from ONAT points to a carpet woven in Tunisia and inspected there; travel advice says the stamp, on the back, certifies hand-weaving in pure wool.
rows.cautions: Only one source read describes the stamp's form (a 2021 radio report). The wording printed on the label, its grade names and knot counts were not seen in an official source. Labels and seals can be removed or moved.

facts.text: ONAT was created by Law no. 133 of 14 October 1959; its duties included technical control of craft products for export.
facts.quote: «أحـدث الديـوان القومي للصناعـة التقليـــدية بمـوجب القـانون عدد 133 لسنة 1959 المؤرخ في 14 أكتوبر 1959»

facts.text: ONAT runs quality control on carpets: its regional figures count the carpets and woven textiles it stamps (الإنتاج المطبوع) by pieces and square meters, and it supervises 'control centers and stamping operations'.
facts.quote: «المتابعة الميدانية والإشراف على مراكز المراقبة وعمليات الطابع» (field follow-up and supervision of the control centers and stamping operations)

facts.text: At Kairouan's stamp house (dar al-tabaa) a carpet's quality and wool density are checked and its measurements recorded before it is stamped with a paper label and a piece of lead.
facts.quote: «حسب المنصوص بالختم (ورقة وقطعة رصاص)» (as written on the stamp: a paper and a piece of lead)

facts.text: The stamp is on the back of the carpet and certifies that the national handicrafts office inspected it and that it is hand-woven in pure wool.
facts.quote: look for the quality-certified stamp on the back.

facts.text: ONAT carries out technical quality control of Tunisian craft products, carpets included, from raw materials and production to export (ONAT); Stone says it controls most contemporary Tunisian rug production.

variants: ONAT stamp: paper label with a lead seal

rows.text: Moroccan craft labels: 'Morocco Hand Made', Label national de l'artisanat, collective labels such as 'Tapis R'bati'
rows.meaning: Since 2009 Morocco's crafts ministry has registered collective certification labels for craft products, grouped under the brand 'Morocco Hand Made', and from 2010 a national labelling strategy with label levels (for example 'Qualité Certifiée', 'Artisanat Régional', 'Qualité Premium').
rows.date_note: 54 collective labels had been filed by 2018 (La Vie éco); the ministry counted 56, then 64, labels and more than 2,300 certified production units by 2021 (Rahel).
rows.what_it_tells: A 'Morocco Hand Made' or national label points to a Moroccan item certified in 2009 or later.
rows.cautions: Which carpet labels exist and what each requires were not read in an official list; a search summary names 'Tapis R'bati', 'Tapis de Médiouna', 'Tapis rural du Maroc' and 'Tapis de Bejaad', unverified. Both sources quote the same official.

facts.text: Since 2009 Morocco has registered collective labels for craft products, all grouped under the 'Morocco Hand Made' brand.
facts.quote: « Depuis 2009, 54 labels collectifs ont été déposés au Maroc et à l'étranger. Ces labels... sont tous regroupés sous la marque «Morocco Hand Made». » (La Vie éco 2018)
facts.note: La Vie éco quotes the official who gave the WIPO talk; not independent.

facts.text: The 2010 national labelling strategy set out labels named 'Qualité Prémium', 'Artisanat Régional', 'Qualité Certifiée', 'Madmoun' and 'Artisan Responsable', and a national label with three levels.

variants: Moroccan craft labels: 'Morocco Hand Made', Label national de l'artisanat, collective labels such as 'Tapis R'bati'
