knots.title: Knot counts as rugs are labeled and sold

rows.name: Knots per square inch (KPSI), and 'a × b knots to the inch'
as_written: Knots to inch horizontally eleven to twenty; perpendicularly, eleven to twenty
rows.where_used: The usual unit in the American and British trade and on US retail tags; used by the older English-language rug books (Hawley 1913/1922, Mumford 1902, Jacobsen 1962). Older books give the two directions separately: knots per inch across the rug (counted along a row, in the direction of the threads that run across the rug, the wefts) and rows per inch along the rug (in the direction of the threads that run the length of the rug, the warps).
rows.unit_meaning: The number of knots in one square inch of the rug. It is the knots per inch across multiplied by the rows of knots per inch along the length. 'a × b to the inch' (Hawley's 'horizontally … perpendicularly') gives the two counts separately: a across, b along.

to_kpsi.words: A KPSI figure is already knots per square inch. For 'a × b to the inch', multiply the two numbers.
to_kpsi.vars: n = stated KPSI; a = knots per inch across (horizontally); b = rows per inch along (perpendicularly)
to_kpsi.formula_source: stone_2013 p.160 (density = vertical count × horizontal count per unit length); hawley_1922 p.48

to_kpdm2.words: Multiply knots per square inch by 15.5 (one square decimeter is 15.5 square inches).
to_kpdm2.formula_source: own arithmetic: 1 in = 2.54 cm, so 1 sq in = 6.4516 cm² and 1 dm² = 100/6.4516 = 15.500 sq in

examples.as_written: Knots to inch horizontally 11–20; perpendicularly 11–20 (Kirman, Hawley p.114)
22 X 22 knots to the square inch (new Nain, Jacobsen 1962 p.267)

facts.text: Knot density is the number of knots per unit area: the count per unit length along the warps (vertically) multiplied by the count per unit length along the wefts (horizontally).
facts.quote: A square inch is a convenient size for measurement
facts.note: stone_2013 p.160; hawley_1922 p.48; abchome: count a 1-inch strip each way on the back and multiply

facts.text: The older English-language books state structure as knots per inch horizontally and perpendicularly, e.g. Hawley's Kirman: eleven to twenty each way.
facts.quote: Knots to inch horizontally eleven to twenty; perpendicularly, eleven to twenty.
facts.note: hawley_1922 p.114; mumford_1902 p.173 ('ten by ten and twenty by twenty knots'; average 'thirteen by thirteen, or one hundred and sixty-nine knots to the square inch'); jacobsen_1962 p.267 ('22 X 22 knots to the square inch')

facts.text: Not every part of a rug is woven equally tightly, so the count should be taken in several places.
facts.quote: the measurement should be made in several places if exactness be required
facts.note: hawley_1922 p.48

facts.text: Counting on the back: where the two warps under each knot lie side by side, each knot shows as two small bumps (nodes), one around each warp, so count two nodes per knot. Where one warp of each pair is pushed deep beneath the other (deeply depressed or 'doubled under'), only one node per knot shows, so count one node per knot.
facts.quote: one thread of warp, included in every knot, has been doubled under so as to be entirely concealed from view
facts.note: stone_2013 p.160 (knot count entry); hawley_1922 pp.50–52 (each half of a knot shows at the back; in Bijar or Sarouk one warp of each knot is doubled under and concealed)

facts.text: The knot ratio (rows per unit length divided by knots per unit length across) differs between rug types and is characteristic for some attributions; many rugs are not square in count.
facts.note: stone_2013 p.161

facts.text: Knot counts are best compared between rugs of the same type; the count depends on the weaving technique as much as on quality, and it is a fair guide for modern commercial rugs more than for older weavings.
facts.note: may_1952 pp.50, 99; abchome (judge against local average counts); hawley_1922 p.48 (coarse yarn can be compact with few knots)

facts.text: China, India and Pakistan each have their own way of writing knot counts; rugs from elsewhere (except China) are often graded by KPSI.
facts.note: cepc (Carpet Export Promotion Council, India); stone_2013 has separate entries for China 'line' (p.175), India (p.134) and Pakistan (p.211)

facts.text: The Carpet Export Promotion Council of India prints a KPSI scale: about 30 very coarse; 30–60 coarse; 60–130 medium fine; 130–160 fine; 160–290 very fine; 290 and up extremely fine.
facts.note: a trade scale, not a standard; the text looks like generic trade copy

rows.cautions: Recompute from the two counts when a book or tag gives both; printed totals are sometimes wrong (Jacobsen 1962 p.218 gives '17 X 19 knots-343 knots to the square inch', but 17 × 19 = 323; Stone p.47 gives 48.8 for 5.55 × 8.88, which is 49.3). A tag's KPSI is the seller's statement, not a count. Count on the back with a ruler at several places; remember two nodes per knot unless one warp of each pair is hidden. Higher KPSI points to a finer weave, not to age, origin or value.

rows.name: Knots per square meter, square decimeter or square centimeter (and per 10 cm)
rows.where_used: European tags and catalogs (German 'Knoten/m²' and similar), Iranian and Turkish export descriptions, museum and scholarly structure notes (per dm²), and Nepalese workshop specifications (knots per 10 cm across and lines per 10 cm along).
rows.unit_meaning: Knots in one square meter (100 × 100 cm), one square decimeter (10 × 10 cm) or one square centimeter. 'Knots per 10 cm' and 'lines per 10 cm' are the two linear counts that multiply to knots per dm².

to_kpsi.words: Per square meter: divide by 1,550. Per square decimeter: divide by 15.5. Per square centimeter: multiply by 6.4516. Knots per 10 cm (a) and lines per 10 cm (b): multiply them and divide by 15.5.
to_kpsi.vars: m = per m²; d = per dm²; c = per cm²; a, b = knots and lines per 10 cm
to_kpsi.formula_source: own arithmetic from 1 in = 2.54 cm (1 sq in = 6.4516 cm²); matches stone_2013 pp.75, 160 (100,000/m² = 1,000/dm² = 65 kpsi, rounded)

to_kpdm2.words: Per square meter: divide by 100. Per square centimeter: multiply by 100. Knots and lines per 10 cm: multiply them.

examples.as_written: Knots 40/10 cm; Lines 40/10 cm (Nepal workshop report)

facts.text: 100,000 knots per square meter = 1,000 knots per square decimeter = about 65 knots per square inch.
facts.note: stone_2013 pp.75 and 160; exact value 64.5 kpsi is our arithmetic (100,000 ÷ 1,550.0)

facts.text: One square decimeter is 15.5 square inches, so knots per dm² ÷ 15.5 = knots per square inch.
facts.note: stone_2013 p.75 gives square centimeter = 0.155 square inch; the rest is arithmetic (1 in = 2.54 cm by definition)

facts.text: Knot density is also written per square decimeter, e.g. a Nepalese average of 45 knots per square inch given as 675 per dm².
facts.note: the journal's 675 uses a factor of 15; with 15.5 it is 697.5 per dm²

facts.text: A Nepalese carpet-production report states density as knots per 10 cm across and lines per 10 cm along (40 and 40), and its total knot count equals width × knots per 10 cm × length × lines per 10 cm (22.5 dm × 40 × 30 dm × 40 = 1,080,000).
facts.note: trade document; arithmetic checked

facts.text: European dealers state Nain densities per square meter (e.g. 500,000–1,200,000 knots/m² for Tudeshk Nains) and per square centimeter (100–120 knots/cm² for early Habibian pieces).
facts.note: dealer text; sathi gives Nain overall 160,000–1,000,000 knots per m²

rows.cautions: Per-m² figures on tags are usually round 'approximately' numbers, not counts. Check which unit is meant: 1,000 per dm² and 1,000 per square inch differ by 15.5 times. 'Knots' on a machine-made rug tag (points per m²) are not hand-tied knots.

rows.name: Raj (row count) per gereh — Iranian raj-shomar
rows.where_used: Iran, in the domestic and export trade. Towns that weave with the symmetric (Turkish) knot, led by Tabriz, count over 7 cm ('Torki-baf' count); towns that weave with the asymmetric (Persian) knot, led by Isfahan, count over 6.5 cm ('Farsi-baf' count). The official Iranian textbook lists Isfahan, Nain, Kashan, Qom, Arak, Hamadan, Yazd, Kerman and Mashhad as Farsi-baf areas and Tabriz, Ardabil, Heris, Mianeh, Marand, Khoy, Bijar, Maragheh and Shabestar as Torki-baf areas. One Iranian dealer gives Kerman its own 6.75 cm basis. Western dealers selling Iranian rugs also quote raj (e.g. a UK retailer's guide, bakhtiyar_kheft_raj).
rows.unit_meaning: The number of knots in one gereh (one-sixteenth of a zar, the old Persian 'arm' or cubit). The zar is 112 cm in Tabriz and 104 cm in Isfahan, so a gereh is 7 cm in Tabriz and 6.5 cm in Isfahan. The count is taken along a row (across the width); the same number is assumed for the rows along the length.

to_kpsi.words: Divide the raj by the gereh length in cm (7 for a Tabriz-type count, 6.5 for an Isfahan-type count) to get knots per cm; multiply by 2.54 to get knots per inch; square it (this assumes as many rows as knots per gereh).
to_kpsi.vars: n = raj; L = gereh in cm
to_kpsi.formula_source: own arithmetic from the textbook definition (Iran textbook pp.107–109) and its worked example; checks against stone_2013 p.235 (20 reg ≈ 53 kpsi)

facts.text: Raj-shomar is the unit for knot density in Iranian hand-knotted carpets: the number of knots in 7 cm or 6.5 cm of length or width. Stone defines reg/raj as knots per gereh.
facts.note: textbook p.107; stone_2013 p.235; farahan (dealer)

facts.text: The raj is counted over one-sixteenth of a zar; the zar is taken as 112 cm in Tabriz and 104 cm in Isfahan, giving 7 cm and 6.5 cm.
facts.note: textbook p.107; farahan (dealer) gives the same values

facts.text: The zar (from Arabic dhar', forearm or cubit) is an obsolete Persian length of about 41 to 44 inches (104–112 cm).
facts.note: stone_2013 p.315; the textbook's 104 cm and 112 cm fall exactly at the ends of Stone's range (41 in = 104.1 cm; 44 in = 111.8 cm: our arithmetic)

facts.text: A count over 6.5 cm is called Farsi-baf and a count over 7 cm Torki-baf, after the knot used in those regions; Tabriz is the 7 cm town and Isfahan the 6.5 cm town.
facts.note: textbook p.107 and its table on p.108; farahan and bakhtiyar are dealer text

facts.text: The textbook's table lists Isfahan, Nain, Kashan, Qom, Arak, Hamadan, Yazd, Kerman and Mashhad as Farsi-baf (6.5 cm) areas and Tabriz, Ardabil, Heris, Mianeh, Marand, Khoy, Bijar, Maragheh and Shabestar as Torki-baf (7 cm) areas.
facts.note: p.108; read from a two-column table in PDF text extraction

facts.text: In Kerman the zar is taken as 108 cm, so the count is over 6.75 cm.
facts.note: dealer text

facts.text: In Isfahan the same 6.5 cm count is also called kheft; in Tabriz it is called raj.
facts.note: dealer text (UK retailer)

facts.text: The count is made along a row across the width (e.g. 50 raj = 50 knots in every 7 cm of the width), and the textbook's worked example applies the same raj to both directions: a 3 × 4 m Farsi-baf carpet of raj 30 has 300 × 30 ÷ 6.5 = 1,385 knots across and 400 × 30 ÷ 6.5 = 1,846 along.
facts.note: textbook p.109; farahan English page; bakhtiyar ('measure 6.5cm across its width')

facts.text: By raj, carpets under 30 are called coarse, 30–50 medium, over 50 fine; over 70 are exceptional pieces mostly woven to order. Iranian customs grades exports as grade 1 (raj 50 and up), grade 2 (30–50) and grade 3 (under 30).
facts.note: textbook pp.107–108

facts.text: Twenty reg is about 53 knots per square inch.

The Persian word raj (رج) means a row or line: Dehkhoda glosses it as saff, rasteh, radeh, radif ('row, file, rank'), as in 'a raj of bricks'. Stone gives the same sense ('row, course'). In carpet use it names the count of knots in one gereh, so the word itself does not say whether knots across or rows along are meant.
facts.quote: رج . صف . رسته . رده . رجه . قطار ... ردیف (Dehkhoda: 'raj: row, file, rank, line')

facts.text: Dehkhoda gives two zar' (ذرع) lengths: the plain zar', also called zar'-e moqassar, of 1.04 m, 'used in Tehran and Fars', and the zar'-e shah of 1.12 m, 'mostly used in Tabriz'. Divided by sixteen these give the 6.5 cm and 7 cm gereh of the raj count.
facts.quote: در ذرع شاه یک متر و دوازده صدم یک متر است (و بیشتر در تبریز متداول است) ('the shah zar' is 1.12 m and is mostly used in Tabriz')

facts.text: A Persian school textbook pairs each warp yarn with the raj it suits: cotton warp 12 la (count no. 20) for raj 46-50, cotton warp 9 la (no. 20) for raj 50-55, 15-la cotton warp for raj 20, 18-la for raj 32, 33-la for raj 10, and a 36-la silk warp for raj 60; for raj 65 the lower weft should be 12 la and the upper weft 42 la.

says.text: p.116 (gereh entry): about 2½ inches (6.35 cm).
p.235 (reg entry): about 2.75 inches (7.0 cm).
7 cm on the Tabriz zar (112 cm), 6.5 cm (2.56 in) on the Isfahan zar (104 cm).
Adds Kerman: 6.75 cm (zar 108 cm).

disagreements.note: Our reading: Stone's two figures fit the two town standards (2.75 in ≈ Tabriz 7 cm; 2½ in ≈ Isfahan 6.5 cm). Not stated by Stone.

says.text: reg/raj (Persian rag, 'row, course') = knots per gereh.
knots in 7 or 6.5 cm of length or width.
knots in 7 cm of the width (English page); density both along and across (Persian page).

disagreements.about: where the 104 cm zar' is used

says.text: Isfahan zar' 104 cm (6.5 cm gereh), Tabriz zar' 112 cm (7 cm gereh).
Plain zar' 1.04 m used in Tehran and Fars; shah zar' 1.12 m mostly in Tabriz.

rows.cautions: A raj number alone does not say which gereh was used: 50 raj is about 329 kpsi on the 7 cm (Tabriz) count and about 382 kpsi on the 6.5 cm (Isfahan) count, a 16% difference. The raj counts one direction; if the rows are packed tighter or looser than the knots across, the true density differs (count both on the back). Raj numbers on tags are sellers' statements. Western books also spell it reg or rag.

formula.note: Counted over a gereh of 7 cm, as in Tabriz; an Isfahan count over 6.5 cm gives about 16% more knots for the same raj.

rows.name: Kerman 'warps / rows per gereh' quality (e.g. 80/40)
rows.where_used: Kerman (Kirman) rugs in the American trade of the 1950s–60s; Jacobsen calls the 80/40 the standard 'contract quality' Kirman.
rows.unit_meaning: First number: warp threads per gereh across the rug. Second number: knots (rows) per gereh along the rug. Each knot sits on two warps, so knots per gereh across = first number ÷ 2, which equals the second number in all the qualities Jacobsen lists.

to_kpsi.words: Halve the first number to get knots per gereh across; take the second as rows per gereh; divide each by the gereh length in inches and multiply.
to_kpsi.vars: a = warps per gereh; b = rows per gereh; L = gereh in cm
to_kpsi.formula_source: own arithmetic from jacobsen_1962 p.242 definition; Kerman gereh 6.75 cm from farahan (dealer, single source)

facts.text: In the trade an 80/40 Kirman has 80 warp threads to the gireh and 40 vertical knots to the gireh, about 15 × 15 knots per inch; lesser qualities are 70/35 and finer ones 90/45 or 100/50.
facts.note: jacobsen_1962 p.242; jacobsen_1969 (same author) calls the contract Kirman 'so-called 80/40 quality'. One author, so single-sourced.

facts.text: Our arithmetic: 40 knots per gereh ≈ 15 per inch implies a gereh of about 2.67 in (6.8 cm), close to the 6.75 cm Kerman gereh one Iranian dealer gives.
facts.note: inference from two sources; not stated by either

rows.cautions: Looks like the Indian '7/52' and Pakistani '16/18' notations but means something different; read it as Kerman only when the rug is a Kerman or the seller says so. The first number counts warp threads, not knots.

rows.name: Kashan 'khuneh' and Yazd 'tun' counts
rows.where_used: Local Iranian trade terms: khuneh in Kashan, tun in Yazd (per one Iranian dealer). Rarely seen on Western tags.
rows.unit_meaning: Khuneh: one khuneh = 10 knots; the number of khuneh across half the width of the carpet. Tun: the number of warp threads across half the width (two warps per knot). The dealer's examples are 'six-meter' (2 × 3 m) carpets, so half the width is 1 m.

to_kpsi.words: For a carpet 2 m wide: khuneh × 10 = knots per meter across; tun ÷ 2 = knots per meter across. Convert knots per meter to per inch (÷ 39.37) and square (assumes square count). For other widths divide by half the width in meters first.
to_kpsi.vars: k = khuneh; t = tun; W = carpet width in m
to_kpsi.formula_source: own arithmetic from farahan definitions (single dealer source)

to_kpdm2.words: Knots per dm across (knots per m ÷ 10), squared.

examples.arithmetic: 460 knots per m = 4.6/cm = 11.68/in; 11.68² = 136.5; dealer: 'equivalent to 30 raj' (460 per m × 0.065 m = 29.9)
840 ÷ 2 = 420 knots per m = 4.2/cm = 10.67/in; 10.67² = 113.8; dealer: '28 raj' (our arithmetic gives 27.3)

facts.text: In Kashan a 'khuneh' is 10 knots and the count is the number of khuneh across half the carpet's width; in Yazd 'tun' is the number of warp threads across half the width.
facts.note: dealer text (Persian page)

facts.text: In Isfahan a '100-tayi' count gives the knots across the carpet's width (in hundreds).
facts.note: dealer text; unclear detail

rows.cautions: Single dealer source; the half-width basis makes the number depend on the carpet's width. Treat as background for readers who meet these words, not as a converter input without the carpet's width.

rows.name: Nain 'la' grades (4 la, 6 la, 9 la, 12 la)
rows.where_used: Rugs of Nain (Na'in), central Iran, and Nain-design rugs; the grade appears in dealer listings in Europe, the US, Australia and Japan (dealer pages read).
rows.unit_meaning: Not a knot count. 'La' is the number of plies (single yarns) twisted together in each cotton warp (foundation) yarn. Fewer plies make a thinner warp, so the warps can be set closer and more knots fit: 4 la is the finest, then 6 la, then 9 la (12 la coarser still, per dealers).

to_kpsi.words: No formula: 'la' describes the warp yarn, not the knots. Count the knots, or use a raj figure if one is given. One Iranian dealer equates 6 la with about 60 raj and 9 la with about 50 raj (Isfahan 6.5 cm count), which would be about 550 and 380 kpsi.
to_kpsi.formula_source: rough association only: farahan (dealer) raj equivalents converted with the persian-raj formula (own arithmetic)

facts.text: 'La' is the number of singles (plies) in each foundation yarn of a Nain rug; four la is the finest and gives the finer weave.
facts.note: stone_2013 p.169; farahan Persian page ('6 لا و 9 لا' = number of plies of the cotton yarn); bizsan: 6-La and 4-La rugs 'woven with six-ply or 4-ply cotton' (dealer)

facts.text: The lower the la number, the finer the rug.
facts.note: stone_2013 p.169 plus four dealer pages; no source read says 9 la is the finest

facts.text: The la grading is a Nain workshop practice.
facts.note: stone_2013 p.169 ('in Nain rugs'); bizsan ('exclusively utilized by Nain workshops', dealer)

facts.text: Usually a 6 la carpet corresponds to about 60 raj and a 9 la carpet to about 50 raj.
facts.note: Persian dealer text

facts.text: Dealer density ranges by grade: Kashmar about 40–80 kpsi, 12 la about 100–150, 9 la about 200–300, 6 la 300–700, 4 la 500–1,100 or more.
facts.note: dealer text; its own summary table says 4 La 500–1000+

facts.text: Nain rugs (from the 1930s) have knot densities between 200 and 800 asymmetric knots per square inch.
facts.note: stone_2013 p.201; persianrugs.com.au gives the same 200–800 range (may copy Stone)

facts.text: Jacobsen counted new Nains of about 1960 at about 22 × 22 knots per square inch (484) and later wrote that the best had some 500 to 600 or more.
facts.note: one author: jacobsen_1962 p.267; jacobsen_1969 (Nain plates and text)

facts.text: Persian sources use la (لا) for the ply count of any yarn, not only Nain warps: a school textbook lists pile wool of 3 and 4 la, cotton warps of 9, 12, 15, 18 and 33 la and a silk warp of 36 la; a Persian study of Nain rugs defines the Nain grade as 'the la of the warp yarn'.
facts.quote: معیار ظرافت فرش از الی نخ چله معین از انواع ۴ ال، ۶ ال، ۹ ال، در نوسان است (Babajamali: 'the fineness of the carpet is set by the la of the warp yarn: 4 la, 6 la, 9 la')

facts.text: Fewer plies mean a finer rug: the textbook pairs a 9-la cotton warp with raj 50-55 and a 12-la warp with raj 46-50; in Nain, the early rugs had raj 40-45 on 9-la cotton warps, and raj 70 with 6-la warps came later under Isfahan influence; 4 la is rare and needs fine fingers and strong eyesight.
Persian authors say the expressions 'Nain 6 la' and 'Nain 9 la' are trade terms used only for the weaving of this town.
facts.quote: واژه نایین شش ال و نایین نه ال (Nasiri, quoted by Babajamali: 'the terms Nain six-la and Nain nine-la')

facts.text: Yasavoli (quoted by Babajamali) writes that Nain rugs are woven 6-la or 9-la and 'one-khaft' or 'two-khaft' (yek-khafti, do-khafti): 6-la one-khaft is fine, high-quality work, 9-la two-khaft is lower in fineness and quality; most current Nain output is 9-la two-khaft, and the first kind is only about 20 percent.

Babajamali's table of usual Nain counts: a 9-la Nain about 2 m long has about 800 knots across the width and 1,500 along the length; a 6-la Nain of 200 x 120 cm about 1,100 by 1,800; a 4-la Nain of 200 x 120 cm (woven in Mazandaran) about 1,600 by 2,700. Our arithmetic: about 250-320, 530 and 1,160 knots per square inch (roughly 40-43, 60 and 87 raj on a 6.5 cm count).
Tajaddod (quoted by Babajamali) gives the usual raj of Nain rugs as 50 to 70 knots in each 6.5 cm or 7 cm.

says.text: the number of singles in each foundation yarn (p.169).
six-ply or four-ply cotton.
the number of twists in the warp threads.
Persian page: the number of plies of the cotton yarn; the same site's English page says layers of cotton yarn 'used in carpet wefts'.
the number of threads used to make each warp strand, but also says the more threads twisted together the thinner the strand, which contradicts its own rule that a lower number is finer.
4 to 6 la.
4, 6, 9 and 12 la, plus Kashmar (entry level).
6 la and 9 la.
9 la ≈ 50 raj (≈ 380 kpsi on a 6.5 cm count, our arithmetic); 6 la ≈ 60 raj (≈ 550 kpsi).

Table: 9 la about 800 x 1,500 knots on about 2 m (about 250-320 kpsi, about 40-43 raj); 6 la about 1,100 x 1,800 on 200 x 120 cm (about 530 kpsi, about 60 raj); text: early Nains 40-45 raj on 9-la warps, later 70 raj on 6-la warps.
A 9-la cotton warp suits raj 50-55; a 12-la warp raj 46-50.
The la (ply) of the warp yarn: 4, 6 or 9 la.
La is the ply of any yarn (wool 3-4 la, cotton warps 9-33 la, silk warp 36 la).

rows.cautions: 'La' is a grade name for the warp yarn, not a measurement of knots; two rugs with the same la can differ in density, and the grade can be used loosely by sellers. Count the knots. The ply count cannot be checked without unpicking a warp.

rows.name: Pakistani 'a/b' qualities (16/18, 9/18, 'doubles')
rows.where_used: Pakistan's export trade (Lahore, Karachi, Hyderabad, Peshawar): Bokhara (Turkmen-design) and Persian-design rugs.
rows.unit_meaning: Knots per inch across (horizontal) / knots per inch along (vertical). 'Doubles' means the vertical count is twice the horizontal (e.g. 9/18).

to_kpsi.vars: a = knots per horizontal inch; b = knots per vertical inch

to_kpdm2.words: Multiply the two numbers, then by 15.5.

facts.text: Pakistani knot densities are written as knots per horizontal inch / knots per vertical inch, so 11/22 = 242 knots per square inch.
facts.note: stone_2013 p.211; no Pakistani source read gives the rule

facts.text: 'Doubles' in Pakistani rug grades means the vertical knot count is twice the horizontal count.
facts.note: stone_2013 p.211

facts.text: Pakistani rugs range from about 40 to 350 knots per square inch.
facts.note: stone_2013 p.211

facts.text: The Pakistan Carpet Manufacturers & Exporters Association lists a product as '8×10 15×15 sotri double knot', a square count written with '×' and labeled 'double knot'.
facts.note: caption only; not explained

facts.text: Pakistan has its own system for writing knot counts.
facts.note: cepc (India) and stone_2013 p.211

facts.text: TDAP gives a 16/16 quality as 16 warps and 16 rows of knots in each inch.
TDAP groups Pakistani rugs as 'single knot' (Bokhara, Jaldar, Silk Touch), 'double knot' (popularly Pak-Persian) and 'Turkish knot' hand-spun vegetable-dyed qualities learned from Afghan refugees.

says.text: 'doubles' = vertical count twice the horizontal (p.211).
labels a 15×15 (equal) count 'double knot', so here 'double' cannot mean twice as many rows; the meaning is not given.
Knots per horizontal inch: 16/16 = 256 kpsi (p.211).
'16 warps and 16 rows of knots' per inch (p.13). Since a knot normally spans two warps, 16 warps would carry about 8 knots, giving about 128 kpsi (our arithmetic). TDAP may be speaking loosely.
'Single knot' and 'double knot' name quality groups: Bokhara/Jaldar vs Pak-Persian (p.6).
'Doubles' means the vertical count is twice the horizontal (p.211).
Dealer: Pakistanis call the symmetric knot the 'single knot'.

rows.cautions: 'Single' and 'double' are used in at least three senses (quality group, knot type, row ratio) The notation looks like the Indian 9-inch system (e.g. 9/60): our rule of thumb, not from a source, is that a second number many times the first (more than about 2½ times) is more likely the Indian 9-inch notation. Counts are sellers' statements; check on the back.

rows.name: Indian (Bhadohi–Mirzapur) 'a/b' qualities (e.g. 5/40, 7/52, 9/60)
rows.where_used: India, especially the Bhadohi–Mirzapur carpet belt of Uttar Pradesh; Stone gives it as the nominal knot count for contemporary Indian rugs generally.
rows.unit_meaning: First number: knots across a 9-inch span, divided by 10. Second number: rows along a 9-inch span, divided by 2. (Stone calls the two figures 'bis' and 'bhutan' in the Bhadohi entry.)

to_kpsi.words: Multiply the first number by 10 and the second by 2, multiply those, and divide by 81 (9 × 9 inches). Same as: knots per inch across = a × 10/9 (≈ a × 1.11); rows per inch along = b × 2/9 (≈ b × 1.333 ÷ 6).
to_kpsi.vars: a = first number; b = second number
to_kpsi.formula_source: stone_2013 p.134 (India) and p.47 (Bhadohi); we checked that the two entries are the same formula: 1.11 ≈ 10/9 and 1.333/6 = 2/9, so (10a/9)(2b/9) = 20ab/81

facts.text: Nominal knot counts for contemporary Indian rugs are two numbers separated by a slash: knots across 9 inches ÷ 10, and knots along 9 inches ÷ 2; kpsi = (first × 10 × second × 2) ÷ 81, e.g. 7/52 = 90.
facts.note: stone_2013 p.134; the Bhadohi entry p.47 is the same author, so one source

facts.text: Common Indian counts are 4/30, 5/40, 7/52, 9/60 and 12/60.
facts.note: stone_2013 p.135

facts.text: Bhadohi rugs are woven at densities between 30 and 225 knots per square inch.
facts.note: stone_2013 p.47

facts.text: India has its own system for writing knot counts.
facts.note: cepc is India's carpet export council; its pages read do not give the system itself

says.text: p.47: 5.55 × 8.88 = 48.8 knots per square inch.
p.134 formula gives (50 × 80) ÷ 81 = 49.4; 5.55 × 8.88 is 49.3. The 48.8 is an arithmetic slip, not a different rule (our check).
9-inch rule: first number = knots across 9 in / 10; second = rows along 9 in / 2 (p.134).
c.1900 Indian 'stitches' were knots per inch across by along, e.g. ten by ten = 100 kpsi (p.24); Mumford (1902, p.261) likewise grades Amritsar rugs 3 x 3 to 12 x 12.

rows.cautions: Counts such as '9/9', '10/10' or '12/12' on modern Indian (e.g. Jaipur, Indo-Persian) rugs were not explained by any modern source read; around 1900 Indian grades were per inch (Holt; Mumford; see Indian 'a by b' per-inch qualities (e.g. 7 x 8, 10 x 10, 12/12, 16 x 16)). Read on the 9-inch rule, 10/10 would be 24.7 kpsi; read per inch (like Pakistan), 100 kpsi: a fourfold difference, so ask the seller or count. The 9-inch rule is single-sourced (Stone); no Indian standard (CEPC, IICT Bhadohi, BIS) was found to confirm it.

rows.name: Chinese line count (道 dào)
rows.where_used: Chinese hand-knotted rugs from the 20th-century export factories (Tianjin, Beijing) to today; Chinese domestic retail guides.
rows.unit_meaning: Knots per linear (English) foot across the width, i.e. pairs of warps per foot; the rows per foot along the length are assumed to be the same number.

to_kpsi.words: Divide the line by 12 (knots per inch) and square it.
to_kpsi.formula_source: stone_2013 p.175 (90 line = 7.5 × 7.5 ≈ 56); cn_patent_cn102619020a (knots per square foot = 道²)

to_kpdm2.words: Divide the line by 3.048 (knots per dm) and square it.

facts.text: 'Line' is the number of pairs of warps (one knot each) per linear foot across the rug, so it equals knots per foot weftwise.
facts.note: stone_2013 p.175; maigoo: 道数 counted per 英尺 (0.3048 m); patent: 100道 = 100 warp lines and 100 weft lines crossing in one square foot

facts.text: The vertical count is taken to equal the horizontal, so knots per square foot = line², and kpsi = (line ÷ 12)².
facts.note: stone_2013 p.175; patent ('道数的平方就是打结的数量', 100道 → 10,000 knots per sq ft)

facts.text: The foot is the English foot (30.48 cm), not the Chinese chi.
facts.note: patent: 平方英尺; maigoo: 英尺 (0.3048m); Stone: 'linear foot'

facts.text: Contemporary woolen Chinese carpets are woven in 70, 80, 90 and 120-line qualities and silk rugs in 120 to 300-line; pile heights for wool are ⅜, ½ and ⅝ inch.
facts.note: stone_2013 p.69; the line entry (p.175) lists 70, 80, 90, 120, 200, 250 and 300 as common

facts.text: A 2012 Chinese patent describes a hand-knotting process for a 250-line wool carpet.
facts.note: wool at 250 line (434 kpsi) is finer than Stone's wool range

facts.text: A Chinese retail guide recommends 90 or 120 line for ordinary homes.
facts.note: user-uploaded guide

facts.text: The Chinese trade name 'Super' means a 90-line rug with ⅝ inch pile and a closed back.
facts.note: stone_2013 p.69

facts.text: Stone describes Chinese rugs in general as not finely knotted, about 30 to 120 knots per square inch (below his 200–300-line silk qualities).
facts.note: stone_2013 p.68

says.text: pairs of warps per foot (one knot per pair).
warp lines (经线) and weft lines (纬线) per foot, with a knot at each crossing.
warp and weft threads (经纬线) per foot.

disagreements.note: All three give the same knots per foot; they differ only in what they call the counted unit.

says.text: wool 70–120 line; silk 120–300.
a 250-line wool carpet.

rows.cautions: Line is per foot, not per inch: a 90-line rug has about 56 knots per square inch, not 90. Rows may not equal knots across; count both on the back. Silk counts such as 160 or 260 line were not confirmed by a source read.

rows.name: Nepalese/Tibetan '60 knot', '80 knot', '100 knot' qualities
rows.where_used: Tibetan-style rugs woven in Nepal (Kathmandu valley) and in Tibet; these rugs are offered by 'knot' grade.
rows.unit_meaning: Not settled by the sources we could read. The grade number is generally treated as (nominal) knots per square inch; a Nepalese workshop production report instead states knots per 10 cm across and lines per 10 cm along.

to_kpsi.words: If the grade is knots per square inch, it is already kpsi. If the seller gives knots (a) and lines (b) per 10 cm, multiply them and divide by 15.5.
to_kpsi.vars: n = grade number; a = knots per 10 cm; b = lines per 10 cm
to_kpsi.formula_source: own arithmetic; reading of the grade as kpsi is unconfirmed

to_kpdm2.words: Grade × 15.5 (if kpsi), or knots × lines per 10 cm.

examples.arithmetic: 60 × 15.5 = 930 per dm² ≈ 30.5 knots and 30.5 lines per 10 cm

facts.text: In the Tibetan technique a continuous pile yarn is looped around two warps and then around a gauge rod; the loops are cut when the rod is removed, so each pile unit sits on two warps like a knot.
facts.note: stone_2013 p.284

facts.text: Tibetan knot densities vary from 20 to 140 per square inch; older rugs are more coarsely knotted.
facts.note: stone_2013 p.284

facts.text: Nepalese knotted carpets average about 45 knots per square inch.
facts.note: Global InCH journal

facts.text: A Nepalese production report gives density as knots per 10 cm and lines per 10 cm (40 and 40 in its example).
facts.note: trade document; attribution to Nepal's Galaincha software maker is our reading

rows.cautions: We could not confirm from a Nepalese authority (CCIA, GoodWeave, TEPC) whether '100 knot' means a counted 100 knots per square inch, a nominal grade, or some other count; treat the grade as approximate kpsi and, when it matters, count knots and rows per inch (or per 10 cm) on the back. Older Tibetan rugs are usually far coarser than modern Nepalese grades.

rows.name: 'a × b' per centimeter (Egyptian tags; also seen as metric grades)
rows.where_used: Contemporary Egyptian rugs (Stone). The same per-centimeter form is used in metric countries; for Turkish (Hereke) grades
rows.unit_meaning: Knots per centimeter across (weftwise) × knots per centimeter along (warpwise).

to_kpsi.words: Multiply the two numbers (knots per cm²) and multiply by 6.4516 (square cm in a square inch).
to_kpsi.vars: a = knots per cm across; b = knots per cm along
to_kpsi.formula_source: stone_2013 p.98 (definition); conversion is own arithmetic

examples.arithmetic: 100 per cm² × 6.4516 = 645.2 (the same as Stone's Hereke average 'about 645')

facts.text: Knot counts in contemporary Egyptian rugs are written like 4 x 5: knots per centimeter weftwise × knots per centimeter warpwise, so 4 x 5 = 20 knots per square centimeter.
facts.note: stone_2013 p.98

facts.text: The average grade of Hereke silk rugs is about 645 knots per square inch; our arithmetic: that is 10,000 per dm², i.e. 10 × 10 knots per cm.
facts.note: stone_2013 p.127; the per-cm reading is our arithmetic, not Stone's

rows.cautions: '10x10' with no unit may be per centimeter (645 kpsi) or per inch (100 kpsi), a 6.45-fold difference: look for 'cm' or ask. Turkish Hereke grades written per decimeter ('60x60' = 3,600 per dm² ≈ 232 kpsi for wool; '100x100' = 10,000 per dm² ≈ 645 kpsi for silk) are reported by Wikipedia, citing Küçükerman 1987, but no Turkish source was read to confirm them.

rows.name: Machine-made Iranian rugs: 'shaneh' and 'tarakom' (e.g. 1200 shaneh, density 3600)
rows.where_used: Power-loom (machine-made) rugs from Iran (Kashan and elsewhere), on labels and listings.
rows.unit_meaning: Shaneh: points per meter across the width (1200 shaneh = 120 per 10 cm). Tarakom: a lengthwise figure; the source says a tarakom of 3600 means 1,800 points per meter of length. These are machine pile points, not hand-tied knots.

to_kpsi.words: Points per inch across = shaneh ÷ 39.37; per inch along = (tarakom ÷ 2) ÷ 39.37; multiply.
to_kpsi.formula_source: own arithmetic from digikala_mag_machine_carpet (single retail source)

facts.text: For machine-made carpets the crosswise density is called shaneh and is counted per meter: a 1200-shaneh carpet has 120 points in every 10 cm; a 'tarakom' (density) of 3600 means 1,800 points in one meter of length.
facts.note: Persian retail magazine

rows.cautions: These numbers describe machine-made rugs only. A '1200 shaneh' label does not mean 1,200 knots per square inch and does not indicate hand knotting; the tarakom rule (figure = twice the rows per meter) comes from one retail source.

rows.name: Indian 'a by b' per-inch qualities (e.g. 7 x 8, 10 x 10, 12/12, 16 x 16)
rows.where_used: Indian factory rugs for Western importers around 1900 (Amritsar, Kashmir); the same per-inch style is seen on some later Indian tags.
rows.unit_meaning: Knots per inch across by knots (rows) per inch along.

to_kpsi.vars: a = knots per inch across; b = knots per inch along
to_kpsi.formula_source: holt_1901 p.24 (gives the products: 7 x 8 = 56, 10 x 10 = 100, 16 x 16 = 256)

to_kpdm2.words: Multiply the two numbers, then by 15.5.

facts.text: Around 1900 Indian factory rug grades were stated as knots per inch across by knots per inch along ('stitches'): 7 x 8 = 56, 8 x 8 = 64, 10 x 10 = 100, 12 x 12 = 144, 16 x 16 = 256 knots per square inch.
facts.quote: ten by ten, or one hundred knots to the square inch

pages.mumford_1902: 261-262 (Amritsar grades 'from three knots by three to twelve by twelve'; pushmina to 'fourteen by fourteen')

facts.text: Hawley's structure notes use the same per-inch style ('knots to inch horizontally ... perpendicularly').
facts.note: See the kpsi item; Hawley is not specific to India.

says.text: Indian grades c.1900 are knots per inch by knots per inch (e.g. ten by ten = 100 kpsi).
Contemporary Indian counts like 7/52 use 9-inch spans: (a x 10)(b x 2)/81 (p.134); read that way 10/10 would be about 25 kpsi.

rows.cautions: A modern tag '10/10' or '9/9' has not been confirmed as per-inch by any source read; the per-inch reading is documented for c.1900 only. If the second number is far larger than the first (5/40, 9/60), use the 9-inch rule; if the two are close (10/10, 12/12), the per-inch reading is more likely, but count on the back to be sure.

checks.title: Hand-knotted, hand-tufted or machine-made: the checks

rows.question: Turn the rug over. Can you see each knot as its own small bump, in rows, with the pattern as sharp on the back as on the front? Or is the back a cloth, a coating, or a perfectly even machine grid?

answers.what_you_see: Rows of small separate bumps (one or two per knot), the pattern clear, with small irregularities from row to row.
answers.note: Each bump is a 'node': one loop of a pile knot around a lengthwise thread.

answers.what_you_see: The back is covered by a glued-on cloth or canvas, or a rubbery coating, with no pattern visible.
answers.note: See the the check on glue/latex check.

answers.what_you_see: An even machine grid of lengthwise and crosswise threads; the pattern may show, but every repeat is identical and there are no knot bumps.
answers.note: Woven Wilton or Axminster. Karastan backs show the pattern clearly.

answers.what_you_see: The back looks almost the same as the front and there is no pile at all.
answers.note: See the the check on front pattern check.

facts.text: A node is one loop of a pile knot around a lengthwise thread (warp), as seen from the back; knot counts are taken by counting nodes on the back (two per knot unless one warp of each pair is hidden).
On power-loomed rugs the stitching on the back is very regular; on hand-knotted rugs it varies slightly because the knots are tied by hand at different tensions.
facts.note: CEPC's wording reads like common dealer copy. Jacobsen (1969 pp. 22, 27, 84-86) makes the related point that machine-made rugs have a 'stamped-out' regularity of design.

facts.text: Karastan's modified Axminster loom pulled the pile through to the back, so the back shows the pattern and looks hand-knotted.

A machine-made copy has no knot at the base of the pile: if you part the pile of a hand-knotted rug you see the loop of each knot around the lengthwise threads; on a machine-made rug the strands are fixed to the base by the machine.

rows.cautions: A pattern showing clearly on the back does not by itself prove hand-knotting (Karastan). Very fine knotting makes the nodes hard to see. Some hand-knotted rugs have had glue, rubber or canvas added to the back later (Jacobsen 1969 pp. 27, 124-25), and older Tibetan rugs often have a red cloth backing (Stone p. 284).

rows.question: Fold the rug pile-side out or part the pile with your fingers down to the base. What holds each tuft: a knot wrapped around the lengthwise threads, a U-shaped tuft lying under a crosswise thread, yarn pushed through a cloth, or loops pulled up through a fabric?

answers.what_you_see: Each tuft comes out of a knot that wraps around lengthwise threads (you may see the loop of the knot at the base of two strands).
Tufts sit in straight machine rows, each a U doubled under a crosswise thread, with no knot; the base is a regular woven grid.
answers.note: Axminster. In Wilton the pile is woven in as extra lengthwise yarns.

answers.what_you_see: Tufts come straight up through a cloth (often with a cotton canvas grid visible at the base) and are held only by glue on the back.
answers.note: Hand-tufted with a gun, or machine-tufted; the two are hard to tell apart.

answers.what_you_see: Loops (or clipped loops) pulled up through burlap or canvas, packed in close rows, no knots.
Cut tufts in rows that overlap like shingles, each row wrapped around two lengthwise threads.
answers.note: The Tibetan rod technique (see the check on pile roots).

facts.text: Jacobsen's test for a good machine-made copy: open the pile and look at the base; a hand-knotted rug shows a tied loop at the base of each pair of strands, a machine-made rug shows none.
In a machine-woven Axminster each tuft is bound in by the weft without being knotted.
facts.quote: the tuft, though inserted in the fabric mechanically, and bound down without being knotted

facts.text: In a hand-tufted rug the pile is shot into a backing cloth with a tufting gun and held by latex and a second cloth; in machine tufting, rows of needles stitch the yarn through a primary backing fabric.
Hooked rugs are made by pulling yarn or fabric strips through canvas or burlap with a hook; the surface is looped and may be clipped.

rows.cautions: In some hand-knotted Chinese rugs (Tianjin 'closed back'), the knot loop sits on the back warp and is not visible from the front when the pile is pushed aside (Stone p. 72), so a missing loop at the base is not proof of machine-made; check the back as well.

rows.question: Follow the fringe into the rug. Are the fringe threads the ends of the rug's own lengthwise threads, running out from under the last row of pile (or a woven band)? Or is the fringe a separate strip sewn or glued on under the edge?

answers.what_you_see: The fringe threads run out of the body of the rug; you can follow them in, sometimes past a narrow flat-woven band.
answers.note: Old hand-knotted rugs may have lost their fringe, or had it replaced.

answers.what_you_see: A separate fringe strip sewn on, often tucked under a binding or stitched across the back of the end.
No fringe at all; the end is bound or folded and sewn.
answers.note: Not decisive on its own.

facts.text: On a hand-woven rug the fringe is the lengthwise threads (warps) running out of the rug's foundation at the ends; artificial fringes are sometimes attached to rugs with damaged ends.
On a hand-knotted rug the fringe is part of the rug; on machine-made rugs it is sewn on.
facts.note: CEPC wording reads like common dealer copy; dealer guides say the same.

facts.text: Warp ends may be braided, knotted or twisted, or a flatweave may simply be folded and stitched at the ends.
Mumford (1902) noted that some Caucasian rugs had warp ends knotted in the manner of 'ordinary machine-made fringe', i.e. machine-made fringe was a familiar product by 1902.
facts.quote: after the manner of ordinary machine-made fringe

rows.cautions: Replaced fringe on a hand-knotted rug looks sewn on (Stone p. 111). Some hand-knotted and flatwoven rugs have no loose fringe. The Karastan fringe was not described in any source read.

rows.question: Look at the long edges. Is the edge yarn wrapped by hand around the outer lengthwise threads (a slightly uneven overcast or a woven cord that is part of the rug)? Or is it a perfectly even machine binding or a sewn-on tape?

answers.what_you_see: Yarn wrapped around the last few lengthwise threads, slightly uneven, continuous with the rug.
A perfectly even, tight machine-stitched binding (serging), or binding tape sewn along the edge.
answers.note: Serging can also be added to any rug to stop fraying.

facts.text: The side edge (selvage) of a hand-woven rug is where the crosswise threads turn back, often strengthened by extra wrapping (overcasting) around the outer warps.
Serging is a binding of heavy yarn, often done by a special machine, on any edge of a carpet to prevent unraveling.
Machine-made rugs typically have serged or machine-stitched sides, while the sides of hand-knotted rugs are a little irregular.
facts.note: CEPC wording reads like common dealer copy.

facts.text: Some new hand-knotted rugs, mainly from Pakistan, are woven without extra edge warps and a 'false selvage' cord is sewn on after weaving.
Indian hand-made carpets are finished by binding the sides with a separate thick, often doubled, thread.

rows.cautions: Hand-knotted rugs are often rebound, and some get sewn-on false selvages when new, so a sewn edge is not decisive.

rows.question: Is the whole back covered by a cloth (often cotton or canvas) or a rubbery coating? Can you lift a corner of the cloth and see glue and tufts underneath?

answers.what_you_see: A cloth glued over the whole back; under it, latex glue and the bases of tufts pushed through another cloth.
answers.note: Hand-tufted or machine-tufted.

answers.what_you_see: A thin coating on an otherwise woven back (you can still see the woven grid).
answers.note: Woven carpets often get thinner back coatings than tufted ones.

answers.what_you_see: A plastic or rubber coating over a back that otherwise shows loops in rows.
answers.note: Jacobsen describes Hong Kong hooked rugs with plastic-covered backs sold as orientals.

answers.what_you_see: Patches of glue, rubber or non-skid coating, or a piece of canvas glued over part of an otherwise knotted back.
answers.note: A later repair or anti-slip treatment on a hand-knotted rug.

facts.text: Hand-tufted rugs have the pile shot into a backing material with a tufting gun; that backing is bonded with latex to a second backing cloth, and a further cloth is used in finishing.
Tufted carpet is made of face yarn, a primary backing, a bonding compound (usually latex) and often a secondary backing; woven carpets have their backing yarns woven in and take thinner coatings.
Jacobsen describes rugs from Hong Kong, hooked in heavy wool yarn with the back covered in plastic, that buyers took for oriental rugs; looking at the underside shows they are hooked.
Owners sometimes put glue, Lastex or non-skid coating, or glued canvas, on the back of hand-knotted oriental rugs.
Older Tibetan rugs often have a red fabric edging and backing.

rows.cautions: A coated or cloth-covered back is typical of tufted rugs but is also found on repaired or anti-slip-treated hand-knotted rugs and on older Tibetan rugs. A smell of latex is often mentioned by dealers but no source was found for it.

rows.question: If the rug is machine-woven, which weave is it? Look at how many colors the design uses, how heavy the rug is for its pile height, and whether it bends easily both ways.

answers.what_you_see: Few colors in any one line of the design; heavy and firm for its pile height.
answers.note: Points to Wilton (unused pile colors buried inside).

answers.what_you_see: Many colors; bends easily across the width but resists bending along the length; back flat or ribbed with jute.
answers.note: Points to Axminster.

answers.what_you_see: Pattern edges a little fuzzy, as if the colors had run from one row into the next.
answers.note: Points to a tapestry carpet (pattern printed on the yarn before weaving).

facts.text: In Wilton and Brussels the pile yarn not on the surface is hidden in the body of the fabric; in Axminster all of the pile is on the surface.
Each Wilton color comes from a separate frame, so a three-frame Wilton has three colors; Axminster offers a wide range of colors.
Axminster carpet bends only across its width.
In tapestry carpet the pattern is printed on the pile yarns before weaving, and the change from one color to the next cannot be made sharp: the colors look as if they had run.
facts.quote: The colour will appear to have run

rows.cautions: These clues sort machine-made weaves from each other; they do not separate machine-made from hand-knotted. Use the back, pile roots and fringe checks first.

rows.question: Pick up a corner and fold it, first across the width and then along the length. Does it fold softly both ways, bend only one way, or feel board-stiff?

answers.what_you_see: Bends readily across the width but resists bending along the length.
answers.note: Typical of Axminster.

answers.what_you_see: Stiff and board-like because of a glued backing.
answers.note: Or a hand-knotted rug coated with non-skid glue.

answers.what_you_see: Supple and limp, folding easily both ways.
answers.note: Not decisive: some hand-knotted rugs are very stiff.

facts.text: Axminster carpet bends only across its width.
Woven carpet has a heavy, firm hand.
facts.note: Brinton: sizing the chain and stuffer adds stiffness; three weft shots give a firmer fabric.

facts.text: Glue or non-skid coating on the back can make an oriental rug stiff and almost board-like.
Some hand-knotted rugs are naturally very stiff: older Bijar rugs, with three wefts beaten hard, are stiff from dense knot packing.
May (1952) wrote that old rugs are always limp and flexible, though limpness alone does not prove age.

rows.cautions: Weight and stiffness vary a great deal within each kind; use this only alongside the back and pile-root checks.

rows.question: Pick one small motif that repeats (a border figure, a flower in the field) and compare two of them a foot or more apart. Are they exactly identical, stitch for stitch? Do colors shift in bands across the rug?

answers.what_you_see: Small differences between repeats of the same motif; slight changes of shade in bands across the rug.
answers.note: Also seen in hand-tufted and hooked rugs.

answers.what_you_see: Every repeat exactly the same; outlines and colors identical throughout.

facts.text: In a machine-made rug each repeated motif is exactly the same, while in a hand-knotted rug no two repeats of a border motif are exactly alike.
facts.note: Brinton: the hand-made carpet has an individuality, 'even in its faults', that no machine product attains.

facts.text: Abrash (bands of slightly different shade across a rug from different dye or wool batches) is sometimes imitated in new hand-knotted and power-loomed rugs.
Some hand-knotted rugs were woven with stiff, very regular designs that dealers called 'machine-made-looking' (Jacobsen cites new Tabriz, Yezd, Romanian and post-WWI Turkish 'Sparta' rugs).
facts.note: Same author; one source.

rows.cautions: Regular drawing alone does not prove machine-made (Jacobsen's 'machine-made-looking' handmade rugs), and imitated abrash does not prove handmade (Stone p. 15).

rows.question: Stroke the pile both ways along the length. Does it lie over toward one end? Is the pile height exactly even everywhere?

answers.what_you_see: The pile leans toward one end of the rug (smooth stroking one way, rough the other).
answers.note: Hand-knotted pile leans toward the end where weaving began; some Axminster weaves also slant the tuft.

answers.what_you_see: Pile stands straight up, perfectly level, with cut ends evenly upright.
answers.note: Weak clue.

facts.text: In hand-knotted rugs the tuft ends do not stand straight up but lean toward the end where weaving began, a feature no machine-made fabric fully imitates.
facts.quote: lie over obliquely towards the starting end of the carpet

facts.text: One standard Axminster weave deliberately sets the tuft at a slant, 'a point of similarity to the hand-tufted carpet'.
facts.quote: adding thereby to the fabric a point of similarity to the hand-tufted carpet
facts.note: Brinton's 'hand-tufted' means hand-knotted (see the label check).

facts.text: Hand-clipped pile on new oriental rugs was often uneven; by the late 1960s some importers used small electric shears to even it.

rows.cautions: A slanting pile is consistent with hand-knotting but is also found in Axminster; an even pile is found on all kinds once a rug has been sheared.

rows.question: Read every word on any sewn label or stamp: how it was made, the fiber, the country, the maker and the design name.

answers.what_you_see: 'Hand-knotted' or 'hand knotted'.
answers.note: Check the back anyway.

answers.what_you_see: 'Hand-tufted' on a modern label.
answers.note: On a British text before about 1950, 'hand-tufted' can mean hand-knotted.

answers.what_you_see: 'Power-loomed', 'machine-woven', 'Wilton', 'Axminster', 'Oriental design'.
'100% polypropylene' or 'olefin' pile.
answers.note: A modern synthetic; most such rugs are power-loomed or tufted.

answers.what_you_see: 'Made in Belgium' (or Egypt, Turkey) with a Persian place name such as 'Kashan'.
answers.note: The place name is the design, the country is where it was made.

answers.what_you_see: Maker names Karastan, Bigelow, Mohawk, Gulistan / Karagheusian, Whittall, Firth.
answers.note: American mills; the Whittall name may be woven into the back.

facts.text: US law requires a rug's label to give the fiber content of the pile (face); the backing is exempt from the fiber disclosure.
facts.quote: backings of, and paddings or cushions to be used under, floor coverings
facts.note: Quote is the exemption in 15 U.S.C. 70j(a)(6). Jacobsen (1962) says a tag stating the pile content was required on all rugs, domestic and oriental.

facts.text: Imported textile products sold in the US, rugs included, must be labeled with the country where they were made ('Made in ...'); wholly US-made goods may say 'Made in U.S.A.'.
'Olefin' is the US generic fiber name for fibers made of at least 85 percent ethylene, propylene or other olefin units, so a label reading 'olefin' usually means polypropylene.
facts.quote: composed of at least 85 percent by weight of ethylene, propylene, or other olefin units
facts.note: Quote from 16 CFR 303.7. Stone lists olefin as a petroleum-derived plastic fiber and polypropylene as used in tufted Chinese rugs and some Belgian Wiltons.

facts.text: Jacobsen wrote that the federal government (the FTC) required machine-made American rugs in oriental patterns to be advertised as 'Oriental Design' rugs rather than as 'American Oriental' rugs; only hand-knotted rugs could be called oriental rugs.
facts.note: Both books are by the same author, so this counts as one source. The FTC rule itself was not found.

facts.text: Brinton (1919, British) uses 'hand-tufted carpet' to mean a hand-knotted carpet; modern trade use means pile shot into a cloth with a tufting gun and glued.
facts.quote: all hand-tufted carpets are superior to all machine-made ones
facts.note: Quote (Brinton p. 22) shows his usage; the full sentence says this is 'far from implying' that all are superior.

facts.text: 'Karastan' is an invented place-like name, and design names such as 'Kirman 717' are pattern names.
'Gulistan' names three different things: a Persian rug type near Kashan (Hawley), a grade of Turkish Oushak rugs (Mumford, Lewis, The Rug Primer), and Karagheusian's machine-woven rug from 1928.
By 1904 the name 'Smyrna rug', once used for Turkish rugs, had been taken over by American makers of domestic (machine-made) rugs.
facts.quote: Now the name has been usurped by United States manufacturers of domestic rugs

rows.cautions: Labels can be removed, replaced or wrong; and old American rugs may carry place names (Kirman, Sarouk, Smyrna, Gulistan) that are design or brand names. Always check the construction.

rows.question: On the back, do you see a woven burlap or canvas with the yarn or fabric strips showing as short running stitches in close rows, and no lengthwise threads or knots of a rug foundation? On the front, are the pile tufts loops (or clipped loops)?

answers.what_you_see: Burlap, canvas or other ready-made fabric with yarn or rag strips showing as rows of short stitches; loops on the front.
The same, but the back covered with a plastic or rubber coat.
answers.note: Hong Kong hooked rugs of the 1960s (Jacobsen).

facts.text: Hooked rugs are made by drawing yarn or strips of fabric with a hook through another fabric, usually canvas or burlap mounted on a frame; the surface is looped and may be clipped. They are a domestic craft of English-speaking countries (earliest about 1840) and are also made in China and India.
Heavy-yarn hooked rugs from Hong Kong, with plastic-covered backs, were sold in the US in the 1960s and taken for oriental rugs; the underside shows they are hooked.

rows.cautions: Hooked rugs in oriental designs exist. A hooked rug has no warps of its own; the foundation is a separate ready-made cloth.

rows.question: Is there any pile at all? If not, compare the two faces: are they the same, or does one side have loose yarn ends or long floats?

answers.what_you_see: No pile; the same design on both faces; small slits where two colors meet along a vertical line.
answers.note: Slit-tapestry kilim.

answers.what_you_see: No pile; one side neat, the other with loose yarn ends or wrapped loops.
answers.note: Soumak or other weft-wrapped weaves, or a kilim with ends left hanging.

answers.what_you_see: No pile; the design appears on both faces with the colors reversed (two cloths woven together).
answers.note: Ingrain / Kidderminster carpet, power-loomed.

facts.text: A flatweave is a textile woven without pile; a kilim is a weft-faced plain weave whose design is made by areas of colored crosswise threads that turn back at the edge of each color.
In the most finished kilims the weft ends are hidden so that both faces are exactly the same; in others the loose ends hang at the back.
facts.quote: permit each surface of the kilim to be exactly the same

facts.text: Soumak is a flatweave in which the crosswise thread wraps around groups of lengthwise threads.
Ingrain carpets are all-wool, flat, power-loomed carpets of two interwoven cloths, with the design on the back reversed in color; made from about the mid-18th century to the 1930s.

rows.cautions: Power-loomed flat carpets (ingrain, Kidderminster) and modern machine-made flatweaves also exist; check the edges and the regularity of the pattern.

rows.question: Part the pile. Are the tufts in rows that overlap like roof shingles, with several plain crosswise threads between rows? On the back, do the knot rows look like loops around pairs of lengthwise threads?

answers.what_you_see: Rows of cut loops that overlap like shingles, wrapped around pairs of lengthwise threads; several crosswise threads between rows.
answers.note: The Tibetan rod technique: hand-made, though not tied one knot at a time.

facts.text: Tibetan rugs are woven by looping a continuous yarn around two warps and then around a rod laid across the rug; when the row is done the loops are cut and the rod removed, giving rows that overlap like shingles.
Tibetan carpets have been woven in Nepal by Tibetan refugees since 1959-60, in the traditional manner, and importers may call them 'Tibetan' though they are made in Nepal.

rows.cautions: Trade terms such as 'hand-loomed' are used for several different hand techniques, and Couristan uses 'hand-loomed' for a flatweave; read the construction, not the term. What 'hand-loomed' means on Indian pile rugs was not settled.

rows.question: Part the pile at a color boundary. Does each tuft keep the same color from tip to base, and are color edges sharp? Does the back show the pattern?

answers.what_you_see: Color edges look smudged, as if the dyes had run from one row into the next.
answers.note: Tapestry carpet (yarn printed before weaving) or a printed rug.

answers.what_you_see: Each tuft is one solid color down to the base and color edges step cleanly from tuft to tuft.
answers.note: Normal for yarn-dyed rugs of every kind.

facts.text: Tapestry carpet gets its pattern by printing the colors onto the pile yarn before weaving, and one color cannot change sharply into the next.
facts.quote: The colour will appear to have run

facts.text: Most woven carpet is made with yarn dyed before weaving, though some is colored afterward by printing; tufted carpet may be dyed or printed after tufting.
Couristan sells digitally printed rug collections.

rows.cautions: No source read describes how to recognize a modern surface-printed rug (for example, color only on the tips of the pile); that test is common in dealer guides but is unsourced here.

features.name: Knot type (symmetric or asymmetric)
how_to_look: Work on the front. Fold the rug across its width, pile outward, so the fold runs along a row of knots and the pile opens like a book; a phone torch held low helps.

Pick one tuft on the fold and, with a pin or the point of a pencil, gently try to separate its two strands so you can see the warp thread (the threads that run the length of the rug, warps) it is tied around.

If the two strands come up together from between the same two warps and will not part to show a warp (they just twist tighter), the knot is symmetric. If one strand comes up between the pair and the other comes up outside it, so you can part them and see a warp, it is asymmetric.
Check several tufts in different colors and in both the field and the border: weavers sometimes mix knots, and solid-color areas may use knots tied over extra warps (jufti).
On the back, both knot types show two small bumps (nodes) per knot, so the back alone usually cannot tell you the knot type.

values.looks_like: Both pile ends rise together in one tuft between the two warps the knot wraps; a collar of yarn passes over both warps; the ends cannot be parted to expose a warp.
values.points_to: Turkish (Anatolian) and Caucasian pile rugs, Kurdish and many tribal and village rugs of western and northwestern Iran (e.g. Heriz area, Bijar, Hamadan villages), Tabriz city rugs; also many Yomud Turkmen rugs. It does not by itself rule out Persia.
values.note: Hawley's 1913 rule that all Asia Minor and Caucasian rugs use it still holds for those groups as he knew them; his rule that Persian rugs with wool warps use it is a tendency, not a law.

values.looks_like: One pile end rises between the two warps, the other outside; the free side lies to the left in the author's convention.
other_names: Senneh / Sehna / Senna knot (Stone calls the name incorrect)
values.points_to: Most common form of the asymmetric knot in Persian city rugs (Iranica says 'more commonly, to the left'); many Turkmen weavings (e.g. Tekke; the 'S group' attributed to the Salor); Indian and Pakistani production; Chinese rugs.
values.note: Open left versus open right depends on which way up and from which side the author views the knot; see pitfalls.

values.looks_like: As above, with the free side to the right in the author's convention.
other_names: right-hand Sehna knot (Hawley's term; Hawley says most Sehna knots are right-hand except many Khorassan rugs)
values.points_to: Less common; Stone gives it for Chaudor Turkmen rugs; Iranica notes it occurs in Persian rugs.
values.note: Because Hawley's 'right-hand/left-hand' and modern 'open left/right' were not defined the same way, do not map one onto the other.

values.looks_like: A symmetric or asymmetric knot tied over four warps (or three) instead of two. Solid-color areas feel thinner than the design outlines when you run your fingers warp-wise across them; from the back, nodes in plain areas are wider and fewer per inch.
values.points_to: Khorasan (Meshed area) weaving, where Jacobsen says it was the regular knot; widespread in Hamadan-area and other commercial Persian production from the late 1930s on (Iranica xii) / after 1945 (Jacobsen 1969). Not a sign of any single place.
values.note: Halves the knots in an area; the rug wears less well and the design is coarser where it is used.

values.looks_like: Each knot wraps one warp only; knots on alternate rows are staggered by one warp, so the back shows a diagonal, offset grid of nodes.
values.points_to: Spanish carpets and some early North African and Coptic material; not expected on an ordinary family rug from Iran, Turkey or the Caucasus.
values.note: Recorded for completeness; outside the main scope.

values.looks_like: No knots at all: loops or cut tufts are punched through a cloth, held by a coat of latex on the back, which is usually hidden under a second glued-on cloth (often canvas). Edges are bound with tape or a sewn strip; fringe, if any, is sewn on.
values.points_to: Modern production (Stone names China and the Philippines); not a knotted rug.
values.note: See the check for hand-knotted, Hand-tufted rugs (India, China and elsewhere) or machine-made.

values.looks_like: Pile inserted on a power loom (Wilton, Axminster and similar): the back shows a perfectly regular grid, often with jute or synthetic weft visible and the pattern only faintly readable; the fringe is usually a separate strip sewn on; identical motifs repeat with no variation.
values.points_to: Factory-made rugs from Europe, the US and elsewhere.
values.note: Jacobsen's practical test: compare two repeats of the same motif a foot apart; on a hand-knotted rug they are never identical.

pitfalls: Open left versus open right: authors view the knot from different sides and with the rug held different ways up, so the same rug can be described both ways. Hawley's 'right-hand' and 'left-hand' Sehna knots are not the same convention as the modern 'open right/left'. Treat any single open-side reading as tentative.
Jufti knots on four warps can look like normal knots in the pile; you find them by the thinner feel of solid areas or the wider nodes on the back.
Worn pile: where the pile is worn to the knot collars, the symmetric collar can look like a pair of asymmetric loops; test where the pile is fuller.
The names are shorthand, not origins: both knots are used in Iran, and Stone calls the 'Senneh' name for the asymmetric knot incorrect.
Knot type is one clue among many; Hawley, May and Stone all say a few weavers in most groups break their group's usual habit.

facts.text: The symmetric knot is tied on two warps with both ends rising together between them; the asymmetric knot wraps one warp fully and passes under or over the next, so its two ends rise on either side of a warp.
facts.quote: In tying the knot, the two ends of yarn appear together at the surface included between two adjacent threads of warp around which they have been passed

facts.text: You can tell the knots apart by parting a tuft: the two ends of an asymmetric (Sehna) knot can be separated to expose a warp, while those of a symmetric (Ghiordes) knot cannot.
facts.quote: If the pile of a rug is carefully parted, the two ends of yarn forming a Sehna knot can be separated; but with the Ghiordes knot this is impossible

facts.text: The asymmetric knot can be open to the right or to the left; in Persian carpets the open-left form is the more common.
Hawley called most Sehna knots 'right-hand' knots but said a large proportion of Khorassan rugs have 'left-hand' Sehna knots.
facts.quote: Most Sehna knots are right-hand knots, but the Sehna knots of a large proportion of Khorassan rugs are left-hand knots.

facts.text: Persians in the trade call symmetric knotting torkībāf and asymmetric knotting fārsībāf; knots of either type tied over more than two warps are called joftī.
Jufti knots save time and material; they lower knot density and give less detailed designs.
In Persian rugs the jufti knot is used in solid-colored areas but not in design outlines, so outlines feel denser when you run your fingers warp-wise across them.
Joftī knotting and 'kimanshi' weaving spread in Persian commercial weaving in the late 1930s (1310s Š.), when production for Tehran companies and export intensified.

Hawley (1913) stated that all rugs of Asia Minor and the Caucasus have the Ghiordes knot, that Central Asian rugs with rare exceptions have the Sehna knot, and that Persian rugs with wool warps have the Ghiordes knot.
facts.quote: all of the rugs of Asia Minor and Caucasia have the Ghiordes knot; that the rugs of Central Asia, with rare exceptions, have the Sehna knot

facts.text: Stone (2013) records both knots in Yomud weavings, with the symmetric knot the more common; Tekke rugs asymmetric; Chaudor asymmetric open to the right.
Tufted rugs have yarn inserted by hand or machine into a cotton backing, then clipped; the back is coated with latex and given an extra fabric backing.
On a machine-made copy every repeat of a motif is identical; on a hand-knotted rug no two repeats are exactly alike.

says.text: Central Asian (Turkmen) rugs, with rare exceptions, have the Sehna (asymmetric) knot.
Yomud weavings use both knots and the symmetric knot is the more common.
Most Sehna knots are 'right-hand'; many Khorassan rugs have 'left-hand' ones.
The asymmetric knot may be open to the right or, more commonly, to the left.
Spread in the late 1930s with contract production for Tehran companies.
Very few old rugs have it; found in rugs woven since 1945.
Khorasan weavers used it as their regular knot 'from time immemorial'.

features.name: Knot count (knots per inch and per square inch)
how_to_look: Turn a corner of the rug over so the back faces up. Lay a ruler along a row of knots (across the rug, parallel to the ends) and count the knots in one inch; then lay it along the length of the rug and count the rows in one inch.

Count knots, not bumps: on most backs each knot shows two small nodes side by side. If both nodes of each knot are visible, count pairs. If the warps are so deeply offset that you see only one node per knot (one bump per colored square instead of two), count each bump as one knot.
Multiply the two counts to get knots per square inch (kpsi). Example: 10 across x 12 along = 120 kpsi.
Count in three or four places (field, border, near each end): knotting is not even across a rug and packing often changes from end to end.
Also note the knot ratio (rows per inch along the length divided by knots per inch across): a ratio well above 1 means rows were beaten down hard.

values.looks_like: Large, distinct nodes; you can count them by eye at arm's length.
values.points_to: Hawley names loosely woven Oushaks and some Genghas at under 20; many tribal, village and Tibetan rugs.
values.note: Coarse is not the same as poor: Hawley warns that knot count alone does not show quality.

values.looks_like: Nodes clearly separate but small; a fingernail drawn across the back catches each row.
values.points_to: The range of most 19th- and 20th-century village and many city rugs in the trade.

values.looks_like: Back looks finely grained, design as clear as on the front.
values.points_to: Fine Persian city rugs (Hawley: Kirman, Bokhara 'several hundred'; Jacobsen: Nain about 500-600).
values.note: Very high claims on tags should be checked by counting.

conversions.to_kpsi: multiply by 0.0645 (1 square inch = 6.4516 cm2); Stone: 1,000 per dm2 = about 65 kpsi
divide by about 1,550; Stone: 100,000 per m2 = about 65 kpsi

Iranica: raj = rows of knots per gereh (6.25-6.95 cm, 2.5-2.78 in). Stone: reg = knots per gereh of about 2.75 in, so 20 reg is about 53 kpsi (assumes the same count both ways). Square the count and divide by the gereh length in inches squared.
knots per cm across x knots per cm along; 4 x 5 = 20 per cm2, about 129 kpsi
Stone: first figure x 1.11 = knots per inch across; second figure is converted from a gaz-based vertical count; see Stone's 'Bhadohi' entry. Single source; another agent may cover tag codes.

pitfalls: Counting nodes instead of knots doubles the figure (four times for a square-inch count) on rugs with level warps.
Jufti areas have half the knots of outline areas; count in a mixed area or count both.
Tags and dealers quote counts in different units (per inch, per square inch, per dm2, per m2, raj, 'quality' codes such as Pakistani 9/18 or 16/18 or Kirman 80/40) that are not interchangeable.
A worn back (shiny, flattened nodes) is harder to count; use raking torchlight.
Higher count is a tendency of older pieces in some groups only (Stone), never a rule.

facts.text: Measure in several places, because all parts of a rug are not woven with equal compactness.
facts.quote: since all parts of a rug are not woven with equal compactness, the measurement should be made in several places if exactness be required

facts.text: Knot density is the product of the knot count across (weft-wise) and the count along (warp-wise) per unit length.
If warp offset is so great that only one node of each knot shows on the back, count one node per knot; with little or no offset, two nodes make one knot.
The number of knots alone does not show quality: a rug can be coarse-knotted yet firm, or fine-knotted yet loose.
facts.quote: The number of knots to the square inch does not of itself demonstrate the quality of texture

facts.text: In Iran, density is traditionally expressed in raj per gereh, a sixteenth of the cubit (ḏaṛʿ) of 100-111 cm.
The knot ratio (warp-wise count divided by weft-wise count) is characteristic for some attributions and shows how hard rows were packed.

says.text: Rows of knots per longitudinal gereh (6.25-6.95 cm).
Knots per gereh of about 2.75 inches; 20 reg is about 53 kpsi.

features.name: Warp material (the lengthwise threads)
how_to_look: Look at the fringe: in a hand-knotted rug the fringe is the ends of the warps themselves, so its material is the warp material.

Wool fringe is springy, slightly hairy and often ivory, gray or brown; cotton is smooth, matte, bright white or cream and soft; silk is very fine and glossy; goat hair is coarse, wiry and usually dark.

Check that the fringe really continues into the rug: fold back the end and see whether the fringe threads run straight into the body under the knots. A fringe sewn on as a separate strip tells you nothing about the warps (and is itself a clue: see ends).

If unsure about cotton versus wool, the old books advise burning a snipped fringe end: only do this on a loose end you are willing to lose, away from the rug, and see materials for what the smell and ash tell you.

values.looks_like: Springy, slightly fuzzy, ivory to brown; may be plied from different natural shades.
values.points_to: Turkish and Caucasian rugs, Turkmen and Baluch rugs, Kurdish and tribal Persian rugs, older village rugs. Hawley: Asia Minor and almost all Caucasian and Central Asian rugs, and about a third of the Persian group.
values.note: Stone: for some types a wool foundation may suggest greater age.

values.looks_like: Smooth, white or cream, matte; may be tightly twisted like string.
values.points_to: Most Persian city and many Persian village rugs (Hawley: about two thirds of the Persian group), Indian, Pakistani and Chinese rugs, many 20th-century Turkish commercial rugs.
values.note: Cotton warps do not rule out age; cotton foundations are an old practice (Stone).

values.looks_like: Very fine, lustrous fringe.
values.points_to: Fine Persian city rugs (Kashan, Qum, Isfahan, Nain), Hereke and other Turkish silk rugs, some Chinese and Indian silk rugs.
values.note: Mercerized cotton or viscose may imitate it; see materials.

values.looks_like: Coarse, wiry, dark brown or black.
values.points_to: Hawley: sometimes warp in Afghan, Baluch and some Turkmen rugs; more often used for side cords.

values.looks_like: Smooth, grayish or tan, strong, slightly stiff.
values.points_to: Hawley says Tabriz rugs very often have linen warp; flax and hemp also in cheap grades.
values.note: Single source on Tabriz linen warps.

pitfalls: Sewn-on fringe on hand-knotted rugs (a repair) or on machine-made rugs does not show the warp material.
Old wool warps can look whitish; cotton warps can be gray with dirt. Feel and twist matter more than color.
Mixed warps exist (e.g. wool and goat hair plied together).

facts.text: The warp of a rug is best observed at the ends.
facts.quote: The warp is best observed at the ends.

facts.text: In most Chinese and Indian rugs and in some Persian rugs the warp is cotton; in others it is wool or goat hair.
About two thirds of Persian rugs (as Hawley classed them in 1913) have cotton warps; the rest, as well as the Asia Minor and almost all Caucasian and Central Asian rugs, have wool warps.
facts.quote: about two thirds of the Persian group have cotton warp; and the remaining third, as well as the Asia Minor and almost all the Caucasian and Central Asian group have woollen warp

facts.text: The use of cotton in the foundation of pile rugs is a common and very old practice.
Goat hair is sometimes used for warp in Afghan, Baluch and some Turkmen rugs, and is preferred by those weavers for side cords.
Cutting off a fringe thread and burning it lets a trained nose tell wool from cotton warp.

features.name: Warp offset (level or depressed warps)
how_to_look: On the back, look closely at a single row of knots: each knot shows as two small bumps (nodes), one on each of its two warps.
If the two nodes of each knot are the same size and lie side by side at the same height, the warps are level.
If one node of each pair is smaller or sits lower, giving the back a slightly ribbed look, the warps are slightly offset (half depressed).
If you see only one node per knot, because every other warp lies directly under its neighbor, the warps are deeply depressed. The rug will feel thick and stiff for its fineness.
Another check: bend the rug back on itself across the width. A deeply depressed rug resists folding and feels like a board; a level-warped rug folds easily.

values.looks_like: Both nodes of each knot equally prominent; back looks flat and evenly beaded.
values.points_to: Hawley: Kazak, Baluch, Feraghan, Yuruk; most Caucasian and Turkish rugs. May: Sehna, Shiraz, Sarabend, Feraghan, Hamadan, Karadagh, Kurdistan, Mosul.

values.looks_like: One node of each knot a little lower; back slightly corrugated.
values.points_to: Hawley: Kulah, Persian Kurdish, Karabagh, Bergama, Ladik; May: Gorevan, Herez, Joshaghan, Niris, Serapi.

values.looks_like: Only one node per knot visible; the other warp is hidden beneath; double-thick, stiff foundation.
values.points_to: Hawley and May: Bijar and Sarouk; May adds Kashan, Kirman, Kermanshah, Tabriz, Khorassan, Herat. Typical of fine Persian city rugs.
values.note: Hawley: about a third of the Persian group has it, almost no rugs of other groups.

pitfalls: Offset is made by weft tension (one tight 'cable' weft and one slack 'sinuous' weft), so it varies within a group and even within one rug.
A worn back flattens nodes and can hide offset.
Do not count only visible nodes as knots when the warps are level; do count one node as one knot when they are deeply depressed.

facts.text: Warp threads can lie all in one plane, have alternate threads depressed, or have alternate threads completely buried under their neighbors.
Offset comes from weft tension: if one weft is pulled tighter than the next, alternate warps are displaced to a second level and one node of each knot is at least partly hidden on the back.
About a third of the Persian group (as classed in 1913) has one warp of each knot doubled under and hidden at the back, and almost no rugs of other groups do.
facts.quote: about one third of the Persian group have one of the two threads of warp encircled by a knot doubled under the other so as to be hidden at the back

facts.text: Rugs with one warp doubled under, such as Bijars, wear better than rugs with every warp equally prominent at the back, such as Mosuls.

features.name: Weft material (the crosswise threads)
how_to_look: On the back, the wefts show between the rows of knots as thin lines running across the rug. Part the back slightly with your thumbnail to see them.
Wool wefts look fuzzy and are often colored; cotton wefts are smooth, white, cream or dyed blue; jute is coarse, hairy and tan.

values.looks_like: Fuzzy, often reddish, brown or natural.
values.points_to: Turkish, Caucasian, Turkmen, Baluch and most tribal rugs; Hawley says 'very many of the best rugs'.

values.looks_like: Smooth white or cream; in some groups dyed blue.
