Very few old rugs have jufti knots; they appear in rugs woven since 1945.

age_and_wear.what_it_tells: Sets a maximum age depending on when machine-spun yarn reached the area (Stone); Stone notes that before 1924 much Tianjin rug wool was hand-spun.
age_and_wear.cautions: Owners cannot reliably tell hand- from machine-spun yarn by eye; dates by region were not found.

facts.text: A maximum age is set for rugs containing machine-spun yarn, depending on when such yarn was introduced into the area.
Machine-spun yarns appeared in Persian weaving in the later decades of the 19th century.

age_and_wear.clue: Fugitive early synthetic colors (faded purples, pinks, oranges)
age_and_wear.what_it_tells: Not before the 1860s, and in most regions not before the 1870s-80s.
age_and_wear.cautions: Their absence does not make a rug older than the 1860s: natural dyes stayed in use in many areas into the 20th century and were revived from 1981.

facts.text: Synthetic (aniline) dyes reached Eastern dyeing in the 1860s (Hawley: about 1860; Kendrick: 1865-70).
Synthetic dyes were noted in Persian carpets by the 1870s.
In Azerbaijan the mass switch from natural to aniline dyes came around 1880, most strongly in Karabagh, Kazak and Ganja and least in Kuba-Shirvan.

says.text: Introduced about 1860.
Began to be used in the East 1865-70.
By 1870 began to displace natural dyes.
Cheap English dyes well known around Kirman by 1876-77.
Mass switch in Azerbaijan about 1880; mauveine in a Kuba rug dated 1868 (citing Eiland 1999).
Most big Turkish manufacturing networks used them by the 1880s.
Vegetable dyes exclusive in Persia until about 1890; 'dangerous aniline period' 1890-1910.

age_and_wear.clue: Greens that have turned blue or blue-green
age_and_wear.what_it_tells: The yellow over-dye has faded faster than the indigo; happens with natural dyes over time.

facts.text: Because yellow dyes fade faster than indigo, greens made of indigo and yellow become blue-green with age.

age_and_wear.clue: Shiny back, ragged or newly overcast edges

facts.text: Antique rugs are usually more or less shiny on the back and their edges are somewhat ragged or have been overcast anew.

repairs.name: Reweaving and reknotting
repairs.how_to_spot: From the back, a patch where the knots are a different size, tighter or looser, or in brighter or different wool; new warps or wefts spliced in; from the front, a slightly different color that may fade differently over the years.

facts.text: Broken warp and weft threads can be mended and missing knots replaced with similar yarn.
facts.quote: Broken threads of warp and weft can be mended; missing knots can be replaced with others of similar yarn

facts.text: Rewoven areas done in new wool that matched when new often fade lighter after a few years and stand out; good repairers use old wool, for example from the back of an old saddlebag.
A little re-knotting can change a woven date and add decades or centuries to a rug's apparent age (post-knotting).

repairs.name: Rebinding (re-overcasting) the sides
repairs.how_to_spot: Edge wrapping in fresher yarn, a different twist or color; wrapping that covers part of the outer border; sides that curl under from tight rebinding; a narrow outer border missing.

facts.text: Worn sides of old rugs are often overcast anew, sometimes covering part of the border, and if overcast too tightly the sides curl under.
A common cure for curled or worn edges was to cut off a quarter to one inch along the edge and overcast it completely.

repairs.name: New fringe sewn on; ends secured
repairs.how_to_spot: A fringe strip machine-stitched or hand-sewn under the end, whose threads do not continue into the rug as warps; rows of knots lost at the ends; a binding or 'serging' along the end.

facts.text: Artificial fringes may be attached to rugs with damaged ends.
In old pieces the end webs often wear away and rows of knots are lost.

repairs.name: Glued patches, latex or cloth backing
repairs.how_to_spot: Rubbery coating, glue or a sewn cloth over areas of the back, often hiding moth damage or holes.

facts.text: Glue, Lastex or non-skid coatings on the back show at a glance from the underside and are used to make moth-eaten rugs usable.
Mechanical stabilization is preferred in conservation; any method should be reversible.

repairs.name: Painted or inked bald spots
repairs.how_to_spot: Worn areas down to the foundation colored to match the design; color comes off on a damp cloth; dye on the back over moth damage.

facts.text: Threadbare places are tinted on the surface to hide that only the foundation remains.

repairs.name: Reduced, cut-and-joined, or re-bordered rugs
repairs.how_to_spot: A seam on the back (stitching across warps, or a line where warps are joined); a design that does not balance (medallion off center, border corners that do not turn properly); borders that do not match the field's wool or knotting; one end with an incomplete border.

facts.text: Badly worn carpets are often cut up and joined into smaller pieces, the joins run along border edges or round the pattern so they are hard to see.
facts.quote: Old carpets which are badly worn, or much damaged in places, while the rest is fairly good, are often cut up and joined together again so as to make up a smaller piece of good appearance.

facts.text: Sometimes whole pieces are removed so a rug is no longer its original length, or the border is replaced by the border of another rug.

repairs.name: Sewn rents and splits
repairs.how_to_spot: From the back, stitching across a tear, often in thread of a different color.

facts.text: In many old rugs the field is full of rents that have been sewn together.

repairs.name: Sizing and straightening
repairs.how_to_spot: Not visible once dry; the rug may feel stiffer than its type.

facts.text: Crooked rugs can be straightened by loosening here and stretching there.
Dealers tacked rugs face down, wet the back with cold-water glue sizing and let them dry to make them lie flat; there is no visible trace afterwards.

dating_rules.rule: A rug containing any synthetic dye was woven no earlier than 1856, the year of the first synthetic dye.
dating_rules.applies_to: All rugs, when a dye is identified as synthetic (usually by laboratory analysis).
dating_rules.cautions: In practice synthetic dyes reached rug weaving in the 1860s-1880s depending on region; an owner cannot identify most synthetic dyes by eye.

facts.text: Perkin made the first commercial synthetic dye, mauve, in 1856.

dating_rules.rule: Fuchsine (magenta) in a rug means not before 1859.
dating_rules.applies_to: Rugs with dye analysis showing fuchsine.
dating_rules.cautions: Visual guesses of 'fuchsine pink' are unreliable.

facts.text: Fuchsine was patented on 8 April 1859.

dating_rules.rule: Synthetic alizarin identified by dye analysis means not before 1869.
dating_rules.cautions: Looks the same as madder; only analysis can tell.

facts.text: Alizarin was first synthesized and patented in 1869.

dating_rules.rule: Acid azo reds and oranges (e.g. Orange II, Ponceau) mean not before about 1876-78.
dating_rules.applies_to: Rugs with dye analysis showing these dyes.

facts.text: Acid orange (1876) and ponceau (1878) were among the first acid azo dyes for wool; azo dyes were made on a manufacturing scale from about 1876-77.

dating_rules.rule: Congo red (a direct azo dye) means not before 1884.

facts.text: Congo red, the first direct dye, dates from 1884.

dating_rules.rule: Chrome (acid-mordant azo) dyes mean not before about 1889-90.
dating_rules.cautions: Single source for the date; Stone's chronology gives 1915 for 'chrome dye'.

facts.text: Important acid-mordant azo dyes for wool, applied with chrome mordants, were synthesized in 1889-1890.

dating_rules.rule: Synthetic indigo in a rug means not before 1897, but it cannot be told from natural indigo, so this rule rarely helps.
dating_rules.applies_to: Blues, only with specialist analysis of impurities.
dating_rules.cautions: Stone says the dye in the fiber is chemically indistinguishable from vegetable indigo.

facts.text: BASF launched synthetic indigo commercially in 1897.

dating_rules.rule: A rug made under the DOBAG natural-dye project is not before 1981.
dating_rules.cautions: Natural dyes alone do not identify a DOBAG rug.

facts.text: The DOBAG project began in 1981.

dating_rules.rule: A tufted rug with a latex-coated back is modern factory or workshop production, not a traditional knotted rug of any age.
dating_rules.applies_to: Rugs with cloth and latex backs and no knots.
dating_rules.what_it_tells: not before the modern tufting era (date not established from sources read)
dating_rules.cautions: Date of first hand-tufted rugs not established (gap).

facts.text: Tufted rugs have yarn inserted into a cotton backing and locked with latex, with an extra fabric backing.

dating_rules.rule: The full bleach-and-repaint treatment points to a rug in the US trade no earlier than about 1905 (Jacobsen) and mostly before about 1955.
dating_rules.applies_to: Persian rugs (chiefly Sarouk) with painted pile.
dating_rules.what_it_tells: not before c. 1905 for the treatment (the rug itself may be older)
dating_rules.cautions: Hawley and Lewis describe treatment by 1911-13; the start date is Jacobsen's alone.

facts.text: Chemical bleaching and painting plants were set up around New York from about 1905; the practice became too costly after about 1955.

dating_rules.rule: The Persian bans on aniline dyes (1900 and later) give no dating rule: Persian rugs made after them can contain synthetic dyes.
dating_rules.cautions: Repeated in many books as if the bans worked.

facts.text: Government efforts to ban synthetic dyes in Persia were ineffective.

gaps: Persian-language sources: the web-search budget ran out before sid.ir, magiran, noormags, Golestan-e Honar or incc.ir could be searched, and ganjineh.nlai.ir refused connection. No Persian-language text of the Qajar or Pahlavi decrees on aniline dyes was found; Mumford's 1900 English translation (from a French/Persian printed copy) is the earliest text found. Native Persian dye names come only from Encyclopaedia Iranica.

Reza Shah-era rules: Stone says Reza Shah banned aniline dyes; Iranica xii mentions the Iran Carpet Company (1935) and regulations c. 1928 but no dye law. Date and text of any 1920s-30s dye law not found.
The 'right hand cut off' penalty: no Persian primary evidence found; earliest source is Mumford (1900), who says it was ordered 'long ago' in 'one part of Persia'.
Iranian natural-dye revival (Shiraz/Fars gabbeh, Zollanvari, Abbas Sayahi, Iran National Carpet Center programs): widely reported, not verified from a source read here.

Turkish-language sources on kök boya beyond Karavar & Öztürk (2019) not reached (search budget). Böhmer's Koekboya (2002) and Oriental Rug Review (1983) article not consulted. Turkish names for weld, buckthorn (cehri), kermes, cochineal and indigo were left out because no source read here gives them.
DOBAG label or certificate: what is sewn on or attached to DOBAG rugs and how a reader can recognize one was not found in a source read here.
Chrome and premetallized dyes: no history-of-chemistry source read for first commercial chrome dyes (Stone 1915 vs Salimov 1889-90) or for premetallized dyes; history-of-chemistry check still owed.
Viscose (art silk) and mercerized cotton: no source read for when they first appear in rugs. 'Bamboo silk' warning rests on a general FTC textile notice, not a rug source.
Hand-tufted rugs: only Stone describes them; date of first production and a second source (e.g. Carpet and Rug Institute) not obtained.
Cotton wefts in Caucasian rugs 'after c. 1900': no source found for this widely repeated rule; Stone's data on 19th-century attributions contradicts it as a firm rule.
Open-left/open-right convention: no museum statement of the viewing convention (e.g. Textile Museum) was obtained; readers should treat open-side readings as tentative.
Cochineal in Caucasian rugs and lac in Turkmen rugs: dye-analysis sources (Whiting, Böhmer, Rageth, Mushak 1984) not consulted directly; Mushak is known only through Iranica's citation.
Eiland & Eiland (1998/1999) is cited second-hand through Salimov (mauveine in a Kuba rug dated 1868; over half of Persian exports in 1913-14 with synthetic dyes); not checked in the original.
Edwards, The Persian Carpet (1953), the main source on Persian dyeing and the identification of esparak as weld, was not available; known only through Iranica.
Museum examples with open images were not collected for this topic (structure details rarely have open back photographs).

motifs.title: Motifs and designs in oriental rugs: what they are called and where they are found

rows.name: Medallion and corners

native.translit: as the Azerbaijan National Carpet Museum spells it in English

rows.literal: Lachak: in Dehkhoda's dictionary, a small triangular head kerchief (چارقد خرد سه گوش); the corner piece is named after it. toranj: no literal meaning found in the sources read.
rows.description: A large central shape in the middle of the field: round, oval, lobed, diamond, shield- or star-shaped, often with a smaller cap or pendant above and below. In the medallion-and-corner layout a quarter of a matching shape fills each corner of the field.
rows.what_it_tells: The commonest layout in Persian city and village rugs and copied in every weaving country, so on its own it places nothing. The drawing helps: finely curved medallions point to workshop weaving from a drawn design; stepped, angular medallions to village and tribal weaving (the angular Heriz medallion is the classic case).
rows.cautions: Many machine-made rugs use the medallion-and-corner layout; check the back. Corner pieces cut off by the border are normal, not a sign of a cut-down rug.

facts.text: Iranica gives the Persian name of the medallion as toranj and calls the design with a central medallion and a quarter-medallion in each corner lachak-toranj.
Medallions are usually curvilinear; the commonest shapes are ogival, circular, shield-shaped and rhomboid, with lobed or stepped edges.
A medallion-and-corner design with angular drawing is associated with Heriz; Stone calls the traditional Heriz design a geometric lobed medallion with pendants.

In a study of village rugs of Ahar county, the parts of the design are named toranj (medallion), sar-toranj (the medallion's end cap), lachak (corner) and border; the prevailing structure there is an angular ('broken') lachak-toranj.
In multiple-medallion designs the field is filled with rows of medallions, linked or overlapping.

images.caption: the central lobed medallion with pendant caps above and below
images.title: Silk Kashan Carpet
images.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Bequest of Benjamin Altman, 1913
images.licence: Public domain (The Met Open Access, CC0)

rows.name: Pole medallion and medallion rows
rows.description: Two, three or more medallions (often diamonds or hooked hexagons) set one above another down the center of the field and joined by a bar, stripe or stem running through them.
rows.what_it_tells: Typical of Caucasian, northwest Persian, Hamadan-area and Fars tribal rugs (Shiraz, Khamseh, Qashqai) and found on runners from many places. It suggests village or tribal weaving but does not by itself name a group.
rows.cautions: Some sources call any vertical row of medallions a 'pole medallion' even when nothing links them; the long Karabagh 'Lampa' design (flattened medallions in a column) is listed here too.

facts.text: Stone defines a pole medallion design as central medallions arranged vertically and connected by a pole, stripe, rod or trunk, and illustrates Gorevan, Kazak and Khamseh examples.
Iranica describes multiple-medallion designs in which rows of medallions, linked or overlapping, dominate the field.
Lewis 1920 names a diamond-shaped pole medallion carrying the Herati design as a Hamadan field design.

images.caption: three hooked diamond medallions joined end to end; the photo shows the rug turned on its side
images.title: Rug
images.credit: Minneapolis Institute of Art, Gift of Gary Forsberg
images.licence: Public domain (Minneapolis Institute of Art)

images.caption: three hooked lozenge medallions linked in a column (black-and-white museum photo)
images.title: Carpet with Triple Lozenge-Medallion Design
images.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, The James F. Ballard Collection, Gift of James F. Ballard, 1922
images.licence: Public domain (The Met Open Access, CC0)

rows.name: Prayer niche (mihrab)
rows.literal: Mehrabi: 'of the mihrab', the niche in a mosque wall that faces Mecca. Stone glosses namazlık and seccade (Turkish) and jaynamaz (Persian) as prayer rug.
rows.description: An arch at one end of the field, pointed, stepped, rounded or three-lobed, so the field reads as a doorway or niche. Columns may hold up the arch, a lamp or ewer may hang from its top, and a panel (cross panel) may run across the rug above or below the niche.
rows.what_it_tells: Woven across the Islamic world, most often in Anatolia, and also in the Caucasus, Persia, Turkestan and India. The shape of the arch, the columns and the cross panels are what separate Ladik, Kula, Ghiordes and other groups. Many prayer-design rugs were made for sale and never used for prayer.
rows.cautions: A double-ended niche, or a niche at each end, still counts as a prayer design. A hanging shape at the top of the arch is usually read as a lamp, but the reading is a convention, not something the weaver wrote down.

facts.text: A prayer rug shows a mihrab (prayer niche); columns may support the arch and a lamp may hang from its apex.
Crude lamp figures, 'like miniature tea-pots', often hang from the niche of Turkish prayer rugs, especially Konya, Ghiordes and Ladik.
facts.quote: like miniature tea-pots

facts.text: Iranica counts prayer-niche (mehrab) designs among the directional designs, meant to be viewed from one end.
The Iran Carpet Company's classification of Persian carpet designs into nineteen groups (as summarized by Egharloo and Zavieh) includes mehrabi (prayer-niche) designs as a group of its own.
Kendrick says Ladik prayer-rug arches have three points and a wide cross panel above or below the niche holding tall upright tulips.
Stone notes that most prayer rugs were woven in Anatolia but that the design occurs throughout Muslim countries, and that a prayer rug need not be used for prayer.

says.text: The lamp may refer to mosque lamps or serve as a symbol of God, described in the Koran as the light of the heavens and the earth.
Lamps hang from the niche and the columns beside them represent the two large altar candles of the mosque.

images.caption: the top of a prayer niche: a stepped arch with a lamp-like form hanging from its apex, flowers below
images.title: Carpet
images.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, The James F. Ballard Collection, Gift of James F. Ballard, 1922
images.licence: Public domain (The Met Open Access, CC0)

images.caption: a stepped niche in a tapestry-woven Ottoman prayer carpet dated 1188 AH/1774 CE
images.title: Carpet
images.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Anonymous Gift, 1962
images.licence: Public domain (The Met Open Access, CC0)

rows.name: Saff (row of niches)
rows.literal: Saff: Arabic 'row, rank'.
rows.description: Several prayer niches side by side across the width of one rug, like a row of worshippers.
rows.what_it_tells: Woven in Anatolia, Turkestan and elsewhere, in pile and as kilims. The layout is unusual and recognizable, but not specific to one place.
rows.cautions: Long rugs with niches side by side are often cut into pieces; a single-niche rug with a partial niche at one side may be a cut saff.

facts.text: Stone defines saff (Arabic 'row, rank') as a prayer rug with multiple niches in a row, sometimes called a family prayer rug; examples were woven throughout the Middle East, including kilims.
Stone suggests the design may derive from mosque arcades rather than from the mihrab itself.
The Art Institute of Chicago holds a Turkish kilim of the early 19th century titled 'Kilim with Six Double-Niches'.

images.caption: two of the six double-ended niche forms set side by side in a kilim
images.title: Kilim with Six Double-Niches
images.credit: Art Institute of Chicago, Gift of the James D. Tigerman Estate
images.licence: CC0 (Art Institute of Chicago, public domain)

rows.name: Lattice (trellis)
rows.description: Lines crossing the whole field to make a network of cells (diamonds, hexagons, ogival shapes or rectangles), each cell holding a flower, a leaf or a small figure. Two or three lattices may be laid over one another.
rows.what_it_tells: Found almost everywhere: classical Persian 'vase' carpets, Caucasian prayer rugs and honeycomb Kuba rugs, Lur and Bakhtiari rugs, and many Turkmen-style Pakistani rugs. The cell contents, not the lattice, help place the rug.
rows.cautions: The herati and mina khani are themselves lattice-based patterns and have their own entries.

facts.text: A lattice is an all-over pattern of ogives, diamonds, hexagons, octagons or rectangles, usually with a floral motif in each cell; two or three lattice systems may be superimposed.
Iranica says lattice designs are best known from 'vase technique' carpets attributed to the Safavid period, and that many lattice designs are still woven.
Stone calls a compact arrangement of diamonds, hexagons or octagons a honeycomb and says it is common in rugs of the northeast Caucasus.
Lewis 1920 says a compact lattice called the 'mirror design' is often found in Hamadan rugs.

images.caption: a diamond lattice with a small flowering plant in each cell
images.title: Prayer Rug
images.credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Gift of Mrs. John H. Walsh
images.licence: CC0 (The Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)

rows.name: Garden panel (kheshti)
rows.literal: Khesht: 'brick'. The field looks laid in bricks or tiles.
rows.description: The field is divided into rows of rectangular panels like tiles. Each panel holds one plant, tree, flower vase, bird or small niche.
rows.what_it_tells: Strongly associated with the Bakhtiari villages of Chahar Mahal; also woven elsewhere in Iran and copied in India and Pakistan.
rows.cautions: Classical garden carpets with water channels are a related but separate design (see Garden carpet).

facts.text: Iranica names the 'brick' (khesht)-patterned rugs of Chahar Mahal-e Bakhtiari as a design associated with a particular weaving center.
Persian studies of Chaharmahal and Bakhtiari rugs treat khesti panels as a design family and study the birds placed in the panels.

images.caption: rectangular compartments, each holding a plant or tree (one with a bird), divided by narrow bands
images.title: Fragment of a Garden Carpet
images.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Theodore M. Davis Collection, Bequest of Theodore M. Davis, 1915
images.licence: Public domain (The Met Open Access, CC0)

rows.name: Garden carpet
rows.literal: Chahar bagh: 'four gardens', the quartered garden. baghi: 'garden-like'.
rows.description: A bird's-eye plan of a formal garden: water channels (often drawn with zigzags or chevrons, sometimes with fish) divide the field into planted beds with trees and flowers, with pools where the channels cross.
rows.what_it_tells: A classical design. A group of consistent design is attributed to northwest Iran or Kurdistan about 1800; later Persian, Indian and modern copies exist. A rug with this layout is not necessarily old.
rows.cautions: Kheshti (panel) rugs look similar but have no water channels.

facts.text: Stone describes garden carpets as rectangular compartments with floral motifs, elaborations of the chahar bagh (quartered garden), delineated by water courses often showing fish and water fowl, with pools at major intersections.
Stone attributes a consistent group of garden carpets to Kurdistan about 1800; the Met catalogs its 'Garden Carpet' 67.156 as northwestern Iran or Kurdistan, ca. 1800.
Egharloo and Zavieh include baghi (garden) designs as one of the seven families of their 'Haft rokh' classification of Persian carpet design.

images.caption: a pool and a water channel drawn with chevrons, with planted beds on either side
images.title: Garden Carpet
images.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift of William R. Pickering, 1967
images.licence: Public domain (The Met Open Access, CC0)

rows.name: Open (plain) field
rows.literal: Kaf-sadeh: 'plain ground'.
rows.description: Most of the field is left as one plain color, or as plain bands, with at most a few small motifs or a small medallion.
rows.what_it_tells: Found on gabbehs, many Talish rugs, and Persian open-field medallion rugs. It shows the weaver chose color over pattern; it does not by itself date the rug.
rows.cautions: A worn rug can look 'open' where the pattern has worn away; look at the edges of the field.

facts.text: Stone calls a carpet with an empty field a 'mirror carpet'.
Stone says many nineteenth-century Talish rugs have empty or almost empty fields.
Ford's classification, as summarized by Egharloo and Zavieh, includes a 'plain-ground medallion' (toranji kaf-sadeh) group among geometric designs.

images.caption: a gabbeh with concentric plain bands around a small central panel (black-and-white museum photo)

rows.name: Stripes
rows.literal: Moharramat: in Dehkhoda (citing Nazem al-Atebba), a cloth-sellers' word for striped cloth with alternating black and white or colored stripes.
rows.description: The field is filled with parallel stripes, running the length of the rug, across it, or diagonally, often each stripe carrying its own row of small motifs (botehs, flowers, stars).
rows.what_it_tells: Persian 'moharramat' rugs, Caucasian diagonal-stripe rugs (Genje), Shiraz and Anatolian Yürük rugs, gabbehs, dhurries and North African and Arabian flatweaves all use stripes, so stripes alone do not place a rug.
rows.cautions: Narrow diagonal stripes in a border are the separate 'barber-pole' stripe.

facts.text: The Iran Carpet Company's nineteen design groups (summarized by Egharloo and Zavieh) include moharramat (striped) designs; Egharloo and Zavieh's own seven-family scheme puts moharramat first.
Dehkhoda records moharramat as a cloth-trade term for striped cloth.
Stone says nineteenth-century Genje rugs often show diagonal stripes with botehs.

images.title: Tent Hanging or Coverlet (Djerbi)

rows.name: Pictorial designs
rows.literal: Naqsh-e ghalat: 'wrong design', a dealers' term Stone reports for pictorial rugs. tablo'i: 'like a picture (tableau)'.
rows.description: A picture fills the field instead of a pattern: people, kings and heroes, animals, buildings (Persepolis), scenes from poetry, or copies of European prints.
rows.what_it_tells: Persian city workshops (Kerman, Tabriz) wove fine pictorial rugs from cartoons; villages wove naive ones; China and others wove many from the 19th century. The subject can sometimes be dated by its print source.
rows.cautions: Pictorial rugs are often copied; a famous subject does not make a rug old.

facts.text: Stone says Iranian dealers called pictorial rugs naqsh-e ghalat ('wrong design') because they were not generally popular, and that fine examples were woven from cartoons in Kerman and Tabriz.
Stone describes Persepolis rugs depicting the ruins and reliefs of Persepolis, some woven by the Qashqai, with designs copied from nineteenth-century French prints, some with French captions.
The Iran Carpet Company's nineteen groups include a group of historical-monument designs (asar-e bastani), as summarized by Egharloo and Zavieh.

rows.drawing_note: No clear open-licence museum photo was found in the Met, AIC, Cleveland and Mia records checked, and no model photo for a drawing was identified.

rows.name: Animals and hunting scenes
rows.literal: Shekargah: 'hunting ground'.
rows.description: Animals, real and mythical, among flowering plants: lions and leopards attacking deer or cattle, birds, sometimes riders hunting with spears and bows.
rows.what_it_tells: A classical Persian and Mughal court design of the 16th–17th centuries, revived in Persian city workshops (Tabriz, Kashan, Kerman) and copied widely since. Tribal rugs with single animals (Qashqai and Bakhtiari lion rugs, Gabbeh animals) are a different tradition.
rows.cautions: Revival rugs with hunting scenes are common; the design alone does not date a rug.

facts.text: Stone defines hunting carpets as Safavid Persian and Mughal carpets showing hunting scenes or animals in combat within a floral setting, many attributed to Kashan, and notes contemporary carpets with the same motif.
Kendrick describes the 'hunting' carpet appearing in the sixteenth century, with riders armed with spears, swords and arrows attacking lions, leopards, wolves and boars.
The Met's 'Silk Animal Carpet' (14.40.721) is a sixteenth-century silk carpet with animals in combat on a red ground.
Shekargahi (hunting-ground) designs are one of the nineteen groups of the Iran Carpet Company's classification.

says.text: Hawley (1913) wrote that in hunting carpets the lion symbolizes victory and the sun, the antelope the moon, and a lion attacking an antelope the victory of day over night.
Stone describes the subject matter (hunting scenes, animals in combat) without assigning symbolic meanings.

rows.name: Sampler (vagireh)
rows.literal: Vagireh: Stone glosses it 'copy, sampler'.
rows.description: A small rug that shows fragments of a design: part of a border, a corner, and part of the field, often ending abruptly, used as a weaver's model.
rows.what_it_tells: Best known from Bidjar; also made elsewhere in Persia. Samplers are working tools, not finished rugs, and are now collected for themselves.
rows.cautions: Iranica records the suggestion that samplers were introduced by Western exporters in the late 19th century, but thinks they may be older.

facts.text: A vagireh is a small sampler rug woven with parts of designs, used as a weaver's guide or to show buyers the designs available.
Iranica says a knotted sampler shows colors and design better than a paper cartoon and lasts longer.
Stone illustrates a Bijar sampler.

rows.drawing_note: No clear open-licence museum photo was found in the Met, AIC, Cleveland and Mia records checked, and no model photo for a drawing was identified.

rows.name: War rug imagery
rows.description: Tanks, helicopters, rifles, grenades, aircraft and maps of Afghanistan woven into the field and borders, sometimes in place of the flowers or guls of a traditional design.
rows.what_it_tells: Woven in Afghanistan and in Afghan refugee camps in Pakistan from shortly after the Soviet invasion of 1979, at first by Baluch weavers around Herat. The imagery places a rug after 1979; later rugs show the events of 2001.
rows.cautions: Many war rugs were made for Western buyers; imagery alone does not say who wove it.

facts.text: Stone says war rugs, with weapons and war imagery, began among Baluch weavers in Herat shortly after the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979.

rows.drawing_note: No clear open-licence museum photo was found in the Met, AIC, Cleveland and Mia records checked, and no model photo for a drawing was identified.

rows.name: Herati

native.translit: 'fish', a Karabakh composition name in the Azerbaijan National Carpet Museum

rows.literal: Herati: 'from Herat'. mahi: 'fish', from the leaves around each rosette. mahi-dar-ham: 'fish intertwined'.
rows.description: A small repeat that covers the field: a flower or rosette inside a diamond, with four long curved leaves (sickle or lancet leaves) lying along the diamond's sides. Repeated, the leaves look like little fish swimming around the flowers. It may be finely curved or drawn in angular steps.
rows.what_it_tells: Woven in many Persian city and village rugs (Farahan and Sarouk, Senneh, Bidjar, Hamadan villages, Khorasan, Tabriz) and copied in the Caucasus, Afghanistan, India and China. By itself it does not place a rug; the drawing, colors and structure do.
rows.cautions: The 'Herati border' (palmettes with hanging leaves) is a different pattern from the herati field; the turtle border is a version of it.

facts.text: The herati unit is a rosette framed in a rhombus with four sickle leaves around it; Persian also calls it mahi ('fish') because the leaves resemble small fish.
Hawley and Mumford both describe a rosette between curved lance-shaped leaves that some call fish, repeated as a diaper over the field.
Mumford lists the herati in Herat, Senneh, Feraghan, Khorasan and Kurdistan rugs and, in rectilinear form, in Afghan pieces.
Malayer-area rugs use the mahi with prefixes (chahar, sag, rudbari, alamdar, herati) as separate named variants.
Mahi-dar-ham is one of the nineteen design groups of the Iran Carpet Company's classification, and herati heads A. C. Edwards's nine Persian design names (both as summarized by Egharloo and Zavieh).

disagreements.about: origin of the name and the 'fish'

says.text: Named after Herat, where it was formerly thought to have been developed.
Hawley (1913): of uncertain antiquity and origin; probably Persian, though some authorities took the leaves for fish and traced them to Egypt or China.
Mumford (1902): some authorities trace it to old Chinese emblems; he wonders whether the fish (sacred to Isis) was meant.

rows.drawing_note: No open museum photo with a clear herati unit was found at usable resolution. Hawley 1922 (public domain) draws the herati as Plate O, fig. 4 (page 291); a simplified drawing could follow it.

rows.name: Mina khani
rows.literal: Literal meaning unknown, possibly from a proper name.
rows.description: A network of stems drawn as linked diamonds, with a large round flower (often white or ivory) at each crossing and smaller flowers between them, on a dark field.
rows.what_it_tells: Associated above all with Varamin, and with Kurdish (Bidjar, Sauj Bulagh), Bakhtiari, Lur, Baluch and Turkmen-area rugs; it is also used by city workshops and copied abroad. It points to Persia or Persian influence, not to a single place.
rows.cautions: Dealers' stories that the name commemorates a 'Mina Khan' are not supported by the sources.

facts.text: Iranica describes the mina khani as a two-plane lattice of scrolling stems with rosettes at the points of contact, particularly associated with Varamin.
Hawley says the mina khani is particularly characteristic of Persian Kurdish rugs: a dark blue field with a network of olive vines and large flowers at the crossings.
Old examples of the mina khani are found in Bidjar and Sauj Bulagh rugs (Imani and Foroughinia, a Persian study of Yalameh and minakhani designs).
Mina khani is one of Edwards's nine named Persian designs (as summarized by Egharloo and Zavieh).

says.text: Hawley (1913): named after Mina Khan, 'a former Persian ruler'.
Iranica: literal meaning unknown, possibly derived from a proper name.

rows.drawing_note: No open museum photo found. Hawley 1922 draws the mina khani as Plate O, fig. 2 (public domain).

rows.name: Afshan
rows.literal: Afshan: 'scattered, strewn' (Stone; Dehkhoda: پراکنده، منتشر، پاشان).
rows.description: An all-over design without a medallion: flowers and leaves scattered evenly over the field. In Caucasian rugs the afshan is drawn as stiff right-angled blossom cups (calyxes) on stems, surrounded by small florets.
rows.what_it_tells: Persian afshan designs are city and village floral allover patterns; the angular Caucasian afshan is typical of Kuba, Shirvan and Baku (Khila) rugs. Look at the drawing to tell which tradition a rug follows.
rows.cautions: The word is used loosely by dealers for almost any all-over floral field.

facts.text: Stone defines afshan (Persian, 'scattered') as an all-over design found in Caucasian, Indian, Persian and Turkish rugs, of stylized right-angle blossom cups or calyxes on a stem surrounded by florets.
Afshan is one of the nineteen groups of the Iran Carpet Company's classification; Persian sources describe it as an all-over design of one kind of motif (for example flowers) linked across the field.
Stone lists Afshan among the named Shirvan design types.
The Azerbaijan National Carpet Museum catalogs an 18th-century Baku carpet under the composition name Xilə-əfşan (Khila-afshan).

rows.drawing_note: No open museum photo of a Caucasian afshan was found. (The Met's 'Chila' rug 22.100.2 is a boteh field, not an afshan.) A drawing would need a public-domain model; none was located.

rows.name: Boteh (paisley)
rows.literal: Bota / boteh: 'bush, shrub' (Iranica; Stone gives 'bush'). Turkish badem: 'almond'.
rows.description: A pear- or teardrop-shaped figure with the narrow tip bent over, the shape known in the West as paisley. It may be small and repeated in rows over the whole field, or large and few. Drawing ranges from finely detailed and curved to stiff and stepped.
rows.what_it_tells: Woven in Persian city, village and tribal rugs (Senneh, Serabend/Mir, Hamadan villages, Fars tribal rugs, Khorasan, Kerman), Caucasian rugs (Baku and Khila, Karabagh, Shirvan, Genje), Turkmen-area and Indian rugs. Rows of small botehs over the whole field, with the tips turning the same or alternate ways, are typical of Serabend (Mir) and Fars rugs; one large, filled boteh is typical of some Caucasian and Afshar pieces. It does not place a rug by itself.
rows.cautions: Many stories explain the shape (flame, cypress, pine cone, closed hand, river bend, crown jewel); none is documented.

facts.text: Iranica and Stone give the Persian word as bota/boteh, 'bush, shrub', and identify it with the pear or teardrop motif of paisley shawls.
Stone says the boteh is usually an all-over repeat in the field and ranges from detailed to simple geometric versions.
Lewis 1920 and Mumford say the boteh covers the whole field in Saraband and Shiraz rugs; Lewis adds Herat, Khorasan and Senna.
Lewis 1920 says that in Saraband and Shiraz rugs alternate rows usually turn the stems in opposite directions, while in Herat, Khorasan and Senna rugs they usually turn the same way.
The Azerbaijan National Carpet Museum catalogs Karabakh and Baku compositions named for the buta: Şabalıd-buta ('chestnut buta'), Gülabdan-buta ('rosewater-flask buta') and Xilə-buta.

Boteh'i (boteh) designs are one of the Iran Carpet Company's nineteen groups and one of Edwards's nine Persian design names, which Edwards glossed as 'pine or palm' design (as summarized by Egharloo and Zavieh).

says.text: Probably originated in Kashmir.
Mumford (1902): the pattern, like the shawl, is Persian and was carried into Kashmir by Iranians.
Hawley (1913): its origin is 'hidden in the mists of the past'.
It has been thought to represent a leaf, a bush, a flame or a pine cone.
Hawley lists a closed hand, Iranian crown jewels, the bend of the Jhelum river, and (after Birdwood) the sacred flame; he treats all as traditions.
Lewis lists fir cone, palm leaf, a loop of the Indus, a crown jewel and a seal made with a hand dipped in blood, and chose 'pear' only because the shape suggests it.

rows.name: Shah abbasi (palmette) design
rows.literal: Shah-abbasi: 'of Shah Abbas'. gol-e eslimi: 'patterned' or 'arabesque flower'. khatai/hatayi: 'Chinese, Cathayan'.
rows.description: A palmette is a fan-shaped flower seen from the side, layered, with a pointed or lobed outline. The shah abbasi design repeats such palmettes and smaller blossoms over the field, linked by stems and often by cloud bands. Stone describes the shah abbasi motif itself as a symmetrical palmette with two sprays at the top.
rows.what_it_tells: Classical Safavid in origin (the Polonaise silk carpets), and since the 19th and 20th centuries a staple of Persian city workshops (Isfahan, Nain, Kashan, Tabriz, Kerman, Mashhad) and of Indian and Chinese copies. Angular versions appear in village rugs.
rows.cautions: The name is a later label: there is no evidence Shah Abbas I had anything to do with the motif.

facts.text: Iranica defines the palmette (gol-e eslimi) as a stylized fan-shaped motif somewhat resembling a lotus flower in section; Stone calls the palmette a conventionalized motif based on the lotus flower, shown in side view.

Iranica calls shah-abbasi ('of Shah Abbas') a repeat pattern of blossoms, cloud bands and palmettes associated with Safavid carpets such as the Polonaise carpets, and more recently with workshops in Tabriz, Kerman, Nain and Isfahan.
A Persian study of rugs at the shrine of Imam Reza in Mashhad classifies the types of gol-e shah-abbasi used there.
Shah-abbasi is one of the Iran Carpet Company's nineteen design groups and one of Edwards's nine Persian design names (as summarized by Egharloo and Zavieh).

images.caption: a large layered palmette seen from the side
images.title: "Floral and Cloudband" Carpet
images.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift of Ralph Dudley, 1953
images.licence: Public domain (The Met Open Access, CC0)

rows.name: Arabesque (eslimi)
rows.literal: Shakheh-ye eslimi: 'patterned' or 'arabesque branch'.
rows.description: Scrolling stems that branch and split, ending in pointed, forked leaves (split-leaf or 'rumi' forms). Arabesques run under or over the flowers of a design, sometimes in two or three overlapping systems, and are also used in borders.
rows.what_it_tells: Found in classical Persian and Turkish court carpets (Lotto and Star Ushak, Polonaise, Ardabil) and in later Persian city rugs; a stiff red-on-blue arabesque on large 19th-century Bidjar rugs is called the Garrus design. The arabesque itself does not place a rug.
rows.cautions: 'Lotto' rugs are named after a painter, not a place.

facts.text: Iranica defines the arabesque (shakheh-ye eslimi) as a stylized vegetal scroll with bifurcated leaves; Stone describes intertwining or scrolling vines, tendrils or branches, including the split-leaf 'rumi'.

Stone describes the Garrus design of large nineteenth-century Bidjar rugs as split-leaf arabesques in red on a blue ground; Garrus was formerly a name for the Bidjar district and a Kurdish subtribe there.
Eslimi designs form one of the nineteen groups of the Iran Carpet Company's classification.

rows.name: Harshang (crab design)
rows.literal: Kharchang: 'crab' (Iranica; Stone gives harshang as the Turkish form of Persian kharchang, 'crab').
rows.description: Shield-shaped or flame-like palmettes with leafy projections that suggest a crab's claws, spaced over the field among smaller flowers. In a crab border the 'crabs' sit where two interlacing scrolling stems cross, with leaves for claws.
rows.what_it_tells: Used in Persian (northwest Iran, Kurdish) and Caucasian (Karabagh, Kazak) rugs of the 18th and 19th centuries; the crab border is especially common in Karabagh and Kazak rugs.
rows.cautions: Hawley and Lewis call 'crab' and 'tarantula' Caucasian border designs; the field harshang and the border crab are related only by name and drawing.

facts.text: Stone describes the harshang as shield-shaped palmettes with foliate extensions suggesting a crab, with interspersed florets, widely used in Persian and Caucasian rugs of the 18th–19th centuries, possibly from Indo-Herat designs.

Iranica describes the crab (kharchang) border as a double-plane system of interlacing S-stems with stylized flame palmettes, or 'crabs', at their points of contact and leaves, or 'claws', on their terminals.
Crab borders are common in Caucasian rugs, especially Kazak and Karabagh.
Hawley says the tarantula and crab designs are found only in the borders of Caucasian rugs and are probably conventionalized stars and palmettes.
The Met titles its fragment 22.100.70 'Fragment of a Red-Ground Harshang Carpet' (northwestern Iran, early 19th century).
Kharchangi (crab) is one of Edwards's nine Persian design names (as summarized by Egharloo and Zavieh).

images.title: Fragment of a Red-Ground Harshang Carpet
images.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, The James F. Ballard Collection, Gift of James F. Ballard, 1922
images.licence: Public domain (The Met Open Access, CC0)

rows.name: Gol hennai (henna flower)
rows.literal: 'henna flower'. Henna is Lawsonia inermis.
rows.description: An all-over repeat of small sprays of henna flowers, usually in a diamond arrangement; each spray shows small bright five-petaled flowers on a stem.
rows.what_it_tells: Typical of Farahan and Sultanabad (Arak) rugs and Sarouks of the 19th century, and woven at Joshaghan; later copied elsewhere. It points to central Persia.
rows.cautions: Hawley's story that the Prophet called henna 'chief of this world and the next' is a quotation he repeats, not a fact about rugs.

facts.text: Stone defines guli hinnai as an all-over pattern of henna flowers usually in a repeated diamond format; Hawley describes it as a formal pattern of bright five-petaled flowers in many Feraghans.
Stone says nineteenth-century Sarouks of the Farahan area often used all-over Herati or Gol Hennai designs, and that rugs of the guli hinnai design are woven at Joshegan.
Gol hennai is one of Edwards's nine Persian design names (as summarized by Egharloo and Zavieh).

rows.drawing_note: No open museum photo found. Hawley 1922 draws the 'Guli Hinnai' as Plate O, fig. 3 (public domain).

rows.name: Gol farang (European rose)
rows.literal: 'European (Frankish) flower' (Stone: 'European rose').
rows.description: Big, shaded, naturalistic roses seen from above or in bouquets and garlands, drawn after European textiles and wallpapers rather than Persian flower forms.
rows.what_it_tells: A 19th-century fashion: Persian Kurdish rugs and kilims (Bidjar, Senneh), Karabagh rugs and Kuba (Seichur) rugs, and Turkish rugs in the Ottoman 'Mejid' style. It points to the 19th century or later.
rows.cautions: Roses on a rug made for the European or American market can be any date after about 1850; the motif gives an earliest date, not a date.

facts.text: Stone defines farangi gul / gul farang (Turkish and Persian, 'European rose') as the Western cabbage rose and its stylizations, found in Savonnerie rugs, mid-nineteenth-century Turkish rugs in the Mejid style and nineteenth-century Karabagh and Kuba rugs.
Stone says the Seishour rose, a field of European cabbage roses, occurs mostly in rugs attributed to Seichur.
Gol farang is one of the Iran Carpet Company's nineteen design groups (as summarized by Egharloo and Zavieh).
Hawley says an all-over pattern of small bushes with flowering roses is frequent in old Persian rugs and that the rose appears in many rugs of Persia and Asia Minor.

rows.drawing_note: No clear open-licence museum photo was found in the Met, AIC, Cleveland and Mia records checked, and no model photo for a drawing was identified.

rows.name: Vase design (goldani) and zel-e soltan
rows.literal: Goldani: 'of the flower vase'. zell-e soltan: Arabic-Persian 'shadow of the ruler', the title of the Qajar prince Mas'ud Mirza, governor of Iran's southern provinces.
rows.description: Flowers growing from a vase, either one large vase at the foot of the field (often in prayer designs) or small vases repeated over the field. In the zel-e soltan design small vases of flowers are repeated in rows; some have birds beside the vase.
rows.what_it_tells: Vases appear in classical 'vase carpets' and throughout Persian city and village rugs (Kashan, Qum, Kerman, Isfahan, Tabriz, Bakhtiari), and in Indian and East Turkestan rugs. The zel-e soltan repeat is a Persian name for a late 19th–20th-century design.
rows.cautions: The classical 'vase carpets' are named for a weaving structure as much as for the motif; a vase motif alone does not make a rug a 'vase carpet'.

facts.text: Stone defines Zill-i Sultan as a common design of all-over repeats of vases with floral sprays, and gives the source of the name.
Jacobsen (cited in the table's Qum row) says many Qum rugs use an all-over small vase-and-flower design that dealers call Zell-i Sultan.

Goldani (vase) designs form one of the Iran Carpet Company's nineteen groups; one summary lists 'thousand-flower vase', 'niche vase' and 'zel-e soltan vase' as kinds of vase design (as reported by Egharloo and Zavieh).
Stone defines 'Vase carpets' as carpets with flowers and tendrils or a lattice with a vase as part of the design, more specifically 16th–17th-century Persian carpets attributed to Kerman.

images.caption: a vase of flowers flanked by pale long-necked birds
images.title: Rug with vases and peacocks

images.licence: Public domain (Minneapolis Institute of Art)

rows.name: Floral sprays and small flowering plants
rows.literal: Millefleurs: French 'a thousand flowers'.
rows.description: Separate sprays or small plants (a stem with leaves and one or more flowers) set in rows or scattered over the field without a lattice; in millefleurs designs the field is packed with tiny flowers. The 20th-century 'American Sarouk' field is made of large detached sprays on a red ground.
rows.what_it_tells: Small flowering plants in rows are typical of Senneh, Sauj Bulagh and other Kurdish rugs and of Mughal-style Indian rugs; millefleurs prayer rugs were woven in Mughal India, southwest Iran (Qashqai) and Hereke; large sprays are the hallmark of Sarouks and Lilihans made for the United States in the 1910s–1950s, and of Chinese and Japanese rugs in that taste.
rows.cautions: Spray designs on a red field are very common in machine-made 'Sarouk-style' rugs; check the back.

facts.text: Stone defines millefleurs as a design of many flower blossoms, often in prayer rugs flanked by cypresses, woven in Mughal India and southwestern Iran, with similar designs at Hereke and by the Qashqai.

Stone describes the seventeenth-century 'Dudley' carpet with flowering trees, shrubs and plants in horizontal rows as a 'Shrub' design and possible precursor of the weeping willow and Joshegan designs.
The Met catalogs a Persian 'Shrub Carpet' (22.100.76), early 18th century, probably Isfahan or Kerman.

images.licence: Public domain (The Met Open Access, CC0)

images.caption: loose floral sprays on an ivory ground (soft museum photo)
