images.credit: Minneapolis Institute of Art, Gift of Mrs. Katharine Neilson Cram
images.licence: Public domain (Minneapolis Institute of Art)

rows.name: Tree of life
rows.literal: Derakht-e zendegi / hayat ağacı: 'tree of life'.
rows.description: A tree with a central trunk and branches spreading up and out, drawn naturally or as a stiff, stepped figure, often filling a prayer niche or the whole field.
rows.what_it_tells: Found everywhere: Persian city prayer rugs (Kerman, Isfahan, Qum, Tabriz), Baluch prayer rugs (where a stiff tree on a camel field is classic), Bakhtiari and Lur rugs, Anatolian prayer kilims and rugs. Stone uses the term for any main motif with a long vertical axis and upward branches. It does not place a rug.
rows.cautions: Meanings given for the tree of life (immortality, paradise, the axis of the world) are general religious readings, not something documented for a given rug.

facts.text: Stone calls the tree of life a pervasive motif, naturalistic, geometricized or abstract, and in general any primary motif with a long vertical axis and horizontal or upward limbs.
Stone describes camel-colored Baluch prayer rugs with a tree-of-life design.
Derakhti (tree) designs are one of the Iran Carpet Company's nineteen groups (as summarized by Egharloo and Zavieh).
A Persian iconological study of a Haji Jalili (Tabriz) prayer rug discusses its composite tree of life in the niche.
Turkish studies of Anatolian kilims treat the tree of life (hayat ağacı) as one of the commonest motifs.

disagreements.about: what the tree of life means

says.text: Hawley (1913) links it to the Tree of Knowledge, the tree of Revelation, the Muslim tree of Paradise and a Taoist tree of immortality, and says it symbolizes knowledge, resurrection and immortality; in Persia 'generally the cypress'.
Lewis (1920): always associated with religious belief, symbolizing divine power and perpetual life.
Stone defines it by shape only and calls it a 'universal symbol' without a fixed meaning.

images.caption: a geometric tree with paired branches rising from a base, in the niche of a prayer rug
images.title: Carpet
images.credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Florence and Charles Abel Oriental Rug Collection
images.licence: CC0 (The Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)

rows.name: Cypress
rows.description: A tall, narrow, pointed evergreen tree, drawn as a spire or a stepped cone, alone or in rows, often flanking a prayer niche or alternating with flowering trees.
rows.what_it_tells: Found in Persian garden, prayer and 'willow and cypress' designs (Kerman, Tehran, Bakhtiari, Bidjar), in Anatolian prayer rugs and in Mughal and Indian rugs. It does not place a rug.
rows.cautions: The reading of the cypress as a symbol of mourning is a Western writers' convention.

facts.text: Stone calls the cypress a design motif in Near Eastern rugs and illustrates a Kerman prayer rug with cypress.
Hawley says the tree of life in Persia is generally the cypress.
Stone's weeping willow design combines geometric willows, cypresses and flowering trees on rugs of Bijar, Zanjan and Ushak.

says.text: It may symbolize mourning.
An emblem of mourning, but in its perennial freshness also a symbol of the life to come.
Hawley treats it as the Persian form of the tree of life, symbolizing knowledge, resurrection and immortality.

rows.drawing_note: No clear open-licence museum photo was found in the Met, AIC, Cleveland and Mia records checked, and no model photo for a drawing was identified.

rows.name: Weeping willow (bid majnun)
rows.literal: Bid-e majnun: the weeping willow, literally 'Majnun's willow' or 'mad willow' (Majnun, 'the madman', is the lover of Persian poetry).
rows.description: Rows of trees across the field: drooping willows alternating with upright cypresses and flowering trees, sometimes in panels.
rows.what_it_tells: A northwest Persian and Kurdish design (Bidjar, Zanjan) also woven in Chaharmahal (Bakhtiari) and copied elsewhere.
rows.cautions: Lewis's reading of the willow as 'death' is a symbolic gloss without evidence from weavers.

facts.text: Stone describes the weeping willow design (Persian bid majnun) as geometricized willow trees, cypresses and flowering trees on rugs of Bijar, Zanjan and Ushak.
Bid majnun (weeping willow) is one of Edwards's nine Persian design names (as summarized by Egharloo and Zavieh); Ford groups 'forest or weeping willow' designs together.

rows.drawing_note: No clear open-licence museum photo was found in the Met, AIC, Cleveland and Mia records checked, and no model photo for a drawing was identified.

rows.name: Pomegranate
rows.description: Round red fruits, sometimes split to show seeds, hanging from branching stems; in East Turkestan rugs whole trees laden with pomegranates rise from a vase and fill the field.
rows.what_it_tells: The pomegranate-tree field is characteristic of East Turkestan (Khotan, Yarkand, Kashgar; sold as 'Samarkand') rugs. Hawley found the fruit conspicuous otherwise mainly in Ladik prayer rugs.
rows.cautions: The fertility reading is widespread but general; Hawley disputes it for Ladik rugs.

facts.text: Stone says the pomegranate tree is a common motif in rugs of Eastern Turkestan, used as an all-over design; Chinese sources list a 'pomegranate flower style' (石榴花式) among Xinjiang carpet patterns.
The Met's Samarkand-region carpet 08.122 (19th century) has a field of pomegranate trees growing from a vase.
Hawley says the pomegranate rarely appears conspicuously in woven fabrics except Ladik prayer rugs, in which it is 'invariably seen'.

says.text: Thought to symbolize fertility in the East and Near East.
Hawley (1913) thought that in Ladik rugs it referred to its old religious associations rather than to fruitfulness.

images.caption: pomegranate trees growing from a vase
images.title: Carpet
images.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Rogers Fund, 1908
images.licence: Public domain (The Met Open Access, CC0)

rows.name: Sickle leaf (saz leaf)
rows.literal: Saz (Turkish): 'reed, bulrush' or 'enchanted forest'.
rows.description: A long, narrow, curved leaf, often with a serrated edge, sweeping across the field or curling around palmettes and rosettes.
rows.what_it_tells: A hallmark of 16th–17th-century Persian 'vase-technique' carpets and of Ottoman court 'saz' style; later geometric versions survive in Caucasian dragon and floral carpets and in Oushak rugs with large leaves. The small curved leaves of the herati are the same kind of leaf in miniature.

facts.text: Iranica defines the sickle leaf as a long, curved leaf with a serrated concave edge; Stone defines lanceolate (sickle) leaves as narrow, curving, tapering leaves, often serrated.
Stone describes a sickle leaf design of large curving lanceolate leaves and palmettes in some sixteenth- and seventeenth-century vase-technique Persian rugs.
Stone defines saz as an Ottoman floral style of long feathery leaves, rosettes and palmettes.
The Met titles its 18th-century Caucasian carpet 30.95.144 'Carpet with a Geometricized Saz-Leaf Design'.

images.caption: a long curved leaf with a serrated edge sweeping among scrolling stems
images.title: Blue-ground Carpet Fragment with Scrolling Floral Vines
images.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift of Joseph V. McMullan, 1970
images.licence: Public domain (The Met Open Access, CC0)

rows.name: Rosette
rows.description: A flower seen from above: a round, symmetrical head of petals around a center, from a fully drawn rose to a simple eight-petaled star-flower.
rows.what_it_tells: Used everywhere as a filler, at the center of herati and mina khani units, and in borders (a rosette border with large blossoms alternating with small florets is typical of Talish rugs). It does not place a rug.

facts.text: A rosette is a stylized, generally symmetrical rendering of a flower seen from above.
Stone says many Talish rugs have a main border of a large blossom alternating with four florets.
Kendrick says a typical Ladik border has large rosettes alternating with sprays of three blossoms; Stone says the Rhodian lily alternates with large rosettes in Ladik borders.

images.caption: an eight-petaled rosette in a lobed frame (black-and-white museum photo)
images.title: Fragment of a Red-Ground Harshang Carpet
images.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, The James F. Ballard Collection, Gift of James F. Ballard, 1922
images.licence: Public domain (The Met Open Access, CC0)

rows.name: Tulip, carnation and other Turkish flowers

native.translit: laleh abbasi ('Abbasi tulip', a border motif)

rows.literal: Lale: Turkish 'tulip'. laleh abbasi: 'Abbasi tulip'.
rows.description: Tulips drawn as tall upright stems topped by pointed or three-lobed flower heads, often in a row in a panel above or below a prayer niche; carnations as fan-shaped flowers on short stems, often bent; in borders, carnations alternate with diagonal leaves.
rows.what_it_tells: Characteristic of Anatolian rugs, above all prayer rugs of Ladik, Ghiordes, Kula and Mudjur; the Ladik cross panel of tall tulips is one of the clearest signs of that group. The carnation also appears in Mughal carpets, Kuba rugs and Persian and Kurdish borders.
rows.cautions: Old books call the upright Anatolian tulip a 'Rhodian lily' after the 'Rhodian' (Iznik) pottery; the name says nothing about Rhodes.

facts.text: Kendrick says certain floral devices are almost peculiar to Anatolian patterns: carnations on short stems, sprays of three blossoms, hyacinths, and tall tulips on upright stems 'often described as Rhodian lilies'.
Kendrick says the cross panel of a Ladik prayer rug holds tall upright tulips.

Stone says the carnation is commonly used as a motif in oriental rugs, particularly in Turkey, and describes a carnation border of reversing fan-shaped carnations separated by diagonal leaves, common throughout the Middle East.
Lewis describes the Rhodian lily as small flowers with three triangular petals on a long stem.

images.caption: the cross panel below a Ladik niche: tall upright stems with paired leaves, each topped by a pointed flower head
images.title: Prayer Rug
images.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, The James F. Ballard Collection, Gift of James F. Ballard, 1922
images.licence: Public domain (The Met Open Access, CC0)

rows.name: Birds
rows.literal: Murgi: from Persian morgh, 'chicken'.
rows.description: Birds drawn naturally (peacocks, songbirds in classical carpets) or as small stiff geometric hens and cocks scattered over the field or around a medallion.
rows.what_it_tells: Small geometric birds (murgi) are typical of southwest Persian tribal rugs, above all Khamseh, and appear in Qashqai, Afshar, Bakhtiari panel and Shiraz rugs and in Caucasian Akstafa (peacocks) and Baku rugs. Birds in a classical floral setting point to Persian court and city work.

facts.text: Stone says geometricized images of chickens occur in southwestern Persian rugs, particularly those of the Khamseh Confederacy, and that rugs dominated by them may be called murgi rugs.
A Persian study (Fakhr, Chitsazian and Safaran) examines the bird motif in khesti (panel) carpets of Chaharmahal and Bakhtiari.
Turkish studies of Anatolian kilims call the bird (kuş) the most used animal motif.
Hawley says that, with few exceptions, modern rugs showing birds are Persian.

says.text: Hawley (1913) gives meanings by species: bird of paradise felicity, peacock fire, eagle power.
Balkanal (after Turkish folklore literature): in Anatolian weaving the bird stands for happiness, joy and love, and also strength.

images.caption: small stiff birds (hens or cocks) around a central tree inside a diamond
images.title: Khamseh Carpet
images.credit: Art Institute of Chicago, Gift of Joseph W. Fell
images.licence: CC0 (Art Institute of Chicago, public domain)

rows.name: Cloud band
rows.literal: Azerbaijani bulud: 'cloud'.
rows.description: A ribbon-like band that curls back on itself in loops and hooks, like a horseshoe or a knot of ribbon, scattered in the field or repeated in a border. In Chinese rugs clouds are drawn as small scrolling lobed clusters (ruyi heads).
rows.what_it_tells: Taken from Chinese art into 15th–16th-century Persian and then Ottoman court carpets; it survives in Persian city rugs, in Caucasian dragon and 'cloudband' Karabagh rugs and in Beshir rugs. In Chinese and Tibetan rugs clouds are everywhere. In a Persian or Caucasian rug it points to a classical model.
rows.cautions: Hawley's reading of the cloud band as a symbol of heaven is his own.

facts.text: The cloud band is a ribbon-like, recurving motif that came into Middle Eastern carpets from Chinese art.

Hawley says the Chinese cloud band appeared in Persia about the middle of the fifteenth century, was conspicuous in carpets attributed to Herat and Tabriz and in Polonaise carpets, passed to Asia Minor, and never appeared in strictly nomadic weavings.
Stone describes a cloud band border of repeated horseshoe-shaped cloud bands, alternating toward and away from the field, from sixteenth-century Persian rugs.
The Met titles its 17th-century Persian carpet 53.214 a 'Floral and Cloudband' Carpet.

images.caption: a blue ribbon-like band curving in a loop around a small flower
images.title: "Floral and Cloudband" Carpet
images.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift of Ralph Dudley, 1953
images.licence: Public domain (The Met Open Access, CC0)

rows.name: Curvilinear and rectilinear drawing
rows.literal: Gardan: 'turning'; shekasteh: 'broken'; hendesi: 'geometric'.
rows.description: Not a motif but the way motifs are drawn. Curvilinear drawing has smooth curves, thin stems and naturalistic flowers; it needs a fine weave and usually a drawn design (cartoon). Rectilinear drawing builds every outline from steps and straight lines, so flowers become stars, diamonds and hooks.
rows.what_it_tells: One of the most useful first questions about any rug. Curvilinear drawing points to city or workshop weaving (or a high knot count); rectilinear drawing to village and tribal weaving, which works from memory. The same motif (a herati, a boteh, a medallion) appears in both styles.
rows.cautions: Fine village rugs can be curvilinear and coarse city rugs angular; and many machine-made rugs imitate both. Use it with the back of the rug.

facts.text: A Persian design scheme (reported by Egharloo and Zavieh) divides Persian carpet design into two styles: designs of straight ('broken') lines and designs of curved lines (gardan).
Stone says motifs vary over time, tending from the complex to the simple and from the curvilinear to the geometric, and that borrowing and reinterpretation confuse attribution.
Hawley contrasts the geometric patterns of nomadic and Caucasian rugs with the floral patterns of Persia and India.
Stone says traditional Heriz designs are thought to be geometricized interpretations of Tabriz designs.

images.caption: curvilinear drawing: smooth stems, palmettes and leaves
images.title: "Floral and Cloudband" Carpet
images.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift of Ralph Dudley, 1953
images.licence: Public domain (The Met Open Access, CC0)

images.caption: rectilinear drawing: a stepped star figure whose every outline runs in steps
images.title: Kilim with Bands of "Star" Motifs
images.credit: Art Institute of Chicago, Dr. and Mrs. Magnus Urnes Memorial Fund
images.licence: CC0 (Art Institute of Chicago, public domain)

rows.name: Mazarlik (landscape or 'cemetery' design)
rows.literal: Mezarlık: Turkish 'cemetery'; türbelik, from türbe, 'tomb'.
rows.description: Rows of small houses or mosques and trees (often cypresses and willows) arranged across the field, usually of a prayer rug, like a village or a graveyard seen in rows.
rows.what_it_tells: An Anatolian design first woven in the 18th century; in the 19th and early 20th centuries made above all at Kula, Gördes and Kırşehir.
rows.cautions: The old story that these rugs were made to wrap the dead or lay on graves is not supported: Stone says there is no evidence they were used for funeral rites.

facts.text: Stone describes landscape (mazarlık, cemetery, türbelik) carpets as Anatolian rugs, first woven in the 18th century, with stylized houses or mosques and trees arranged horizontally, made in the 19th–early 20th centuries mainly at Kula, Gördes and Kırşehir.

says.text: Mumford (1902) wrote of türbelik 'grave carpets' spread on graves, with cypress, willow and myrtle designs, now made for export.
Stone: it was incorrectly supposed that such carpets enfold the dead; there is no evidence they were used for funeral rites, so 'cemetery carpet' has no foundation.

rows.drawing_note: No open museum photo found among the Met, AIC, Cleveland and Mia records checked.

rows.name: Memling gul
rows.literal: Named in the West after the painter Hans Memling, whose paintings show rugs with the motif.
rows.description: A small stepped figure, roughly a diamond or octagon, whose stepped outline throws off hooks; it is repeated in rows over the field or used as a minor motif. Stone illustrates Kazak, Moghan, Kurdish and Anatolian versions.
rows.what_it_tells: Common in Caucasian (Kazak, Moghan, Genje), Anatolian, Kurdish and Persian tribal rugs (Qashqai, Afshar, Lur), and in Turkmen weaving. It points to village or tribal weaving but is shared too widely to name a group.
rows.cautions: Despite the name it is not a Turkmen tribal gul; the Turkmen gul explorer covers those.

facts.text: Stone says the Memling gul is a widely used motif named after Hans Memling, a fifteenth-century Flemish painter whose paintings show rugs with the motif, and that the earliest Memling gul rugs were probably flatwoven.
Stone says Moghan rugs usually have Memling guls or hooked medallions, and that Genje rugs may show Memling guls.
Stone lists the Memling gul among motifs shared by Persian tribal groups and in Kurdish village rugs.

rows.drawing_note: No open museum photo with a clear Memling gul was found at usable resolution; the Met's yastik 22.100.9 may show hooked polygons of this family but its image is 512 px wide and the identification is not certain.

rows.name: Octagon and other polygons
rows.description: Eight- or six-sided figures used as medallions or repeated in rows, often with an inner star, cross or interlace. Large octagons framed in squares make the 'large-pattern Holbein' design; small octagons in rows the 'small-pattern Holbein'.
rows.what_it_tells: Octagons run from 15th-century Anatolian 'Holbein' carpets and Mamluk carpets to 19th-century Caucasian, Anatolian (Bergama, Canakkale), Baluch and Uzbek rugs. Octagonal Turkmen guls are a separate system (see the Turkmen gul explorer). Hexagonal medallions in a column are typical of Serab and Karadagh runners.

facts.text: Stone defines the octagon as any regular eight-sided figure and the hexagon as any regular six-sided figure.

Hawley describes a small octagonal disc crossed by hour-glass-like figures, probably related to the large designs of the 15th-century Holbein carpet, frequent in nomadic rugs: Baluch, nearly all Caucasians, some Anatolian, very few Persian.
The Met and Cleveland catalog 15th–16th-century carpets with rows of octagons as 'Holbein' carpets (Met 2009.458.1) or 'Spanish Carpet with a Turkish Pattern' (Cleveland 1952.511).
Stone describes Serab runners with repeating diamond or hexagon medallions on a camel-colored field.

says.text: Hawley (1913) reports that it 'is sometimes regarded as a dial symbolising the diurnal motion of the earth'.
Lewis (1920) says it represents the eight directions.

images.caption: a small octagon with a hooked, interlaced outline
images.title: 'Holbein' Carpet
images.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift from the Collection of Hillary Black Dumas and Dr. D. Gilbert Dumas, 2009
images.licence: Public domain (The Met Open Access, CC0)

images.caption: a large octagon with an inner stepped figure
images.title: Hearth Rug
images.credit: Minneapolis Institute of Art, Bequest of Miss Lily Place
images.licence: Public domain (Minneapolis Institute of Art)

rows.name: Diamond (lozenge) medallion
rows.description: A diamond standing on its point, used singly as a medallion, in a column (see pole medallion), or repeated; its edges are often stepped, serrated or fringed with hooks, and it may hold a smaller diamond or a star.
rows.what_it_tells: Universal in village, tribal and flat-woven rugs. A diamond with hooked or serrated edges and spurs, central in the field, is typical of Qashqai and other Fars tribal rugs; a lattice of small diamonds each holding a flower is the Joshaghan design. The diamond itself places nothing.

facts.text: Stone defines a diamond as a square or rhombus oriented with one diagonal vertical, and a rhomb motif as any design dominated by the diamond.
Stone describes the Qashqai-type medallion as a hexagon or diamond with projections, curvilinear in earlier versions and rectilinear in later ones, used on many Qashqai rugs and bag faces.
Stone says the design for which Joshegan is famed is an all-over lozenge pattern, each lozenge holding a geometricized floral motif, widely copied.
Iranica lists the rhomboid among the commonest medallion shapes.

images.caption: a diamond (lozenge) medallion with a serrated outline
images.title: Carpet
images.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, The James F. Ballard Collection, Gift of James F. Ballard, 1922
images.licence: Public domain (The Met Open Access, CC0)

images.caption: stepped diamonds outlined in white in a kilim
images.title: Rug
images.credit: Art Institute of Chicago, Gift of Ada K. Rew
images.licence: CC0 (Art Institute of Chicago, public domain)

rows.name: Sunburst (eagle) medallion

native.translit: the composition name in the Azerbaijan National Carpet Museum

rows.literal: Chelaberd is, per Stone, a corruption of Chelabi, a town of southern Karabagh; Azerbaijani Çələbi.
rows.description: A large lozenge at the center with long parallel arms radiating outward like rays, and hooked brackets facing outward above and below; one to four of these fill the field, usually on red.
rows.what_it_tells: A Karabagh design of the 19th century, also made later and copied (including in Iranian Karadagh and modern Turkish rugs). It is one of the best-known Caucasian designs.
rows.cautions: Many late and contemporary copies exist; the design alone does not date a rug.

facts.text: Stone describes Chelaberd (Eagle, Sunburst, Adler Kazak) rugs as 19th-century Karabagh rugs with a lozenge medallion with parallel radiating arms and outward-facing hooked brackets above and below.
Lewis calls the 'Palace' or 'Sunburst' design very common in Kazaks and Shirvans and never found outside the Caucasus.
Stone says the design is thought to derive from Dragon carpets, and that there are 17th-century Caucasian carpets with this medallion.

says.text: Karabagh (Chelabi in southern Karabagh).
Common in Kazaks and Shirvans.
Hawley called rugs with this medallion Tcherkess (Circassian) rugs.

images.caption: one sunburst medallion: a lozenge with long radiating arms
images.title: Carpet
images.credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Gift of Charles and Irma Wilkinson in honor of Evan and Brenda Turner
images.licence: CC0 (The Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)

rows.name: Lenkoran medallion

native.translit: composition name in the Azerbaijan National Carpet Museum

rows.literal: Named after Lenkoran (Lənkəran), the main town of Talish on the Caspian.
rows.description: A large medallion with two or four curling arms or hooked projections, often read as a geometricized calyx or dragon, repeated down the field and alternating with smaller medallions.
rows.what_it_tells: Characteristic of Talish rugs; also used in Kazak and Karabagh rugs.

facts.text: Stone says the Lenkoran medallion may be a large geometricized calyx or derived from a dragon motif, has two or four arms, and is used in Talish, Kazak and Karabagh rugs.
The Azerbaijan National Carpet Museum catalogs a late-19th–early-20th-century carpet named Lənkəran among its Karabakh carpets.

rows.drawing_note: No open museum photo found.

rows.name: Lori Pambak medallion
rows.literal: Named after Lori Pambak, a town south of Tbilisi in the Kazak region.
rows.description: A large octagonal medallion filled with two pairs of opposed calyx (cup) forms joined at the base, usually one or two in the field of a Kazak rug.
rows.what_it_tells: A Kazak design of the 19th century, still used by Turkish and Kurdish weavers around Kars, so it is found on both Caucasian and modern east Anatolian rugs.

facts.text: Stone describes the Lori Pambak motif as a large octagonal medallion filled by two pairs of opposing calyxes joined at the base, evolved from an Anatolian medallion and still used by Turkish and Kurdish weavers around Kars.

rows.drawing_note: No open museum photo found.

rows.name: Shield medallion (Sewan Kazak)
rows.description: A very large cruciform medallion with a shield-like outline, projecting arms at the top and bottom and stepped sides, filling most of a Kazak rug's field; in 'Shield Kazak' rugs, smaller shield shapes with hooked extensions are repeated on the diagonal.
rows.what_it_tells: A Kazak design (Sewan or Shield Kazak) of the 19th century; the smaller repeated shields are also found in some Shirvan rugs.
rows.cautions: Writers use 'Sewan' and 'Shield' Kazak for two related designs; check which one a source means.

facts.text: Stone defines the Shield Kazak as a south Caucasian rug with an all-over pattern of diagonally arranged shield-shaped motifs with hooked extensions, also found in some Shirvan rugs.
The Art Institute of Chicago titles its rug 2014.1173 (Caucasus, about 1875) 'Sewan Kazak Rug'; it has one large central shield-shaped medallion.

images.caption: the large central shield-shaped medallion
images.title: Sewan Kazak Rug
images.credit: Art Institute of Chicago, Gift of Joseph W. Fell
images.licence: CC0 (Art Institute of Chicago, public domain)

rows.name: Latch hook
rows.literal: Çengel: Turkish 'hook'.
rows.description: Small hooks projecting at right or acute angles, all turned the same way, along the edges of diamonds, medallions, bands and borders. A long row of them standing on a line is a 'running latch hook'.
rows.what_it_tells: Found in almost all Caucasian, Turkmen and Anatolian rugs and in Persian tribal rugs (Shiraz, Qashqai, Kurdish); rare in Persian and Indian city rugs. Plenty of latch hooks points to village or tribal weaving.

facts.text: Stone describes latch hooks as parallel projections with short right- or acute-angle ends pointed the same way, on the sides of diamonds and other figures or on the edges of broad stripes.
Hawley says latch hooks are found in all Caucasian and Central Asian rugs and most Anatolian rugs, but rarely in Indian or Persian rugs except Shiraz.
Hawley suggests the hook softens the abrupt change from one color to another; Lewis calls it a modification of the swastika.
Turkish studies list the çengel (hook) among motifs woven against the evil eye.

says.text: Its function is to soften the harsh effect of a sudden change of color; probably derived from the Chinese fret.
A modification of the swastika, carrying the same meaning.
In Anatolian tradition (after Turkish folklore studies) the hook protects against the evil eye.

images.caption: white bands ending in right-angle hooks around a dark panel
images.title: Star Kazak Carpet
images.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, The James F. Ballard Collection, Gift of James F. Ballard, 1922
images.licence: Public domain (The Met Open Access, CC0)

rows.name: Star (eight-pointed star)
rows.literal: Yıldız: Turkish 'star'. Mühr-ü Süleyman: 'seal of Solomon'.
rows.description: A star with eight points, often drawn as two squares laid over each other or as a cross with notched arms; also six-pointed and many-pointed stars. Large stars fill the field of 'Star Kazak' rugs; small ones are scattered or set in rows.
rows.what_it_tells: Chiefly a village and tribal motif, most frequent in Caucasian rugs (Kazak, Shirvan), Anatolian rugs and kilims (Konya, Bergama, Canakkale), and Persian tribal bags (Shahsavan). The large blue lobed 'stars' of 16th–17th-century Star Ushak carpets are a different, court design.
rows.cautions: Meanings given for stars (Solomon's ring, the Medes' god, happiness) are writers' traditions.

facts.text: Stone defines the octagram as an eight-pointed star, which may take the form of superimposed squares or a cross with triangular cut-outs at the arm ends.
Hawley calls the eight-pointed star chiefly a nomadic symbol, rarely seen in Chinese or Indian rugs, only occasionally in Persian, and most frequent in Caucasian rugs.
Balkanal (after Turkish weaving studies) says five-pointed stars are rare in Anatolian weaving because they are hard to weave, while six-, eight- and many-pointed stars are common.
Stone describes Star Ushak carpets as large eight-lobed blue stars with yellow arabesques alternating with indented diamonds on red, from 16th–17th-century Ushak workshops.

says.text: Hawley (1913) ties the eight-pointed star to ancient star worship and the female principle of the Chaldean sun god, and repeats a tradition about King Solomon's ring.
Balkanal (after Karahan 1992): in Anatolian weaving the star stands for happiness, goodness, light and heroism.

images.caption: a large eight-pointed star at the center of the rug
images.title: Star Kazak Carpet
images.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, The James F. Ballard Collection, Gift of James F. Ballard, 1922
images.licence: Public domain (The Met Open Access, CC0)

images.caption: small eight-pointed stars in rows (small museum photo)
images.title: Shahsevan Saddle Bag Face
images.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift of Inger G. and William B. Ginsberg, 2018
images.licence: Public domain (The Met Open Access, CC0)

rows.name: Lesghi star
rows.literal: Named after the Lesghis (Lezgins), mountain peoples of Daghestan.
rows.description: A stepped eight-pointed star with four arrow-like projections, usually large and in a column of two or three down the field.
rows.what_it_tells: Especially associated with 19th-century Daghestan rugs, and also found in Kuba and Shirvan rugs, Shahsavan flatweaves and eastern Anatolian rugs.

facts.text: Stone describes the Lesghi star as an eight-pointed stepped star with four radiating arrows, used in Shahsavan flatweaves, eastern Anatolian rugs and Caucasian rugs, especially associated with 19th-century Daghestan rugs.

images.caption: a white stepped star with arrow-like projections
images.title: Carpet
images.credit: Art Institute of Chicago, Gift of Margaret Walbank
images.licence: CC0 (Art Institute of Chicago, public domain)

rows.name: S motif

native.translit: shakheh-ye mavvaj ('wavy branch', the floral S-stem)

rows.literal: Ajdaha: Persian 'dragon' (Stone cross-refers the S motif to it).
rows.description: S or Z shapes, angular or curved, used singly as fillers or in chains along borders and ends; very large S forms fill the field of some Caucasian soumaks and pile rugs.
rows.what_it_tells: Found in almost every group except Chinese: Caucasian, Turkmen, Baluch and Anatolian rugs and Persian tribal rugs. Large S forms point to Caucasian 'dragon' soumaks (silehs) and related pile rugs.
rows.cautions: The floral S-stem of Persian borders (Iranica's 'wavy branch') is a different pattern.

facts.text: Stone says S or Z shapes are common in tribal and nomadic rugs, singly or in chains in borders and ends, and are thought to represent the dragon.
Hawley says the S form appears in each group of oriental rugs except the Chinese, and in almost every Caucasian and Anatolian class.
Lewis 1920 calls an S-shaped arrangement of latch hooks a 'Caucasian border design' because it is seldom found outside Caucasian rugs.

says.text: Thought to represent the dragon.
Hawley (1913): 'accepted belief' links it to sun worship as an emblem of light; possibly a serpent, emblem of superhuman knowledge.

images.caption: a large S-shaped band filled with small S and Z shapes, in a rug the Met calls a Dragon Carpet
images.title: Dragon Carpet
images.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, The James F. Ballard Collection, Gift of James F. Ballard, 1922
images.licence: Public domain (The Met Open Access, CC0)

images.caption: part of a large S-shaped band in a soumak sileh
images.title: Carpet (Sileh)
images.credit: Art Institute of Chicago, Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Dave Chapman
images.licence: CC0 (Art Institute of Chicago, public domain)

rows.name: Ram's horn
rows.literal: Koçboynuzu: Turkish 'ram's horn'; buynuz: Azerbaijani 'horn'.
rows.description: Pairs of curls turned outward like a ram's horns, on a stem or at the ends of a bar; in felts and Kyrgyz and Turkmen work the curls are large and bold, in pile rugs small and repeated.
rows.what_it_tells: Found in Turkmen, Kyrgyz, Uzbek and Kazakh weaving and felts, in Anatolian rugs and kilims (Döşemealtı, central Anatolia) and in Caucasian rugs (Perepedil, Karabakh 'Buynuz' rugs).
rows.cautions: Turkish meanings (strength, masculinity, fertility) come from modern folklore studies.

facts.text: Stone defines kochak (aina kotchak, kochanak) as the ram's horn, a design with many variations often used in Turkmen rugs, and cross-refers vurma.
The Azerbaijan National Carpet Museum catalogs a late-19th-century Karabakh carpet named Buynuz ('horn').
Stone says Perepedil rugs have stylized ram's horns or flower calyxes.

says.text: Balkanal (after Erbek 2002): a symbol of abundance, heroism, strength and masculinity, used after or together with the mother goddess.
Oyman (2019): the motif has many names because in different regions it stands for masculinity, fatherhood and courage.
Stone describes the shape and its use without assigning a meaning.

images.caption: bold curling horn-like scrolls in appliqué felt
images.title: Rug
images.credit: Minneapolis Institute of Art, Gift of Richard L. Simmons
images.licence: Public domain (Minneapolis Institute of Art)

rows.name: Tarantula
rows.description: An old trade name for a small Caucasian figure with a central body and several hooked arms or legs, used in rows in borders and sometimes in the field. Lewis says it is so modified that the resemblance to a spider is almost lost.
rows.what_it_tells: Lewis calls it almost omnipresent in Caucasian rugs, especially Kazak, Kabistan (Kuba) and Shirvan; Hawley puts it only in Caucasian borders.
rows.cautions: The name is a Western dealer's label; the sources do not agree on exactly which figure it means.

facts.text: Lewis says the tarantula design is almost omnipresent in Caucasian rugs, especially Kazaks, Kabistans and Shirvans; Hawley says tarantula and crab designs are found exclusively in borders of Caucasian rugs.
Hawley thought tarantula and crab designs were probably conventionalized stars and palmettes, since they hardly resemble the animals.
Mumford mentions a tarantula device referred to by the Russian writer Simakoff.

says.text: In the field and borders of almost all Caucasian rugs.
Only in borders of Caucasian rugs.

rows.drawing_note: No clear open-licence museum photo was found in the Met, AIC, Cleveland and Mia records checked, and no model photo for a drawing was identified.

rows.name: Scorpion (akrep)
rows.literal: Akrep: Turkish 'scorpion'; toplu çengel: 'ball with hooks'.
rows.description: A diamond or rectangle with hooked appendages projecting from its sides, or a long body with many legs; used as a field motif or filler.
rows.what_it_tells: An Anatolian and Caucasian village motif; at Döşemealtı (Antalya) 'akrepli' (scorpion-filled) is the name of a rug design.

facts.text: Stone defines the scorpion motif (Turkish toplu çengel, 'ball with hooks') as a diamond with projecting hooks or a rectangle with appendages.
Balkanal says akrep is used both as a motif name and as a rug-type name, 'akrepli halı', as in Döşemealtı rugs.
Hawley says the scorpion does not often appear in weaving but is sometimes drawn with careful precision in Caucasian rugs.

says.text: Balkanal (after Deniz 2010): woven in Anatolia for protection against evil and enemies; people believe it protects the rug.
Hawley (1913): supposed to represent knowledge.

rows.drawing_note: No clear open-licence museum photo was found in the Met, AIC, Cleveland and Mia records checked, and no model photo for a drawing was identified.

rows.name: Elibelinde (hands on hips)
rows.literal: Elibelinde: Turkish 'hands on hips'.
rows.description: A highly geometric human figure: a body (often a stepped diamond or hourglass) with arms bent so the hands rest on the hips, and sometimes a head and legs; usually in kilims, singly, in rows or as a border.
rows.what_it_tells: Common in Anatolian kilims, less so in pile rugs. It points to Anatolian flat-weaving, not to a date.
rows.cautions: The popular reading of the figure as a 'mother goddess' descended from Neolithic Çatalhöyük comes from James Mellaart's 1980s work; that theory is disputed and the evidence he published has been challenged. Do not treat the meaning as fact.

facts.text: Stone defines elibelinde (Turkish 'hands on hips') as a motif common in kilims consisting of a highly geometricized human figure with hands on hips.

Stone says James Mellaart theorized that some designs in contemporary Anatolian kilims derive from Neolithic images of a mother goddess at Çatal Hüyük, and that the theory is disputed and the credibility of his archaeological evidence challenged.

Marla Mallett found that the 'reconstruction' drawings of Çatal Hüyük wall paintings in The Goddess from Anatolia (1989) had no verifying photographs and contradicted Mellaart's own 1960s excavation reports, and that the first 'elibelinde' figures attributed to the site, published in 1984, had no supporting photos.
Turkish studies of kilim motifs cite Mellaart, Hirsch and Balpınar, The Goddess from Anatolia (1989), as a source for kilim pictures and motifs.

says.text: Balkanal (after Erbek 2002): a symbol of motherhood, fertility, femininity and productivity, also luck, abundance and happiness.
Oyman (2019): despite its stylization, the elibelinde symbolized motherhood and female fertility.
Stone describes the figure only, and records Mellaart's mother-goddess derivation as a disputed theory.
Mallett argues the Neolithic 'evidence' for the goddess link appears to be fabricated.

rows.drawing_note: No open museum photo with a clear elibelinde was found among the records checked; a public-domain kilim photo would be needed.

rows.name: Swastika (wan)
rows.literal: 卍字纹 / 万字纹: 'pattern of the 卍 (wan, ten thousand) character'.
rows.description: A cross whose arms are bent at right angles, all the same way. In Chinese rugs swastikas are linked into a continuous fret (a swastika meander) that fills borders or a whole field.
rows.what_it_tells: The swastika fret border is one of the commonest borders of Chinese rugs (Ningxia, Baotou, Peking) and of East Turkestan rugs; single swastikas also appear in Caucasian and other rugs. It has nothing to do with the 20th-century European political emblem.
rows.cautions: Readers may be startled by the shape; on Chinese and Asian rugs it is an old auspicious sign.

facts.text: Stone describes the swastika (Chinese wan) as an ancient design shared by many cultures, and a border of linked swastikas as often found in Chinese rugs.
The Palace Museum (Beijing) describes a Qing Ningxia tribute carpet whose field is surrounded by the 'traditional 卍-character pattern' with a peony border outside it.
Hawley says the swastika is very frequent in Samarkand (East Turkestan) rugs, occasional in Caucasian rugs, and seldom in Persian, Anatolian or Turkmen rugs.
The Palace Museum's 2010 catalogue of its carpets identified a 'swastika-pattern carpet' (万字纹地毯) laid in the Huangji Hall for the Empress Dowager Cixi's sixtieth birthday.

says.text: Hawley (1913): its primitive meaning of abundance, fertility and prosperity 'has never been lost'.
The Palace Museum, describing one carpet as a whole, says its patterns symbolize wealth, honor and auspiciousness without end.

images.caption: a border of interlocked swastikas forming a continuous fret
images.title: Carpet

images.licence: Public domain (The Met Open Access, CC0)

rows.name: Fret (key pattern)
rows.literal: Leiwen: 'thunder pattern'.
rows.description: Lines that turn at right angles to make a continuous key, meander or T-shaped pattern, usually in a border; in Chinese rugs frets also form corner pieces and medallions.
rows.what_it_tells: The fret border is standard on Chinese rugs and common on East Turkestan rugs; geometric 'Greek key' versions appear in Baluch and some Caucasian borders.

facts.text: Stone describes frets as winding or interlaced designs with right-angle turns, common in the borders of Chinese rugs, where the swastika is connected by lines or T or rectilinear S (leiwen, 'thunder pattern') shapes.
Lewis says the 'Greek key' border is common in the borders of Samarkand, Kashgar, Yarkand, Baluch and nearly all Chinese rugs.

images.caption: a key-fret (meander) border
images.title: Carpet
images.credit: Minneapolis Institute of Art, The John R. Van Derlip Fund
images.licence: Public domain (Minneapolis Institute of Art)

images.caption: a key-fret corner piece, with a small bat
images.title: Carpet
images.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift of Miriam and Ira D. Wallach, 1991
images.licence: Public domain (The Met Open Access, CC0)

rows.name: Bat
rows.literal: Wufu: 'five blessings' (Stone: five bats are emblematic of blessings).
rows.description: A small bat with spread wings, drawn as a curved scalloped shape with a little head; scattered over the field, set in rows, or grouped around a medallion or a shou character.
rows.what_it_tells: Typical of Chinese rugs (Ningxia, Baotou, Peking, Tianjin) and of Tibetan rugs; it places a rug in the Chinese tradition, not in a particular town.

facts.text: Stone says the bat appears singly or in groups in Chinese and Tibetan rugs and that five bats (wufu) are emblematic of blessings.
Hawley describes a Chinese field covered with a swastika-fret with diagonal rows of bats; Leitch lists the bat among favorite Chinese border themes and shows dragon, bat and lotus in a Peking rug.
The Met tags its Chinese carpet 1991.198 (late 18th–19th century) with bats and dragons.

images.caption: a single stylized bat with spread wings
images.title: Carpet
images.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift of Miriam and Ira D. Wallach, 1991
images.licence: Public domain (The Met Open Access, CC0)

rows.name: Shou (longevity character)
rows.literal: Shou: 'long life'.
rows.description: The Chinese character for long life, drawn as a round medallion or in tall rectangular forms, used as a central medallion, in rows in the field or repeated in borders.
rows.what_it_tells: A Chinese motif, found on Ningxia, Baotou, Peking and later Chinese rugs and on Tibetan rugs; often paired with bats.
rows.cautions: Round fret medallions can resemble a round shou; the character itself has distinct strokes.

facts.text: Stone says shou is a group of Chinese characters symbolizing long life, most commonly circular, used as a central medallion or repeated border element in Chinese rugs.
A Beijing palace-carpet piece exhibited in 2005 showed nine dragons with fortune-and-longevity (福寿) characters.

rows.drawing_note: No open museum photo with a clear shou character was located; Hawley 1922 Plate M, fig. 1 (public domain) draws an octagonal Shou medallion.

rows.name: Dragon

native.translit: shuanglong xi zhu ('two dragons playing with a pearl')

rows.literal: Əjdahalı: Azerbaijani 'with dragon(s)'.
rows.description: In Chinese rugs a scaly, five-clawed (or fewer) dragon, coiled in a roundel or chasing a flaming pearl among clouds; or an 'archaic' dragon reduced to scrolls with a small head. In Caucasian 'dragon carpets' the dragons are broken into angular S-shaped and lattice forms among large palmettes.
rows.what_it_tells: Chinese dragons point to Chinese (Ningxia, Baotou, Peking, Qing palace) and Tibetan rugs and East Turkestan pieces; Caucasian dragon carpets are a 17th–18th-century group with 19th-century descendants (dragon soumaks).
rows.cautions: Chinese makers and Western writers sometimes link the number of claws to rank; check the source before repeating it.

facts.text: Stone says the dragon (lung) is an important motif in Chinese rugs, represents the Emperor, and that two opposing dragons are sometimes shown in combat over a flaming pearl; Hawley calls the dragon an emblem of imperial power.
Stone says stylized opposing Chinese dragons may have been the source of the dragons in Caucasian dragon carpets.
Hawley says archaic dragons in early Chinese rug medallions were conventionalized into scrolls until only their heads betray their origin.
The Palace Museum's carpet catalogue identifies a large carpet with two dragons playing with a pearl (双龙戏珠) before the throne of the Hall of Supreme Harmony.
The Azerbaijan National Carpet Museum's oldest exhibit is a 17th-century Karabakh 'Ajdahali' (Dragon) carpet.

images.caption: a coiled dragon in a central roundel
images.title: Carpet
images.credit: Minneapolis Institute of Art, The John R. Van Derlip Fund
images.licence: Public domain (Minneapolis Institute of Art)

images.caption: a stylized scroll-bodied dragon with a small head
images.title: Carpet
images.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift of Miriam and Ira D. Wallach, 1991
images.licence: Public domain (The Met Open Access, CC0)

rows.name: Lotus

native.translit: goulian ('hooked lotus': single flowers joined by hooked lines; Palace Museum glossary)
chuanzhi lian ('lotus on a linked stem')

rows.literal: Goulian: 'hooked lotus'; chuanzhi: 'linked branches' (Palace Museum glossary).
rows.description: A water-lily flower with pointed petals, seen from the side or from above, often on scrolling stems that link the flowers into a continuous pattern.
rows.what_it_tells: Common in Chinese and Tibetan rugs; the lotus also appears in classical Persian carpets and Indian rugs. Stone notes the lotus has been proposed as the source of some Turkmen guls.

facts.text: Stone calls the lotus a Buddhist and Taoist symbol of perfection and purity and a motif in Chinese rugs; Hawley says it is a favorite design of Chinese weavers and was realistically drawn in classical Persian carpets.

The Palace Museum describes a Qing Ningxia tribute carpet whose field is a pattern of lotus-shaped flowers on linked stems (串枝莲花形花卉), and defines goulian (勾莲) as single flowers linked by hooked lines.
The lotus is one of the eight Buddhist emblems.

images.caption: a lotus-like flower with pointed petals, cut off by the lower edge of the photo; from a woven silk velvet carpet
images.title: Incomplete Carpet

images.licence: CC0 (Art Institute of Chicago, public domain)

rows.name: Peony
rows.literal: Kani-botan: Japanese 'crab peony'.
rows.description: A large, round, many-petaled flower seen from the side or above, often with leaves and buds, in borders and fields.
rows.what_it_tells: A favorite of Chinese rugs (often in Ningxia borders) and of Japanese dantsu, where a crab-like peony (kani-botan) is the signature design of Nabeshima dantsu. Peonies are also drawn naturally in Mughal carpets.

facts.text: Stone says the peony is a common motif in Chinese rugs, often used in the borders of Ningxia rugs; the Palace Museum describes a peony border around a Qing Ningxia tribute carpet.
The table's Nabeshima dantsu row (from a Japanese dictionary) says its signature design is the kani-botan, a crab-like peony, with karakusa scrolls.

says.text: It may symbolize riches, honor, beauty, love or spring.
Lewis: in China a symbol of wealth and official rank.

images.caption: a layered, many-petaled flower head of peony type; from a woven silk velvet carpet
images.title: Incomplete Carpet
images.credit: Art Institute of Chicago, Gift of Mrs. Chauncey McCormick and Mrs. Richard Ely Danielson
images.licence: CC0 (Art Institute of Chicago, public domain)

rows.name: Scrolling vine
rows.literal: Karakusa: Japanese 'Tang (Chinese) grass'; tak: Persian 'vine'.
rows.description: A continuous wavy stem that curls back on itself, carrying leaves, buds and flowers, used in borders and as a ground pattern beneath other motifs.
rows.what_it_tells: Universal: in borders of Persian, Indian and Anatolian rugs, as the ground of Chinese and Japanese rugs (karakusa in dantsu). It does not place a rug.
rows.cautions: Hawley's reading of the endless vine as 'continuity of purpose' is his own.

facts.text: Hawley says almost every rug of Persia, India and Asia Minor has a vine with pendant leaves, flowers, rosettes or palmettes in some part of the border, and that conventionalized vines appear even in geometric Caucasian rugs.
Iranica calls repeated S-shaped stems ending in small vegetal motifs (shakheh-ye mavvaj, 'wavy branch', or tak, 'vine') usually a border pattern.
The Palace Museum defines chuanzhi (串枝) as a traditional pattern in which flowers are linked vertically into strips, such as linked lotus.

images.caption: scrolling leafy stems with curling ends
images.title: Carpet
images.credit: Minneapolis Institute of Art, The John R. Van Derlip Fund
images.licence: Public domain (Minneapolis Institute of Art)

images.caption: a blue scrolling vine with a many-petaled flower; from a woven silk velvet carpet
images.title: Incomplete Carpet
images.credit: Art Institute of Chicago, Gift of Mrs. Chauncey McCormick and Mrs. Richard Ely Danielson
images.licence: CC0 (Art Institute of Chicago, public domain)

rows.name: Sea waves and mountains
rows.description: At the foot of the field or around a border: diagonal multicolored stripes ('standing water'), rolling scalloped waves above them, and sometimes a rocky mountain peak rising from the water.
rows.what_it_tells: Chinese and East Turkestan rugs (Hawley found the mountain-and-waves emblem more often in Samarkand and Yarkand rugs than in Chinese ones); common on Chinese pillar rugs, saddle rugs and Qing palace carpets.
rows.cautions: Hawley calls the zigzag 'water motive' widespread far beyond China; a zigzag line alone is not a Chinese wave border.

facts.text: Hawley lists the Sacred Mountain rising out of the waves of eternity as an old Chinese emblem, more frequently found in rugs of Samarkand and Yarkand.
Hawley (quoting Mumford) says a zigzag line stood for water and that rows of zigzags representing the sea were a recognized carpet design in India, China and Persia.

images.caption: a band of scalloped waves above diagonal multicolored stripes, with part of a dragon above
images.title: Rug
images.credit: Minneapolis Institute of Art, Bequest of William E. Goodfellow
images.licence: Public domain (Minneapolis Institute of Art)

rows.name: Buddhist emblems and the hundred antiques
rows.literal: Babao: 'eight treasures'. bogu: 'broad antiquity'. dorje: Tibetan 'sacred stone'.
rows.description: Small emblems scattered in the field or border: the eight Buddhist symbols (wheel, conch, umbrella, canopy, lotus, vase, paired fish and endless knot), often tied with ribbons; or the 'hundred antiques', vases, bronzes, books and scholars' objects. Tibetan rugs may show crossed dorjes (ritual thunderbolts).
rows.what_it_tells: Chinese and Tibetan rugs; the hundred antiques are typical of Peking and Baotou rugs and of 20th-century Chinese export rugs.
rows.cautions: The dorje is a Tantric ritual object, not one of the eight emblems.

facts.text: Stone lists the eight Buddhist symbols (wheel, conch, umbrella, canopy, lotus, vase, fish and endless knot) as used singly or together in Chinese and Tibetan rugs; Hawley names the conch, wheel of law and two fishes as Buddhist emblems in Chinese rugs.
The Palace Museum describes a Tibetan tribute hanging woven with a monk and the eight treasures (八宝).
Stone defines bogu as a Chinese rug motif of bronze, jade or porcelain vessels and other antiques; Leitch says the hundred antiques can be seen in the borders, corners and medallion of a Peking rug.
Leitch says the corners of some Chinese rug fields carry the swastika or the endless knot.
Stone says crossed dorjes are sometimes shown in Tibetan rugs.

images.caption: an endless knot tied with ribbons, in a corner of the field
images.title: Carpet
images.credit: Minneapolis Institute of Art, The John R. Van Derlip Fund
images.licence: Public domain (Minneapolis Institute of Art)

rows.name: Tiger stripe
rows.description: The field woven as a tiger's skin: wavy dark stripes on orange, sometimes with the outline of the head, legs and tail.
rows.what_it_tells: A Tibetan design (tiger rugs), also in Nepalese-Tibetan production.
rows.cautions: Old Tibetan tiger rugs are scarce and widely copied.

facts.text: Stone describes tiger rugs as a large group of Tibetan rugs woven in imitation of tiger skins.

rows.drawing_note: No clear open-licence museum photo was found in the Met, AIC, Cleveland and Mia records checked, and no model photo for a drawing was identified.

rows.name: Checkerboard
rows.description: Squares of two or more colors alternating like a checkerboard, filling a field or a narrow border.
rows.what_it_tells: A checkerboard field is typical of Tibetan (Wangden) rugs; check borders are common minor borders on Kazak and Kurdish rugs, and Lewis found checkerboards mainly in Bergama and Yomud rugs.

facts.text: Lewis says the checkerboard arrangement is seldom found in any rugs except Bergama and Yomud; Stone calls the check border a very common minor border, especially in Kazak and Kurdish rugs.

rows.drawing_note: No clear open-licence museum photo was found in the Met, AIC, Cleveland and Mia records checked, and no model photo for a drawing was identified.

rows.name: Kufesque border
rows.literal: Kufesque: 'like Kufic', the angular early Arabic script.
rows.description: A border of tall, angular, letter-like uprights joined at the base, sometimes knotted or interlaced, that imitates (without spelling) angular Arabic script. In Caucasian rugs the same idea survives as a white border of stiff angular figures.
rows.what_it_tells: Found in 15th–17th-century Anatolian 'Holbein' and 'Lotto' carpets and in 19th-century Caucasian rugs of Kuba, Konaghend, Perepedil and Shirvan; also in some North African rugs.
rows.cautions: Whether these borders really derive from the word 'Allah' or lam-alif is disputed.

facts.text: Stone says kufesque borders are thought to derive from Arabic script with elongated angular letters, illustrated from Holbein, Kuba and Lotto rugs.
Stone says Konaghend rugs often have an all-over honeycomb within kufesque borders, and Perepedil rugs often a kufesque border.

images.caption: a section of the white main border of angular, letter-like figures on a dark ground
images.title: Kufesque-Border Lattice Shirvan Rug
images.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, The James F. Ballard Collection, Gift of James F. Ballard, 1922
images.licence: Public domain (The Met Open Access, CC0)

images.caption: the narrow interlaced border of a small-pattern Holbein carpet
images.title: 'Holbein' Carpet
images.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift from the Collection of Hillary Black Dumas and Dr. D. Gilbert Dumas, 2009
images.licence: Public domain (The Met Open Access, CC0)

rows.name: Turtle (samovar) border
rows.description: A main border of large palmettes alternating with smaller flowers on curling stems; the big palmettes are simplified into rounded, segmented shapes that look like a turtle's shell.
rows.what_it_tells: Typical of Farahan, Sarouk, Mushkabad, Serapi and Heriz rugs, very often with a herati field. It points to northwest and central Persia.
rows.cautions: Hawley's 'turtle stands for constancy' is a symbolic gloss.

facts.text: Stone describes the turtle or samovar border as a palmette border used in Sarouks and other rugs, in which the large palmettes suggest a turtle shell, often with the herati field.
Hawley and Lewis both relate the turtle border to the Herati border; Hawley thought it derived from interlacing arabesques.

rows.drawing_note: No open museum photo of a Farahan or Heriz border was found at usable resolution.

rows.name: Wine-glass (leaf and calyx) border
rows.description: Diagonal serrated leaves alternating with a geometric cup or goblet shape (a stylized calyx) along the main border.
rows.what_it_tells: A Caucasian border, especially common on Shirvan and Kazak rugs; also on some Anatolian rugs (Ezine). It points to the Caucasus or rugs made in Caucasian style.
rows.cautions: Contemporary Turkish rugs in Caucasian designs copy this border.

facts.text: Stone describes the leaf and calyx (leaf and goblet, wineglass) border as diagonal serrated leaves alternating with a geometric calyx suggesting a goblet, used in Caucasian rugs, especially of the Kazak region.
Hawley says the serrated leaf and wine cup border is found only in Caucasian and old Armenian rugs and in about half of Shirvans.

images.caption: the red main border: diagonal serrated leaves alternating with goblet-like shapes
images.title: Prayer Rug
images.credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Gift of Mrs. John H. Walsh
images.licence: CC0 (The Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)

rows.name: Reciprocal trefoil (laleh abbasi)
rows.literal: Madakhel: 'doorways' (Iranica; Stone medahil). laleh abbasi: 'Abbasi tulip'.
rows.description: A narrow guard stripe of two interlocking rows of three-lobed (trefoil) shapes, one row pointing in, the other out, in two contrasting colors; extreme versions are rows of triangles each topped by a small diamond.
rows.what_it_tells: Very common in Caucasian guard stripes (Hawley and Lewis especially Karabagh) and in Persian rugs; rarer in other groups. On its own it points to the Caucasus or Persia.

facts.text: Iranica describes the reciprocal-trefoil (madakhel, 'doorways') pattern, common on borders, as two interlocking systems of stylized trefoils; Stone gives laleh abbasi and medahil ('doorways') for the same reciprocating trefoil.

Hawley calls the reciprocal trefoil very usual in Caucasian and Persian rugs, often in Indian and Baluch rugs, and rare in other groups; Lewis says it is found in rugs of nearly all classes, especially Caucasian, most often Karabagh.

says.text: Probably a conventionalized lily or three-leaf spray.
A tulip calyx (lâle in Turkish), from curvilinear to extreme geometric versions.

rows.drawing_note: No clear open-licence museum photo was found in the Met, AIC, Cleveland and Mia records checked, and no model photo for a drawing was identified.

rows.name: Running dog (wave) border
rows.description: A border of repeated wave shapes, each curling over into the next like a breaking wave (a Vitruvian scroll); angular versions turn into a hooked key or 'Greek key'.
rows.what_it_tells: Especially associated with Seichur rugs of the Kuba region, where it is often drawn in blue; also on Shahsavan and other Caucasian and Persian tribal pieces.

facts.text: Stone describes the running dog (Seishour) border as repeated wave shapes like a Vitruvian scroll, geometric versions of which may be called Greek key, frequently used in Seishour rugs in shades of blue.

images.caption: a narrow border of repeated hooked wave shapes (small museum photo)
images.title: Shahsevan Saddle Bag Face
images.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift of Inger G. and William B. Ginsberg, 2018
images.licence: Public domain (The Met Open Access, CC0)

rows.name: Chichi border

native.translit: a Kuba composition name in the Azerbaijan National Carpet Museum

rows.description: A main border in which large rosettes alternate with groups of diagonal bars, set on a dark ground.
rows.what_it_tells: The mark of Chichi rugs of the Kuba region; it points to northeast Caucasian (Kuba) weaving.

facts.text: Stone says the distinctive Chichi border consists of diagonal bars alternating with large blossoms; Lewis describes the Chichi border as an eight-petaled flower set on the alternate steps of a Greek meander, seldom found outside Tchetchen rugs.
The Azerbaijan National Carpet Museum catalogs Kuba carpets under the composition name Sırt Çiçi.

disagreements.about: what the Chichi border looks like

says.text: Diagonal bars alternating with large blossoms.
An eight-petaled flower on the alternate steps of the Greek meander.

rows.drawing_note: No open museum photo of a Chichi border was found.

rows.name: Barber-pole stripe
rows.description: A narrow border or edge binding of short diagonal stripes in alternating colors, like a barber's pole.
rows.what_it_tells: Found in rugs of nearly all classes; used in Caucasian, Persian tribal (Shiraz, Neyriz) and Turkmen weaving, in borders and on overcast edges.
rows.cautions: An overcast edge wrapped in alternating colors gives the same effect; that is a finish, not a woven border.

facts.text: Stone defines the barberpole as diagonal stripes, sometimes in the field but more often in borders and selvages, and also a selvage overcast to produce diagonal stripes.
Hawley describes sides overcast in a barber-pole stripe on Shiraz rugs, and says barber-pole stripes are characteristic of the borders of Niris (Neyriz) rugs.

images.caption: a narrow band of diagonal bars in alternating colors, some holding small hooks (small museum photo)
images.title: Shahsevan Saddle Bag Face
images.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift of Inger G. and William B. Ginsberg, 2018
images.licence: Public domain (The Met Open Access, CC0)

rows.name: Cartouche
rows.literal: Ghabi: 'framed, in frames'.
rows.description: An elongated frame with rounded, cut or lobed ends, used in borders (alternating with rosettes or other shapes) or overlapping across the field; cartouches often hold inscriptions.
rows.what_it_tells: Found in classical Persian carpets (the Ardabil border), Tabriz and Kashmar workshop rugs with inscribed cartouches, Mamluk borders and 'Transylvanian' Anatolian rugs. Inscribed cartouches are where to look for verses, names and dates.

facts.text: Iranica defines the cartouche as an elongated ogival compartment, repeated or alternating in borders as in the Ardabil carpet, and says inscriptions are generally framed in cartouches; Stone defines it as an enclosed area, often with an inscription, with a rectangular outline and rounded, cut or scalloped corners.
Qabi (framed) designs form one of the Iran Carpet Company's nineteen groups and one of Egharloo and Zavieh's seven families.
The Met titles its 17th-century carpet 56.185.1 'Vase-technique Carpet with Overlapping Cartouches'.

guls.title: Turkmen guls: which tribes wove them, on what, and how to tell them apart

rows.name: Tekke gul
rows.meaning: No agreed meaning. Moshkova (1946) recorded the weavers' names for its parts: kush 'bird', dunguz burun 'pig's snout', chakkan 'one that bites or stings', kovacha 'cotton boll', and read the gul as a plant with birds or animals at its sides. The Turkmen state book offers several readings without choosing: red poppies and tulips of the Kopet Dagh foothills, an oasis with herds at water, the four seasons, an all-seeing eye.
rows.shape: An octagon with stepped (indented) sides, usually a little wider than tall, divided into quarters; opposite quarters share a color, so the coloring runs on the diagonal. Small hooked figures (the 'birds' or 'feathers') sit in the quarters around a small central star, diamond or hexagon. On main carpets the guls stand in straight rows on a grid of thin dark lines that run through their centers; smaller cross-shaped or diamond minor guls sit between them.

tribes.note: Moshkova: the Ali-Eli, living among the Tekke, weave Tekke designs, as do the Nokhurli near Bakharden.

formats: later also rugs of every size in 20th-century state production and in Pakistani and Afghan copies
rows.period_note: Moshkova (1946): until recently Tekke weavers kept the large Tekke gul for the main carpet alone and did not put it on bags or other small pieces. In the 20th century it became the standard design of Soviet and present-day Turkmen production and of Pakistani 'Bokhara' rugs.
rows.minor_guls_note: Lewis (1920): rows of octagons alternate with rows of diamond forms. Berdimuhamedov (2011) names the cross-shaped 'ak bashly chemche gyol', the openwork 'gurbaga' and the 'chakmak' and 'dyrnak' guls as the in-between figures. The Rijksmuseum labels the cross-shaped figures on a Tekke rug (BK-1975-268) 'so-called chemche guls'.

facts.text: Hawley describes the commoner 'Royal Bokhara' pattern as an octagon around a quartered hexagon, with one pair of opposite quarters white or cream and the other red; in large rugs the centers of the octagons are joined by straight dark blue lines.
facts.quote: In large rugs the centres of the octagons are generally joined by straight lines of dark blue colour.

facts.text: Lewis describes Tekke rugs as rows of elongated, quartered octagons alternating with rows of diamond forms, with straight lines connecting the octagons' centers.
facts.quote: Elongated octagon forms arranged in rows alternating with rows of diamond forms with straight lines connecting the centres of the octagon

facts.text: The Ballard catalogue describes a 'Bokhara' rug with four rows of medallions connected by heavy blue vertical and horizontal lines through their centers, dividing each medallion into quarters.
facts.quote: connected by heavy blue vertical and horizontal lines running through their centres, dividing each medallion into quarters

facts.text: The Turkmen state book says a grid of thin dark lines dividing the field into rectangles, each holding a gul, is a characteristic mark of Tekke carpets, while on Merv (Salor) carpets the guls lie on an undivided field.
Moshkova says the Tekke kept their large tribal gul for the main carpet only; Tekke weavers told her it could not be used on everyday small pieces.
Moshkova recorded the Tekke weavers' names for elements of the Tekke gul: kush (bird), dunguz burun (pig's snout), chakkan (one that bites or stings) and kovacha (cotton boll).
Stone defines the traditional Tekke gul as an indented octagon.
The Turkmen state book calls the Tekke gul the main ornament and mark of Tekke carpets.

says.text: Groups the Merv Tekke and part of the Akhal Tekke with the Salor and Saryk in one 'Salor' ornament group: the Salor rose stayed the basic element of Saryk and most Tekke (especially Merv) ornament, and the Akhal Tekke version was changed for the worse under Yomut influence.
The Tekke gul is the Tekke's own tribal gol, one of the 'living' guls kept on the main carpet.
The teke-gyol is close to the salor-gyol in form and filling: the Salor gul is the archetype of the Salor (Soinkhan) confederation and the Saryk, Ersari and Tekke guls branched from it.
A central plant motif flanked by birds or animals; the 'birds' look more like plant parts in later versions.
Poppies and tulips, an oasis with herds, the four seasons or an all-seeing eye; the book leaves the choice open.
On guls generally: a flower (the Persian sense of gul), totemic animal designs, or Chinese cloud collars and early silk roundels have all been proposed.

rows.name: Salor main-carpet gul
other_names: Rose of Salor (old books; also used for the turret gul)
rows.shape: A large rosette close to a circle with a scalloped (many-lobed) outline, divided on two axes into quarters colored on the diagonal, with a complex filling. Tsareva sees long-necked birds at the ends of the vertical axis and short-necked ones at the horizontal axis. Clusters of small clover-leaf figures fill the quarters; on the Met's Salor main carpet small H-shaped figures sit near the center.

tribes.note: Cleveland: the gul with three clover-leaf devices in each quarter was a Salor hallmark 'often copied by other Turkmen tribes', here on a Saryk carpet.
Moshkova and Bogolyubov say the Merv Tekke took over Salor ornament; Cole (dealer text) says the Salor main-carpet gul itself was not regularly copied by other tribes, only the Salor chuval guls.

rows.period_note: Museum examples are dated late 18th to early 19th century (Met 1974.149.46). Moshkova says the Salor stopped weaving carpets after their defeat on the date.
minor_guls_with_it: small octagonal minor gul (Met 1974.149.46; unnamed in the record)
stepped octagon minor gul copied by the Saryk (Cleveland 2006.201)

facts.text: Tsareva describes the Salor gul as a scalloped rosette close to a circle, with a cross-shaped two-axis structure, complex filling and diagonal coloring, and calls it the archetype for main carpets of all tribes of the Salor confederation.
The Cleveland Museum of Art says the main gul with three clover-leaf devices in each quarter was a hallmark of the Salor and was often copied by other Turkmen tribes.
Iranica describes old Salor pieces as having asymmetric knots open to the left on closely packed warps lying on two levels.

Stone reports that some scholars accept only the 'S group' (asymmetric knots open left, highly offset warps, long pile, bluish-red or pink silk highlights, rust to brick red overall) as Salor work, and attribute Salor-gul pieces without these features to the Tekke or Saryk after the Salor defeat.

disagreements.about: date the Salor stopped weaving / were defeated

says.text: At the end of the 18th century the Salor lived in the Yolatan and Pende oases; pressed by the Saryk, most left in 1780 for the Hari Rud and Sarakhs, handed their art to the Saryk and almost stopped weaving carpets.
About 1830 a quarter of the Tekke moved east and captured Merv.
The Salor held Merv until defeated by the Tekke and Persians in the 1830s.
The Salor were routed by the Tekke and Saryk at the end of the 19th century and gave up carpet weaving.
Dealer text: defeat by the Tekke about 1842.
Weavings with the S-group features were attributed to the Salor; the exclusive attribution is questioned.
Old Salor pieces are characterized by asymmetric knots open to the left on warps on two levels (stated as a characteristic, without the dispute).

disagreements.about: which Salor gul passed to other tribes

says.text: The famous Salor gol passed to the Saryk, who reproduced it in modernized form on chuvals under the old name; its use on Saryk and Merv Tekke carpets dates from the colonial period and reflects Russian buyers' demand.
Dealer text: what passed to the Saryk were the Salor chuval guls; the Salor main-carpet gul was not regularly used by any other tribe.
The Salor main gul with clover-leaf devices was often copied by other Turkmen tribes (shown on a Saryk main carpet).

images.caption: One main gul: a round, many-lobed outline, quartered with diagonal coloring; clusters of small round (clover-leaf) figures and small H-shaped figures in the quarters.
images.title: Salor Main Carpet
images.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Bequest of Joseph V. McMullan, 1973
images.licence: Public domain (The Met Open Access, CC0)

rows.name: Turret gul (Salor chuval gul)
rows.shape: An octagon whose frame carries a row of small turret- or tooth-like points (Berdimuhamedov: small triangular 'pyramids' topped by a stylized ram's head, giving a saw-toothed edge), with ram's-horn hooks inside and a stepped cross or star at the center. Usually two or three rows of them on a chuval face.

tribes.note: Rijksmuseum BK-1975-315 is labeled a Tekke chuval with this kind of gul; Bogolyubov says the Merv Tekke use Salor ornament.
Moshkova: the Kizil Ayak use a 'mar-gol' borrowed from the Merv Saryk or Salor.

formats: main carpet (later Saryk and Merv Tekke work)
rows.period_note: In early rug literature this gul was tied to the Salor; in Afghanistan the Saryk weave 'Sariq Mauri' rugs with it. Moshkova: its use on Saryk and Merv Tekke carpets belongs to the colonial (Russian) period.
minor_guls_with_it: quartered cross-shaped minor figures (Rijksmuseum BK-1975-314 and -315)

facts.text: Stone describes the turret gul as an octagon with projections around the perimeter, used by the Salor, Sariq, Ersari and Kizil Ayak, tied to the Salor in early literature and sometimes called the 'Rose of Salor'.
The Rijksmuseum describes BK-1975-314, a chuval face with octagonal turret-framed guls, as a Salor chuval (weaver: Salor people, southern Turkestan, 1800–1900).
Moshkova says the Salor gol was transferred to chuvals and that the Saryk reproduced it on chuvals in a modernized form under its old name.
Bogolyubov says the Salor rose remained the basic element of the ornament used by the Saryk and by most Tekke, especially those of Merv.
facts.quote: Das Muster der Rose von Salor ist dessenungeachtet das Grundelement der Ornamentik geblieben (the Salor rose pattern nonetheless remained the basic element of the ornament)

facts.text: The Turkmen state book says the Salyr gul with its saw-toothed edge spread in slightly changed form to carpets of all Turkmen regions and influenced Tekke patterns, so it is sometimes hard to attribute.

says.text: 'Salor gul' = the turret gul.
The salor-gyol of Salor main carpets is a scalloped, near-circular rosette (a different shape).
Dealer text: distinguishes the Salor main-carpet gol from the Salor chuval gols.

images.caption: The middle gul of the chuval face: an octagon with a row of turret-like points along its inner frame, ram's-horn hooks inside, and a stepped cross at the center.
images.title: Tentzakvoorblad (tent bag face); museum description: 'Salor Chuval'
images.credit: Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam, BK-1975-314
images.licence: Public domain (Rijksmuseum)

images.caption: One gul of a Salor chuval face: an octagon with a row of turret-like points along its inner frame, small ram's-horn hooks inside, an outer ring of hooked projections, and a stepped cross at the center; parts of the cross-shaped minor figures (small squares with stars) at the corners.

rows.name: Saryk gul
rows.shape: A stepped octagon with a central hexagon. On the oldest known Saryk bag face (Cleveland 2008.223) the guls are divided into quarters and alternate with angular minor guls in staggered rows. Moshkova saw a single bird figure in it, a step between the Tekke gul and the old Yomut gul.
rows.period_note: From the beginning of the 20th century the Saryk used their tribal pattern widely on chuvals. Stone: late pieces (after 1880) have a purple-brown, brown or purple field; earlier pieces crimson with cotton and silk highlights; the earliest all wool with an orange-tan field.
minor_guls_with_it: angular minor guls in staggered rows (Cleveland 2008.223)

facts.text: The most common Sariq gul is a stepped octagon with a central hexagon.

Cleveland describes 2008.223 as the oldest known weaving of the Saryk tribe, with main guls subdivided in quadrants alternating with angular minor guls in staggered rows, and white cotton and magenta silk highlights.
Moshkova counts the Saryk among the tribes that kept their tribal gul, and says the Saryk used their tribal pattern widely on chuvals from the beginning of the 20th century.

images.caption: One gul from a bag face: a stepped octagonal outline split down the middle, a central octagon, and white triangles in the quarters.
images.title: Turkmen Bag Face
images.credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Gift of Arlene C. Cooper
images.licence: CC0 (The Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)

rows.name: Temirchin gul
rows.meaning: Stone gives 'onurga' as another name. Cole's captions (dealer text) report that Tsareva reads one element as a fish.
rows.shape: An octagon with a row of fish-like elements in each quarter (Stone: four overlapping 'angelfish' shapes per quarter) and a rectangular central medallion.

tribes.note: Stone: in early Sariq main carpets; Cole (dealer text): a Saryk gul.
Moshkova lists it as an Ersari tribal gul; the Turkmen state book lists it among Ersari ornaments; Stone: also in some old Ersari carpets.

rows.period_note: Early Sariq main carpets and some old Ersari carpets.

facts.text: Stone describes the temirchin (temerchin) gul as an octagonal gul of early Sariq main carpets and some old Ersari carpets, with four overlapping angelfish-like shapes in each quarter.
Moshkova names the gulli gol and the temirdzhin gol as the Ersari tribal guls, each known in several variants.
The Turkmen state book lists bash-ai, gulli-gyol, beshir-gyol and temirdzhik-gyol among Ersari ornaments.

says.text: An Ersari tribal gul.
An Ersari ornament ('темирджик-гёль').
In early Sariq main carpets and some old Ersari carpets.
Dealer text: a Saryk gul; Moshkova 'curiously' calls it Ersari.

rows.drawing_note: A facsimile candidate from Bogolyubov Plate XXVIII is listed, but the gul-name match is uncertain; a drawing should wait for a source that names the gul on a photographed piece.

rows.name: Gulli gul
rows.meaning: In the Ersari gul the side figures have become trefoils and the weavers call them gul, 'flower'. Stone: 'elephant's foot' (fil-pai) is also a loose name for any octagonal Turkmen gul.
rows.shape: A large octagon, quartered, each quarter holding a clover-leaf (trefoil) figure; many variants. Bogolyubov (Plate xxvi, Char Vilayet): five parts, an inner part in the field color and four outer parts alternately dark green and light brick red with clover leaves and stars. On Ersari and Afghan carpets usually three upright rows of large octagons almost touching, with small diamonds between.

tribes.note: Cleveland 2006.201: a Saryk main carpet with the Salor-type gul with clover-leaf devices.

rows.period_note: Ersari tribal guls appear only on large carpets, never on small pieces. Large octagon guls of this family are the standard design of 20th-century Afghan Ersari carpets ('Afghan', Daulatabad).
minor_guls_with_it: small diamonds or clusters of eight-pointed stars, some fringed with hooks (Hawley, 'Afghans')
gaz ayak 'goose' figure (Tsareva: an intermediate motif of the Ersari group)

facts.text: The gulli gul is associated with the Ersari, Salor and Saryq; each quarter contains a clover-leaf motif, and there are many variations.
Moshkova names the gulli gol as an Ersari tribal gul and says Ersari tribal guls never appear on small pieces, only on main carpets.
Bogolyubov says the octagonal Ersari 'rose' is larger and simpler than the Salor and Yomud roses and is laid out symmetrically on a one-color field ranging from dark red to yellow.
facts.quote: Die achteckigen, ersarischen Rosen sind im Gegensatze zu den beiden vorhergehenden größer und einfacher (the octagonal Ersari roses are larger and simpler than the two preceding)

facts.text: Hawley describes the traditional pattern of the 'Afghan' class as upright rows, usually three, of large octagons almost touching, with much smaller diamond designs between.
facts.quote: perpendicular rows, usually three in number, of large octagons, that are almost in contact

facts.text: Tsareva lists the Ersari gulli-gyol among the guls that kept bird motifs and served as tribal emblems on main carpets.

says.text: An Ersari tribal gul.
Associated with the Ersari, Salor and Saryq.
The gul with three clover-leaf devices in each quadrant was a Salor hallmark copied by other tribes.

images.caption: One main gul: lobed outline, quartered, with clover-leaf clusters in the quarters. The museum's text calls this gul a Salor hallmark copied by other tribes.
images.title: Turkmen Main Carpet
images.credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Gift of Arlene C. Cooper
images.licence: CC0 (The Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)

images.title: Oosters tapijt; museum description: 'Ersari-tapijt, achthoekenkleed' (octagon carpet)
images.credit: Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam, BK-18095
