rows.name: Keyik gul
rows.meaning: The Turkmen state book says some art historians see a priestly sign combined with horsemen and banners in the Ersari gul; over time the horsemen came to be read as gazelles (keyik), hence the name.
rows.shape: Not described in detail; the book speaks of an octagonal Ersari medallion with large light details in yellow-gold and red-terracotta on an indigo ground set against the field color.

facts.text: The Turkmen state book names the Ersari medallion gul 'keyik gyol' (gazelle gul) and lists other Ersari ornaments: bash-ai, gulli-gyol, beshir-gyol and temirdzhik-gyol.

rows.note: Which Western-named gul this is (gulli gul or another) is not stated; kept separate until a second source ties them.

rows.name: Kepse gul
rows.meaning: Stone glosses kepse as Turkish 'sheaf' (single source).
rows.shape: A complex gul: a horizontal lozenge made of upright bands with an octagonal element in the middle, set in diagonal rows on Yomut main carpets (Stone; thought to derive from a serrated-leaf gul).
formats: torba and chuval (later, by Moshkova's account)
rows.period_note: Kepse and dyrnak guls appear on newly made torbas but not on old ones. Cole (dealer text): old chuvals and torbas with the kepse gul are rare but known.

facts.text: Moshkova names the kepse gol and the dyrnak gol as the basic tribal guls of the Yomut.
Stone describes the kepse gul as a horizontal lozenge of vertical bands with an octagonal element in the middle, woven in diagonal rows on Yomut main carpets.

says.text: Found on bags (torbas) of recent manufacture, not on old bags.
Dealer text: old chuvals and torbas with the kepse gul are rare but not unknown.

rows.drawing_note: No open-licence photograph that clearly shows a kepse gul was identified with confidence. Met 1974.149.45 (Yomut Main Carpet, TP364) has octagons with comb-like outlines in horizontal rows that may be relevant; not matched to the kepse description with enough confidence to crop.

rows.name: Dyrnak gul
rows.meaning: 'Claws, clawed'; 'bird's claw'; Turkish 'claw'. Tsareva suggests that some dyrnak-type diamonds are no-longer-recognizable two-headed eagles.
rows.shape: A diamond, quartered, whose edges carry rows of hooks like the teeth of a comb (Stone: external and internal hooks; Tsareva: rhomboid motifs outlined with hook-shaped figures).
rows.period_note: On newly made torbas, not on old ones.

facts.text: The dyrnak (Turk. 'claw') gul is a quartered diamond with external and internal hooks, used in Yomud, Chaudor, Chub Bash and Ersari weavings.
The Turkmen state book says the dyrnak-gyol ('bird's claw') and anchor-like symbols prevail in the field of Yomut carpets.

disagreements.about: role: main gul or in-between figure

says.text: A basic tribal gol of the Yomut, on main carpets.
In one passage, an in-between ('second violin') ornament alongside the chakmak gyol.
Speaks of rhomboid in-between figures 'of the dyrnak type'.

images.caption: One diamond gul in a diagonal row, with rows of white comb-like hooks along two of its edges.

rows.name: Tauk noska gul
rows.meaning: The Arabachi call it tauk nuska, 'figure of a hen'; Stone: Turkish 'chicken design gul'. Tsareva (in a note) prefers tavak, Persian-Tajik 'dish', the Central Asian word for round rosettes and medallions.
rows.shape: An octagon divided into quarters, each holding a pair of small animals; in early versions the animal has two heads. Without its bird-like upper heads the figure reads as the letter H, and the H form spread widely.

tribes.note: Moshkova: the Arabachi regard it as their tribal gul; carpets with it survive in the Denau district of Chardzhou, where the Arabachi kept their identity best.
Moshkova: borrowed by the Chodor from the Arabachi, replacing the ertmen on their carpets.
Stone: the major gul of the Kizil Ayak. Bogolyubov's Kizil Ayak carpet (Plate XXVII) has quartered octagons with stylized animals like two joined heads, which fits but is not named.

rows.period_note: Moshkova dates the Arabachi carpet she studied to about 100 years before 1946 by its border and composition; Stone reports an origin proposed in 11th-century Luristan.
minor_guls_with_it: erre gul on a Chodor main carpet (Cole, dealer text)

facts.text: The tauk noska gul is used by the Kizilayak, Ersari, Arabachi, Yomut and Chodor and contains two small animals in each quadrant; in early versions the animal has two heads.
Moshkova says the Arabachi regard the tauk nuska as their tribal gul and that the Chodor borrowed it from them, where it replaced the Chodor's own ertmen on carpets.
Bogolyubov describes Kizil Ayak carpets with octagonal guls in regular rows, each split into four fields holding stylized animals that can be read as two joined heads.

says.text: 'Figure of a hen'.
'Chicken design gul'.
More correctly tavak, 'dish', the Central Asian name for round rosettes.
The H form spread widely; the bird heads are the older form preserved in some carpets.
Dealer text: the H form without animal heads is a later version; tauk noska elements also sit in the Salor main-carpet gul.
Its origin has been assigned to 11th-century Luristan.
A tribal emblem of the Arabachi, whose bird form links it to Oghuz bird totems.

images.caption: One octagonal gul, quartered, with two small H-shaped hooked figures in each quarter around a central panel.
images.title: Yamut Carpet with Octagonal Guls
images.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, The James F. Ballard Collection, Gift of James F. Ballard, 1922
images.licence: Public domain (The Met Open Access, CC0)

rows.name: C gul
rows.shape: An octagonal or stepped-diamond gul with C-shapes or crescents inside, some facing left and some right.

tribes.note: The Cleveland Yomud main carpet 2010.190 shows guls matching the description; the museum does not name the type.

rows.period_note: Cleveland 2010.190 is dated to the mid-1850s.
minor_guls_with_it: small barred cross figures between the guls (Cleveland 2010.190)

facts.text: The 'C' gul is a Turkmen octagon gul with C-shapes or crescents facing both left and right, found in Yomud rugs.

images.caption: One gul: a stepped, hooked diamond outlined in white, quartered, with small C-shaped (crescent) figures facing left and right in the quarters.
images.title: Turkmen Main Carpet
images.credit: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Gift of E.B. and Joan C. Long
images.licence: CC0 (The Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)

rows.name: Ertmen gul
other_names: Kushly (Amu Darya Chodor name for the composition)
rows.meaning: A plant flanked by two birds; the Chodor could no longer name its parts, but Chodor on the Amu Darya call the composition kushly, 'with birds'. The Turkmen state book reports a folk reading as the houses of bride and groom.
rows.shape: A stepped diamond standing upright, with curled ram's-horn projections at its top and bottom corners and a single vertical axis; flat (not diagonal) coloring; inside, pairs of long-tailed birds or bird-and-plant figures on either side of the axis. Unlike most Turkmen guls, which are wider than tall, it is oriented vertically.

tribes.note: Stone: 'possibly' the Yomud.
Dealer text: an Ersari interpretation from the middle Amu Darya.

rows.period_note: The ertmen deformed within 20–30 years and stopped being woven on Chodor carpets, replaced by the tauk noska; it survived on chuvals and torbas, where weavers still called it the Chodor tribal gul. Tsareva illustrates a Chodor main carpet with it dated to the early 19th century and says it was also used on chuvals by tribes close to the Esen-khan confederation.

facts.text: The ertmen (Chodor) gul is a stepped diamond with ram's-horn projections at its upper and lower corners and a vertical axis.
Moshkova says the Chodor's own ertmen gul went out of use on their carpets, replaced by the tauk noska borrowed from the Arabachi, and survived on chuvals and torbas.
Moshkova says the Chodor supplied carpets to the markets of the Khiva and partly the Bukhara khanates, and that this commercial role changed their ornament.

says.text: Long gone from Chodor carpets; preserved on small items (chuval, torba).
Shows it on an early 19th-century Chodor main carpet and says Esen-khan-group tribes used it on chuvals.
Dealer text: shows it on a 19th-century Chodor main carpet; doubts Moshkova's view that its use on torbas and trappings is degenerate.

rows.drawing_note: Superseded: a facsimile from Bogolyubov's plates is now listed (status 'facsimile').

images.caption: One white gul of a Chodor carpet: an upright stepped hexagon or diamond with a curled, horn-like projection at its top and bottom points, flat (not diagonal) coloring, filled with small stepped figures; no bird figures can be seen.
images.holder: Bogolyubov, Tapis de l'Asie Centrale (1908), Qatar National Library copy

rows.name: Eagle gul
rows.meaning: Tsareva reads its outline as schematized eagles with spread wings. Stone reports it is thought to be a stylized floral palmette.
rows.shape: A hexagon within a border of spikes and rams' horns, not quartered. Tsareva: an outline of schematized eagles with spread wings.

tribes.note: Stone: possibly Yomud; Bogolyubov describes a Yomud carpet whose large guls look like raised eagle wings.

rows.period_note: Tsareva cites radiocarbon ranges for an Imreli main carpet with igl-gyol (1655–1824 at 68.1 percent, or 1827–1887).

facts.text: The eagle gul is thought to be used by the Göklan and possibly the Yomud and is no longer associated with the Imreli; it is a hexagon in a border of spikes and rams' horns, not quartered.

says.text: The Imreli created the 'igl' composition; igl-gyols are a tribal marker of Imreli main carpets.
No longer associated with the Imreli; the Imreli attribution (first made in 1980) was never supported and is questionable; Göklan and possibly Yomud.

rows.drawing_note: Superseded: a facsimile from Bogolyubov's plates is now listed (status 'facsimile').

images.caption: One large gul of an old Yomud carpet: a small hexagonal center inside a stepped medallion edged all round with spiky, feather-like projections and hooks; not quartered.
images.holder: Bogolyubov, Tapis de l'Asie Centrale (1908), Qatar National Library copy
images.title: Quart de vieux tapis iomoude, au 1/3 de sa grandeur
images.credit: Bogolyubov, Tapis de l’Asie Centrale (1908), plate Plate XIII; Qatar National Library copy
images.licence: Public domain (1908)

images.caption: One large gul of a small Yomud carpet: a hexagonal center with a small diamond, inside a green medallion with a jagged, spiky outline of hooks.
images.holder: Bogolyubov, Tapis de l'Asie Centrale (1908), Qatar National Library copy

rows.name: Gushly gul
rows.meaning: Gush, 'bird'.
rows.shape: Large eight-sided medallions with stepped outline, a little wider than tall, holding an octagon edged by small triangles on stalks like bird tracks, with a small horizontal diamond at the center and diagonally colored parts.

tribes.note: The book places it in the Tekke group.

rows.period_note: The Turkmen state book says the 193 m2 giant carpet 'Türkmen kalby' woven in 1941–42 has a red field with gushly-gyol.

facts.text: The Turkmen state book places the 'gush' or 'gushly-gyol' in the Tekke group: large stepped eight-sided medallions with bird-track triangles around an inner octagon.

rows.note: No Western source read names this gul; it may be a Tekke gul variant under a Turkmen name.

rows.name: Yomut gul with anchor figures
rows.shape: An octagon (often with a zigzag or stepped center) with small anchor- or arrow-shaped figures around it (Met 22.100.47) or inside it, set in offset rows.

tribes.note: Met 22.100.47 'Yomut Main Carpet' shows this layout.
Bogolyubov's old Ogurjali carpet from Cheleken has diamond guls decorated with arrows and anchors.

rows.period_note: Met 22.100.47 is dated probably mid-19th century.

facts.text: Anchor-like figures are typical of the field of Yomut carpets: Bogolyubov saw stylized anchors inside small Yomud guls and arrows and anchors in Ogurjali guls; the Turkmen state book says anchor-like symbols prevail in Yomut fields.

images.caption: One octagonal gul with a zigzag center, ringed by small anchor- or arrow-shaped figures.
images.title: Yomut Main Carpet
images.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, The James F. Ballard Collection, Gift of James F. Ballard, 1922
images.licence: Public domain (The Met Open Access, CC0)

rows.name: Chuval gul
rows.shape: Guls of bag faces, smaller than main-carpet guls, often two or three rows of three. Moshkova's old Yomut chuval gul has no 'birds' and sharp geometric angles; the Rijksmuseum's Ersari chuval bk-1975-316 has stepped, quartered guls with hooked projections at top and bottom.

tribes.note: Dealer text: the gul Moshkova tied only to the Yomud is also used on Kizil Ayak chuvals.
Rijksmuseum BK-1975-316, an Ersari chuval with stepped quartered guls.

tribes.tribe: all Central Asian Turkmen and Karakalpak (small chuval guls)

formats: also as in-between figures on main carpets (Tsareva)
rows.period_note: Moshkova's 'dead gul': once a Yomut tribal gul, by the 1940s used on chuvals only and seen as ornament.

facts.text: Moshkova says the old Yomut gol, now used only in the field of chuvals, is called chuval gyul rather than gol and is used alongside purely ornamental patterns.
Tsareva calls 'small chuval guls' a group of small guls common to all Turkmen, used on wall bags and as in-between motifs in gul layouts, and also used by the Karakalpak and by Anatolian weavers.
Moshkova says that in the chuvals of her day one finds tribal guls that had gradually lost their tribal meaning.

says.text: A Yomut gul.
Dealer text: also Kizil Ayak; possibly derived from Tekke chuval guls.

images.caption: The middle gul of the chuval face: a lobed outline, quartered with diagonal coloring, white and red hooked figures in the quarters.
images.title: Storage Bag (Chuval) Face
images.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, The James F. Ballard Collection, Gift of James F. Ballard, 1922
images.licence: Public domain (The Met Open Access, CC0)

images.caption: One chuval gul: a stepped, quartered gul with hooked projections at top and bottom and small crosses in the quarters. Photograph turned 90 degrees.
images.title: Tentzakvoorblad (large tent bag face, chuval)
images.credit: Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam, BK-1975-316
images.licence: Public domain (Rijksmuseum)

rows.name: Erre gul
rows.shape: An indented rectangle with a flower at the center and crosses at top and bottom, with arrowheads pointing in at the sides; in a variant a diamond fills the center.

tribes.note: Stone cross-refers erre gul to Yomud; Cole (dealer text) ties it to Yomud chuvals.

formats: minor gul on some main carpets

facts.text: Stone describes the erre gul as an indented rectangle with a central flower, crosses at top and bottom and in-pointing arrowheads at the sides.

Cole (dealer text) says the erre gul is best known on Yomud chuvals, appears as a minor gul on a Chodor main carpet, and was used by the Arabachi, Chodor and Yomud and by Uzbek, Karakalpak and Kyrgyz weavers.

rows.drawing_note: No open-licence photograph found.

rows.name: Chemche gul
rows.meaning: Chemche means 'spoon' or 'scoop'; the same word names the spoon bag, chemche torba. The Turkmen state book lists chemche among signs for ram's horns.
rows.shape: A small quartered diamond with arms, giving a cross shape; it may have eight radiating arms, alternately ending in a ram's-horn curl. The Turkmen state book calls the cross-shaped chemche guls the 'coordinate system' that keeps the main guls apart.

tribes.note: Stone: the Kizil Ayak minor gul.

facts.text: Chemche gul is a common minor gul in Turkmen rugs, a quartered diamond that may have eight radiating arms alternately ending in the ram's-horn motif.

Cross-shaped minor guls set between the main guls are called chemche guls; the Turkmen state book says these cross-shaped 'ak bashly chemche' guls set a clear grid that keeps the large ornaments from running together.

images.caption: The cross-shaped minor gul between two rows of main guls: a small quartered diamond with arms reaching left and right and short finials up and down.
images.title: Tekke Main Carpet
images.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, The James F. Ballard Collection, Gift of James F. Ballard, 1922
images.licence: Public domain (The Met Open Access, CC0)

rows.name: Gurbaga gul
rows.meaning: Frog (Stone: Turkish kurbage, 'frog').
rows.shape: A secondary field figure between the main guls; the Turkmen state book calls it an openwork pattern that lightens the composition. No detailed shape found.

tribes.note: Dealer text: the kurbaghe minor gul may be originally Arabachi.

facts.text: Stone defines the kurbage (frog) gul as a secondary field motif in Turkmen rugs.
The Turkmen state book names the openwork 'gurbaga' among the in-between patterns of Tekke-group carpets.

rows.drawing_note: No crop identified with a source naming the gul on that piece.

rows.name: Chakmak gul
rows.meaning: Chakmak, 'flint and steel' (fire-striker); the book links it to fire and the hearth.
rows.shape: A strongly elongated cross with the elements inside it also arranged as a cross.

facts.text: The Turkmen state book names the chakmak gyol as one of the most widespread ornaments of Dashoguz carpets: a strongly elongated cross.

rows.where_found_note: Dashoguz province covers the old Khiva oasis, home of Yomut and Chodor groups (see tribes); the book does not name a tribe.

rows.name: Sagdak
rows.meaning: Sagdak, 'quiver'; the book counts it among protective and wishing ornaments.
rows.shape: A row ornament: on the wedding tent band (ak ýüp), on a carpet made of tent-band strips where three of five rows carry sagdak and tegbent, and along the edges of a modern carpet.

facts.text: The Turkmen state book lists sagdak with tegbent, gulyaidy, dogajyk, keyik okara, daragt ogajy, sekiz gochak and dagdan as protective and wishing ornaments on ak ýüp bands of the wedding tent.

rows.note: Western books read do not use 'sagdaq' as a gul name; whether it is a field gul or only a row ornament is not settled (gap).

rows.name: Aina gul
rows.meaning: Aina, 'mirror' (Stone: Persian âyena); gochak, ram's horns, a sign of courage and strength.
rows.shape: A quartered diamond in a rectangle, or a stepped diamond inside a diamond inside a rectangle; these are called compartment guls.

tribes.note: Rijksmuseum BK-1975-317, a Tekke torba with the aina-gochak motif in rectangular compartments.

facts.text: The aina (mirror) gul is a quartered diamond in a rectangle, or a stepped diamond within a diamond within a rectangle; these are termed compartment guls.

rows.name: Sekme gul
rows.shape: A rectangle holding two concentric stepped diamonds.

facts.text: The sekme gul is a rectangle containing two concentric stepped diamonds, used in Tekke weavings.

rows.name: Dagdan
rows.meaning: An amulet well known in Turkmenistan; Moshkova says weavers give it a religious-magical (protective) meaning.
rows.shape: A small amulet figure in a narrow border.

tribes.note: Stone: a minor border design in Sariq weavings.
Moshkova: on almost every carpet then being made, woven at the very start as the first ornamental border.

facts.text: Dagdan is a Turkmen amulet design used as a minor border.
Moshkova says dagdan was on almost every carpet being made in her day, woven at the very start of the carpet as the first ornamental border.

rows.name: Ashik design
rows.meaning: Moshkova reads it as a late, simplified form of an older bird ornament.
rows.shape: Serrated or stepped diamonds, sometimes concentric, filling the field of an asmalyk as a lattice.

tribes.note: Moshkova: knotted wedding trappings (osmolduk) were kept only by the Yomut in her day.

rows.period_note: Osmolduks made in the colonial period often have the ashik design; the two or three early 19th- or late 18th-century osmolduks in Moscow and St Petersburg museums show an older form, a colored rhomboid rosette with white zigzags and a bird (sometimes an animal) at its center.

facts.text: The ashik gul is a gul of serrated or stepped diamonds, which may be concentric.
Moshkova says modern osmolduks (asmalyks) are often filled with the ashik design, which she considers a later version of an older bird ornament.

says.text: The ashik field is the later, colonial-period form.
Dealer text: some ashik asmalyks are quite old, contemporary with the 'archaic' type.

rows.drawing_note: No open-licence asmalyk photograph found.

rows.name: Bird asmalyk design
rows.shape: Repeated birds within a lattice of serrated leaves on a red field, with white borders carrying a meandering vine; running or standing birds.

tribes.note: Stone: rare Tekke asmalyks; Tsareva: an 18th-century Akhal Tekke asmaldyk in the Russian Ethnographic Museum.
Old Yomut osmolduks with a bird at the center of each rosette.
Arabachi asmaldyks with two-headed 'eagles' (REM).

facts.text: Bird asmalyks are rare Tekke asmalyks with a repeated pattern of birds in a lattice of serrated leaves.

rows.drawing_note: Superseded: a facsimile from Bogolyubov's plates is now listed (status 'facsimile').

images.caption: Detail of the field of a seven-sided Yomud piece: rows of stylized bird figures with spread wings in white, red and black on a dark red ground, with small stars between.
images.holder: Bogolyubov, Tapis de l'Asie Centrale (1908), Qatar National Library copy
images.title: Moitié de tchoval iomoude, au 1/3 de sa grandeur
images.credit: Bogolyubov, Tapis de l’Asie Centrale (1908), plate Plate XIX; Qatar National Library copy
images.licence: Public domain (1908)

rows.name: Darvaza design
rows.meaning: Darvaza, 'gate' (Persian-Tajik, also Turkmen).
rows.shape: The field of an asmalyk with three large central rosettes and two rows of arches running lengthwise; also a Salor wedding panel. Stone: a complex symmetrical polygon with six to eight small hexagons.

tribes.note: Charshango Ersari.

facts.text: Darvaza is the Turkmen name for an asmalyk field composition of three large central rosettes and two rows of lengthwise arches.
The darvaza medallion is a complex symmetrical polygon with six to eight small hexagons, used in Charshango Ersari, Salor and Kizil Ayak weavings.

says.text: A whole asmalyk field layout (three rosettes and arches).
A single complex polygonal medallion or gul.

rows.name: Kejebelik (wedding-caravan) design
rows.meaning: From kejebe, the tent-like litter in which the bride rode on a camel.
rows.shape: Asmalyks picturing the wedding caravan itself.

facts.text: The Turkmen state book says asmalyks showing the wedding caravan are popularly called kejebelik; the UNESCO inventory lists kejebelik as a rug for decorating a camel at the wedding.

rows.name: Torba designs
rows.shape: No single design. Torbas carry compartment guls (aina gul), old tribal guls that left the main carpet (ertmen, Salor gul), later Yomut kepse and dyrnak guls, and many borrowed patterns.

facts.text: Moshkova says prayer rugs, torbas and other small everyday pieces show most clearly both borrowed elements and the weaver's own invention; there she was least bound by tribal rules.

Bogolyubov says the finest Turkmen work is found in the small pieces (chuval, torba, namazlyk) rather than the large carpets, because mothers wove the bags for their daughters' dowries with special care.
facts.quote: Deshalb begegnet man den besten Erzeugnissen nicht unter den großen Teppichen, sondern bei den verhältnismäßig kleineren Stücken.

images.caption: Half of a Pende torba: a field of small stepped cross-shaped figures in a lattice on a dark ground, several narrow borders, a lower end panel of diamonds, and a long dark fringe hanging below.

images.credit: Bogolyubov, Tapis de l’Asie Centrale (1908), plate Plate XI; Qatar National Library copy

rows.name: Ensi (hatchli) layout
rows.meaning: Hatchli/khatchli means 'cross-like': Stone derives it from Turkish haçlı 'cruciform'; Lewis and Hawley say it comes from Armenian.
rows.shape: The pile door hanging of the tent. Its field is split into four roughly equal panels by an upright band and a cross band, forming a broad straight cross. The panels are often filled with rows of small Y-shaped or 'candlestick' figures. An arch (mihrab) panel sits at the top, often crowned by ram's horns (gochak), and a wide lower end panel (elem) often carries tree or plant figures. Moshkova names a central figure kuchuk izi, 'puppy's track'.

tribes.note: Stone: the 'Pende khatchli', with a panel of turret-like figures, is probably Saryk.

rows.period_note: Many Tekke rugs have the katchli pattern. The trade sold them as 'Princess Bokhara' prayer rugs.

facts.text: The ensi field is divided into four parts by crossing vertical and horizontal bands.
The ensi hung over the outside of the tent entrance against sun, cold and dust; a small rug, the germech, closed the threshold.

Hawley describes the Princess Bokhara ('katchli') as nearly square, divided into four equal sections, with a Y-shaped motif in field and border and a small tent-shaped prayer arch in a panel inside the upper border.
facts.quote: the field is divided into four equal sections by perpendicular and horizontal bands. Because of this pattern they are called "Katchlis,"

facts.text: Moshkova names a central ensi figure kuchuk izi, 'puppy's track', and a mihrab pattern with a protective meaning.
The Turkmen state book says ensis are densely knotted, up to 500,000 knots per square meter (about 323 per square inch).

says.text: A very large percentage of these pieces are namazliks (prayer rugs); doors had a hemmed upper selvage with braided cords for hanging.

Armenian 'khatchlie', a cross; the Armenians call them Khatchlie Bokhara.

tribes.name: Tekke
tribes.where_19th_century: The Akhal oasis along the Kopet Dagh (Ashgabat, Tejen) and, from about 1830, the Merv oasis; groups also lived along the Persian border and later in northern Afghanistan.
tribes.weaving: Knot: Asymmetric, generally open to the right; Stone: asymmetric. Wefts: Usually two wefts between rows of knots, a few single-wefted (Stone; Hawley gives two). Density: Stone: about 150 knots per square inch; Tekke torbas may be very finely knotted. Turkmen state book: 220,000–400,000 knots per square meter (about 142–258 per square inch). Sides: Dark blue overcasting; Hawley: double overcasting or a three-cord goat-hair selvage. Palette: Dark red to red-brown with dark blue and ivory (Hawley, 'Royal Bokhara'); the Turkmen state book says even modern Tekke carpets in unusual colors keep warm, golden shades. Formats: Main carpets, chuvals, torbas, ensis, asmalyks (bird asmalyks), khalyks, kapunuks, tent bands; Stone says most khalyks are Tekke.
tribes.where: The Akhal oasis along the Kopet Dagh (Ashgabat, Tejen) and, from about 1830, the Merv oasis; groups also lived along the Persian border and later in northern Afghanistan.

tribes.name: Salor
tribes.where_19th_century: Bogolyubov: the Yolatan and Pende oases at the end of the 18th century, most leaving for the Hari Rud and Sarakhs in 1780; Stone: around Merv until defeated in the 1830s; later scattered, some in Afghanistan.
tribes.weaving: Knot: Asymmetric, open to the left, on closely packed warps lying on two levels; Stone's 'S group': asymmetric open left, highly offset warps, long pile. Palette: Rust red to brick red with bluish-red or pink silk highlights (Stone, 'S group'); Bogolyubov notes silk in Pende and Merv chuvals and torbas; the Turkmen state book cites an 18th-century Salor carpet in the Hermitage with silk in nine colors. Formats: Main carpets, chuvals (turret gul), torbas, ensis, kejebe trappings and wedding panels (darvaza).
tribes.where: The Yolatan and Pende oases at the end of the 18th century, most leaving for the Hari Rud and Sarakhs in 1780; Stone: around Merv until defeated in the 1830s; later scattered, some in Afghanistan.

tribes.name: Saryk
tribes.where_19th_century: Merv, then the Pende (Penjdeh) oasis on the Murghab, which Bogolyubov says they took from the Salor; later some in northern Afghanistan.
tribes.weaving: Knot: Almost always symmetric (Iranica; Cleveland records); Stone: very late pieces may be asymmetric. Palette: Stone: earliest pieces all wool with an orange-tan field; then crimson with white cotton and magenta silk highlights; after 1880 purple-brown, brown or purple. Cleveland 2008.223: soft red with cotton and magenta silk. Formats: Main carpets, chuvals, ensis (Pende khatchli), kapunuks; Bogolyubov illustrates a Saryk namazlyk used as an ensi and a Saryk door surround from Takhta Bazar.
tribes.where: Merv, then the Pende (Penjdeh) oasis on the Murghab, which Bogolyubov says they took from the Salor; later some in northern Afghanistan.

tribes.name: Yomut
tribes.where_19th_century: The east Caspian coast and the Gorgan and Atrek plains (into Iran) and the Khiva oasis; subgroups include the Atabai, Jafarbai, Ogurjali and Igdyr (Stone). Bogolyubov's Yomud ornament group adds the Chodor, Abdal, Khoja and Goklan.
tribes.weaving: Knot: Both symmetric and asymmetric, sometimes in one carpet; Stone: symmetric more common. Density: Stone: typically 100–150 per square inch; Cleveland 2010.190: 128–136 symmetric. Palette: Brownish red dominant, main borders usually on a white ground, wider range of colors than other tribes; the Turkmen state book: more white, green, lilac and blue than other Turkmen carpets. Formats: Main carpets with decorated end panels (elem), chuvals, torbas, asmalyks (the only tribe still making knotted wedding trappings in Moshkova's day), ensis, hearth rugs (ojakbashy), tent bands.
tribes.where: The east Caspian coast and the Gorgan and Atrek plains (into Iran) and the Khiva oasis; subgroups include the Atabai, Jafarbai, Ogurjali and Igdyr. Bogolyubov's Yomud ornament group adds the Chodor, Abdal, Khoja and Goklan.

tribes.name: Chodor
tribes.where_19th_century: The Khiva (Khorezm) oasis; one group settled on the Amu Darya between Daynau and Sayat at the end of the 18th century (Moshkova).
tribes.weaving: Knot: Asymmetric, open to the right. Wefts: Two-ply, sometimes wool, sometimes cotton. Palette: Often a purple-brown field; Bogolyubov's Chodor carpet (Plate xxiii) has a chestnut-brown ground, which he calls rare in Turkmen carpets. Formats: Main carpets (ertmen, later tauk noska guls), chuvals, torbas; Moshkova: the Chodor supplied carpets to the Khiva and Bukhara markets.
tribes.where: The Khiva (Khorezm) oasis; one group settled on the Amu Darya between Daynau and Sayat at the end of the 18th century.

tribes.name: Arabachi
tribes.where_19th_century: The middle Amu Darya; Moshkova: the Denau district of Chardzhou, where they kept their identity best.
tribes.weaving: Knot: Asymmetric, open to the left, some warp offset; wefts of wool and white cotton. Palette: Purplish-brown field with outlines in natural brown wool. Formats: Main carpets (tauk noska), chuvals, kapunuks, asmalyks with eagle figures.
tribes.where: The middle Amu Darya; Moshkova: the Denau district of Chardzhou, where they kept their identity best.

tribes.name: Ersari
tribes.where_19th_century: The middle Amu Darya from Charjou to Kerki and into northern Afghanistan. Bogolyubov's Ersari group: Bashyr, Kashyr, Burdalyk, Chakyr, Ali-Eli, Toncha, Topcha and other Ersari in Russia, Bukhara and Afghanistan, plus the Karakalpak.
tribes.weaving: Knot: Asymmetric (Stone, for Beshir); Iranica: often more coarsely woven than other Turkmen. Palette: Bogolyubov: Ersari roses on one-color fields from dark red to yellow. Turkmen state book: more yellow than in other styles, light details on indigo set against the field. Formats: Main carpets (gulli gul), chuvals (including striped chuvals, Rijksmuseum bk-1975-313), ensis, prayer rugs; many non-tribal designs (Herati, ikat, boteh).
tribes.where: The middle Amu Darya from Charjou to Kerki and into northern Afghanistan. Bogolyubov's Ersari group: Bashyr, Kashyr, Burdalyk, Chakyr, Ali-Eli, Toncha, Topcha and other Ersari in Russia, Bukhara and Afghanistan, plus the Karakalpak.

tribes.name: Kizil Ayak
tribes.weaving: Knot: Asymmetric, open to the right; light undyed wool warps, brown wefts. Quality: Bogolyubov ranks Kizil Ayak carpets first among Turkmen work of the Amu Darya for knotting and clipping, as Pende carpets are first on the Murghab. Formats: Main carpets (tauk noska major gul, chemche minor gul), chuvals, flat-woven kilims.

tribes.name: Chub Bash
tribes.where_19th_century: Northern Afghanistan (Ersari area); possibly an Ersari subtribe (Stone).
tribes.weaving: Note: Stone: some Kizil Ayak and Chub Bash weavings may not be separable by structure or design.
tribes.where: Northern Afghanistan (Ersari area); possibly an Ersari subtribe.

tribes.name: Goklan
tribes.where_19th_century: Khurasan in Iran (Stone); Bogolyubov: the Sumbar valley (Kara).
tribes.weaving: Note: Stone: their work may have been attributed to the Yomud; symmetric knot over three warps in outlines; red silk wefts occasionally. Bogolyubov: they made no pile carpets, only flatweaves (palas).
tribes.where: Khurasan in Iran; Bogolyubov: the Sumbar valley (Kara).

tribes.name: Igdyr
tribes.where_19th_century: Near the Yomut, on whom they depended (Moshkova); Stone: a tribe related to the Yomud.
tribes.weaving: Note: Bogolyubov counts the Igdyr in the Yomud ornament group (his Plate xxiv is an Igdyr ensi); Moshkova says they weave Yomut patterns, having lost their own gul.
tribes.where: Near the Yomut, on whom they depended; Stone: a tribe related to the Yomud.

tribes.name: Imreli
tribes.where_19th_century: Tsareva: for centuries between the Gurgan and Atrek rivers; pushed out from the 18th century, partly into Akhal and the Khiva oasis.
tribes.weaving: Note: Moshkova: weave Yomut patterns. Tsareva: creators of the eagle (igl) gul. Stone: the attribution of carpets to the Imreli (from 1980) is questionable.
tribes.where: For centuries between the Gurgan and Atrek rivers; pushed out from the 18th century, partly into Akhal and the Khiva oasis.

structures.title: Knots, weaves, sides and ends: how rugs are made, drawn

rows.name: Symmetric knot
other_names: Turkbaff / torkībāf (Persian trade term; Stone, Iranica)
'double' knot (Leitch's term for the knot as used in China; Turkish 'çift düğüm')
Complete knot (English term cited by Öztürk)
Symmetrical knot (Kendrick & Tattersall 1922, the earliest use Öztürk found)

native.translit: çift düğüm ('double knot') / çift bağlama düğüm ('double-tie knot')
kapalı düğüm ('closed knot'; Turkish literature after 1990)

native.note: Türkmenhaly names two knots, 'двойной и полуторный' (double and one-and-a-half), and separately codes 'SY' (symmetric) and 'AS' (asymmetric) knots without pairing the words with the codes. 'Double' = symmetric is our reading, by analogy with Cordwell 1979 as cited by Öztürk ('double knot' for the symmetric knot, 'one and a half knot' for the asymmetric).

how_made: Seen from the front: lay the pile yarn across the front of the two warps W1 and W2. This crossing is the collar.
Take the left end around the outside (left) of W1, behind W1, and bring it forward through the gap between W1 and W2.
Take the right end around the outside (right) of W2, behind W2, and bring it forward through the same gap.
Pull both ends down toward the finished part of the rug, which tightens the collar and slides the knot down onto the wefts; cut the ends to pile length.
Both ends now rise together from the gap between W1 and W2, just below the collar. The next knot is tied on W3 and W4, so the gap between W2 and W3 has no yarn ends.
how_made_sources: ozturk_2025 pp. 171-172 (collar above, ends pulled down)
rows.front: One tuft per pair of warps, rising from between them; if you part the pile you see a collar of yarn lying across both warps, with the whole tuft coming out from under it. The two ends cannot be parted to show a warp: trying only twists them tighter (Hawley p. 48; May pp. 42-43). Across a row, gaps between warps alternately hold two yarn ends and none (Mumford p. 87; Kendrick p. 94).
rows.back: Two nodes per knot, one lying across the back of each of the two warps. On level warps the two nodes are the same size and side by side, like two beads (Hawley Plate B 7-a; May Fig. 20). If one warp of each pair is depressed its node is smaller (Plate B 8-a); if it is fully doubled under, only one node per knot shows (Hawley p. 52; Stone p. 160). On the back the symmetric and asymmetric knots look alike, so the back alone rarely tells which knot was used.
rows.where_typical_note: Rows whose first-listed knot is symmetric in rugs_current.json. Also used in some rows listed under other knots: tehran, mashhad, mahal, classical-garden, shahsavan, yalameh, shiraz, khamseh, isparta, beshir, soviet-turkmen, afghan-ersari, mushwani-herat-baluch, kashgar, samarkand, ningxia, peking, tianjin, tibetan-khaden, agra, pakistani-bokhara, romanian.
rows.what_it_tells: Typical of Anatolian (Turkish) and Caucasian pile rugs, and of Kurdish, Hamadan-area, Heriz-area and much other village and tribal weaving in western and northwestern Iran; also Tabriz city rugs, the Saryk and most Yomut Turkmen, Moroccan and Algerian pile rugs. Because it is used across the whole rug-weaving belt, it narrows a rug's origin; it does not settle it.
rows.cautions: The names are shorthand, not origins: Persia uses both knots (Iranica; Jacobsen p. 159; Öztürk). On warps that lie on two levels a symmetric knot leans to one side and can look asymmetric (Kendrick p. 95; Öztürk after Azadi). Worn pile can reduce a symmetric collar to two loops that look like asymmetric knots: test where the pile is full. Weavers in one rug may mix knots (Leitch p. 120; Iranica on the Yomut).

facts.text: In the symmetric knot the yarn lies across the front of two warps and both ends pass around behind them and come out together between them.
facts.quote: the yarn lies across and in front of the two warp-threads and its free ends pass round behind them and then emerge again between them

facts.text: The two ends of a symmetric knot cannot be parted to show a warp; those of an asymmetric knot can.
facts.quote: If the pile of a rug is carefully parted, the two ends of yarn forming a Sehna knot can be separated; but with the Ghiordes knot this is impossible

facts.text: Turkish geographical-indication registrations call the symmetric knot 'Türk düğümü', also known as the Gördes or 'double' (çift) knot, tied around two warps and wrapping both equally.
facts.quote: Türk düğümü; Gördes düğümü ve çift düğüm olarak da bilinir. Gördes düğümü simetriktir. (The Turkish knot is also known as the Gördes knot and the double knot. The Gördes knot is symmetric.)

facts.text: Hawley shows three ways of tying the Ghiordes knot and calls the second a 'right hand' and the third a 'left hand' knot.
facts.quote: of which the second is known as a "right hand" and the third as a "left hand" knot

facts.text: Azadi (1975) described three forms of the symmetric knot, depending on whether the two warps lie level or one in front of the other and on weft tension; the Turkmen state carpet corporation likewise codes three symmetric knots (SY I-III).
Kendrick & Tattersall wrote that a Ghiordes knot tied on warps on two levels may incline either to right or left, and that the Ghiordes knot is rarely found on warps on very different levels.
facts.quote: the Ghiordes knot is rarely found with a warp on very different levels

facts.text: The first naming of the symmetric knot after Gördes that Öztürk found is from 1904; he calls the link to ancient Gordion, which Hawley repeats, a false equation and advises against the name in scholarly work.

says.text: Named after the town of Ghiordes, where some of the finest pieces were made, 'which tradition states was once the ancient Gordion' (p. 48).
Gordion lies near Polatlı (Ankara), not at Gördes; the name, first found in 1904, rests on a false link and should not be used in scholarly work.

disagreements.about: symmetric knot on deeply offset warps

says.text: The Ghiordes knot is rarely found with a warp on very different levels (p. 95).
Bijars have the Ghiordes knot with one warp of each knot doubled under and hidden (p. 52; Plate B fig. 9).
Bijar: symmetric knot (Bijar entry); warps may be offset so that only one node shows (warp offset, p. 304).

rows.name: Asymmetric knot, open to the left
other_names: Sehna / Senneh / Senna / Sena knot (Hawley, Lewis, May, Jacobsen; Stone calls the name incorrect)
'single' knot (Leitch, for the knot as used in China)
'right-hand Sehna knot' in Kendrick & Tattersall's sense (encircled warp on the right as seen by the weaver), which under Heirloom's convention is this knot
'asimetrik düğüm sol' (Turkish, some publications cited by Öztürk)
'one and a half knot' (English term cited by Öztürk)

native.translit: gereh-ye taki ('single knot', i.e. tied on two warps, not jufti)
Sine düğümü ('Senneh knot'; Öztürk calls the name wrong)
tek düğüm ('single knot') / tek bağlama düğüm ('single-tie knot')

native.note: Mapping to the asymmetric knot is our reading (see symmetric-knot, Russian note).

how_made: Seen from the front, warps W1 (left) and W2 (right). Leave one end of the pile yarn (A) in front, to the left of W1.
Pass the yarn behind W1, from left to right, and bring it forward through the gap between W1 and W2.
Carry it across the front of W2 (this is the collar, which crosses one warp only), around the right side of W2, and back behind W2 from right to left.
Bring it forward again through the gap between W1 and W2 as end B, below the collar. W2 is now fully encircled; W1 is only passed behind.
Pull both ends down and cut: end A rises to the left of W1 and end B between W1 and W2, so the two ends straddle W1 and the tuft leans left, toward the open side.
how_made_sources: jacobsen_1962 p. 109 ('one end is left outside the two warp threads, and the other ... passed under the first warp, and over and under the second, and is then drawn between the two warps' — paraphrased)
rows.front: Each tuft has one end coming up between the two warps and one outside the pair, so across a row every gap between warps holds one yarn end (Mumford p. 87; Kendrick pp. 94-95). Parting a tuft, the collar crosses only one warp, with part of the tuft from under it and part beside it (May p. 43; Kendrick pp. 94-95); the two ends can be separated to show a warp (Hawley p. 48). The pile leans slightly toward the open side, here left (Kendrick p. 94; Lewis p. 93).
rows.back: Two nodes per knot on level warps, one on each warp (May p. 40). On warps on two levels, one node per knot may be smaller or hidden (Hawley Plate B 10-a; Stone p. 304). Whether the encircled warp lies to the front or the back is disputed; in Chinese usage a back with the wefts hidden is called 'closed back' (Stone pp. 72, 208).
rows.where_typical_note: Rows that state 'open left'. Rows that give only 'asymmetric' (side not recorded): kashan, kashan-manchester-mohtasham, kashan-silk, isfahan, nain, qum, kerman, kerman-lavar, kerman-american-market, kermanshah-trade-name, yazd, tehran, najafabad, mashhad, khorassan, kashmar, farahan, sarouk, sarouk-american, mahal, lilihan, arak-modern, classical-ardabil, classical-polonaise, classical-hunting, classical-garden, yalameh, varamin, shiraz, qashqai, khamseh, baluch, isparta, ersari, beshir, chub-bash, bokhara, soviet-turkmen, afghan-ersari, daulatabad, khal-mohammadi, mauri, war-rug, khotan, kashgar, yarkand, samarkand, qing-palace-carpet, baotou-suiyuan, peking, tianjin, chinese-art-deco, chinese-modern-export, chinese-silk, agra, lahore, amritsar, mirzapur-bhadohi, jaipur, kashmir-pile, indo-trade-names, indo-savonnerie, pakistani-bokhara, pak-persian, romanian, greek-refugee, chinese-persian-design, classical-mamluk. Iranica says open left is the commoner form in Persian carpets.
rows.what_it_tells: The asymmetric knot is typical of Persian city and workshop rugs (Kashan, Kerman, Sarouk, Isfahan, Nain, Qum), most Turkmen weaving (Tekke, Salor and others), Baluch, Indian, Pakistani and Chinese rugs. Open left in particular is recorded for Salor and Arabachi Turkmen work, classical 'vase technique' carpets, Khorasan jufti work and Ningxia rugs. The side is a minor clue that only specialists record, and authors differ on how to name it.
rows.cautions: Read every 'right-hand/left-hand' or 'open right/left' with its author's definition; never convert one author's term into another's without saying so. In tightly woven rugs on offset warps it can be very hard to tell the knot type at all (Kendrick p. 95). The name 'Senneh knot' is a misnomer: Senneh rugs are mostly symmetric-knotted.

facts.text: In the asymmetric knot the yarn fully encircles one warp of the pair; one end comes out between the two warps and the other passes behind the second warp and comes to the front outside it.
facts.quote: the yarn completely encircles one warp-thread of a pair; one yarn-end emerges between them, while the other passes behind the second warp-thread and comes to the front outside it

facts.text: The asymmetric knot can be tied two ways, open on one side or the other; in Persian carpets the open-left form is the more common.
Knotted pile in the asymmetric knot leans toward one corner of the rug, right or left according to which way the knot is tied, while symmetric-knotted pile leans straight toward one end.
facts.quote: those that are tied with the Senna knot have a nap which runs towards one corner, right or left, according to whether the right or left Senna knot is employed

facts.text: Because one end comes up in every gap between warps, the asymmetric knot allows closer knotting and a finer, more even surface than the symmetric knot.
facts.quote: the Sehna knots, which permit of closer weaving and clearer definition of pattern, appear in rugs of shorter nap

facts.text: Calling the asymmetric knot the 'Senneh knot' is a misnomer: the knot is not peculiar to Senneh, both knots are used throughout the region regardless of the weavers' ethnicity, and Senneh's own fine rugs are described as symmetric-knotted.
Jacobsen (1962) wrote that 'Persian knot' would be a better name than 'Sena knot', and 'Turkish knot' better than 'Ghiordes knot'.

Chinese pile rugs are tied mostly with the asymmetric ('single') knot, with symmetric ('double') knots mainly at the edges and ends of some pieces; Leitch says a Chinese knot never takes in more than two warps.
facts.quote: In Chinese rugs, two warp threads, never more, are included to form a knot

facts.text: Chinese sources call the pile knot the '8' (figure-eight) knot, 8字扣: the Palace Museum for a Qing Ningxia rug, the Ningxia heritage listing, and a 2012 patent for modern export carpets; none of them says whether it is the symmetric or the asymmetric knot.
facts.quote: 用彩色羊毛在经线上拴“8”字扣形成栽绒 (colored wool tied on the warps in '8' knots to form the pile)

facts.text: In Nain the knot has been the Persian knot tied singly on two warps; jufti, 'rubafi' and 'kamanshib' knots are counted as fraudulent in Iranian weaving.
facts.quote: گره تکی نامتقارن و اصلی‌ترین گره در فرش نایین است (the single asymmetric knot is the main knot of the Nain carpet)

says.text: Right-hand or left-hand 'according as this thread of warp [the adjacent, unencircled one] is to the right or the left of the one they encircle' (p. 48). Most Sehna knots right-hand; many Khorassans left-hand. Viewing side not stated.
Figure captions 'Sehna knot, right-hand system' and 'left-hand system'; the Sehna 'is sometimes reversed and worked from left to right' (p. 87). No definition.

Right-hand or left-hand according as the ENCIRCLED warp is the right-hand or left-hand one of the pair 'as seen by the weaver'; right-hand much more common, its pile leaning left (p. 94). This is the opposite way round from Hawley's wording.
Senna-knotted pile runs toward one corner, right or left, according to whether the right or left Senna knot is used (p. 93). No definition.
Right-hand when the second warp lies to the right of the warp the yarn is first tied around; left-hand when it lies to the left (p. 120): the same wording as Hawley.
The asymmetric knot may be open to the right or, more commonly, to the left (shown in Figures 65b, 65c; viewing side not stated in the text).
May be open to the right or left (drawings only, p. 34).

Some publications call them 'asimetrik düğüm sol / sağ' because in some places the left and in others the right side of the knot is made as a half knot; Azadi (1975) counts four asymmetric forms (warp position x left/right).
Codes four asymmetric knots, AS I-IV, without definitions on the page read.

disagreements.about: which warp the asymmetric knot encircles when warps lie on two levels

says.text: The encircled warp is always the one nearer the front of the carpet (p. 95).
Either: 'open back' when the loop encircles the warp nearest the front (wefts show on the back); 'closed back' (Tianjin) when it encircles the warp nearest the back (pp. 72, 208).
Plate B fig. 10 (Sehna knot, one warp doubled under) appears, as we read it, to show the yarn fully round the lower (back) warp; the text does not say.

disagreements.about: knot of Chinese rugs from about 1925

says.text: Mostly the 'single' (asymmetric) knot; some pieces symmetric ('double') throughout; never more than two warps per knot (pp. 119-120).
From about 1925 'the Chinese employed the double Persian knot' (p. 82); what 'double' means here is not explained.

rows.name: Asymmetric knot, open to the right
other_names: 'left-hand Sehna knot' in Kendrick & Tattersall's sense (encircled warp on the left as seen by the weaver)

'asimetrik düğüm sağ' (Turkish, publications cited by Öztürk)

native.translit: Sine düğümü ('Senneh knot'; Öztürk calls the name wrong)

how_made: Seen from the front, warps W1 (left) and W2 (right). Leave end A in front, to the right of W2.
Pass the yarn behind W2, from right to left, and bring it forward through the gap between W1 and W2.
Carry it across the front of W1 (the collar), around the left side of W1, and back behind W1 from left to right.
Bring it forward through the gap between W1 and W2 as end B, below the collar. W1 is fully encircled; W2 is only passed behind.
Pull down and cut: end A rises to the right of W2, end B between W1 and W2; the tuft straddles W2 and leans right.
how_made_sources: kendrick_1922 p. 94 (mirror of the right-hand knot)
hawley_1922 p. 48 and Plate B figs. 4 and 6 (yarn around the left warp, end outside the right warp)
rows.front: As the open-left knot, mirrored: the collar crosses W1 only; the free end comes up to the right of W2; the pile leans right (Kendrick p. 94, for his 'left-hand' knot).
rows.back: Two nodes per knot on level warps, as for the open-left knot.
rows.where_typical_note: Rows that state 'open right'. Iranica gives it as the less common form in Persian carpets; Hawley reports many 'left-hand' Sehna knots in Khorassan rugs, but his term cannot be mapped with certainty.
rows.what_it_tells: Recorded as the usual knot of Tekke, Chodor (Chaudor) and Kizil Ayak Turkmen weaving in the Turkmen literature, and as the less common form in Persian carpets.
rows.cautions: As for the open-left knot. One reading of the knot side does not fix a tribe: the salor row already notes that some later Salor pieces are reported open to the right.

facts.text: Tekke and Chodor knots are asymmetric and open to the right, unlike Salor knots, which open to the left.
Kendrick & Tattersall's left-hand Sehna knot, with the encircled warp on the left as seen by the weaver, is the less common form, and its pile inclines to the right.
facts.quote: while the pile of the left-hand inclines towards the right

facts.text: Hawley (1913) called most Sehna knots 'right-hand' and said a large proportion of Khorassan rugs have 'left-hand' Sehna knots.
facts.quote: Most Sehna knots are right-hand knots, but the Sehna knots of a large proportion of Khorassan rugs are left-hand knots.

says.text: Right-hand or left-hand 'according as this thread of warp [the adjacent, unencircled one] is to the right or the left of the one they encircle' (p. 48). Most Sehna knots right-hand; many Khorassans left-hand. Viewing side not stated.

Senna-knotted pile runs toward one corner, right or left, according to whether the right or left Senna knot is used (p. 93). No definition.

rows.name: Jufti knot, symmetric form (symmetric knot on four warps)
other_names: Double knot (Stone; not to be confused with 'double knot' = symmetric knot)
how_made: Treat W1 and W2 together as if they were one warp, and W3 and W4 together as a second.
Lay the collar across the front of all four warps.
Take the left end around the outside of W1, behind W1 and W2 together, and forward through the gap between W2 and W3.
Take the right end around the outside of W4, behind W4 and W3 together, and forward through the same gap.
Pull down and cut: both ends rise together between W2 and W3. One knot now covers four warps where two ordinary knots would.
how_made_sources: kendrick_1922 p. 95 ('two warp-threads are taken together and treated as one')
jacobsen_1962 p. 111 (Fig. 48: Turkish jufti, top and side views)
rows.front: One tuft per four warps, so solid-colored areas have half as many tufts across as areas knotted normally; Stone says outlines are knotted normally, so they feel denser than the plain areas when you run a finger along the warps.
rows.back: Two nodes per knot, each lying across two warps instead of one, so in jufti areas the nodes are wider and there are half as many across an inch. Babajamali warns that jufti and other 'fraud' knots show the same curve on the back as regular knots, so they are hard to see.
rows.where_typical_note: Rows that list or mention jufti and also list the symmetric knot; the row notes do not always say which form of jufti is used. Jacobsen reports many jufti knots in Hamadan-area and Gorevan rugs of the 1950s.
rows.what_it_tells: Jufti knotting in solid areas is a time-saving practice of commercial Persian weaving from the mid-20th century on, and an old local habit in Khorasan; it says nothing by itself about where in Iran a rug was made.
rows.cautions: Jufti is not a fault that makes a rug unusable (Jacobsen 1969 says a jufti rug with good wool will still last a lifetime), but it halves the knot count where it is used. Do not count jufti nodes as ordinary knots when estimating knot density.

facts.text: Jufti knots are symmetric or asymmetric knots tied over four (or three or more) warps instead of two; the knot itself is not different, two warps are simply treated as one.
facts.quote: it only means that two warp-threads are taken together and treated as one

facts.text: Jufti knotting halves the number of knots and the pile wool in the area where it is used, and gives a less detailed design.
In Persian rugs the jufti knot is used in solid-colored areas but not in design outlines, so outlines feel denser when you run your fingers warp-wise across them.
Iranian sources count jufti knotting among fraudulent knots.
Early 20th-century writers saw knots on four warps only rarely: Hawley calls them 'a few rare instances' and Kendrick & Tattersall say they are found 'rarely throughout the whole of a carpet'.
facts.quote: In a few rare instances a knot is tied to four threads of warp.

facts.text: The Textile Museum describes classical (16th-17th-century) Khorasan carpets as usually knotted around four warps rather than two, often offset row by row.
Turkbaff weavers in Mashhad, trained in the Tabriz manner, tie knots with a hook, with which jufti knotting is impractical.

says.text: Knots on four warps are 'a few rare instances' (p. 48, 1913 text).
Found sometimes, 'though rarely throughout the whole of a carpet' (p. 95).
Spread in commercial Persian weaving in the late 1930s.
Very few old rugs have it, only those woven since 1945; but Khurasan (Meshed) weavers have used it as their regular knot 'from time immemorial' (jufti check point).
Khurasan weavers 'have also used the Jufti knot for years as their standard' (p. 111); in 1950s Hamadans perhaps a quarter of the knots are jufti (p. 204).
Classical Khorasan carpets usually have knots on four warps.
'I know of no other country which uses this false knot' than Iran (p. 109); 1969: not used in Pakistan and Afghanistan.
Most contemporary Kashmir rugs are jufti-knotted (Kashmir entry).

images.credit: Drawing by Heirloom, after Iranica, Carpets; Stone (2013)

images.caption: The back: a jufti knot’s nodes each lie across two warps, so they are wider and fewer than ordinary knots’ nodes.
images.credit: Drawing by Heirloom, after Iranica, Carpets; Stone (2013)

rows.name: Jufti knot, asymmetric form (asymmetric knot on four warps)
other_names: Khurasan jufti (Stone: asymmetric and open to the left)
how_made: Treat W1+W2 as one warp and W3+W4 as another (open-left form shown).
Leave end A in front, to the left of W1.
Pass the yarn behind W1 and W2 together and bring it forward in the gap between W2 and W3.
Carry it across the front of W3 and W4 (collar), around the right side of W4, back behind W4 and W3, and forward in the W2-W3 gap as end B.
Pull down and cut: end A left of W1, end B between W2 and W3.
how_made_sources: jacobsen_1962 p. 111 (Fig. 48, fourth column: Persian jufti)
rows.front: One tuft per four warps; ends straddle the W1+W2 pair.
rows.back: Two wide nodes per knot, each across a pair of warps.
rows.where_typical_note: Rows that list or mention jufti and also list the asymmetric knot.
rows.what_it_tells: Typical of Khorasan work (Mashhad, Birjand, Dorokhsh, Kashmar area) and of mid-20th-century commercial Kerman and Arak-area rugs; also most contemporary Kashmir rugs.
rows.cautions: As for the symmetric jufti.

facts.text: Khorasan carpets use the asymmetric knot tied over four warps; Stone gives the Khurasan jufti as asymmetric and open to the left.

images.caption: An asymmetric jufti knot, open to the left, seen from the front: the knot goes round two warps at a time.
images.credit: Drawing by Heirloom, after Stone (2013); knots/findings.json

rows.name: Single-warp knot (Spanish knot)

native.translit: İspanyol düğümü ('Spanish knot') / tek çözgüye düğüm ('knot on a single warp')

native.note: Seen only in a search-result summary of the page, not verbatim; treat as unconfirmed.

how_made: Row 1 uses every other warp: W2, W4, W6...
Lay the yarn across the front of W2, take both ends around behind W2 so that they cross each other at the back.
Bring the ends forward, one on each side of W2: one in the W1-W2 gap and one in the W2-W3 gap.
In the next row tie the knots on the warps left empty before (W1, W3, W5...), so each knot sits between two knots of the row below.
rows.front: Each tuft straddles one warp; knots in successive rows are staggered by one warp, so diagonal lines in the design are much smoother than vertical ones (Kendrick p. 97).
rows.back: One node per knot, on a single warp; the nodes form a staggered, diagonal (brick-like) grid because alternate rows use alternate warps (Kendrick pp. 96-97).
rows.where_typical_note: No row of rugs_current.json uses this knot as its main knot. The holbein row lists a Spanish copy of a Turkish pattern (Cleveland 1952.511, 'Spanish knot').
rows.what_it_tells: Points to Spain (early Spanish carpets); not expected on a rug from Iran, Turkey or the Caucasus.
rows.cautions: Do not confuse with offset symmetric or asymmetric knots (each on two warps) or with the 'Senneh loop' of early Egyptian fragments, which spans three warps (Stone p. 254).

facts.text: The single-warp (Spanish) knot is tied around one warp, and the knots of successive rows are staggered onto the alternate warps.
facts.quote: The yarn completely encircles the single warp-thread, one end crosses the other at the back and then the ends come to the front, one at each side

facts.text: Kendrick & Tattersall found the single-warp knot almost exclusively in early Spanish carpets; Stone thinks it originated in North Africa and notes a similar knot in Coptic weaving of the 8th-9th centuries.
Because its knots fall into diagonal lines, a carpet with the single-warp knot shows smoother diagonals than verticals.
facts.quote: single-warp knots are tied on those warps left blank in the previous row, and so fall into diagonal instead of vertical lines

rows.name: Tibetan technique (yarn looped over a rod and cut)

native.translit: chuāngān shì liánhuán bāzì kòu ('rod-threaded linked figure-8 knot')
kǎdiàn (the rug: Chinese rendering of Tibetan khaden)

native.note: Tibetan script for the rug name as recorded in rugs_current.json (tibetan-khaden row); no Tibetan-language name for the knotting technique was found.

how_made: Lay a rod (gauge rod) across the front of the warps at the height of the knot row.
With a continuous length of pile yarn, wrap a knot around two warps (W1 and W2), then take the yarn up and once over the rod.
Without cutting, wrap the next two warps (W3 and W4) and go over the rod again; continue across the color area.
When the row is done, cut the loops along the rod and remove it: each wrap becomes a knot with two cut ends.
Weave several rows of plain ground weft before the next row of knots.
rows.front: Rows of cut pile that overlap like roof shingles or the planks of a boat (Stone p. 284).
rows.back: Rows of knots around pairs of warps, separated by bands of several ground wefts; older Tibetan rugs often have a red cloth backing that hides the back (Stone p. 284).
rows.what_it_tells: Points to Tibet or to Tibetan weaving in Nepal and India (refugee production since 1959-60, Stone).
rows.cautions: Stone notes that some Tibetan rugs are tied with ordinary symmetric knots. The sources read do not say exactly how the yarn passes around the two warps, so do not draw more detail than they give.

facts.text: Tibetan pile is made with a continuous yarn wrapped around two warps and then around a rod laid across the rug; when the row is finished the loops on the rod are cut and the rod removed.

In Chinese the Gyantse technique is called 穿杆式连环八字扣, 'rod-threaded linked figure-8 knot'; Tibetans call the rug khaden (卡垫), and Tibetan khaden weaving has been national intangible heritage since 2006.

says.text: A weft-wrapping technique with cut loops, not a knot; some Tibetan rugs use the symmetric knot.
Chinese usage calls the method a knot (八字扣, figure-8 knot) threaded on a rod.

images.caption: Tibetan knotting, seen from the front: one yarn wrapped around pairs of warps and over a rod, later cut along the rod.
images.credit: Drawing by Heirloom, after Stone (2013); knots/findings.json

rows.name: Offset knots (knots shifted by one warp in alternate rows)
other_names: Packing knots (Stone, when no weft separates the rows)
how_made: Tie a row of ordinary knots on the usual pairs: W1-W2, W3-W4, W5-W6.
In the next row, break up the pairs and tie each knot on W2-W3, W4-W5, so each sits midway between two knots of the row below.
Where the pattern needs it, return to the usual pairs; Kendrick says Yomud weavers do this by tying a knot on three warps at each end of the shifted run.
rows.front: Smoother diagonal lines in the design at about 45 degrees; the knots of shifted rows sit like bricks in a half-brick wall.
rows.back: Two nodes per knot as usual, but in shifted runs the pairs of nodes are staggered by one warp from the row below.
rows.where_typical_note: Yomut (Kendrick; Stone); Kurdish and Turkmen pile weaving, early Chinese and Moroccan rugs (Stone); classical Khorasan carpets (Textile Museum).
rows.what_it_tells: Used only where needed in the pattern; a feature specialists note for Yomud Turkmen work, some Kurdish rugs and early Chinese rugs.
rows.cautions: Not the same as the single-warp (Spanish) knot, whose every row is staggered; offset knots are ordinary two-warp knots shifted in places.

facts.text: Some weavers break up the usual pairs of warps and tie a row of knots midway between those of the row below, to draw smooth diagonal lines.
facts.quote: The knots are thus arranged like the bricks in a half-brick wall

facts.text: Kendrick & Tattersall say the Yomud restore the usual arrangement by tying a knot on three warps at each end of a row of shifted knots.
Packing knots are rows of pile knots put in with no weft between them and the row below; they may be shifted by one warp, and were used in Chinese rugs for design effects.

images.caption: The back of offset knots: in alternate rows the knots shift by one warp, so the pairs of nodes are staggered.
images.credit: Drawing by Heirloom, after Stone (2013); knots/findings.json

rows.name: Symmetric knot tied across a skipped warp (Uzbek strip rugs)
how_made: Tie a symmetric knot on two warps that are not neighbors (for example W1 and W3), leaving the warp between them (W2) inside the knot; extra wefts lie behind and around each row.
rows.front: Long shaggy pile; tufts spaced more widely than the warps.
rows.back: Knots hardly visible because of the extra wefts.
rows.what_it_tells: A feature recorded for Uzbek long-pile strip rugs (julkhyr).
rows.cautions: Single source; not enough detail for a reliable diagram.

facts.text: Uzbek pile strip rugs use the symmetric knot tied so that it skips a warp, with extra wefts that hide the knots on the back.

rows.name: Berber knot (Middle Atlas, Morocco)
how_made: The yarn encircles two warps twice; on the front the tufts come out in opposite diagonal directions from under a diagonal loop. It may be shifted by one warp either way and combined with symmetric knots on four warps.
rows.front: Tufts emerging diagonally in opposite directions from under a diagonal loop.
rows.back: Not described in the sources read.
rows.what_it_tells: Points to Middle Atlas Berber weaving.
rows.cautions: Single source; Stone's text is not enough for an exact diagram.

facts.text: The Berber knot encircles two warps twice, uses more yarn than the symmetric or asymmetric knot, and is more durable.

rows.name: Hand-tufted pile (tufting gun, latex and backing cloth)
other_names: Machine-tufted (the factory form, with rows of needles)
NOTE: before about the 1920s 'hand-tufted' was also used in English for hand-KNOTTED carpets
how_made: Stretch a primary backing cloth on a frame (Stone: a cotton backing; cri: woven or non-woven polypropylene in machine-tufted carpet).
Shoot the pile yarn into the cloth with a hand-held tufting gun; the yarn is not knotted to anything. Machine tufting does the same with rows of hundreds of needles.
Leave the loops as loop pile, or cut them for cut pile.
Coat the back with latex (or another bonding compound) to lock the tufts in the cloth.
Bond a secondary backing cloth to the back with the latex; CEPC says a third cloth is then used and the rug finished. With no warps, any fringe has to be a separate strip sewn on.
rows.front: Dense, even pile with no knots at its base: part the pile and the tufts come straight up out of a cloth (Stone; Jacobsen 1969 p. 131 for the absence of knots in machine-made pile). Edges are bound, not woven; any fringe is a separate sewn-on strip.
rows.back: No knots or warps: a plain cloth (often cotton canvas) glued over the whole back, with latex underneath; lift a corner and you may see the rows of tufts in the first cloth.
rows.what_it_tells: A tufted rug, not a knotted one, whatever its design or label; Stone names China and the Philippines, and CEPC says Indian exporters also make hand-tufted rugs.
rows.cautions: A later cloth or rubber backing on a hand-knotted rug (a repair or anti-slip treatment) can hide knots; look at the pile roots and the fringe too. Old English books use 'hand-tufted' for knotted carpets.

facts.text: In a hand-tufted rug the pile is shot into a backing cloth with a tufting gun and held by latex and a second cloth; in machine tufting, rows of needles stitch the yarn through a primary backing.
Tufted pile can be cut or looped.
Brinton (1919) used 'hand-tufted carpet' for hand-knotted carpets made in Britain, Europe and the East.
facts.quote: there is no method of combining the pile with the foundation so good as the knot

images.caption: Hand-tufted, in section: no warps and no knots; yarn is pushed through a cloth and held by latex under a glued backing.
images.credit: Drawing by Heirloom, after Stone (2013); knots/findings.json

rows.name: Hooked rug (loops pulled through a cloth)
how_made: Mount a ready-made cloth, usually burlap (sacking) or canvas, on a frame.
With a hook, pull yarn or narrow strips of fabric up through the cloth from the back to form loops on the front, row after row, close together.
Leave the loops, or shear them for a cut pile.
rows.front: Loops (or clipped loops) packed in close rows; no knots and no warps of the rug's own.
rows.back: The burlap or canvas, with the yarn or strips showing as short running stitches in rows; some commercial ones have the back covered in plastic.
rows.where_typical_note: No type row; see the checks system rows the check on back and the check on pile roots, and the Hand-tufted rugs (India, China and elsewhere) row (Jacobsen's Hong Kong hooked rugs).
rows.what_it_tells: A hooked rug, a different craft from knotted pile: a domestic craft of English-speaking countries since the 19th century, also made commercially in China, India and Hong Kong.
rows.cautions: Hooked rugs in oriental designs exist (Jacobsen 1969, Hong Kong rugs of the 1960s).

facts.text: Hooked rugs are made by pulling yarn or fabric strips through canvas or burlap with a hook; the surface is looped and may be clipped.
facts.quote: The New England Hooked or Rag rug has for its foundation a strip of burlap or sacking. Through this, strips of cloth are hooked, which form loops

facts.text: Heavy-yarn hooked rugs from Hong Kong with plastic-covered backs were sold in the US in the 1960s and taken for oriental rugs; the underside shows they are hooked.

rows.name: Wilton and Brussels (power-loomed, pile yarns as extra warps over wires)
how_made: The pile yarns run lengthwise as extra warps, one set (frame) for each color; a Jacquard mechanism lifts the color wanted at each point.
The lifted pile yarn is formed into a loop over a wire laid across the loom.
In Brussels the loops stay uncut; in Wilton the wire ends in a blade that cuts the loops when it is drawn out.
Weft shots (two or three per row of pile) and a chain and stuffer warp bind the pile in; pile colors not on the surface run buried inside the body of the fabric.
rows.front: Cut (Wilton) or looped (Brussels) pile in perfectly regular rows; few colors in any one lengthwise line (one per frame).
rows.back: A machine-woven grid of chain, stuffer and weft yarns with no knots; heavy and firm for its pile height because unused pile yarns are buried in the body.
rows.what_it_tells: A machine-woven rug, not hand-knotted.
rows.cautions: The pattern can show on the back; that alone does not mean hand-made.

facts.text: In Wilton the pile is formed over a flat wire and the loops are cut as the wire is withdrawn; if left uncut, the carpet is Brussels.
In Wilton and Brussels the pile yarn not on the surface is hidden in the body of the fabric; in Axminster all the pile is on the surface.
Each Wilton color comes from a separate frame, so a three-frame Wilton has three colors.

rows.name: Axminster (power-loomed, tufts inserted row by row)
other_names: (historic) hand-knotted Axminster carpets of Axminster and Wilton, England
how_made: Pile yarns are set up beforehand in the colors of each row of the design (on spools, or presented by grippers or 'fingers').
For each row the loom inserts tufts between the warps, cut to length, and binds them in with weft shots; the tufts are not knotted.
Chain warps bind the weft above and below; a stuffer warp runs straight through the middle.
rows.front: Cut pile only, many colors possible; tufts in straight machine rows; in one common weave the tufts slant like hand-knotted pile.
rows.back: Flat or ribbed with jute weft showing; no knots; the rug bends across its width but resists bending along its length (cri).
rows.what_it_tells: A machine-woven rug. Karastan's modified Axminster pulled the pile through to the back so the back shows the pattern.
rows.cautions: 'Axminster' was also the name of hand-knotted English carpets (1755-1835) and of hand-knotted carpets later made at Wilton (Stone p. 36).

facts.text: In a machine-woven Axminster each tuft is inserted mechanically and bound in by the weft without being knotted.
facts.quote: the tuft, though inserted in the fabric mechanically, and bound down without being knotted

facts.text: Depending on the weave, an Axminster back is flat or ribbed, with a heavier bottom weft showing across it.

rows.name: Chenille Axminster (pile woven in as ready-made 'fur' wefts)
how_made: First a 'fur' cloth is woven: colored woolen wefts held by fine cotton warps set in groups; the colors follow strips of the design.
The cloth is cut lengthwise between the warp groups into strips of fur, which are steamed and folded into a V so the cut ends all face one way.
The fur strips are then woven into the carpet as weft on a second loom, held down by a fine catcher warp, with chain, stuffer and filling wefts forming the ground.
rows.front: Cut pile; the pattern is formed by the weft, row by row.
rows.back: Machine-woven ground with jute chain and stuffer; no knots.
rows.what_it_tells: A machine-made rug.

facts.text: Chenille carpet is made in two stages: a cloth of colored wefts on fine warps is cut into strips of 'fur', and the strips are then woven into the carpet to form a cut pile.
facts.quote: about the only cut-pile carpet fabric in which the pattern is distinctively formed by the weft

rows.name: Tapestry carpet (pile yarn printed before weaving)
how_made: The pattern is printed in sections onto the pile yarns before weaving; the yarns are then woven as loop pile (or cut, 'velvet') on a simple loom.
rows.front: Color changes cannot be made sharp; the colors look as if they had run.
rows.back: Machine-woven ground; no knots.
rows.what_it_tells: A machine-made carpet.
rows.cautions: Not the same thing as hand-woven tapestry (kilim, Aubusson).

facts.text: In tapestry carpet the pattern is printed on the pile yarns before weaving, and one color cannot change sharply into the next.

rows.name: Modern power-loomed 'oriental design' rug
how_made: Woven on power looms, mostly in Wilton weaves (Stone names polypropylene Wilton weaves from Belgium); fringes are usually separate strips sewn on; edges serged (overcast) by machine.
rows.front: Every repeat of a motif identical; pile straight or slightly crushed; machine-stitched (serged) sides.
rows.back: A regular machine grid, often with the pattern visible but slightly blurred; no knots; no fringe running out of the body.
rows.what_it_tells: A machine-made rug.
rows.cautions: The pattern may show clearly on the back (Karastan); check pile roots and fringe, not the back alone.

facts.text: On a machine-made copy every repeat of a motif is identical; on a hand-knotted rug no two repeats are exactly alike.
Machine-made rugs have serged or machine-stitched sides and sewn-on fringes; on a hand-knotted rug the fringe is the end of the warps.

rows.name: Slit tapestry (slit-woven kilim)

native.translit: kilim; palaz (Azerbaijani word for flat-woven floor covers in general)
native.note: Given by Selçuk in Turkish spelling.

native.translit: ilikli kilim ('kilim with slits'); ilik (the slit)

how_made: Weave weft-faced plain weave: each weft goes over one warp and under the next, beaten so tightly that the warps are hidden.
Weave each color only across its own area of the design, turning back at its edge (discontinuous wefts).

Where two colors meet along a warp line, the left color turns back around the last warp of its area (W2) and the right color around the first warp of its area (W3); the two warps are not tied together, so a slit opens between them for as long as the color boundary runs straight up.
rows.front: A flat, pileless face with the design in blocks of color; small vertical slits where colors meet; vertical lines short or stepped, diagonal edges stepped.
rows.back: The same as the front when the weft ends are hidden; otherwise loose ends of colored wefts hang on the back.
rows.where_typical_note: Rows that mention kilim or slit tapestry; also the plain kilim bands at the ends of many pile rugs.
rows.what_it_tells: A kilim. Slit tapestry is the commonest kilim structure in Anatolia and in Persian village and tribal work; Senneh kilims are very fine slit tapestries with curving (eccentric) wefts.
rows.cautions: Long slits weaken the fabric, so designs avoid long vertical lines; some slits are sewn up later. Power-loomed flat carpets (ingrain, Kidderminster) also exist.

facts.text: Slit tapestry is a weft-faced plain weave in which wefts of different colors turn back around neighboring warps, leaving a slit between them where the color boundary runs along the warp.
Because the weft turns back at the edge of each pattern, a straight vertical line in a kilim is kept short (Hawley: never more than about an inch), and long vertical edges are stepped.
facts.quote: a straight perpendicular line never exceeds an inch in length

facts.text: In the most finished kilims the weft ends are hidden so that both faces are the same; in others the loose ends hang at the back.
facts.quote: permit each surface of the kilim to be exactly the same

facts.text: Wefts that run at an angle to the warps to follow curves (eccentric wefts) are used in fine kilims such as those of Senneh (Sanandaj).

rows.name: Dovetailed tapestry (shared warp)
how_made: As slit tapestry, but at the boundary the wefts of both colors turn back around the same warp (W3), in turn, so no slit forms.
rows.front: No slits; the boundary between colors is a slightly toothed, blurred line (Krody: outlines blurred, crisp color changes hard).
rows.back: Same as the front.
rows.where_typical_note: Stone lists dovetailing among dhurrie structures; the Met's Bakhtiari flour bag 2015.490.8 is recorded with 'tapestry (kilim) with dovetailing'; Krody gives Zarand gelims as dovetailed with eccentric wefts.
rows.what_it_tells: A kilim structure; stronger than slit tapestry.

facts.text: In dovetailed tapestry the wefts of two adjacent color areas turn back around a common warp, so no slit is formed; the join is stronger but less crisp.
