images.credit: Drawing by Heirloom, after Iranica, Carpets; Stone (2013)

rows.name: Interlocked tapestry (single and double interlocking)
how_made: Single interlocking: at the boundary, each weft of one color is looped once around the corresponding weft of the other color, between two neighboring warps (W2 and W3), before both turn back.
Double interlocking: the wefts of the two colors are wrapped around each other in pairs, giving a closer join; the loops lie on one face.
rows.front: A smooth, continuous color boundary that can run straight up; no slits.
rows.back: Single interlock: same as the front. Double interlock: a ridge along each color boundary on the back (Sherrill; Krody).
rows.where_typical_note: Double interlocking is particularly characteristic of Bakhtiari tapestry weaving (Sherrill; Krody; Stone p. 90).
rows.what_it_tells: Double interlocking with a ridge on the back points to Bakhtiari work among Persian kilims, and to Kazakh and Uzbek weavers of Afghanistan.

facts.text: In interlocked tapestry the wefts of neighboring colors loop around each other between two warps instead of turning around warps; double interlocking leaves the face smooth and a ridge on the back.
Double interlocking is particularly characteristic of Bakhtiari tapestry-woven pieces.

images.caption: Interlocked tapestry: the two colors’ wefts loop round each other between two warps.
images.credit: Drawing by Heirloom, after Iranica, Carpets; Stone (2013)

rows.name: Weft-faced plain weave (plain kilim)
other_names: Kilim band (at the ends of pile rugs)
how_made: Each weft passes over one warp and under the next, the next weft the reverse; the wefts are packed so closely that they hide the warps. Wefts may run edge to edge (continuous) in one color or in stripes.
rows.front: Flat, finely ribbed across the width; only weft visible.
rows.back: The same as the front.
rows.where_typical_note: As the end band (kilim, web) of the pile rugs listed; also the backs of many bags.
rows.what_it_tells: The basic kilim weave; as an end band it is part of how a pile rug was started and finished.

facts.text: In weft-faced plain weave the wefts are packed so tightly that the warps are hidden; in Persia this structure is called gelīm.
Because pile knotting sets the warp spacing, the kilim bands at the ends of pile rugs are usually weft-faced.

images.caption: Weft-faced plain weave: over one, under one, packed so tightly that only the wefts show.
images.credit: Drawing by Heirloom, after Iranica, Carpets; Stone (2013)

rows.name: Soumak, plain (weft wrapping, not countered)
other_names: 'Kashmir' (old US trade name for Caucasian soumaks)

native.note: Selçuk gives the Turkish spelling; the table's soumak row has 'Sumaq / Сумах'.
The textbook lists 'گلیم پیچ' beside 'گلیم کرباس' (plain gelim) in a yarn table; that gelīm-pīč means weft wrapping (soumak) is our reading, not stated there.

how_made: A pattern weft wraps the warps: go forward over four warps (W1-W4) in front, back under two (W4, W3) behind, forward over four again, and so on across the row (Fo4 Bu2); finer work uses forward two, back one.
In plain soumak every row wraps in the same direction, so all the slanting spans on the face lean the same way.
Between rows of wrapping, one or more plain ground wefts may be woven; some soumak has no ground weft (sources differ).
Each color is wrapped only across its own area; the yarn ends are left on the back.
rows.front: A flat face of small slanting stitches lying in rows, like a fine braid; all rows slant one way.
rows.back: Long floats of weft and many loose cut ends of the colored yarns, a shaggy back (Hawley's 'Kashmir' back).
rows.what_it_tells: A soumak (weft-wrapped) flatweave: Caucasian soumak carpets and bags, Shahsevan, Afshar, Lur and Bakhtiari bags.
rows.cautions: Reverse soumak shows the short spans on the face and the long ones on the back. 'Brocade' is sometimes used loosely for soumak (Stone p. 54).

facts.text: Soumak is a flatweave in which the weft wraps around groups of warps, going forward over several and back under fewer, for example forward four and back two.
In plain soumak all rows wrap in the same direction; in countered soumak the direction is reversed in alternate rows, giving a herringbone effect.
Reverse soumak shows the shorter spans on the front and the longer on the back, and is used as a ground weave and for decoration especially in Shahsevan flatweaves.

disagreements.about: ground wefts between rows of wrapping

says.text: A thread of weft crosses and recrosses between each row of stitches in old soumaks and between each second and third row in new ones (p. 47).
In the Salyan-type soumak at the Nakhchivan State Carpet Museum the pattern yarns wrap the warps in pairs and no weft is put in between.
Persian weft-wrapped flatweaves may have a simple ground weft between rows of wrapping or none.
The soumak weave may be used without ground weft (p. 266).

images.caption: Soumak: the pattern weft wraps forward over four warps and back under two, so each wrap shows as a slanting stitch.
images.credit: Drawing by Heirloom, after Iranica, Carpets; Stone (2013)

rows.name: Soumak, countered (herringbone)
other_names: Balıksırtı sumak (Turkish; seen only in a search summary)

native.note: Selçuk gives the Turkish spelling; the table's soumak row has 'Sumaq / Сумах'.

how_made: As plain soumak, but each row wraps in the opposite direction to the row before (left to right, then right to left), so the slanting spans of alternate rows lean opposite ways.
rows.front: Rows of stitches slanting alternately left and right, a herringbone or braided look.
rows.back: As plain soumak; Hawley says each pair of encircled warps shows as a separate cord at the back.
rows.what_it_tells: A soumak flatweave; the herringbone face is typical of many Caucasian soumak carpets.

facts.text: In Caucasian soumaks the yarn crosses two adjacent warps in front, encircles them behind and recrosses in front, so that at the back each pair of encircled warps shows as a separate cord and at the front the yarn runs diagonally across four warps; the diagonal is reversed in each row, giving a herringbone surface.
facts.quote: at the back of these rugs each of the two threads of warp encircled by the yarn appears as a separate cord, while at the front the yarn passes diagonally across four threads of warp

images.caption: Countered soumak: alternate rows wrap the other way, so the stitches make a herringbone.
images.credit: Drawing by Heirloom, after Iranica, Carpets; Stone (2013)

rows.name: Cicim (supplementary-weft brocading, overlay-underlay)
how_made: Weave a plain (balanced or weft-faced) ground.

Lay extra colored pattern wefts in the same sheds as the ground wefts, floating over several warps on the face where the motif needs color and passing to the back (or floating on the back) where it does not.
In Turkish usage the pattern yarns of cicim are also carried upward around warps to build motif outlines; the face is often woven on the side away from the weaver (Yıldırım).
rows.front: Raised motifs in floats of colored weft on a plain ground.
rows.back: Floats of the pattern wefts where they were not needed on the face, and loose ends.
rows.where_typical_note: Rows that mention brocade or jijim/cicim (kyrgyz: brocaded flatweaves; qashqai: brocade at the ends; varamin: Met bag 'brocaded'; shahsavan: jijim).
rows.what_it_tells: A brocaded flatweave; cicim is mainly an Anatolian term.
rows.cautions: Stone says the name cicim has been used indiscriminately for flatweaves; jijim/jajim also names warp-faced weaves (see jajim).

facts.text: Brocade is patterning with supplementary (extra) wefts interlaced into a ground weave; cicim usually means weft-float or overlay-underlay brocade on a plain-weave ground.
Stone says the term cicim has been used indiscriminately for flatweaves.

says.text: Weft float or overlay-underlay brocade on a balanced or weft-faced plain weave; used indiscriminately (p. 72).
Colored pattern yarns carried vertically or horizontally to make raised motifs; in cicim the pattern yarns wrap upward to form contours, unlike zili.

museum_examples.licence: Public Domain (Open Access); API isPublicDomain: true, as recorded in rugs_current.json
museum_examples.title: Salt Bag
museum_examples.shows: two images; medium 'balanced plain weave with pattern in supplementary brocaded weft (front)'

images.caption: Cicim: a colored pattern weft floats over the plain-woven ground on the face, building small motifs.
images.credit: Drawing by Heirloom, after Stone (2013); knots/findings.json

rows.name: Zili / sileh (supplementary-weft float brocade with regular skips)
how_made: Weave a plain-weave ground.
After each ground weft (or pair), lay a colored pattern weft that floats over two, three or five warps on the face and goes under one (2-1, 3-1, 5-1), ignoring the warp pairs of the ground.
Repeat row after row to fill motifs solidly; the single warps where the floats go under line up into fine vertical ribs.
rows.front: Motifs filled solidly with short floats; a ribbed look where the plain weave is completely covered; fine vertical lines where the binding warps line up.
rows.back: Floats and loose ends of pattern yarn.
rows.where_typical_note: The soumak row mentions sileh (Caucasian flatweaves with the S-shaped dragon motif).
rows.what_it_tells: A brocaded flatweave of Anatolia and the Caucasus; in the West 'sileh' names Caucasian flatweaves with large S-shaped motifs.
rows.cautions: The names sileh and verneh mean different things in the West and in Russia and the Caucasus. Easily confused with reverse soumak.

facts.text: In zili weaving colored pattern wefts float over two, three or five warps and go under one, filling motifs solidly on a plain-weave ground.
Stone says the term sileh means a Caucasian flatweave with S-shaped dragon motifs in overlay brocade in the West, but in Russia and the Caucasus can mean flatweaves in a mix of soumak and tapestry.

images.caption: Zili: pattern wefts go over three warps and under one, and the binding warps line up in columns.
images.credit: Drawing by Heirloom, after Stone (2013); knots/findings.json

rows.name: Jajim (warp-faced plain weave)

native.note: Iranica gives the transliteration jājīm; the Persian script is the standard spelling of that word.

how_made: Set the warps very close together; weave plain weave so that the warps cover the wefts completely. The design is in the warps: stripes along the length, or warp-patterned motifs. Often woven in narrow strips that are sewn together.
rows.front: Lengthwise stripes or warp patterns; wefts invisible.
rows.back: The same as the front for plain warp-faced weave.
rows.where_typical_note: bedouin-sadu (warp-faced plain weave per UNESCO and Stone); shahsavan (jijim); wangden (the trade's 'warp-faced back', unsourced).
rows.what_it_tells: A warp-faced flatweave, often in strips: Persian and Caucasian jajims, Bedouin sadu.
rows.cautions: Stone says jijim is used ambiguously, also for brocaded flatweaves and, in India, for a printed cotton floor cloth.

facts.text: If the warps are packed so closely that they cover the wefts, the structure is warp-faced plain weave, which Persians call jājīm.
Jijim (jajim) can mean narrow warp-faced strips sewn together or a warp-patterned weave, but the term is used ambiguously.

images.caption: Jajim: a warp-faced weave in narrow strips sewn side by side.
images.credit: Drawing by Heirloom, after Stone (2013); knots/findings.json

rows.name: Level warps (both warps of each knot side by side)

native.note: Iranica gives the transliteration; Persian script is the standard spelling.

how_made: No weft is pulled tight: each weft passes with some slack, folding around the warps, so all warps stay in one plane.
rows.front: No difference visible from the front.
rows.back: Both nodes of every knot equally prominent, side by side; the back looks flat and evenly beaded; the rug folds easily.
rows.what_it_tells: Typical of Caucasian and most Anatolian rugs and of many Persian village rugs (Hawley: Kazak, Baluch, Feraghan, Yuruk).
rows.cautions: Offset is a matter of degree and can vary within one rug.

facts.text: Warps may lie all in one plane, with alternate warps depressed, or with alternate warps buried under their neighbors.
If no weft is pulled taut the warps lie level and both nodes of each knot show on the back.
facts.quote: each of the two threads of warp encircled by a single knot lie side by side with equal prominence

images.caption: Warps level, looking along them: both warps of each knot side by side, the two wefts equally wavy.
images.credit: Drawing by Heirloom, after Hawley, Plate B, fig. 7

images.caption: Hawley’s Plate B, fig. 7: Ghiordes knots, in section.
images.credit: Hawley, Oriental Rugs, Antique and Modern (1913; 1922 printing), Plate B, fig. 7
images.licence: Public domain

images.caption: Hawley’s Plate B, fig. 7-a: the back of fig. 7.
images.credit: Hawley, Oriental Rugs, Antique and Modern (1913; 1922 printing), Plate B, fig. 7-a
images.licence: Public domain

rows.name: Partly offset warps (slightly offset, half depressed)

native.note: Stone gives the transliteration 'nim-lool' (p. 204); the script is the standard spelling.

how_made: One weft of each pair is pulled tighter than the other: the tight (cable) weft holds one set of alternate warps forward while the slack (sinuous) weft lets the other set sink part way back.
rows.front: No difference visible from the front.
rows.back: One node of each knot smaller or lower than the other; the back looks slightly corrugated or ribbed.
rows.where_typical_note: rugs_current.json uses both 'slightly offset' and 'half depressed'; the sources read draw no firm line between them.
rows.what_it_tells: Kulah, Persian Kurdish, Karabagh; many Turkmen and some Arak-area rugs in the table.
rows.cautions: Degrees of offset grade into each other; 'slightly offset' and 'half depressed' are not separately defined by any source read.

facts.text: When one weft is pulled tighter than the next, alternate warps are displaced to a second level and one node of each knot is at least partly hidden on the back.
facts.quote: one thread of warp to each knot is depressed, so that the back has a slightly corrugated appearance

facts.text: Stone describes a 45-degree warp offset in which both nodes show on the back but one is much smaller than the other.

images.caption: Warps partly offset: one warp of each knot sits lower, held by a straight cable weft and a wavy sinuous one.
images.credit: Drawing by Heirloom, after Hawley, Plate B, fig. 8; Stone (2013)

images.caption: Hawley’s Plate B, fig. 8: Ghiordes knots, one warp of each depressed.
images.credit: Hawley, Oriental Rugs, Antique and Modern (1913; 1922 printing), Plate B, fig. 8
images.licence: Public domain

images.caption: Hawley’s Plate B, fig. 8-a: the back of fig. 8.
images.credit: Hawley, Oriental Rugs, Antique and Modern (1913; 1922 printing), Plate B, fig. 8-a
images.licence: Public domain

rows.name: Deeply depressed warps (one warp of each knot hidden)
how_made: One weft is pulled taut and straight across one set of warps; the other weft is slack and sinuous. Pulled hard enough, alternate warps sink until each lies directly behind its neighbor. Kendrick says many fine Persian carpets have three shoots after each row, the middle one very sinuous and the outer two straight.
rows.front: No difference from the front; the rug is thick and stiff for its fineness.
rows.back: Only one node per knot shows; the back looks finely ribbed. In Chinese rugs with a 'closed back' the wefts are hidden as well.
rows.what_it_tells: Typical of fine Persian city rugs (Kashan, Kerman, Sarouk, Tabriz) and of Bijar; also later Chinese export rugs ('closed back').
rows.cautions: Count one node per knot on such backs when estimating knot density (Stone p. 160). Hawley says it makes a rug stronger.

facts.text: In rugs such as Bijar or Sarouk one warp of every knot is doubled under and hidden, giving the foundation a double thickness.
facts.quote: one thread of warp, included in every knot, has been doubled under so as to be entirely concealed from view

facts.text: When warps are offset, one weft is straight (cable weft) and the other bends (sinuous weft).
facts.quote: The second weft is put in straight, the first one loose, zig-zag, or vandyked, so as to fill up the back of the carpet

facts.text: In Chinese trade usage a 'closed back' is an asymmetric knot on fully offset warps with the wefts hidden on the back; an 'open back' shows the wefts.
In India the cable weft is called thari and the sinuous weft lackchi.

images.caption: Warps deeply depressed: one warp of each knot lies right under the other; the back shows one node per knot.
images.credit: Drawing by Heirloom, after Hawley, Plate B, figs. 9–10; Stone (2013)

images.caption: Hawley’s Plate B, fig. 9: Ghiordes knots, one warp doubled under.
images.credit: Hawley, Oriental Rugs, Antique and Modern (1913; 1922 printing), Plate B, fig. 9
images.licence: Public domain

images.caption: Hawley’s Plate B, fig. 10: Sehna knots, one warp doubled under.
images.credit: Hawley, Oriental Rugs, Antique and Modern (1913; 1922 printing), Plate B, fig. 10
images.licence: Public domain

rows.name: One weft between rows of knots (single-wefted)
how_made: After each row of knots, pass one weft across, over and under alternate warps; after the next row, pass the next weft through the opposite shed. So each weft goes only one way between knot rows.
rows.front: No difference visible.
rows.back: Between knot rows, tiny bits of warp and weft alternate in a checkered (quincunx) pattern; the warps show between rows.
rows.what_it_tells: Typical of Hamadan-area rugs (heavy weft) and of Senneh rugs (fine weft); also Arak-area village rugs.
rows.cautions: Hawley counts 'crossings': 'crosses once' = one weft; 'crosses twice' = two wefts.

facts.text: With one weft between rows, the back shows a checkered (quincunx) look where small bits of warp and weft cross at right angles; Sehna and Hamadan rugs are single-wefted.
facts.quote: only a single thread of weft between every two rows of knots, which winds in front of and behind alternate threads of warp

facts.text: If only one shoot of weft is made after a row of knots, the shoot after the next row goes through the reverse shed.

images.caption: Hawley’s Plate B, fig. 15: one thread of weft between two rows of knots.
images.credit: Hawley, Oriental Rugs, Antique and Modern (1913; 1922 printing), Plate B, fig. 15
images.licence: Public domain

rows.name: Two wefts between rows of knots (double-wefted)

native.translit: süzme ('strained', the slack weft) and basma ('pressed') weft
native.note: The Döşemealtı registration names the two wefts put in after each knot row; which is taut and which slack is our reading of the names.

how_made: After each row of knots, pass the weft across through one shed and back through the other, so it fully encloses each warp; where warps are offset, one of the two is taut (cable) and the other slack (sinuous).
rows.front: No difference visible.
rows.back: A continuous band of weft between rows of nodes; on level warps both wefts show, on offset warps mostly one.
rows.what_it_tells: The usual arrangement in most rugs.

facts.text: In almost all rugs the weft crosses twice between rows of knots, across and back once, the most usual number of shoots being two.
facts.quote: In almost all other rugs the weft crosses twice, that is, across and back once, between every two rows of knots

images.caption: Hawley’s Plate B, fig. 16: two threads of weft.
images.credit: Hawley, Oriental Rugs, Antique and Modern (1913; 1922 printing), Plate B, fig. 16
images.licence: Public domain

rows.name: Three (or more) wefts between rows of knots
how_made: After each row of knots, pass three shoots of weft (twice one way, once the other); in fine Persian carpets on offset warps the middle shoot is very sinuous and the two outer ones straight. Some coarse rugs have many shoots, varying in number.
rows.front: No difference visible; in coarse many-wefted rugs the pile rows overlap and the rug may be more lustrous (Lewis p. 92).
rows.back: A thicker band of weft between rows of nodes; in many-wefted rugs the wefts look like strings of beads (Hawley, Genghas).
rows.what_it_tells: Three wefts: Safavid 'vase technique' carpets, Kerman and Bijar today, early Bijars; many wefts: some Kazak, Gendje and Bergama rugs and many rugs over 150 years old.
rows.cautions: Khorassan and Herat rugs vary the number at intervals.

facts.text: Many finer Persian carpets on two-level warps have three shoots of weft after each row of knots, the middle one very sinuous and the other two straight.
facts.quote: a common plan is to have uniformly three shoots of weft after each row of knots, the middle shoot being very sinuous and the other two straight

facts.text: Some Anatolian rugs show the weft crossing three times between rows; Genghas, Tcherkess, Bergamos and many rugs over 150 years old often have many crossings, varying within one rug.

disagreements.about: which of three wefts is the sinuous one

says.text: The middle shoot is very sinuous, the other two straight (p. 96).
Early Bijars: three wefts, one of them very heavy (Bijar entry; which one not stated in our notes).

images.caption: Hawley’s Plate B, fig. 17: three threads of weft.
images.credit: Hawley, Oriental Rugs, Antique and Modern (1913; 1922 printing), Plate B, fig. 17
images.licence: Public domain

rows.name: Overcast side (single cord wrapped by the weft)
other_names: Shirazeh (Persian: the wrapped edge; see shirazeh)
how_made: At each side a heavier cord (or a few warps) is strung beside the warps; at each pass the weft, after crossing the warps, is wound around this cord for the height of the knot row before it turns back.
rows.front: A narrow, round edge wrapped in yarn, usually one color.
rows.back: The same wrapped cord.
rows.what_it_tells: With few exceptions the side finish of Persian rugs (Hawley p. 283).
rows.cautions: Sides are the first part of a rug to be redone; much overcasting on old rugs is a repair (Hawley p. 57).

facts.text: In weft overcasting the weft, after crossing the warps, is wound around a heavier cord at the side of the rug.
facts.quote: the thread of weft, after encircling the threads of warp to which the knots are tied, is wound about a much heavier cord that is strung at the side of the rug

says.text: Weft overcasting is done by the ground weft itself (p. 56).
Overcasting is a yarn that wraps the edge warps and is NOT continuous with the foundation weft (p. 209).

images.caption: Hawley’s Plate B, fig. 11: weft-overcasting.
images.credit: Hawley, Oriental Rugs, Antique and Modern (1913; 1922 printing), Plate B, fig. 11
images.licence: Public domain

rows.name: Double overcast side (extra yarn wound over the cord)
other_names: Attached double overcasting (figure-eight to the adjacent warps)
how_made: After the weft has wrapped the side cord, a heavy separate yarn is wound around the cord again, covering it; if it also passes figure-eight around the neighboring warps it is 'attached'.
rows.front: A thick, round, firmly wrapped edge; may be in a contrasting color or in barber-pole stripes.
rows.back: The same.
rows.what_it_tells: Common on Persian city and village rugs in Hawley's analyses.

facts.text: In double overcasting, heavy yarn is wound about the side cord that the weft has already encircled; several yarns may take the place of a single heavy cord.
facts.quote: heavy yarn is wound about the cord that has previously been encircled by the weft

images.caption: Hawley’s Plate B, fig. 12: double-overcasting.
images.credit: Hawley, Oriental Rugs, Antique and Modern (1913; 1922 printing), Plate B, fig. 12
images.licence: Public domain

rows.name: Weft selvage (two or more cords wrapped figure-eight)
how_made: Place two or more heavy cords (or groups of warps) at the side instead of one; the weft passes around them in figure-eight fashion, making a flat band beyond the knotted area.
rows.front: A flat band a few cords wide along the side, without pile, often in color blocks or a checker of two colors.
rows.back: The same flat band.
rows.what_it_tells: Typical of Caucasian, Anatolian and Turkmen rugs and some northwest Persian ones.
rows.cautions: A cord sewn on after weaving (false selvage) imitates it (Stone p. 254).

facts.text: A weft selvage is made by placing two or more heavy cords at the side and encircling them with the weft in figure-eight fashion; Iranica calls this kenārapīč.
facts.quote: made by placing two or more heavy cords instead of a single one at the side of the warp, and encircling them by the weft in figure-eight fashion

images.caption: Hawley’s Plate B, fig. 13: weft-selvage.
images.credit: Hawley, Oriental Rugs, Antique and Modern (1913; 1922 printing), Plate B, fig. 13
images.licence: Public domain

rows.name: Double and added selvage
how_made: Double selvage: the weft is carried around the heavy cords as in weft selvage, then an extra yarn is wound over them figure-eight fashion.
Added selvage: the cords are not wrapped by the weft at all, but attached to the side by an extra yarn that winds around them and two or more neighboring warps.
Mixed: the weft wraps only one or two cords, and an extra yarn wraps these and the rest.
rows.front: A heavy, raised multi-cord edge.
rows.back: The same.
rows.what_it_tells: Nomadic weavers such as Baluch and Afghan use the double selvage for hard wear.

facts.text: The double selvage, used by nomadic weavers such as Baluch and Afghans, has an extra yarn wound figure-eight over the weft-wrapped cords; in an added selvage the cords are attached only by the extra yarn.
facts.quote: the heavy cords are not encircled by the weft, but are attached to the side of the rug by the extra yarn that winds about them figure-eight fashion

images.caption: Hawley’s Plate B, fig. 14: double-selvage.
images.credit: Hawley, Oriental Rugs, Antique and Modern (1913; 1922 printing), Plate B, fig. 14
images.licence: Public domain

rows.name: Shirazeh (Persian name for the wrapped side edge)
how_made: Not a separate structure: the word names the wrapped side edges of a rug, which may be overcast or a multi-cord selvage (see side-overcast, side-double-overcast, side-weft-selvage).
rows.front: The wrapped side edges, sometimes in two or three colors.
rows.back: The same.
rows.what_it_tells: Persian-language descriptions use it for the side finish; colored shirazeh in two or three colors are noted for Yalameh rugs.
rows.cautions: No source read gives a technical definition separating shirazeh from overcasting or selvage.

facts.text: Persian-language sources call the wrapped side edges of a rug shirazeh: Yalameh rugs are made with colored shirazeh in two or three colors, and a rug's limits are the shirazeh of the two sides and the fringes at top and bottom.

rows.name: Machine-serged, taped or false selvage
how_made: Serging: heavy yarn stitched over the edge, often by a special machine. False selvage: cords sewn or woven along an edge after weaving to replace or reinforce edge warps. Tufted rugs are bound with tape or a sewn strip.
rows.front: A perfectly even binding, or a cord clearly sewn on rather than woven in.
rows.back: Machine stitches visible; on false selvages, sewing thread through the edge of the rug.
rows.what_it_tells: Machine-made or tufted rugs; or a repaired or modern hand-knotted rug (Stone: some new Pakistani rugs are woven without edge warps and given false selvages).
rows.cautions: A sewn edge alone does not prove machine-made: check the fringe and back.

facts.text: Some new rugs, mainly from Pakistan, are woven without extra edge warps and get a false selvage sewn on after weaving.
Machine-made rugs typically have serged or machine-stitched sides.

rows.name: Kilim band (plain-woven web) at the end
other_names: Skirt, elem (Turkmen, when patterned or piled)

native.translit: gelīm (the protective plain-woven strip at the start and end)

how_made: Before the first row of knots and after the last, weave weft-faced plain weave across the warps for a short or long distance; the band may be plain, striped, patterned or embroidered.
rows.front: A flat woven strip between the last row of knots and the fringe.
rows.back: The same.
rows.what_it_tells: Very long webs: Turkmen, Afghan and Baluch rugs; moderately long: some Turkmen and Anatolian rugs, Shiraz and Niris.
rows.cautions: On old rugs the web is often worn away with a few rows of knots (Hawley p. 57).

facts.text: The simplest end finish is a web of warp and weft woven like a kilim beyond the pile, short or, as in Baluch and Afghan rugs, several inches long.

images.caption: An end with a flat-woven band before the fringe.
images.credit: Drawing by Heirloom, after Hawley (1922); Stone (2013)

rows.name: Knotted, braided or netted fringe

native.translit: gereh zadan ('to knot into fringes', Stone)

native.text: çiti (plaited end at the fringe, Döşemealtı)

how_made: The warp ends left after cutting the rug from the loom are tied in groups (simple knots), or knotted in alternate groups row after row to make a net, braided in flat plaits, plaited diagonally into a band, chained, or twisted in pairs or groups.
rows.front: Groups of warp ends tied together; the fringe threads run straight into the body of the rug as its warps.
rows.back: The same; the fringe continues the warps.
rows.what_it_tells: Warp ends finished by hand; on a hand-woven rug the fringe is the warps.
rows.cautions: Machine-made fringe also exists (Mumford 1902 already mentions 'ordinary machine-made fringe'); always check that the fringe threads continue into the rug.

facts.text: The warp of the end finished last generally forms a fringe; the warp ends may hang loose, be twisted into cords, knotted, or tied to one another diagonally to form a network.

images.caption: A fringe of warp ends knotted in groups.
images.credit: Drawing by Heirloom, after Stone (2013)

rows.name: Looped warps (uncut loops at one end)
how_made: The warps were wound around a rod or bar at the start of weaving; when the rug is taken off, the loops at that (lower) end are left uncut, or braided around the last weft.
rows.front: A row of small uncut loops beyond the end band; the other end usually has cut fringe.
rows.back: The same.
rows.what_it_tells: Common at the lower (first-woven) end of Caucasian and many village and Chinese rugs.

facts.text: Very often the loops formed where the warp went around the loom rod are left at the lower end of the rug.
facts.quote: Very frequently the loops formed by the warp that encircled the rod extend beyond the web at the lower end of the rug

images.caption: Looped warps at one end.
images.credit: Drawing by Heirloom, after Stone (2013)

rows.name: Chained or twined end (weft chaining, zanjireh)
how_made: At the start (and again at the end) a chain of yarn is worked across the warps to space them evenly before the kilim band is woven; it can be done by hand or with a hook on the loom, or after the rug comes off.
rows.front: A narrow raised chain-like line across the end, next to the kilim band.
rows.back: The same line.
rows.what_it_tells: A normal end detail of Persian workshop rugs; not diagnostic by itself.

facts.text: Weft chaining, weft twining or soumak may be worked across the ends to lock wefts and knots in place; Iranian textbooks describe a chain (zanjireh) at the start and end of a carpet that sets the warps for the kilim band.

rows.name: Sewn-on fringe
how_made: A separately made fringe strip is sewn under or across the end of the rug.
rows.front: Fringe threads that stop at a sewn strip and do not run on into the rug.
rows.back: A stitched band across the end; the fringe threads do not continue as warps.
rows.what_it_tells: Machine-made and tufted rugs; or a repair to a hand-knotted rug with damaged ends.
rows.cautions: Do not judge the knotting from an added fringe.

facts.text: Artificial fringes may be attached to rugs with damaged ends; on machine-made rugs the fringe is sewn on, while on a hand-knotted rug it is part of the rug.

plate_b.caption_group: PLATE B. — Nos. 1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 9, Ghiordes knots. Nos. 4, 5, 6, 10, Sehna knots. No. 11, Weft-overcasting. No. 12, Double-overcasting. No. 13, Weft-selvage. No. 14, Double-selvage. Nos. 15, 16, 17, illustrate one, two, and three threads of weft passing between two rows of knots.
plate_b.hawley_text: Caption: Ghiordes knot. Text: 'The three different ways of tying this knot are shown in Plate B, Figs. 1, 2, and 3'.
